Since the rule is already established by the principle of *tadantavidhi* (application to that which ends with the specified element), the inclusion of the term *bhastrā* in the rule "also for those preceded by *nañ*" is for the sake of clarity; it serves to include compounds where *bhastrā* is an *upasarjana* (subordinate member), whereas for other cases, the result is already established by the subsequent rule.

In these two cases, however, because the preceding [elements] possess the status of *net*, the prohibition "not when followed by a suffix" (*an-supi*) applies by relying on the case-ending (*vibhakti*) situated between them; thus,
[the form] is *aneṣakā*.
The supreme seekers, the peerless ones; the supreme, the peerless.
The inclusion of the term *svaśabda* is for the sake of [excluding] technical names (*saṃjñā*) and secondary members (*upasarjana*).
For here, the phrase "in place of *āt*" (*ātaḥ sthāne*), which is carried over from the previous rule, qualifies *svaśabda*;
it does not qualify *dvi* and *e*, because those two are impossible [in this context].
Nor does it apply to others, because there is no deviation [in that case].
However, the word *sva* itself, when not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*), denotes "one's own" and is eligible for the suffix *-kaC*;
but in other meanings, it is not feminine.

However, when it functions as a subordinate member of a compound (*saṃjñopasarjanībhūta*), it certainly becomes an example [of the rule] because it ends in the suffix *kap*. Thus, in the case of *ātmīyāyām*, the forms *svikā* and *paramasvikā* always have the substitution of *it* (short *i*), as in *nirbhastrakā*.
A small bellows,
a seeker, one who seeks.
Since the designation of the number six has already been established, there is no optionality here;
[the forms] *etike* and *etikāḥ* are both correct.
The goat,
the she-goat,
the knower.
The knower of the two pairs.
Devoid of self and devoid of "mine.
According to Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.48,
for the *at* substituted in place of that [suffix] prescribed after this [root], there may optionally be *it* instead; thus,
*gaṅgakā*.
Since *gaṅgikā* is a bahuvrīhi compound and is treated as a word whose masculine form has been previously stated (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the suffix prescribed after it is always [replaced]; thus,
*ajñātā akhaṭvā* becomes *akhaṭvikā*.
But when the secondary suffix *kap* is applied, there is indeed an option [regarding the elision of the final vowel and consonant], according to Pāṇini 7.3.49.
In the scope of the preceding sūtra, there may optionally be the substitution of *ā* for the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, as in *gaṅgākā* or *gaṅgikā*.
But from a word denoting a woman who has already spoken as a man [the suffix *kan* is applied], as in *śubhrikā*.
(SK 469; Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.14)

This governing rule (adhikāra), extending up to *yūnastiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.77), indicates that the principle of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies to feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). (SK 470)

After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ya*, *ṭi*, or the like, which is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*) and ends in *a*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied; for example, *kurucarī*.
Because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) here, *nadat* does not occur in the compound *bahukurucarā*.
In the case of *nadī*, which will be discussed later, the suffix *ṅīp* would have been applicable due to its being marked with the indicator *ṭi* and its being a stem ending in an *uk* vowel.

Because the *ṅit* status of *yāsuṭ* indicates that a grammatical operation based on an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) applies only to the substitute (*ādeśa*) and not to the original element (*sthānin*), [the substitution does not apply here]. Alternatively, because the *śit* status of *śānac* (the substitute for *śna*) indicates that even in certain operations based on an indicatory letter, the prohibition "not when there is a rule concerning a letter" (*analvidhau*) applies,
[the suffix] becomes *sauparṇeyī*.
Aindrī,
autsī, and ūrudvayasī.
It is knee-deep, reaching up to the thighs, and fivefold.
Such as that which pertains to dice and that which pertains to salt.
In the sense of "temporary" (itvarī), even when the suffix *ṇa* is used in the sense of characterizing a habit (*tācchīlika*), [the feminine form] is *caurī*.
The addition of *nañ*, *snañ*, *īk*, *kak*, *hyuṃ*, *staruṇa*, and *taluna* [to the list of bases] is prescribed (as an option). For example:
*straiṇī* and *pauṃsnī*.
The Śāktī is the one who makes [the body] prosperous and is youthful.
Taluṇī SK 471 AS 4-1-16
The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied to a feminine noun ending in *yañ*, once the elision of the vowel *ā* has been performed. (SK 472)
There is elision of the penultimate *y* of a *taddhita* suffix that follows a consonant (*hal*), when *ī* follows;
[e.g.,] *gārgī*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is not applied [after a word ending in *a*] when it stands in the sense of "belonging to one who has no offspring" (Vārttika); thus, those born on an island (*dvīpa*) are called *dvaipyāḥ*, because of the inclusion of the term "belonging to" (*adhikāra*), this does not apply here.

The suffix *yañ* in *daivya* (the offspring of a god) is indeed the *prāgdīvyatīya* [suffix] *yañ* prescribed by the rule "devād yañañau," and not the one read in the section on "offspring" (*apatya*).
After a stem ending in *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* may optionally occur in the feminine; and that [suffix] is a *taddhita*.
The initial sound of an affix (pratyaya) shall be marked with the indicatory letter *ṣ*.

For *pha* and the others that have become suffixes (*pratyaya*), *āyan* and the other substitutes shall take their place respectively; because they end in a *taddhita* suffix, they possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

By virtue of the technical designation *ṣit*, even though femininity has already been expressed by the suffix *ṣpha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.41) applies,
resulting in *gārgyāyaṇī*.
After words ending in *kata* that begin with *lohita* and end in the suffix *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* shall always be applied; [e.g.,] *lauhitāyanī*.
Kātyāyanī, SK 477,
The suffix *ṣpha* shall be applied after these two [roots], as an exception to *ṭāp* and *ṅīṣ*;
and the suffix *ṇya* is applied after [the group of roots] beginning with *kṛ*.
From *maṇḍūka*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.109] "kauravyāyaṇī-ḍhak ca maṇḍūkāt," the suffix *aṇ* is applied,
resulting in *māṇḍūkāyanī*.
The addition of *āsuri* [to the list] is proposed (as an alternative);
[the feminine form is] *āsurāyaṇī*.
AS 4.1.20: After a word denoting the first stage of life that ends in the vowel *a*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine; for example, *kumārī*.
Or it should be stated that "vayasyā" means "caramā"; furthermore, "vadhūṭī" and "ciraṇṭī" [are synonyms].
The words *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī* denote youth;
what follows from this? [It means] that a young girl is not a child (*śiśu*).
Because of the grammatical rule [Pāṇini 6.4.164]: "The forms *nyāyaḥ* and *kanīna* [are derived from the root *nay*]," [as stated in] SK 479 and AS 4.1.21.
The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in a consonant; for example,
*trilokī*,
and *triphalā* [is formed] because it belongs to the *ajādi* group.
An army consisting of three divisions (the elephant corps, the chariot corps, and the infantry).
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* shall not be applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in an immeasurable (*aparimāṇa*) or a *biṣṭa* measure when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix; for example,
"bought with five horses" is *pañcāśvā*, where the suffix *ṭhak* belonging to the *ārhīya* group has been elided.
According to *Adhyardha-śata-saṃdarbha* 1693, there is elision (*luk*); thus,
"he cooks two *bista*s" becomes *dvibistā*, and "two *ācita*s" becomes *dvyācitā*.

What about "dvikambalyā," which ends in a measure [denoting] a limit? And what about "dvyāḍhakī"? [This applies] when there is elision of the taddhita suffix; for example, "pañcāśvī" in the sense of a collective compound (samāhāra).
After a *dvigu* compound ending in *kṣetra* that ends in *kāṇḍa*, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur when there is elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix.

The division of the field has two *kāṇḍas* as its measure; thus it is called *dvikāṇḍā*. According to the rule *pramāṇe dvayasac-daṭ-mātracaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.37), the suffix *mātrac* is prescribed [to form *kāṇḍamātra*]; however, by the rule *pramāṇe lo dvigornityam* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.2.37), there is the compulsory elision (*luk*) of this suffix after a *dvigu* compound.
What [is the result] in the case of a field? A rope two *kāṇḍas* long.
When a *puruṣa* is the final member of a *dvigu* compound denoting a measure, the suffix *ṅīp* may optionally be applied after the elision (*luk*) of the *taddhita* suffix;
for example, "a trench two *puruṣas* in length" is *dvipuruṣī* or *dvipuruṣā*.
According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.131, the substitute anaṅ is applied for a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas* when used in the feminine;
once anaṅ has been applied, the suffixes ṅīp and ṅīṣ would otherwise be applicable, but they are prohibited by specific rules.
After a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied when the word denotes a feminine.
Why [is it] "kuṇḍodhnī" in the feminine? [Because] here, in "kuṇḍodha dhainukam," even the *anaṅ* substitution does not occur.
In the formation of that [word], there is an addition [to the rule] stating "optionally in the feminine" (SK 485).
AS 4.1.26: An exception to the suffix *ṅīṣ*;
[the word] *dvyūdhnī*.
By the rule "atyūdhnī from a bahuvrīhi," [the form] *atyūdhāḥ* means "those who have passed beyond the udder."
The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with a numeral, ending in *dāman*, or ending in *dhāyana*.
This statement is made because, at the end of *dāman*, both the suffix *ḍāp* and its prohibition would apply; at the end of *hāyana*, the suffix *ṭāp* would apply.
Thus, [the forms] *dvidāmnī* and *uddāmā vaḍavā* are established, where both *ḍāp* and its prohibition optionally occur due to the non-continuation of the mention of "indeclinables."
In the word *dvihāyanī* ("two-year-old female"), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in *hāyana* should be stated [by rule] after the words *tri* and *catur*;
furthermore, this *ṅīp* suffix and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* are desired only when *hāyana* denotes age.
A three-year-old or a four-year-old [cow], except for other ages.
A hall three years old or four years old.

From an *annanta* (ending in -an) *bahuvrīhi* compound that undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; for example, *surājñī* as the name of a city. Otherwise, in other cases, there is only the aforementioned optionality.
But in the Veda, [the word] "śatamūrdhni" [is used].
After these nine [stems], the suffix *ṅīp* shall always occur in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or in Vedic literature (*chandas*); for example:
*athota indraḥ kevalīr viśaḥ māmakīḥ*.
The unfortunate one is wicked.
Equal is the noble deed,
most auspicious.
The mention of "my own" (*māmaka*) in the passage beginning with "the medicinal herbs elsewhere are exclusively... is for the purpose of restriction.
Since the proof is established precisely because [the suffix] is *aṇ*, by that [rule], in common usage (*loke*) when it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*), [the form] is *māmikā*.

According to Pāṇini 4.1.32, the augment *nuk* shall be applied to these two [words] in the feminine; furthermore, by Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. In the case of "pregnant" (*garbhiṇī*) and "whose husband is living" (*jīvadbhartṛkā*), the original forms (*prakṛti*) are established as exceptions (*nipātana*).

In that regard, in the analysis (vigraha) "there is a fetus within her" (*antar asyām garbhaḥ*), because the word *antar* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); thus, the suffix *matup*, which would otherwise not apply, is introduced by nipātana.
However, in the case of *pativatnī*, it is the *vat* [substitution] that is introduced by nipātana; hence the form *antarvatnī*.
The counter-example for *pativatnī* is:
"There is a jar in this house."
The earth possesses a master.
There shall be the substitution of *na* for the word *pati* when it is connected with a sacrifice;
the meaning is that "the wife of Vasiṣṭha" is one who enjoys the fruit of the sacrifice performed by him.
Because the husband and wife have joint authority, [the result belongs to both]. (SK 491; AS 4.1.34)
For a nominal stem ending in the word *pati* that is preceded by another member, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* may optionally occur; for example:
*gṛhasya patiḥ* (the master of the house) becomes *gṛhapatiḥ* (householder), and [with the optional suffix] *gṛhapatnī*.
The term *anupasarjanasya*, although carried forward here for the sake of subsequent rules, is not a qualifier of *pati* itself, but rather of that which ends in *pati*;
therefore, even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, one has *dṛḍhapatnī*.
Dṛḍha is the husband,
the Vṛṣala is the wife; the Vṛṣala is the husband.

If it is asked how [the term] "vṛṣalasya patnī" (the wife of a low-caste man) is used when [the two words] are separate, it is because she is metaphorically designated as a "patnī" (wife) since she is like a wife;
or else:
In this alternative view, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent to the nominal stem *ācāra* which already ends in *kvip*, resulting in the forms *patniyau*.

Regarding the specific rule that *patnī* takes the short *ī* vowel (*iyaṅ*) in this context, [the sūtra asks]: "What if it is preceded by another word? For example: *gavāṃ patiḥ strī* ("a female cowherd").
An exception to the previous alternative.
The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* is also prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*):
she whose husband (*pati*) is the same (*samāna*) is *sapatnī*, while she who has one husband is *ekapatnī*.
The wife of a hero (vīrapatnī) [is one who has not been violated].
This *trisūtrī* is desired only in the sense of a relationship with a male (*puṃyoga*); [for example],
the wife of Pūtakratu is *pūtakratāyī*,
but she by whom the sacrifices (*kratavaḥ*) have been purified is simply *pūtakratuḥ*.
For these [vowels], there shall be the substitution of the udātta vowel *ai* and the suffix *ṅīp*.
The wife of Vṛṣākapi is Vṛṣākapāyī;
according to Amara, "Vṛṣākapī" refers to Hara and Viṣṇu,
and "Vṛṣākapāyī" refers to Śrī and Gaurī.
Agnāyī, Kusitāyī, and Kusidāyī.
The word *kusida* has a short vowel in its middle, and not a long one; [this is according to] Pāṇini 6.2.38.

The vowel *au* should be substituted for the word *manu*, and it is optionally acute; furthermore, by the rule of simultaneous prescription (*sanniyoga-śiṣṭa*), the suffix *ṅīp* is also applied after those two [substitutions].
Thus, the feminine of *manu* is *manāvī* or *manāyī*.
Manu, SK 496;

The suffix *ṅīp* may optionally be applied after a non-initial nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a vowel denoting color (*varṇa-vācin*), which has an unraised (*anudātta*) final vowel and a *t* or *th* as its penultimate (*upadhā*), provided it is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*); furthermore, there is the substitution of *n* for the *t*. Thus:
*enī* (variegated) and *etā* (mare).
The word *rohiṇī* is udātta on its first syllable by the Phiṭ-sūtra: "The words *rohitā*, *varṇānām*, and those ending in *taṇa*, *tini*, and *tānta*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 33).

Regarding the *Gṛhyasūtra* passage "with a three-striped porcupine quill" (*tryeṇyā ca śalalyā*), the term *tryeṇī* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has these three. Why [is the rule] stated as "from a word with an anudātta vowel"? Consider the example: *śvetā*.
And because of the rule *ghṛtādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), this [suffix] is udātta on the final syllable;
thus, by the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.4),
the feminine form is *śiti*.
An addition [to the rule] for *piśaṅga* (Vārttika):
*piśaṅgī* and *piśaṅgā*.
Neither in the black nor in the grey hairs are there black or grey hairs.
In the Vedic language, some [grammarians] maintain that the suffix *kna* is optionally applied [to form feminine nouns], as in the examples *asiknī* and *paliknī*.
But the word *avadāta* does not denote color; rather, it denotes purity.
Therefore, they are simply called *avadātāḥ*.
After a nominal stem denoting color that ends in an unaccented vowel and does not have *t* or *p* as its penultimate letter, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine; for example,
*kalmāṣī*.
According to the rule *sāraṅgī laghāvante dvayośca bahvaco guruḥ* (Pāṇini Śikṣā 42), these two [words] have the middle syllable as udātta;
[the question is] why [is it asked] "from what ending in anudātta"? [The answer is: *kṛṣṇā*.
Kapilā SK 498 AS 4-1-41
The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after stems ending in *ṣit* and after the group beginning with *gaura*; for example: *nartakī*, *gaurī*.
In the feminine of *anaḍuh*, there is optionally [the form] *anaḍuhī* or *anaḍvāhī*.
(ga) And *pippaly-ādayaḥ*; this is an *ākṛti-gaṇa* (class of words defined by its form). (SK 499)
The *upadhā* vowel *ya* of a stem is elided if that *ya* is a constituent of the word *sūrya*, etc.,
provided it occurs before a feminine suffix (*ṅīp*) [or optionally in the case of *matsya*].
The elision of *y* in *tiṣya* and *puṣya* when followed by the suffixes *cha*, *ṅi*, or *ām* should be stated as optional;
[examples are] *matsī*.

Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established for the word *mātṛ* by the rule *mātari ṣicca* (vā), its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group— along with the form *mātāmahī*— indicates that the *ṅīṣ* added after roots marked with the marker *ṣ* is not compulsory; thus,
[the feminine form] is *daṃṣṭrā*.
After these eleven nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied in the sense of "occupation" (*vṛtti*) and so forth, respectively.
If it is the *jānapadī* vṛtti,

then another *jānapadī* [is required]; however, because of the elision (*utsādana*) [of the suffix], when the form ends in *añ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, resulting in an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*).
If *kuṇḍī* means a vessel, it is derived from *kuṇḍa*; if it means a fire-pit, it is derived from the root *kuḍi*, meaning "to burn."
By the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103), the suffix *ap* is applied [to form *amatra*].

As for the word *kuṇḍa*, which denotes a human caste as in "one born of adultery from an unmarried woman" (*amṛte jārajaḥ kuṇḍaḥ*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* indeed occurs there by virtue of the characteristic of a genus (*jāti*).
For in the case of *amatra*, since it refers to a female object, the application of *ṅīṣ* was not otherwise established; therefore, it is prescribed here, rather than being restricted.
If "goṇī" means a sack, then it is a measure for sowing; if it means a field, then it is an unartificial plot of land.
If one vegetable dish is cooked on dry ground and another is cooked in a pot,
they are distinct.

If the word *nāgī* means "thick," then the word *nāga*— which elsewhere denotes an elephant— is used in another sense due to its association with the quality of thickness; this is an example [of metaphorical usage].
However, when the word *sarpa* (serpent) is applied elsewhere due to its association with the quality of length, it serves as a counter-example:
if *kālī* refers to the color black, then *kālā* is something else.
If *nīlī* is not a garment, it means a blue cloth dyed with indigo; that is, a *śāṭī* (a lower garment) colored by indigo.
It should be stated that [the rule] "or with *nīlī*" applies not everywhere, but rather only when there is no covering.
*Nīlī* refers to a blue medicinal herb (*oṣadhi*) or a living being (*prāṇin*).
The word *nīlī* optionally [retains its long vowel] when it denotes a specific name (*saṃjñāyām*). [Otherwise,
it becomes *nīlā*].
If the blue *kuśī* is an iron product, then the *kuśī* is something else.
If "kāmukī" means a desire for sexual union, then "kāmukā" refers to another [woman]; if it means a braid, it refers to the arrangement of the hair.
"Another variegated [form]" means "various.
AS 4-1-43: *śoṇī* [becomes] *śoṇā*.
After a word ending in /u/ that denotes a quality, the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally occur.
Is "mṛdvī" (feminine) and "mṛduḥ" (masculine) [the same]? [Yes,] it is "śuciḥ" (pure).
What is the purpose of the word "guṇa"? [It is to exclude cases such as:

*ākhuḥ* (mouse), *kharuḥ* (one who has a connection with the suffix *kharu*), and *patiṃvarā* (a maiden choosing her own husband). These do not [take the feminine suffix *ī*] because they have a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as their penultimate (*upadhā*).
Pāṇḍu (the pale one) SK 503, AS 4.1.45.
Or, the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally be applied after these [words],
as in *bahvī* or *bahu*.
(ga) From a word ending in the *ik*-affix, provided it is not the feminine suffix *ktin*:
*rātriḥ* or *rātrī*.
(ga) Some say that [the feminine suffix ṅīp] is applied after every word ending in a kṛt-affix that does not have the sense of "artha" (object/purpose); thus,
*śakaṭiḥ* and *śakaṭī*.
Why [is it] not [formed] from the root *a-kṛ* with the suffix *ktin*?
Because *ajananiḥ* would not otherwise be established due to ending in *ktin*, the word *paddhati* is recited in the list [of roots] for the purpose of a specific rule;
by the rule "and in the case of *himakāṣihatiṣu*" (Pāṇini 6.3.54), there is the substitution of *pad* for *pād*.
The manual, the manuals.
SK 504
The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after a word denoting a male that refers to a female by virtue of her connection with that male; for example, the wife of a cowherd (*gopa*) is a *gopī*.
A woman who tends cattle is a *gopālikā*; a woman who tends horses is an *aśvapālikā*.
The feminine suffix *āP* should be stated for the word *sūrya* when it denotes a deity;
that is, [the form] *sūryā* is used when the deity is the wife of Sūrya. Why "when it denotes a deity"? [Consider: *sūrī*, as in the case of Kuntī.
This is a human being.

The augment *ānuk* and the suffix *ṅīṣ* are applied to these six beginning with Indra, as well as to *mātula* and *ācārya*; however, this is intended only in the sense of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*).
Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established there, only the addition of the augment *ānuk* is prescribed.
For the other four, both [types of compounds apply]; however,
*indrāṇī* is used for the greatness of *himā* and *araṇya*.
*mahaddhimam* becomes *himānī*, and *mahadaraṇyam* becomes *araṇyānī*;
[the suffix] *ānīk* is applied after *yava* when it denotes a fault (*doṣa*).
*Duṣṭa-yava* means "bad barley";
*yavanānī* refers to the script of the Yavanas, or the script of the Yavanas (*yavanānāṃ lipiḥ*). It may also be [derived from] the Yavana.
The female descendants of a maternal uncle or a teacher are called *mātulānī* or *mātulī*.
In the case of *upādhyāyānī* and *upādhyāyī*,
which refers to one who teaches by herself, the suffix *ṅīṣ* should be stated as optional (*vā*).
The feminine forms *upādhyāyī* and *upādhyāyā*, as well as [the suffix] *aṇ* after *ācārya*.
The wife of the teacher (ācārya) is called *ācāryānī* by the rule *puṃyoga*; however,
when she herself is the expounder [of the Veda], she is called *ācāryā*.
Or, when used in its own sense, [the suffix ṅīṣ] is applied after "ārya" and "kṣatriya," as in "āryāṇī" and "āryā."
The meaning is "the mistress" or "the Vaiśya woman"; "kṣatriyāṇī" means a Kṣatriya woman.
But in connection with a male, [the feminine forms] are *aryī* and *kṣatriyī*.
Why is she called Brahmāṇī?
Because she brings Brahman (the Supreme) near and gives it life; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here in the sense of an object (*karman*).
After a word ending in *krīta* that ends in a short vowel and begins with the name of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; for example, *vastrakrītī*.
In some places, she was not purchased with wealth.

After a word ending in the suffix *kta* that denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*) or similar, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied when smallness (*alpatva*) is to be expressed; e.g., *abhraliptī dyauḥ* ("the sky [is] thinly covered with clouds"). Why "when expressing smallness"? [Consider: *candanaliptāṅganā* ("a woman whose limbs are smeared with sandalwood paste").

SK 508 / AS 4.1.52: After a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a suffix marked with *k* (i.e., a past passive participle), which is oxytone and ends in the vowel *a*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied.
It should be stated that [the suffix *ini* is added] after a word preceded by *jāti*;
therefore, *ūrubhinnī* is not formed from words preceded by *bahu*, *nañ*, *su*, *kāla*, *sukha*, and so forth.
Nor have many [births] been made here, ending in death.
When teeth have appeared,
she becomes a wife by the grasping of the hand; or, another [woman] may be taken as a wife by the grasping of the hand.
This is an optional rule (vikalpa) where the preceding rule would have applied invariably (nitya).
*surāpītī* and *surāpītā* [are examples]; why [is it specified] "from that which has its acute accent on the final syllable"? [Consider: *vastracchannā*.
Because of the prohibition [of the udātta accent] by the rule *anācchādanāt*,
for this very reason, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply even by the preceding rule. (SK 510)

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is optionally applied after a nominal stem ending in short *a*, provided that it has as its final member a word denoting a part of the body (*svāṅga*) which does not have a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyoga*) as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*) and is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Example:
*atikeśī* (one who has hair that exceeds [the norm]).
She with the long hair, moon-faced, moon-faced.
But [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a compound ending in *gulpha* when it is a subordinate member; why [is this mentioned]? Because a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*) is of three kinds.
One's own body, being non-fluid, material, residing in a living being, and not produced by transformation,
is easily known through perspiration because of its fluidity; [otherwise], it would be difficult to know due to its lack of material form.
The word *sumukhā* refers to a hall because it does not reside in a living being;
*suśophā* refers to a swelling because it arises from a morbid condition (*vikāra*);
and [the suffix *ka*] is applied when something not residing therein is observed there.
Whether it be *sukeśī* or *sukeśā*, [the feminine suffix] occurs in the case of a street (*rathyā*),
because it is seen even in non-living things;
therefore, if that [street] is thus endowed with that [quality].
An image with or without breasts is so called because it exists as something possessing life or resembling a living being.
After these [stems], the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally occur;
in the case of the first two, the prohibition conditioned by the presence of many vowels (*bahvack*) is set aside.
By the principle of "prior exception" (*purastādapavādanyāya*),

since the five [consonants] beginning with *oṣṭha* would otherwise fall under the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogopadhāt*), this statement is made by the principle of "exception in the middle" (*madhye'pavādanyāya*).
However, a negation characterized by coexistence (*sahanañlakṣaṇa*) sublates this [rule] due to its higher status,
as in examples such as *tuṅganāsikī* and *tuṅganāsikā*.
Here, there is neither with nose nor without nose.
Regarding this, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states:
it should be stated that [the suffix *ini*] is applied after the words *aṅga*, *gātra*, and *kaṇṭha*; thus, one who has beautiful limbs is called *svaṅgī*.
Regarding the passage beginning with *svaṅga*,
some maintain that this should be included by the particle *ca* (and), which serves to collect what has not been explicitly mentioned;
however, those who follow authoritative tradition (*prāmāṇika*) hold that it is not a valid authority because it is not stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works.
Regarding this, there are Vārttikas:
[the suffix *ini* is added] after the word *puccha*, optionally (*vā*),
as in *supucchī*.

"Supucchā" means one who has a beautiful tail; "kabara" refers to a variegated or multicolored tail, as in the case of a peahen (*mayūrī*), whose tail is always variegated (*kabara*) like a jewel or a poisoned arrow. Thus it is said.
Based on the comparison,
the wings, and the tail, it is always [called] "ulūkapakṣī śālā" (the house with the owl's wings).
An army with tails like those of owls.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied after words such as *kroḍa* when they denote a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*) and consist of more than two syllables; for example,
*kalyāṇakroḍā* (a mare with a beautiful chest) and *aśvānām uraḥ kroḍā* (the chest of horses).
This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); for example:
*sujaghanā* (SK 513).
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied after a word ending in the group beginning with *saha*, provided that three elements precede it; for example,
*sakeśā*.
One who is hairless yet possesses a nose.
SK 514
The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall not occur [after a word ending in *nakha*], as in the case of *śūrpaṇakhā*.
Why [is it] "gauramukhā" in the sense of a name? [Answer: "tāmramukhī" refers to a girl. (SK 515)

For a feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* following a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that has a word denoting a direction as its prior member and ends in a word for a part of the body (*svāṅga*), there shall be the substitution of *ṅī*. Example:
*prāṅmukhī* (facing east).
A word is acute-accented on its first syllable [when it is a compound].
The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after a nominal stem ending in *vāhan*;
only *ṅīṣ* is understood here, not *ṅīp*.
[Examples: *dityavāṭ ca me*, *dityauhī ca me*.
The word "iti" (SK 517) should be understood as occurring immediately after the rule "AS 4.1.62: *iti* śabdaḥ prakāre bhāṣāyām".
Therefore, even in the Vedic language, the word *sakhī* sometimes appears as *aśiśvī*.
Let the non-cows low, though they have no calves.
From a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) that is not restricted to the feminine and does not have *y* as its penultimate letter, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine.
"Genus" (*jāti*) is defined by its form (*ākṛtigrahaṇā*);
the meaning is that it is manifested by a recurring configuration (*anugata-saṃsthāna-vyaṅgyā*).
And the gender of [words denoting] riverbanks is not shared by all [words];
it is to be grasped through a single mention.

Another definition is that a genus (*jāti*) is easily grasped when, while not possessing all genders, it is stated in one individual instance; thus, even without being stated in another individual instance, it is easily understood. What is the purpose of the phrase ending in "being real" (*satyantam*)? [The answer is: "white" (*śuklā*).

What is the meaning of "once" (*sakṛt*) and so forth? It means that a word ending in a patronymic suffix— whether it denotes a *gotra* (clan name) together with a *caraṇa* (Vedic school), or whether it denotes one who studies a particular branch (*śākhā*)— receives the grammatical operations applicable to a genus (*jāti*).
Aupagavī,
Kaṭhī,
Bahvṛcī.

In the case of *brāhmaṇī*, however, because it is listed in the *śārṅgaravādi* group, the suffix *ṅīn* supersedes *ṅīṣ*. [Question: Why is it specified as "denoting a genus" (*jāti*)? [Answer: [To exclude cases like] *muṇḍā*. [Question:
Why is it specified as "not referring to a female" (*astrīviṣaya*)? [Answer: [To exclude cases like] *balākā*.
Why [is it specified] "after a word ending in *ya*"? [Consider the case of] *kṣatriyā*.
Regarding the prohibition of [the suffix *ṅīṣ*] after words ending in *ya*, there is no prohibition for *hayā*, *gavayā*, *mukayā*, *manuṣyā*, and *matsyā*. [Thus:
*hayī*.
By the rule *gavayī-mukayī-hala-staddhitasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.154), there is the elision of *ya*.
The feminine form of *matsya* is *matsī* when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
After a word ending in *pāka* or similar terms, which denotes a genus (*jāti*) and is used in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied.
Odanapākī,
Śaṅkukarṇī, and Śālaparṇī.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, dāsīphalī, and darbhamūlī.
These two terms are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for specific medicinal plants.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied [after a word ending in *a*] to form *dākṣī*.
Even from a word ending in *u* as an upadhā, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied]:
*audameyī*, the female descendant of Audameya.
Why [is the example] "human" (*manuṣyā*) given? [To show that it does not apply to non-human beings: *tittiriḥ*.
After words denoting a human class that end in *u* and have *y* as their penultimate letter, the suffix *ūṅ* shall be applied in the feminine.
The suffix *ṇya* is applied after "Kuru" and similar stems [according to Pāṇini 4.1.172],
and there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix in the feminine according to [Pāṇini] 4.1.177 and subsequent rules.
Why [is there] the exclusion of words ending in *ay*? [The answer is: An *adhvaryu*.
There is an addition to the rule [that it applies] to words not denoting living beings, with the exception of *rajju* and others (*rajjvādīnām upasaṅkhyānam*).
Or rather, because of the exclusion of *rajju* and others, it applies only to those ending in the vowel *u*.
In the case of *alābvā* and *karkandhvā*,
although these two words end in long vowels, the prohibition of the acute accent on the case-ending— by the rule *noṅdhātvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.175)— is the purpose for the presence of the suffix *ūṅ*.
Among the classes of living beings, the cock is [the foremost];
among ropes and the like, the rope; and the jawbone.
In the feminine gender, the suffix ūṅ shall be applied [after the word *pṛthu-*].
In the case of a name, as in *bhadrabāhuḥ*; why [is it not so] in the case of *vṛttabāhuḥ*? (SK 523)
*paṅguḥ* [is formed from *paṅgur*] after *śvaśura*, with the elision of the phonemes /u/ and /a/ (optionally).
The suffix *cāp* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṅīṣ* prescribed for words denoting a male connection;
by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*, the case-endings beginning with *su* (*svādayaḥ*) are applied.
The word *śvaśrūḥ* [is formed by the suffix *ūṅ*] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.69.

The feminine suffix *ūṅ* shall be applied after that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which has a word denoting a point of comparison as its prior member and the word *ūru* (thigh) as its subsequent member; for example:
*karabhorūḥ* ("she whose thighs are like the trunk of an elephant").
This sūtra is for the purpose of expressing that which cannot be compared; [example:
*saṃhitorūḥ* (she whose thighs are joined together).
She herself has shaphorū (shapely calves);

because they are closely joined like two hooves (śaphau), which are literally "hooves" (khurau), the term is applied figuratively through the use of the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *adarśa*.
The term *lakṣaṇoru* and *vāmoru* [should be included];
it should be stated that [the suffix *u* is applied] after the words *sahita* and *saha*.
She whose thighs (*ūrū*) are joined together (*sahita*) is *sahitorū*;
she whose thighs are capable (*saha*) is *sahorū*. Alternatively, the word *saha*, which expresses existence, is employed here to convey the excellence of her thighs.
After the words *kadru* and *kamaṇḍalu*, the suffix *ūṅ* shall be applied when they denote a feminine name.
Why is the word *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name) used? [Answer: *kadruḥ*. *Kadrūḥ* and *kamaṇḍalūḥ* [are examples]. Why [is the suffix *ūṅ* applied]? [Answer: *kadruḥ*.
The water-pot [is mentioned] for the purpose of excluding [the use of] vessels;
this is the statement [of the Sūtra].

After the suffix *añ* in the group beginning with *śārṅgarava*, and after a word denoting a genus that ends in the vowel *a* derived from that *añ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīn* shall be applied; for example, *śārṅgaravī*.
Because the term *baidī* follows from the recurrence [of the rule], only the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied when expressing connection with a male (*puṃyoga*).
Furthermore, there is the *Gaṇasūtra*: "In the case of *nṛ* and *nara*, there is vṛddhi."
A woman (nārī) [is formed by adding the suffix ṅīṣ] after [the word nara-], according to Pāṇini 4.1.74.
After a word ending in *yaṅ*, the suffix *cāp* shall occur in the feminine; here, the term *yaṅ* is used as a general designation for both *ñyaṅ* and *ṣyaṅ*, as in the case of *Āmbaṣṭhyā*.
The suffix *āp* should optionally be stated after *kārīṣagandhī* and after a word ending in *ṣyañ*;
[thus] *pautimāṣyā*.
And from this [suffix], the suffix *cāp* shall also occur.
By the rule *yañaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.16), which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṅīṣ*,
the word *avaṭa* belongs to the *garga*-class; thus,
[the feminine form] is *āvaṭyā*.
This is the governing rule (adhikāra) up to the end of the fifth book.
From the word *yuvan*, the suffix *tip* shall be applied, and it is a *taddhita*.
Since [the desired form] is established by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*, the heading *taddhitāḥ* (secondary suffixes) is for the sake of what follows; thus,
in the case of *yuvatiḥ*, it is precisely because of the rule *anupasarjanāt*.

That [woman] in whom there are many youths is called *bahuyuvā*; however, it should be understood that the form *yuvatī* is derived from the root *yu* with the suffix *śatṛ* (forming *yuvan*) and the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
Thus ends the section on feminine suffixes.
Now begins the section on grammatical relations (kāraka).
The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is necessarily present;
the word *mātra* is to be construed with each [term].
The nominative case (*prathamā*) shall occur when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem, or when there is the addition of gender alone, measure alone, or number alone.
Kṛṣṇa is both high and low.

The word *śrīḥ* is an example of a term whose gender is not fixed (*aliṅga*), while those with fixed genders (*niyataliṅga*) are examples of the category "the mere meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātra*).
But those with indeterminate gender (*aniyataliṅga*) [take the neuter] when there is a mere excess of gender, as in *taṭas*,
*taṭī*, *taṭam* (bank);
and [the masculine] when referring to a mere measure, as in *droṇo vrīhiḥ* (a *droṇa* measure of rice).

The meaning is that the rice grain is delimited by that specific measure which constitutes the form of a *droṇa*. The distinction is this: the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) qualifies the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)—namely, the measure—through a relation of non-difference; however, the meaning of the suffix qualifies the rice grain through the relation of the delimiting and the delimited.
The word for number is *saṅkhyā*:
one (*ekaḥ*),
two (*dvau*).
Since many [words] are mentioned here, the case-ending would not otherwise be applicable; therefore, this statement is made. (SK 533)
In this case, the nominative case ending should be used:
"O Rāma."
Thus ends the first [section],
With reference to this,
[it is said] in Sāṃkhyakārikā 53 and Yogasūtra 1.4–49.
The *kāraka* which the agent most desires to obtain through his action shall be designated as the *karman*. Why specify "of the agent"? [Consider: "He binds a horse among the beans.
The beans are desired by the object (*karman*), but not by the agent.

What is the purpose of including the mention of *tamap*? When the word *karman* (object) is being carried over [from a previous rule], the repetition of *karman* here is for the sake of excluding the *ādhāra* (locus/receptacle);
otherwise, it would apply only in cases such as "he enters the house" (*gehaṃ praviśati*).
Having introduced [the topic] with "SK 536 AS 2-3-1" as the heading.
When the object (karman) is not expressed [by another means], the second case ending (dvitīyā) shall be used.

When "he worships Hari" is stated, since the object (karman) has already been expressed, only the first case ending (prathamā) is used, signifying merely the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha);
and this expression is generally effected by means of finite verbs (tiṅ), primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa).
Verb (tiṅ): Hari is served;
Primary derivative (kṛt): Lakṣmī is served;
Secondary derivative (taddhita): Bought for a hundred, "śatya."
The compound is *prāptānandaḥ* (one who has attained bliss), where the bliss that has been attained is expressed by means of a nipāta (an indeclinable particle).
For example, there is expression by means of a nipāta as in: "Even a poison tree, having been nurtured, is not fit (*asāṃpratam*) to be cut down by oneself.
For the word *sāṃpratam*, the meaning is "it is proper" (*yujyate*).
A factor of action (kāraka), even if not desired, shall be designated as the object (karman) when it is connected with an action that involves that which is most desired.
Going to the village, he touches grass;
eating rice, he eats poison. (SK 539)

A *kāraka* that is not intended to be specified by particular designations such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth shall be designated as *karman* (object), [in the case of the verbs] *duh* (to milk), *yāc* (to beg), *pac* (to cook), *daṇḍ* (to fine), *rudh* (to obstruct), *pracch* (to ask), *ci* (to gather), *brū* (to speak), *śās* (to command), *ji* (to win), *math* (to churn), and *muṣ* (to steal).

That which is connected with the object (*karman*) is called "unspoken" (*akathita*); likewise, it should be understood that for the twelve verbs beginning with *duh* (milk) and the four beginning with *nī* (lead), that which is joined with the object is specifically designated as the "unspoken object. For example: *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (he milks milk from the cow).
He begs Bali for the earth;
he asks the ill-behaved for discipline;
he cooks rice grains into boiled rice.
He fines the Gargas a hundred; he shuts up the cow in the pen;
he asks the boy the way.
He gathers fruits from the tree;
he tells or instructs the boy in the Dharma;
he wins a hundred from Devadatta.
He churns the ocean of milk for nectar;
he steals a hundred cows from Devadatta;
he leads or takes away the village goat. He drags or carries it.
This notion is based on meaning:
[one says] "he begs alms," "he dwells on the earth," "he speaks the Dharma," "he articulates it," "he expresses it," and so forth.

What is the *kāraka*? [The answer is: When used in conjunction with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and the distance to be traveled (*gantavya-adhvā*) are to be designated as the object (*karman*). This is stated in a Vārttika: "In connection with intransitive roots, place, time, state, and the way to be traversed are to be called the object. For example:
*kurūn svapiti* ("He sleeps in the Kuru country").
He sits for a month; he sits for the duration of milking a cow;
he sits for the distance of a *krośa*.

Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.52: In the case of roots meaning "motion" (gati) and so forth, as well as those having sound as their object (śabdakarma), and those that are intransitive (akarmaka), that which is the agent (kartṛ) in the active voice (aṇi) shall be the object (karman) in the causative voice (ṇau).
He caused his enemies to go to heaven, he made his own people know the meaning of the Vedas,
he offered nectar to the gods, and he taught the Veda to Brahmā.
"He who caused the earth to rest upon the water—that Śrī Hari is my refuge.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "refuge" and so forth? Consider: *pācayaty odanaṃ devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to cook the rice"). Why is it said "of roots that do not end in a causative marker (*aṇi*)"? Consider: *gamayati devadatto yajñadattam* ("Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to go"), and another person employs him: *gamayati devadattena yajñadattaṃ viṣṇumitraḥ* ("Viṣṇumitra causes Devadatta to cause Yajñadatta to go").
In the case of the roots *nī* and *vah*,
one says either *nāyayati* or *vāhayati* "he causes the servant to carry the load"; there is no prohibition [of the *ṇic* suffix] for the root *vah* when the driver (*niyantṛ*) is the agent.
The charioteer causes the horses to draw the chariot;
he causes the boy to eat or consume food.
[The rule] does not apply to the root *bhakṣ* when it means "not to injure" (*ahiṃsā*). [Example:
*na vā bhakṣayaty annaṃ baṭunā* ("or he does not eat the food with the boy").
What [is the purpose] of [specifying] "when it means not to injure"? [Counter-example: *bhakṣayati balīvardān sasyam* ("he causes the oxen to eat the grain").
There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the roots beginning with *jalpati* (Vārttika):
"Devadatta causes his son to speak or to recite the Dharma.
And there is an addition regarding the root *dṛś* (Vārttika).
By demonstrating Hari to His devotees,
it is made known through this [sūtra] that only those meanings which are common to knowledge are to be grasped, and not its specific instances;
therefore, [the rule does not apply to] "he remembers," "he smells," and so forth.
One causes Devadatta to be reminded or caused to smell by means of [another],
or one causes Devadatta to be caused to sound by means of [another].

Since [these verbs] are intransitive because their object is subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), they are included here; those for whom an object distinct from place, time, and so forth is not possible are "intransitive" in this context,
but not those whose object is merely not intended to be expressed.
Therefore, in expressions such as *māsam āsayati devadattam* ("He causes Devadatta to sit for a month"), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) indeed occurs;
however, in expressions such as *devadattena pācayati* ("He causes Devadatta to cook"), it does not.

When the affix *ṇi* follows the roots *hṛ* (to take) or *kṛ* (to do), that which is the agent [of these roots] may optionally be designated as the object (*karman*) when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. For example:
*hārayati kaṭaṃ bhṛtyam* or *hārayati kaṭaṃ bhṛtyena*; *kārayati kaṭaṃ bhṛtyam* or *kārayati kaṭaṃ bhṛtyena*. (He causes the servant to take/make the mat.)
It should be stated that for the roots *abhivādi* and *dṛś*, the Ātmanepada [ending] is optional:
*abhivādayate* or *darśayate* [he causes himself to be saluted or seen] the Lord by the devotee or through the devotee.
For these verbs preceded by *adhi*, the substratum shall be the object (*karman*).
Hari dwells in Vaikuṇṭha—whether one says *adhiśete*, *adhitiṣṭhati*, or *adhyāste*.
Following the word *abhinītya*, the locus of the root *viś-* preceded by a compound shall be the object (*karman*).

In the rule *abhiniviśate sanmārgam parikrayaṇe saṃpradānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.47), by skipping over [the intervening rules] like a frog (*maṇḍūkapluti*) and carrying forward the term *anyatarasyām* from that sūtra, one adopts a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); thus, in certain cases, there is no application of the accusative case to the word *pāpa*.
When preceded by *upa* and other such prefixes, the locus (*ādhāra*) of the root *vasati* (to dwell) shall be the object (*karman*).
Hari dwells in Vaikuṇṭha— he inhabits, resides, endures, or stays there;
however, [the root] *upa-vas* does not mean "to eat," as in "he fasts in the forest."

The second case ending is to be employed after the words *ubha* and *sarvatas*, as well as after the three beginning with *dhik* and *upari* when they end in a reduplicated form; it is also seen elsewhere than these. For example:
*ubhayataḥ kṛṣṇaṃ gopāḥ* ("the cowherds [are] on both sides of Kṛṣṇa") and *sarvataḥ kṛṣṇam* ("on all sides of Kṛṣṇa").
Fie upon the non-devotee of Kṛṣṇa!
Hari is higher than the highest world,
and even higher than that world.
In the sense of "below and below," "on all sides," "around," "near," or "along with"— even when not used in conjunction with a word expressing a specific relation—
one says *abhitaḥ kṛṣṇam*.
Around the village of Kṛṣṇa,
near and close to Laṅkā.
"Alas! That which is not a devotee of Kṛṣṇa is to be pitied"—this is the meaning;
nothing at all appears [attractive] to one who is hungry.
When used in conjunction with these two [words], the second case ending is employed.
Hari is between you and me;
there is no happiness without Hari.
Under the heading of AS 1.4.83,
[it is stated in] SK 547:
AS 1.4.84: When indicating a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the word *anu* shall bear the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*;
this is an exception to the designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*).
By this [rule], the second case ending shall be used when there is conjunction (yoga).
"Following the recitation" (japamanu) means that the raining occurred characterized by the recitation as its cause; thus,
this [usage] sets aside the third case ending prescribed by the rule "parāpi hetau" (Pāṇini 2.3.23).

Since [the application of the suffix] is already established by rules such as *lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna* (Pāṇini 2.3.21), the force of the formulation of this specific technical name (*saṃjñā*) [in Pāṇini 1.4.85] serves [to restrict its scope].
When this [meaning] is expressed, it shall bear the designation *anurukta*;
"the army has encamped along the river" means that it is connected with the river.
The root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding" takes the suffix *kta*. (SK 550; AS 1.4.86)
When inferiority is expressed, *anu* functions as previously described; for example,
*anu hariṃ surāḥ*, meaning "the gods are inferior to Hari."
When superiority or inferiority is to be expressed, the indeclinable *upa* shall be designated as a prefix (*prāk*).
The locative case will be explained when there is superiority; when there is inferiority, as in "the gods are subordinate to Hari" (upa harim).
AS 1.4.90: When these meanings function as objects (*viṣaya*), words such as *prati* and others receive the aforementioned designation (*saṃjñā*).
[Example: *vṛkṣaṃ prati*, *paryanu* vā *vidyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes toward the tree").
In the sense of describing a state of being (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), as in "a devotee toward Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ prati*);
or in the sense of a share (*bhāga*), as in "Lakṣmī belongs to Hari" (*hariṃ prati*) or "Lakṣmī is a portion of Hari" (*hareḥ*). This is the meaning.

In the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*): *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati*, *pary*, or *anu siñcati*. Here, because there is an absence of the status of a prefix (*upasarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. Why [is it] in these cases? [Because in] *pariṣiñcati*, [the prefix condition applies].
In the sense of "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) and so forth, excluding the sense of "portion" (bhāga), the word *abhi* shall have the designation of *ukta* (stated).
The devotee turns toward Hari; he pours himself out toward the god, toward the god.
Why [is it stated] "when there is no share"? [Consider: "Whatever belongs to me here, let that be given. (SK 554; AS 1.4.93)
They are designated as such because from where does he come,
and from where does he go forth?
Because the notion of "motion" (gati) is sublated by [the subsequent term], there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent) according to the rule *gatir gatau* (Pāṇini 8.1.70).
In *susikta* and *sustuta*, there is no substitution of *ṣ* because they are not *upasargas*.
What is the purpose of the honor? "Is it well-sprinkled for you here?"—this is a reproach. (SK 556)
AS 1.4.95: The particle *ati* shall be designated as a *karmapravacanīya* when it expresses either transgression or honor;
for example, *ati devān kṛṣṇaḥ*.
When these meanings are to be expressed, the word *api* shall have the technical designation *ukta*.
There would also be [the substitution] of *sarpiṣ-* because it is not preceded by a prefix; the suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

The word "api" (even/also), while indicating the rarity resulting from the difficulty of finding a donor with respect to that very house which serves as the object, is connected with the word "syāt" (might be).
As for the genitive case in "sarpiṣaḥ" (of ghee), it expresses the relationship of part and whole between the drop—which is understood through the force of the word "api"—and the ghee;
for this indeed is what is meant by the word "api" being a "clarifier of the meaning of the word" (*padārthadyotaka*).
But the second [alternative] does not apply here, because it has been stated that there is no connection with even a drop of clarified butter (*sarpiṣo bindunā*), as in the example:
"one might praise Viṣṇu even (*api*)."
*Saṃbhāvanā* is hyperbole used to manifest an excellence of power; *api stuhi* [is an example]. *Anvavasarga* is permission for acting according to one's desire.
Shame on Devadatta! One may praise even a low-born man;
one may revile, one may pour water [on the fire], and one may praise.
In the case of conjunction (samuccaya), [the suffix -vat is used], according to Pāṇini 2.3.5.
In this case, the second case ending would occur:
*māsaṃ kalyāṇī*,
*māsam adhīte*.
He eats rice with molasses for a month;
the river is winding for a krośa;
he studies for a krośa.

In the case of *atyantasaṃyoga* (continuous connection), why [is the genitive used] for *krośam giriḥ*? [Answer: Because there is a mountain at one part (*ekadeśe*) of the *krośa*, as in *māsasya dvir adhīte*.
Thus ends the second [section], SK 559; AS 1.4.54.
The object intended to be expressed as independent with respect to an action shall be the agent (kartṛ). (SK 560; Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.42)
That which is the most effective instrument (*prakṛṣṭopakāraka*) in the accomplishment of an action shall be designated as the *karaṇa* (instrument).
Why is the term *tamap* (the superlative suffix) included? [Consider: "A cowherd settlement on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).
AS 2-3-18: When not already expressed, the third case ending shall be used for the agent and the instrument; as in "Vālī was killed by Rāma with an arrow."
An addition [to the rule] should be made for words such as *prakṛti* and others:
"beautiful by nature" (*prakṛtyā cāruḥ*),
"mostly a performer of sacrifices" (*prāyeṇa yājñikaḥ*).
By his lineage he is a Gārgya; he goes by even [means], he goes by uneven [means].
"He buys grain for two *droṇas*, he goes with ease or with difficulty," and so forth. (SK 562)

That factor which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the action denoted by the root *div* (to play/gamble) shall be designated as the object (*karman*), and optionally as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Example: *akṣair dīvyati* or *akṣān dīvyati* ("He plays with dice").

*apavarga* means the attainment of the result; when that [attainment] is to be illuminated, the third case ending shall be used for words denoting time (*kāla*) or distance (*adhvan*) in the sense of uninterrupted connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

If a section (*anuvāka*) has been studied by the day or by the *krośa* [of distance], what [is the result] upon completion? [If one says: "I have studied for a month," [and yet] has not arrived [at the goal]. (SK 564)

AS 2-3-19: When joined with a word having the sense of "together" (saha), the third case ending shall be used for the subordinate element; as in: *putreṇa sahāgataḥ pitā* ("the father has come together with the son").
Thus, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs even when there is conjunction with *sākam*, *sārdham*, or *samam*, and even in the absence of such conjunction,
as indicated by rules such as *vṛddho yūnā* (Pāṇini 1.2.65).
The third case ending shall be used for that limb by which, when it is modified, a modification of the whole body is indicated.

"Blind in the eye" (*akṣṇā kāṇaḥ*) means characterized by blindness pertaining to the eye. What is the purpose of the rule regarding "bodily defect" (*aṅgavikāra*)? [Consider: "His eye is blind" (*akṣi kāṇam asya*).
When there is a definition of something that has attained a certain state, the third case ending may be used.
"An ascetic by his matted locks" means one who is distinguished as an ascetic by the knowledge [indicated] by his matted locks; this is the meaning.
In the case of the verb *jñā* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the third case may optionally be used for the object:
*pitṛā* or *pitaram saṃjānīte*.
In the sense of a logical reason (hetu), the third case ending (tṛtīyā) should be used.
The status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is common to substances and so forth, and is independent of activity; however,
the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) pertains exclusively to action and is restricted to activity, as in "a jar [is produced] by means of a staff."
Hari was seen because of merit;
here, even the fruit is the cause,
as in "he dwells because of his study."
Even an action that is currently being performed (gamyamāna) serves as the motivator for the case-ending of the *kāraka*;
the meaning is: "Enough with this effort, there is nothing to be accomplished."
In relation to the act of accomplishing [the milking], "effort" (śrama) is the instrument (*karaṇa*);
"he causes the calves to drink milk by the hundreds" means he distinguishes them by the hundreds.

In the usage of *dāṇ* in the sense of an unrefined transaction, the third case is used [optionally] in place of the fourth case: *dāsyā saṃyacchate kāmukaḥ* ("the lustful man gives to the slave-girl"). But in a righteous transaction, one says *bhāryāyai saṃyacchati*.
Thus ends the third [section], SK 569, AS 1.4.32.
That person whom one intends to reach by means of the act of giving shall be designated as the recipient (sampradāna). (Pāṇini 1.4.32)
"He gives a cow to a Brahmin who has not been solicited"— thus, the Brahmin is one to whom a gift should be given.
That which one intends through an action is also the recipient (*saṃpradāna*); [alternatively],
for the root *śī* ("to lie down"),
the object is termed the instrument (*karaṇa*), and for the root *yaj* ("to sacrifice"), the recipient is termed the object (*karman*).
The meaning is that one sacrifices an animal to Rudra; one gives the animal to Rudra. (SK 571)
When roots meaning "to please" (rucy-artha) are used, that which is being pleased shall be the *sampradāna* [recipient]. Example:
*haraye rocate bhaktiḥ* ("Devotion is pleasing to Hari").
*Abhilāṣa* (desire) has another as its agent; *ruci* (liking) is the agent of the pleasure residing in Hari; what is being pleased? "The sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta on the road."
When these [verbs] are employed, that which is intended to be informed [by the agent] shall be the recipient (saṃpradāna).
Does the cowherd girl praise, hide, stand, or curse for Kṛṣṇa out of love? Or is she being informed [of something] regarding Devadatta on the road?
In the employment of the verb *dhārayati* (to owe), the creditor shall receive the designation [of the recipient]. For example:
*bhaktāya dhārayati mokṣaṃ hariḥ* (Hari owes liberation to his devotee).
What is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*)? "He owes a hundred to Devadatta in the village" (SK 574, AS 1.4.36).
When used in conjunction with the verb *spṛh* (to desire), that which is desired shall be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). For example:
*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati* (he desires flowers). What if it is not desired? *puṣpebhyo vane spṛhayati* (he desires flowers in the forest).
This designation [of *saṃpradāna*] applies merely when there is a desire;
however, when excellence is intended to be expressed, the designation *karman* (object) takes precedence, as in:
"he longs for flowers" (*puṣpāṇi spṛhayati*).
When verbs having the sense of *krudh* (to be angry) and others are employed, that person toward whom the anger is directed shall bear the technical designation [of the "object"].
He becomes angry with Hari, bears malice toward him, and feels envy for him.
What is anger directed toward someone? Envy is the resentment that thinks, "May no one else see my wife.
Resentment is indignation.
Betrayal is doing harm; envy is intolerance;
and malice is the pointing out of faults in virtues.
Even Druha and the others are understood to arise solely from anger; therefore, the qualification "toward whom" is used in a general sense. (SK 576)

AS 1.4.38: When these two [roots] are accompanied by a preposition (upasarga), that kāraka toward whom the anger is directed shall be designated as the object (karman); for example, *krūram abhikrudhyati* ("he is angry with the cruel one").
He acts with malice.
The agent of these two [verbs] would be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), when various questions are posed concerning him, as in:
"He deliberates or examines on behalf of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇāya rādhyati īkṣate vā*).
The meaning is that Garga, when questioned, deliberates upon what is auspicious and inauspicious. (SK 578, AS 1-4-40)

When these two [roots] are used in conjunction with the verb *śṛṇoti* (to promise), the agent of the preceding action, which consists of the activity of instigation (*pravartana*), shall be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). For example:
*viprāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti* or *āśṛṇoti*.
The meaning is that, having been instigated by the Brahmin with the words "Give [the cow] to me," he gives his assent.
By these two [sūtras], the participant (kāraka) of the root *gṛ* which has become the agent of the preceding action shall receive the designation *ukta*.
"He responds to the Hotṛ" means that the Hotṛ recites first and the Adhvaryu encourages him.

*parikrayaṇa* (the act of hiring) is the acceptance of service for a fixed period; the most effective factor (*sādhakatama*) in that action may optionally be designated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
For example: *śatena parikrītaḥ* or *śatāya parikrītaḥ* ("hired for a hundred [pieces of gold]").
The dative case should be stated [to express] the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*);
e.g., *muktaye hariṃ bhajati* ("He worships Hari for the sake of liberation").
It is also used in the senses of "fitness" (*klṛpi*) and "becoming" (*sampadyamāne*).
Devotion conduces to knowledge; that is, it is accomplished, born, and so forth. And when [an event] is indicated by a portent, such as tawny lightning for wind.
And in connection with "beneficial" (hita),
as in "beneficial for a Brahmin" (brāhmaṇāya hitam).
SK 581

When an action [expressed by a verb] has another action as its object (upapada), the fourth case ending shall be used for the object of the *tumun* suffix (*-tum*) which is not actually employed but is understood;
as in *phalebhyo yāti* ("he goes for the sake of fruits").
The meaning is that he goes to gather fruits;
the meaning is that we pay homage to Nṛsiṃha in order to propitiate Nṛsiṃha.
The same applies to such passages as "Having thus paid homage to the Self-existent One" (SK 582) and so forth (AS 2.3.15).

By the rule *bhāvavacanāśca* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), the fourth case ending shall be applied after a word ending in that which is prescribed by this sūtra; for example, *yāgāya yāti*, meaning "he goes in order to sacrifice."
When used in conjunction with these [words], the fourth case ending shall be employed.
Salutation to Hari;
the case ending denoting the grammatical relation (kāraka) is stronger than the case ending used for a qualifying word (upapada);
[as in] "he pays homage to the gods."
May there be well-being for all creatures;
Svāhā to Agni! Svadhā to the ancestors!
The word *alam* is taken here in the sense of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*).

Consequently, in constructions with words such as *prabhu* (master), *samartha* (capable), and *śakta* (able)— as in "Hari is sufficient for the Daityas," "He is the master," "He is capable," or "He is able"— the use of the genitive case is also correct.
Based on the grammatical indications "he has power over that" (Pāṇini 1.4.57) and "he is the leader of these" (Pāṇini 1.4.54),
it is established that [the word *indra*] signifies one who desires to be the lord of the three worlds; thus,
*vaṣaṭ indrāya*.
The particle *ca* serves to re-enjoin [the rule];

therefore, when a benediction (*āśis*) is intended to be expressed, even though a sixth case ending would otherwise apply by the rule "also in a benediction" (*cāśiṣi*), it is superseded and only the fourth case ending occurs:
*svasti gobhyo bhūyāt* ("May there be well-being for the cows").
In the sense of contempt, the fourth case may optionally be used for the object of the verb *man* (to think), except when it refers to living beings.

I do not consider you to be even a blade of grass, nor do I regard you as something comparable to grass; for according to the grammatical rule regarding the use of the *tṛn* suffix in the sense of "thinking" (*manana*) and so forth,
I do not think of you as grass.
Excluding the word *aprāṇiṣu* ("in the case of non-living beings"), one should state instead: "excluding boats, food, parrots, and jackals" (*naukākānnaśukaśṛgālavarjyeṣu*).
By this rule, in the example *na tvāṃ nāvaṃ annaṃ vā manye* ("I do not consider you a boat or food"), the fourth case ending does not occur despite the lack of life;
however, in the example *na tvāṃ śune manye* ("I do not consider you a dog"), the fourth case ending does indeed occur despite the presence of life.
For verbs meaning "to go," when there is a distinction of paths, these two [suffixes] are used in the sense of the object, provided there is physical effort involved.
In the sense of movement, [what is the purpose of using] *grāmaṃ* or *grāmāya* in "he goes to the village"? [The answer is: "He goes to Hari mentally.
Why [is it said] "not on a path" (*anadhvany*)? [Because in] "he goes along the road," [the accusative is used].
This prohibition applies only when the path is already occupied by a traveler;
however, when one intends to proceed from a wrong path onto the correct path itself, the fourth case ending is indeed used, as in:
*utpathena pathe gacchati* ("He goes from the wrong path onto the path").
Thus ends the fourth [section],
When separation (*viśleṣa*) is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), that factor which is fixed as the limit (*avadhi*) therein shall be the *apādāna* (ablative).
From what [case-role] does one come from the village? From what [case-role] does one fall from a galloping horse? The leaf falls from the tree.
There is an addition [to the rule] regarding words meaning "disgust," "cessation," and "negligence" (Vārttika):
one feels disgust toward sin, one desists from it.
One becomes negligent regarding the Dharma. (SK 588; AS 1.4.25)
In the usage of words meaning "fear" and words meaning "protection," the cause (hetu) shall be the *apādāna* [ablative case]; for example:
*corād bibheti* ("he fears the thief") and *corāt trāyate* ("he protects from the thief").
What is the cause of fear? One fears or is protected in the forest. (SK 589; AS 1.4.26)

In the employment of the root *parā-ji* (to defeat), an unbearable object shall be the *apādāna* (ablative case); for example, *adhyayanāt parājayate*, which means "he falters because of his studies."
Is it "endured"? It means he conquers or overcomes his enemies; (SK 590).
*Pravṛttivighātaḥ* (obstruction of activity) is *vāraṇa* (prevention).
When verbal roots having the sense of prevention are used, that which is desired [by the agent] shall be the *apādāna* (ablative case).
In "He keeps the cow away from the barley," is [the barley] the desired object? He keeps the cow away from the barley in the field. (SK 591)
When there is an intervention, that from which the agent desires the absence of the self's perception shall be the *apādāna* (ablative case);
for example, "Kṛṣṇa hides from his mother."
Why "in the case of disappearance"? [Example: *caurān na didṛkṣate* ("he does not wish to see the thieves").
Why the inclusion of the word "wishes" (*icchatigrahaṇam*)? So that it may apply even when there is actually seeing, provided there is a desire for non-seeing. (SK 592)
When there is the acquisition of knowledge preceded by restrictive rules, the speaker shall be designated as "prāk" (the former); [as in] "he studies from the upādhyāya."
What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the case of usage"? [The purpose is to exclude cases such as: "He hears his verse" (tasya gāthāṃ śṛṇoti).
For that which is being born, the cause would be the *apādāna*;
from Brahman, the creatures are born. (SK 594)
The root *bhū* signifies "becoming" (*bhavana*), as well as the source of origin for that which becomes.
The meaning is that the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat; it shines forth there.
[This is an example of] the locative case used for the object or the locus when a gerund (*lyap*) is elided.
The meaning is that he looks from the palace,
he looks from the seat;
that is, having ascended the palace and having sat down upon the seat, he looks.
"She is bashful before her father-in-law" means "she feels shame upon seeing her father-in-law";
for even an action that is merely implied can be the cause for case-endings of the factors of action (*kāraka*).
Why [is this said]? From the river—whereby the construction of distance and time occurs—the fifth case ending (pañcamī) is used;
or, when connected with that [fifth case], the first (prathamā) and seventh (saptamī) case endings are used for the distance.
The locative case should also be stated [after a word denoting time], optionally:
"a village is a *yojana* from the forest," or "a village is at the distance of a *yojana*";
"the month of Āgrahāyaṇī is [after] the month of Kārttikī."
When these [words] are used in conjunction, the fifth case ending shall be employed.
The term "anya" (other) includes both "itarat" (the other) and "prapañca" (elaboration); thus,
"anya" means distinct or "itara" in relation to Kṛṣṇa.
Far from the forest, apart from Kṛṣṇa,
before the village.
A word denoting direction is a "direction-word" (*dikśabda*); by means of that, even when joined with something existing in space or time, [the suffix *tasi*] occurs, as in:
"Phālguna is prior to Caitra."

But when used in connection with a word denoting a part [of the body], it is not the subsequent repetition of that [word] which is called *amreḍita*, because of the rule: "In the case of *kāya*, the preceding [part] is [so called]. (Pāṇini 8.1.8). Thus, it is the preceding [part of the body].

However, although *añcu* has a directional meaning as its final member, it is mentioned separately in order to override the genitive case prescribed by *ṣaṣṭhyatasartha-pratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.30). Thus, one says *prāk* or *pratyak* *grāmāt*,
or *āc* *dakṣiṇā* *grāmāt*.

Regarding the rule *āṅmaryādāvacane* (Pāṇini 2.3.10), which prescribes the ablative case (*pañcamī*) for the sense of "starting point" (*apādāna*) when used with words like *ā* or *dakṣiṇā*, the usage in the Bhāṣya— *kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti* ("from the full moon of Kārtika")— shows that the ablative is employed in connection with words having the sense of "starting from" (*prabhṛti*).
Thus, in the expression *bhāvāt prabhṛti* or *ārabhya*, Hari is to be served.
Because of the rule for compound formation stating "apaparibahir" (Pāṇini 2.1.12), it is known that the ablative case is used in connection with *bahiḥ* (outside); thus,
in the example "grāmād bahiḥ" (outside the village).
AS 1.4.88: These two [words, *ati* and *anu*], when used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*), are termed *karmapravacanīya*. (SK 597)

AS 1.4.89: The term *āṅ* shall have the designation [of *upasarga*] when it denotes a limit (*maryādā*); because of the inclusion of the word "mention" (*vacana*), it also [has this designation] when it denotes inclusive limit (*abhividhi*).
SK 598 / AS 2.3.10: When used in conjunction with these *karmapravacanīya*s, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be employed.
"Excluding Hari," "around Hari"— in these cases *pari* signifies exclusion (*varjana*);
however, in cases such as indication (*lakṣaṇa*), one says "around Hari."
Saṃsāra exists until liberation;
Brahman exists until it is fully realized.
In these two senses, the word *prati* shall be designated as *ukta-saṃjñaka*.
AS 2-3-11: In this context, when used in conjunction with *karmapravacanīya*s, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be employed; for example: *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇāt prati*.
He exchanges sesame seeds for beans.
When a debt (*ṛṇa*) serves as the cause (*hetu*) and is distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*), the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used;
for example, *śatād baddhaḥ* ("bound because of a hundred").
Why "other than the agent"? [Consider: *śatena bandhitaḥ* ("caused to be bound by a hundred").
When a non-feminine gendered word expressing a quality serves as the cause (hetu), the fifth case ending may optionally be used.

What is the use of a quality to one bound by dullness or even by further dullness? What is the use of wealth to a family that lacks a woman? One who is liberated through wisdom—what need has he for anything else?
By the rule of *vibhāṣā*, there is optionally the suffix *a* after a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*) or a feminine noun; for example:
"there is fire because of smoke" (*dhūmād agnimān*), and "the jar does not exist because it is not perceived" (*anupalabdher na ghaṭaḥ*).
In conjunction with these [words], the third case-ending shall be used, as well as the fifth and the second case-endings.
The inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of conjunction; the fifth and second case endings are understood to follow, as in:
*pṛthag rāmeṇa*, *rāmāt*, or *rāmam*.
Thus, without variety.

After these words, when they do not denote a substance (*adravyavacana*), the third and fifth case endings occur in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*): *stokena* or *stokāt muktaḥ*. However, when denoting a substance (*dravya*), [only the third case is used]: *stokena viṣeṇa hataḥ*.
After these [words], the second case ending shall be used; furthermore, the fifth and third case endings may also be used.
This rule applies to the mere meaning of the nominal stem:
*grāmasya dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*; likewise, *antikam*, *antikāt*, or *antikenā*.
Because the phrase "of a word denoting a non-substance" (asattvavacanasya) is understood [from the preceding rule],
the fifth case ending is not used here in the expression *dūraḥ panthāḥ*.

That which is distinct from the meaning of the case-factor (*kāraka*) and the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), namely a relationship such as that between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), is the "residual" (*śeṣa*); the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used in that context.
In the case of "the king's man" (rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ),
when there is a desire to express merely the relationship even among [the factors] such as the action (karman) and so forth, the genitive alone is used by those who know the truth.
He knows ghee;
he remembers his mother;
he prepares fuel for water.
Satisfied by the fruits [of my practice], I worship the two feet of Śambhu. (SK 607)
When the word *hetu* (cause) is employed to indicate the cause, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used; for example:
*annasya hetor vasati* (he dwells for the sake of food).
When pronouns and the word *hetu* are used, the third case ending shall be employed to indicate the cause (*hetu*), and the sixth case ending as well.
For what reason does it abide, and for what purpose?
In the application of synonyms for signs, there is generally the observation of all [of them].
For what cause does he dwell? By what cause? For what purpose? And so forth.

Thus, because of the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāya*), the nominative and accusative cases do not occur for non-pronouns [when used as interrogatives] such as *kiṃ kāraṇam*, *ko hetuḥ*, and *kiṃ prayojanam*. For example:
*jñānena nimittena hariḥ sevyaḥ* ("Hari is to be served by means of knowledge as the cause").
"For the sake of knowledge, for the sake of the sign," and so forth (SK 609; AS 2.3.30).
In connection with this [suffix], the sixth case ending (ṣaṣṭhī) shall occur;
this is an exception to the fifth case ending (pañcamī) prescribed by the rule *dikśabdād digdeśakāleṣu* (Pāṇini 5.3.27). For example:
*grāmasya dakṣiṇataḥ* ("to the south of the village").
In front (puraḥ), from the front (purastāt), above (upari), from above (upariṣṭāt).
SK 610
In connection with a word ending in the suffix *enap*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) should be used; however,
by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *enapā*, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may also be employed.
To the south of the village, or to the north of the village, in this manner. (SK 611)
In connection with these [words], the sixth case ending shall be used, and optionally the fifth case ending as well; for example: *dūraṃ nikaṭaṃ grāmasya* or *grāmāt*.
When the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the verb *jñā* (to know) is intended to be expressed as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*)— that is, not as a kāraka— the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used.
The cognition of clarified butter [arises] from [the word] "sarpiḥ" (SK 613;
The sixth case ending shall be used for these [verbs] when the object remains unexpressed:
*mātuḥ smaraṇam* (the remembering of the mother), *sarpiṣo dayanam* (the giving of ghee), or *īśanam* (the ruling).
When a quality is imparted, the sixth case ending shall be used for the object of the verb *kṛ* (to do/make) when it remains as a residual relation (*śeṣe*).
Fuel is an accessory for water.

The sixth case ending shall be used for the object of roots meaning "to afflict" (*ruj*), provided they are not intransitive (*abhāvakartṛka*) and exclude *jvari* and *saṃtāpi*, when [the agent] is treated as residual (*śeṣe*). For example:
*caurasya rogasya rujā* ("the affliction of the thief's disease").
It should be stated that this does not apply to *jvari* and *saṃtāpi*.
"Thief-fever" (*caurajvara*) or "thief-torment" (*caurasantāpa*) regarding disease means fever and so forth caused by disease and related to thieves; such is the meaning. (SK 616)
After the verb *nāth* when it has the sense of "blessing" (*āśis*), the sixth case ending shall be used for the remaining object; e.g., *sarpiṣo nāthanam*.
Why [is it specified] "in the sense of a blessing"? [Consider the example: *māṇavakanāthanam*, which means a request related to that [boy].
After these [roots] meaning "to injure," when used in a non-causal sense (śeṣe), the sixth case ending shall be used for the object; for example, *caurasyojjāsanam* ("the killing of the thief").
The prefixing of *ni* and *pra*— whether joined together, reversed, or separated—
constitutes the killing of a thief (*caurasya niprahaṇanam praṇihananam*).
The roots *niha* and *praha*, meaning "to strike" or "to kill," belong to the *cur*-class (*curādi*) when used in the sense of leaping upon or attacking.
The uprooting of the thief,
the tearing apart of the thief, and the grinding of the low-born man.
What is the example for "in the case of injury"? The crushing of roasted grains (dhānāpeṣaṇam).
The sixth case ending shall be used for the remaining objects;
in the context of gambling and the business of buying and selling, these two [roots] have the same meaning,
as in "the wagering or staking of a hundred."
What is the purpose of [specifying] "when both are capable"? [The examples are: *śalākā-vyavahāraḥ*, meaning counting;
and *brāhmaṇa-paṇanam*, meaning praise.
The sixth case ending shall be used for the object of the root *div* when it means "gambling" or "transaction in the form of buying and selling."
In "he plays for a hundred," what is the meaning of that [accusative case]? It means he praises the Brahmin; that is the sense.
