An exception to the preceding rule; [one plays] for a hundred, or one wins back a hundred.
When the meaning is "offering to a deity," the sixth case ending shall be used after a word denoting a specific oblation that is the object of the verbs *preṣya* ("command") and *brū* ("speak").
"Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the fat of the omentum of the goat-offering to Agni, or recite [the invitatory verse].

When a word expressing time is used as a locative (adhikaraṇa) in connection with the employment of numerals (*kṛtvas*), the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the remaining relation (*śeṣe*); for example:
*pañcakṛtvo 'hno bhojanam* (eating five times a day), *dvir ahno bhojanam* (eating twice a day).
What is the purpose of the word "śeṣe" (in the remaining cases)? [It is to exclude examples such as: *dvir ahany adhyayanam* (study twice a day).
In connection with a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive case shall be used for both the agent and the object:
*kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ* (the deed of Kṛṣṇa) and *jagataḥ kartā kṛṣṇaḥ* (Kṛṣṇa is the creator of the world).

The designation *netṛ* is desired when it denotes a quality or an action (in the sense of "one who leads"), as in *aśvasya netā* ("the leader of the horse") or *srughnasya/srughnaṃ netā* ("the leader to/from Srughna").
Why [is this rule stated]? So that it does not apply in the case of a *taddhita* suffix.
"One who has previously made a mat" (kṛtapūrvī kaṭam). Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.66.

When both [the agent and the object] are applicable in a formation ending in a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive case should be used for the object alone; however, this restriction does not apply to feminine suffixes ending in *ā* or *ī* (Vārttika). For example: *āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful").

According to some, when the word *rudra* occurs in the sense of "one who divides" or "one who desires to divide" the world, the feminine suffix is optionally applied in the remaining cases (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*).

The creation of the world is diverse, whether by Hari or by a lion; or rather, some maintain that there is no distinction between the two, [just as] they accept the teaching of words either by the Teacher or as belonging to the Teacher.
In connection with a *kta* suffix having the sense of the present tense, the sixth case ending shall be used.
This is an exception to the prohibition [stated in] *loka-sandarbhah* 627:
[the suffix *kta* is used after the word *rājan*] when it means "esteemed," "known," or "honored" by kings (*rājñām mataḥ*, *buddhaḥ*, or *pūjitaḥ*).
AS 2-3-68: In connection with a word ending in a *kta* suffix, the sixth case-ending shall be used; for example: *idam eṣām āsitam*, *śayitam*, *gatam*, or *bhuktam*.
When these [words] are used, the sixth case-affix shall not occur.
Hari, performing or having performed the creation,
is *uḥ*.
One who desires to see Hari, or one who wishes to adorn himself, is called *alaṃkariṣṇu*.
Hari is the slayer of the Daityas;
there is no prohibition against [the use of] the suffix *kamu* (in the sense of desiring),
as in "Hari is the lover of Lakṣmī."
Having created the imperishable world,
[he acts] to bring about happiness.
The Daityas were destroyed by Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu slew the Daityas.
The *khalartha* suffixes are easily formed; the expansion [of the rule] by Hari is as follows:
the pratyāhāra *tṛn* is formed starting from the word *tṛ* in the rule *śatṛśānacau* up to the *n* of *atṛn*.
Pavamāna, purifying the Soma, has attained it.
Adorning himself while studying this Veda, O Śatru.
The agent of the suffix *tṛn* [is expressed by the first case],
or that of the suffix *dviṣ* [is expressed by the sixth case], or that of the suffix *śatṛ* [is expressed by the sixth case].
Whether one hates Mura or Murāri,
this is a total prohibition of the genitive case used for the agent; however, the genitive case for the "remainder" (śeṣe) would certainly still apply.
The conqueror of hell, while acting for the sake of the Brahmin.
When used with a future verb or with a word expressing a debt (ādhamarṇya), the genitive case shall not be employed for a word denoting existence;
as in "The purifier descends upon the existent."
He who goes to Vraja is a giver of a hundred.
The genitive case may optionally be used;
for example, "Hari is to be served by me" (*mayā*) or "Hari is to be served of mine" (*mama*).

What is the purpose of the word "kartari" (in the sense of the agent)? [Consider the example: *geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* ("The boy is one who should sing the Sāman hymns"). Since the suffix *ya* is prescribed here in the sense of the agent according to *bhavyageya* Pāṇini 3.4.68, the object (*karman*) is not already expressed; therefore, this rule is divided [from the preceding].
The phrase "in the case of the attainment of both for verbal derivatives" (kṛtyānām ubhayaprāptau) and "not" (na) carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore,
it must be understood that "the cows were led to the cow-pen by Kṛṣṇa."
Therefore, the meaning has been stated [as applying] to the agentive suffix (kartari).
When joined with words having the sense of "equal," the third case ending may optionally be used; otherwise, the sixth case ending is used.

What is the point of the words *atulopamābhyām* (incomparable and peerless), since [the terms] *tulyaḥ*, *sadṛśaḥ*, or *samaḥ* mean "equal to Kṛṣṇa" or "like Kṛṣṇa"? For there is no scale (*tulā*) or comparison (*upamā*) for Kṛṣṇa.

According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.73, when used in conjunction with words having this meaning, the fourth case (caturthī) may optionally be employed, and in its alternative, the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī); [this applies] in the sense of a benediction: "May long life, [or] a long-lived existence, belong to Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇāya* or *kṛṣṇasya bhūyāt*).

In this way, may there be welfare (*madram*), prosperity (*bhadram*), well-being (*kuśalam*), freedom from disease (*nirāmayam*), happiness (*sukham*), tranquility (*śam*), purpose (*arthaḥ*), motive (*prayojanam*), benefit (*hitam*), or that which is salutary (*pathyam*).

Why [is it used] in the sense of a benediction? Because of the explanation that "it exists for the longevity of Devadatta" (*devadattasyāyuṣyam asti*), the term *artha* is understood in all these cases.
Since *madrabhadra* and *paryāya* are synonyms, only one of them should be recited;
thus, [the compound takes] the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī).
AS 1.4.45: A factor (kāraka) that serves as the locus (ādhāra) of an action residing in the agent or the object, by means of those [two], shall be designated as the locus (adhikaraṇa).
AS 2-3-36: The locative case (saptamī) shall be used for the locus (adhikaraṇa); by the word "and" (ca), it is also used after words expressing distance or proximity.
The locus (ādhāra) is threefold: contact-based (aupaśleṣika), objective (vaiṣayika), and pervasive (abhivyāpaka); as in "he sits on a mat" and "he cooks in a pot."
There is a desire for liberation in everyone; there is a Self both far from and near to the forest.

By the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.34], four case endings are thus established here along with the three [already mentioned]. Regarding the Vārttika *ktasyenviṣayasya karmaṇyupasaṅkhyānam*, [the example is]:
*adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("one who has studied grammar").

In the analysis "this person has studied" (*adhītam anena*), the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *iṣṭādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.88) to denote the agent; furthermore, according to the Vārttika *sādhvasādhuprayoge ca*, [the genitive is used] as in:
"Kṛṣṇa is virtuous toward his mother."
An unvirtuous person [is so called] because of his maternal uncle;
here, "cause" refers to the fruit within the application of action.
Union consists of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*):
one kills the leopard for its skin, the elephant for its tusks,
the yak for its hair, and the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland.
1. (This is the commentary:
In this context, the third case ending would have applied to express the cause; this [sūtra] is intended to prevent that.
The words *sīmā*, *aṇḍakośaḥ*, *puṣkalakaḥ*, and *gandhamṛgaḥ* [are used] when referring to a specific kind of yoga; why [is this so]? [Because] one reaps grain for wages (*vetanena*).
When one action is characterized by another action, the seventh case ending shall be used after that [word denoting the characterizing action].
While the cows were being milked, he departed;
and while those who are worthy act and those who are unworthy do not act— or the reverse—
while the virtuous cross over, the wicked remain behind.
While the good remain, the wicked cross over; while the wicked remain, the good cross over;
when the wicked have crossed over, the good remain.
When there is a mark indicating a state (bhāva-lakṣaṇa) characterized by disregard or excess, the sixth and seventh case endings are used.
"He went forth while [others] were weeping, or he went forth as they were weeping";
the meaning is that he renounced the world, disregarding his weeping son and others.
In connection with these seven [words], the sixth and seventh case endings occur;
since only the sixth case ending would have been applicable, this rule is stated for the purpose of optionally allowing the seventh case ending as well.
The meaning is that he is the master of cows, or among cows,
or produced among cows; that is to say, he was born to experience cows alone.
When used in conjunction with these two [words], the sixth and seventh case endings occur in the sense of "intention" (tātparya).
*Āyukta* means employed or engaged;
or, *āyukta* means skilled in the worship of Hari, or in the practice of the worship of Hari.
What [is it]? A yoked ox at the cart (*āyukto gauḥ śakaṭe*).
The meaning is "slightly joined.

Selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is the separation of one part from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*saṃjñā*); after that [word expressing the whole], the sixth and seventh case endings occur:
*nṛṇāṃ* or *nṛṣu* *brāhmaṇaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* (among men, the Brāhmaṇa is the best);
*gavāṃ* or *goṣu* *kṛṣṇā bahukṣīrā* (among cows, the black one yields much milk).
Among those going or while they are going, he runs swiftly;
among the students or for the students, he is friendly and skillful.
AS 2-3-42: Where there is a distinction (*vibhāga*) consisting of the separation (*vibhakta*) of that which is being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*), the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used.
The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra. (SK 640; AS 2-3-43)
When used in conjunction with these two [words], the seventh case ending shall be employed in the sense of "reverence" (*arcā*), but not when used with *prati*. For example:
*mātari sādhuḥ* or *nipuṇaḥ* ("skilled or proficient toward his mother").
Why "in the sense of reverence"? Consider: *rājño bhṛtyo nipuṇaḥ* ("the king's servant is skillful [toward him]").
In this context, it should be stated that the intention [of the author] is to explain the reality by means of words such as *apraty* and so forth; or [alternatively],
a virtuous or skillful person might inquire of his mother.
In connection with these two [words], the third case ending shall be used, and optionally the seventh case ending as well.
*Prasita* or *utsuka* [are used] with *hariṇā* or *harau*. (SK 642;

When [a word] denotes a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) in its primary sense, the third and seventh case endings occur after that word—provided it expresses the meaning of a suffix that has been elided by the technical term *lup*—in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example:

"one should invoke the Goddess under Mūla" (*mūlenāvāhayed devīm*) or "one should dismiss her under Śravaṇa" (*śravaṇena visarjayet*), or alternatively, "under Mūla" (*mūle*) or "under Śravaṇa" (*śravaṇe*).
What is the purpose of [mentioning] *lupi*? [For example: "Saturn is in Puṣya" (*puṣye śaniḥ*).
Between the two powers, those which are the paths of time (kālādhvan), these [two] exist by means of them:
"Having eaten today, he will eat in two days" or "after two days"; this is time situated between the two powers of the agent (kartṛśakti).
"Standing here, one might pierce a target at a distance of one *krośa* or from one *krośa* away"; in the context of the relationship between the agent and the object,
the locative (*saptamī*) and ablative (*pañcamī*) case endings are prescribed when used in conjunction with the word *adhika*.
This is because of the indications in the Sūtras, "tadasminnadhikam" (SK Sandarbha 1846) and "yasmādadhikam" (SK Sandarbha 645),
[it follows that] Hari is superior to the world or from the world (loka). (SK 644)
AS 1.4.97: In the sense of the relationship between owner and owned, the prefix *adhi* shall be designated as a *karmapravacanīya*.
In this case, the seventh case ending shall be used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya* [particle], as in:
"The qualities of Hari are near the ultimate limit (*upa parārdhe hareḥ guṇāḥ*)."
The meaning is that they exceed a parārdha;
however, regarding sovereignty, the locative case is used alternatively for both the location and the possessor,
as in "Rāma [rules] over the earth."
In the case of forming a compound according to the rule *adhi-rāme bhūḥ saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.40),
the suffix *kha* (īna) is applied by the rule *rāmādhīnā aṣaḍakṣa-* (Vārttika 2079).
The prefix *adhi* may optionally have the designation [of *karmapravacanīya*] when used with the verb *kṛ*, in the sense of "lordship" (*īśvara*).
That which will authorize me here— meaning that which will employ me;
from this, the sovereignty of the employer is understood.
Because it is not preceded by another verb (*agatitvāt*), there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent) according to Pāṇini 8.1.28 (*tiṅi codāttavati*).
Thus ends the section on the seventh case (*saptamī*) within the topic of grammatical relations (*kāraka-prakaraṇa*).
Now begins the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds (SK 647; AS 2.1.1).
A rule that relates to words should be understood as depending on semantic competency (samartha).
From the rule *kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 2.2.38) onwards, until that point, the term *samāsa* (compound) is understood as the governing heading (adhikāra). Pāṇini 2.1.4.
The rule *saha* is analyzed as a *yogavibhāga*:
a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is compounded with a compatible word (*samarthena*).
Since this analysis of the rule is for the purpose of achieving desired results, this compound consists of a few words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) as its final members.
And he adorned himself with that very desire and moved along in accordance with it.
A case-inflected word (sup) is compounded with another case-inflected word (sup) or a word ending in a kṛt or taddhita suffix (sup-supā);
by virtue of being a compound (samāsa), it possesses the status of a nominal stem (prātipadika). (SK 650)
According to AS 2.4.71, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) of the member of these two [compounds].
Due to the rule "caraṭ" in the context of "bhūtapūrve" (AS 5.3.53), the word *bhūta* takes the prior position.

The word *bhūtapūrva* is a compound meaning "formerly been," formed with the prefix *pūrva-*; optionally, there is a compound with the particle *iva*, and there is no elision of the case-ending, as in *jīmūtasyeva*.
This is a heading.
The rule "avyayam" (SK 652, AS 2.1.6) is analyzed as a separate yoga.
An indeclinable is compounded with a word that has the same case-ending;
that is an *avyayībhāva*. (SK 653)
In a rule concerning compound formation, that which is designated by the nominative case shall bear the technical name *upasarjana*.
In a compound, the subordinate member (upasarjana) should be placed first.
In a compound, that which has a fixed case-ending in its analysis (vigraha) shall be designated as an *upasarjana*, but it does not necessarily undergo prior placement [in the compound]. (SK 656)
AS 1.2.48: "The word *go* when it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and that which ends in a feminine suffix—there shall be shortening of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in those;
and [the compound] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of AS 2.4.18. Thus, it possesses the status of an indeclinable.
After an avyayībhāva compound ending in a vowel other than *a*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*); rather, with the exception of the fifth case, it is replaced by *am*.
"Apadiśa" is the intermediate point between two directions; it is a neuter indeclinable, whereas "vidiś" (the intermediate direction) is feminine— so says Amara (SK 658).
AS 2.4.84: After an avyayībhāva compound ending in a vowel other than *a*, there is optionally the absence of the third and seventh case endings;
for example, *apadiśam*.
By means of pointing out, pointing out, in pointing out.
Due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely), in cases such as *sumadram* and *unmattagaṅgam*, there is invariably the substitution of *am* for the locative case ending.

This is the meaning of the rule beginning with *vibhakti*: an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that denotes the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*) and so forth is compounded with a word ending in a case suffix (*subanta*), and that compound is called *avyayībhāva*.
First, regarding the case ending: in the example *adhi hari*, the word *adhi* indicates only the sense of the locative case (*saptamī-artha*).
*Hariḥ adhi* is the extraordinary (*itthalaukika*) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*);
here, although the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is already expressed by the particle (*nipāta*), the seventh case (*saptamī*) occurs by virtue of the power of the explicit statement.
AS 2.4.18: This [suffix] shall be neuter;
[and] there is shortening of the final vowel of the nominal stem when it is neuter (SK 318).
"He protects" (*gopāyati*) or "he guards the cows" (*gāḥ pāti*), thus he is a "cowherd" (*gopā*); "in him" means "near the cowherd" (*adhigopam*).
In the examples "near Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya samīpam upakṛṣṇam*),

"near the village" (*samayā grāmam*), "near Laṅkā" (*nikaṣā laṅkām*), and "far from the forest" (*ārād vanāt*), there is no *avyayībhāva* compound; this applies also to the words *abhitaḥ* and *paritaḥ*.
By the force of the rule prescribing the second and fifth case endings in the sense of "other than" (anyārāt) [Pāṇini 2.3.29],
*sumadram* means "the prosperity of the Madras," and *duryavanam* means "the misfortune of the Yavanas."
The departure of prosperity is the loss of wealth;
the absence of flies is flyless; the passing of the cold is the end of frost.
*Atyaya* means destruction;
*nidrā* means sleep. Since "sleep is not appropriate at this time," there is an excess of sleep (*atinidram*).
Thus, *hari* is the manifestation of the word *hari*.
In the expression *viṣṇoḥ paścādanuviṣṇu*, this is not a compound;
for there is the usage in the Bhāṣya: *tataḥ paścāt sraṃsyate*.
The meanings of *yathā* are fitness (*yogyatā*), repetition (*vīpsā*), non-transgression of the word-meaning (*padārthānativṛtti*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*). For example,
in the phrase "anurūpaṃ rūpasya" (suitable for the form), the meaning is "fitting."

In the expression *artham arthaṃ prati* (*pratyartham*), because the designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the word *prati* when used in a distributive sense (*vīpsā*), the resulting sentence— even though it contains an accusative case—
does not exceed its expressive power (*śakti*) in accordance with that capacity (*yathāśakti*).
The similarity of Hari is with Hari; by the rule "sa" is substituted for "saha," as in "jyeṣṭhasyānupūrvyeṇa" [Pāṇini 2.1.60], it becomes "anujyeṣṭham."
In the analysis of the compound *cakreṇa yugapat*, [the rule] applies according to Pāṇini 2.1.4 (SK 660; AS 6-3-81).
In an *avyayībhāva* compound, that [word] would be *sahasya*, but not when it refers to time; however, when referring to time, one says *sahapūrvāhṇam*.

In the case of *sadṛśaḥ sakhyā* (similar to a friend), since the sense of "having a friend" (*sasakhi*) is already established by the literal meaning [of the compound], the inclusion of the term *sādṛśya* (similarity) is for the purpose that it may apply even when similarity is subordinate. Thus,
*kṣatrāṇāṃ saṃpattiḥ* (the prosperity of the Kṣatriyas) is *sakṣatram*.
The distinction is that *samṛddhi* is the excellence of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*),
while *saṃpatti* is a corresponding physical form; thus,
he eats even with the grass, not abandoning even a blade of grass.
The meaning is "in its entirety";
there is no intention here, at the end, for the consumption of grass.
One who studies up to the *Agnigrantha* is called *sāgni*.
The word *yathā* is compounded only when there is dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*); therefore, in this case, *yathā haristathā haraḥ* is not a compound,
because the word *yathā* indicates that Hari possesses the status of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
By this [sūtra], the attainment of [the cognition] as "similarity" or as "according to the object" is negated.
As many verses as there are, so many prostrations to Acyuta; for as long as a verse [is recited], [so many prostrations are made].
A small portion of a vegetable is "śākapratiḥ";
in the sense of measure, [it is used as in] "kim vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut" (the lightning flashes toward every tree).
In the context of gambling transactions, this compound refers specifically to defeat.
A roll of the dice that has turned out unfavorably;
[a roll] of the dice, of the sticks, or of the single [die].
This is a heading.
Precisely by virtue of this capacity, the compounds of the ancients are mandatory (*nityasamāsa*); however, the rule *sup supā* does not constitute a mandatory compound,
as is evidenced by the injunctions for forming compounds such as *avyayam* (Pāṇini 2.1.6).
Transmigration is devoid of Viṣṇu; it is apart from Viṣṇu.
Having circumambulated, he goes around Viṣṇu’s enclosure;
from the enclosure he goes to the forest; from the forest to the eastern forest; from the eastern forest—
With these two [words], *āṅ* is optionally compounded with a word ending in the fifth case; that is an *avyayībhāva*.
May there be saṃsāra until liberation;
may there be devotion to Hari from childhood; may there be [devotion] unto children.

The prefixes *abhi* and *prati*, which indicate direction toward something, when used with a word denoting a mark or boundary, are treated as in the preceding rule [i.e., they form an avyayībhāva compound]. For example:
*abhyagni śalabhāḥ patanti* (moths fly toward the fire). *Agnim abhi*.
Toward the fire, [he places] the fire.
When a word-meaning is illuminated by a term that serves as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that [term] is compounded with *anu*; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound.
For example, *anuvanaṃ aśanir gataḥ*, which means "the thunderbolt has gone near the forest."
The prefix *anu* is compounded with that which, being a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), has its length illuminated by it.
"Anugaṅgam" means Vārāṇasī is characterized by a length similar to that of the Ganges; that is, it is along the Ganges. (SK 671)
These [words] are formed by irregular derivation (nipātana).
When cows stand [to be milked], that time is *tiṣṭhadgu*, meaning the milking time.

In *āyatīgava* and similar forms, the substitution of the suffix *śatṛ*, the absence of the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), and the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) are all irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*).
The words *pāra* and *madhya* are optionally compounded with a word ending in the genitive case,
and the final *e* is prescribed as their substitute.
In this alternative view, it is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound:
*pāregaṅgāt* means "from the far side of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāḥ pārāt*),
and *madhyegaṅgāt* means "from the middle of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāḥ madhyāt*).
According to the Mahāvibhāṣā, even a sentence [is divided] from "from the far bank of the Gaṅgā" and "from the middle of the Gaṅgā."
Lineage is twofold: by way of learning and by way of birth.
In this context, a word denoting a descendant (*vaṃśya*) is optionally compounded with a numeral along with a word expressing that [descendant]; for example,
"two ancestral sages" is *dvimuni*.

Regarding grammar, one should know "the three Munis" (*trimuni*); when there is no intention to express a distinction between the science and its masters, it is "grammar of the three Munis" (*trimuni vyākaraṇam*), and "twenty-one Bhāradvājas."
A numeral followed by words denoting rivers is treated as before.
And this [term] is intended to denote a collective aggregate, as in "seven Gaṅgās" or "two Yamunās."
A nominal stem ending in a case-suffix, which denotes something other than its own constituent members, is always compounded with feminine names of rivers when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

Even though this falls under the scope of the *vibhāṣā* (optional) rule, because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not understood through the individual words alone, it is here a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*):
*unmattagaṅgaṃ nāma deśaḥ* (the region named Unmattagaṅgā) and *lohitagaṅgam*.
Having introduced [the topic] with the rule *SK* 676 (*AS* 5.4.68): "Under this heading..."
Pāṇini 5.4.107: The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied after [compounds beginning with] *śarat* and others as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) in the case of an *avyayībhāva*.
Near the autumn, in the vicinity of the Vipāś river,
[there was] autumn.
O Vipāś, O Anas, O Manas!
The leather sandals are from the Himalayas.
Behold the direction of the ox.
O you of fourfold consciousness.
That which is that.
How much?
From old age (*jarā*), the state of being old is *jaras*, and [the comparative form] is *upajarasam*.
(ga) From *prati*, *para*, *sama*, and *anu* [the suffix *ṭhak* is added] after *akṣan*;
and [the suffix *ṭhak* is added] after a word ending in *yasya*. (Pāṇini 5.2.9–10) *Pratyakṣam* (direct perception).
In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *akṣṇaḥ param*, it is an *avyayībhāva* compound by virtue of the rule prescribing the suffix for compounds;
and because of the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule *parokṣe liṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.115), the substitute *au* is applied to *para*,
resulting in *parokṣam*.

In the expression "parokṣā kriyā" and so forth, however, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*, such that it means "that which is beyond direct perception" (*anvakṣam*).
The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied after an avyayībhāva compound ending in *anna*.
In a taddhita suffix, there is elision of the /ṭ/ of a bha-stem ending in /n/.
The internal counterpart of the viceroy.
After an avyayībhāva compound ending in a neuter word that ends in the suffix *ann*, the suffix *ṭac* may optionally be applied;
for example, *upacarma*.
upacarma SK 681 AS 5-4-110:
"near the skin" (a compound formed according to Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.110).
Or the suffix *ṭac* may be applied [to form a feminine noun], as in *upanadam* or *upanadī*.
The Upapaurṇamāsa,
the Upapaurṇamāsī, and the Upāgrahāyaṇa.
The suffix *cha* (forming the word *upāgrahāyaṇī*) is applied after the word *upāgrahāyaṇa*.
The suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after an indeclinable *avyayībhāva* compound ending in a semivowel (*jhay*); thus,
from *upasamit*, one forms *upasamitam*.
The suffix *ṭac* may optionally be added after an avyayībhāva compound ending in a word denoting a mountain (*giri*).
The mention of Senaka is for the sake of honor; "upagiram" means near the mountain.
Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds;
now begins the section on *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
This is a governing heading (adhikāra) extending forward up to the rule on bahuvrīhi compounds.
A *dvigu* compound shall also bear the designation of *tatpuruṣa*.
This sūtra can be dispensed with;

for after reading "a dvigu compound preceded by a numeral" (*saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguśca*), it is easy to state that two designations apply simultaneously by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), and thus the purpose [of the sūtra] is merely to provide a specific suffix for the compound.
The Five Kings (Pañcarāja) SK 686 AS 2-1-24
A word ending in the second case is optionally compounded with words such as *śrita* (resorted to) that end in case-terminations; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. For example:
*kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ* becomes *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa"), and *duḥkham atītaḥ* becomes *duḥkhātītaḥ* ("one who has transcended suffering").
An addition should be made [to the rule] for words such as *gamin* (going):
*grāmaṃ gamī* (one who goes to the village), *grāmagamī* (one who goes to the village);
*annaṃ bubhukṣuḥ* (one who desires to eat food), *annabubhukṣuḥ* (one who desires to eat food).
[The rule] "dvitīyā" (SK 687) from the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* does not connect with [the previous rule] "AS 2-1-25," because of incompatibility.
The offspring of one who has produced it himself is a *svāyaṃkṛti*. (SK 688; AS 2.1.26)

A word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) whose base form is *khaṭvā* is compounded with a word ending in a *su*-affix whose base form ends in a *kta*-suffix, provided there is censure (*nindā*). For example: *khaṭvārūḍho jālmaḥ* ("the wretch who has mounted the couch").
This is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*).
For censure is not understood from the sentence itself.
That which is performed by the master (sāmikṛta).
The mention of the *kta* suffix is for the purpose of excluding absolute connection; thus,
"the moon measured by a month" refers to the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
The meaning is that he began to delimit the month.
The word "kāla" is stated for the sake of specifying the end of the time; "muhūrta-sukham" means happiness for a moment.
In the sūtra *tatkṛta* (SK 692, AS 2.1.30), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) has been elided.

A word ending in the third case, together with a quality-word (guṇavacana) that expresses the meaning of that which ends in the third case, and with the word *artha*, follows the same rules as before:
*śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* becomes *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*; *dhānyenārthaḥ* becomes *dhānyārthaḥ*.
If it were produced by that [eye], why is one blind in the other eye?
AS 2-1-31: A word ending in the third case is compounded with these [words], as before; for example, *māsapūrvaḥ*.
Like a mother, like a father, for the sake of what is deficient.
A kārṣāpaṇa minus one māṣa, or a kārṣāpaṇa lacking a māṣa,
is a verbal quarrel.
Skilled in conduct,
mixed with molasses,
and smooth in conduct.
When "mixed" (*miśra*) is mentioned, that which includes a prefix is also included;
this is because of the mention of "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) in the rule *miśraṃ cānupasargam asaṃdhau* (Pāṇini 2.1.69), as in the example:
*guḍasaṃmiśrā dhānāḥ* ("barley grains mixed with molasses").
An addition [to the rule] regarding "inferior" (*avara*) is as follows: (Vārttika) "Inferior by a month" (*māsāvara*) means one who is inferior by [the measure of] a month.
The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument when combined with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, frequently, as before; e.g., *hariṇā trātaḥ* = *haritrātaḥ* ("saved by Hari").
"Nakhabhinnaḥ" means "pierced by nails";
in the rule concerning *kṛt* suffixes, there is the inclusion of even those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*, as in "nakhanirbhinnaḥ."
Regarding the rule "kartṛkaraṇe" (Pāṇini 2.3.18), why [is this example given]? [Answer:
He dwelt by means of alms;
this third case ending is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
The inclusion of the term *bahula* (in various cases) is for the purpose of avoiding deviation from all qualifying conditions (*upādhi*);
therefore, in examples such as *dātreṇa lūnavān*, why is the suffix *kta* not applied?
"He cooks better with wood.

A statement of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) that has the fruit of either praise or censure is called "a statement of additional meaning" (*adhikārthavacana*). In that context, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent or the instrument, as before, when combined with gerundives (*kṛtya*); for example:
"grass to be cut by the wind" (*vātacchedyaṃ tṛṇam*) and "a river to be drunk from by crows" (*kākapeyā nadī*).
A word denoting a substance that effects a refinement, ending in the third case, [is compounded] with *anna* as before.
In the compound *dadhyodanaḥ* ("curd-rice"),
there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) by means of the action of sprinkling (*upaseka*) which is included within the compound itself;
this is stated in SK 697.
*guḍena dhānāḥ* (barley grains with molasses) becomes *guḍadhānāḥ*; the semantic connection [between the members of the compound] is established through the action of mixing.

That which denotes something for the sake of what is expressed by a word ending in the dative case may optionally be placed before it, as previously [stated], along with the words *artha* and so forth.
By that meaning, only the relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) is understood,
as indicated by the evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the mention of "Bali-rakṣita"; thus, *yūpāya dāru* (wood for the sacrificial post) is called *yūpadāru*.
In this case, there is no cooking pot for cooking;
however, compounds such as "horse fodder" (*aśvaghāsa*) are genitive (ṣaṣṭhī) compounds.
It should be stated that [the word] "artha" always forms a compound and takes the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣyaliṅgatā*):
*dvijārthaḥ sūpaḥ* ("soup for the twice-born") and *dvijārthā yavāgūḥ* ("barley-gruel for the twice-born").
Milk for the sake of the twice-born, an offering to the spirits, and what is beneficial for cows.
The cow's happiness is protected by the cowherd.
AS 2-1-37: "Fear from a thief" is *corād bhayam* or *corabhayam*; it should be stated that [the sixth case ending is used] with the words *bhaya*, *bhīta*, *bhīti*, and *bhī*.
Afraid of a wolf, having fear of a wolf, fearful of a wolf.
A word ending in the fifth case is compounded with these [words], forming a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Free from pleasure, devoid of conceptual construction, and released from the cycle of existence.
Having fallen from heaven,
what little use is there for one who is terrified by the waves?
Fallen from grace,
One who has been released for a short time, one who has been released for a little while, or one who has come from nearby.
Come from nearby,
come from afar,
come from a great distance.

The suffix *pañcamī* (the ablative case ending) is applied after words such as *stoka*, etc., when used with the sense of "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*), and there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending according to Pāṇini 5.4.45 and 6.3.1.
The king's man is "rājapuruṣaḥ" (king-man). (AS 2-2-8;
"With these [words], a word ending in the genitive case is compounded;
this is an exception (pratiprasava) to the rule [AS 2-2-15] stating that [compounding occurs] with *tṛc* and *aka* when the agent is denoted."
The suffix *yā* is applied after the word *brāhmaṇa* to form *brāhmaṇayājaka*;
it is also to be stated that the suffix *ka* is applied after *deva* to form *devapūjaka*, and that there is the elision of the *ra* in the case of *guṇāt taraṇe*.

This is a counter-exception (pratiprasava) to the prohibitions found in Pāṇini 2.2.11 (*na nirdhāraṇe*) and 2.1.67 (*pūraṇaguṇa*), which state that a word expressing a quality (*guṇavācin*) cannot form a compound with a comparative suffix (*tarap*) and that the suffix *tarap* is elided [in such cases]. Thus,
*sarveṣāṃ śvetataraḥ* ("the whitest of all") becomes *sarvaśvetaḥ*.

It should be stated that the sixth case ending is compounded when it denotes "the agent" (*kartṛ*) and signifies "greater than all" (*sarveṣāṃ mahattaraḥ*) or "the greatest of all" (*sarvamahān*); for example:
*idhmasya vraścanaḥ* becomes *idhmavraścanaḥ*.
The genitive case used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is not compounded.
Among men, the twice-born is the best;
"the sixth [case] is not compounded with *pratipadavidhāna*"—this is what should be stated (or: it is said)—as in the example:
*sarpiṣo jñānam* ("knowledge of ghee").
A genitive case ending is not compounded with words meaning "filling" and so forth, nor with words such as "existent" (sat) and the like.
In the completion [of the list] of the virtuous, he is the sixth in merit.
When the qualifier "the crow's blackness" and "the Brahmin's white [teeth]" are understood as being specifically "teeth" through context and other such means, then this serves as an example.
This negation by means of a quality (*guṇa*) is non-eternal;
for this is established by such indications as [the rule] *tadāśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.53),
whereby [constructions such as] *arthagaurava* (weightiness of meaning) and *buddhimāndya* (slowness of intellect) are proven.
The words *suhita* and *tṛpta* have the sense of "satiation";
thus, *phalānāṃ suhitaḥ* would indeed form a genitive tatpuruṣa compound.
A twice-born man, whether performing or causing [another] to perform, incurs sin through a specific defect in his pronunciation.
The meaning is "servant";
[this] is an indeclinable used after the word *brāhmaṇasya*.
Rakṣita maintains that, due to its association with what precedes and follows, only the *kṛt*-derived indeclinable is understood here; thus, forms such as *tadupari* are established.
This applies to the suffix *tavya*.
The suffix *tavyat* is indeed used for the obligation (*kartavya*) of a Brahmin; however, there is a difference in accent regarding one's own duty (*svakartavya*).
In this case, a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the coreferential term *takṣakasya sarpasya* does not occur because of the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*).

In cases such as *gordhenūḥ*, since the rules beginning with *poṭāyuvatistoka...* (Pāṇini 2.1.65) have already found their scope in other case-endings (*vibhaktyanta*), the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would apply by virtue of its higher priority;
however, even that is precluded by this [present rule].

The sixth case (genitive) is not compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta* prescribed by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.12); for example: *rājñāṃ mato buddhaḥ pūjito vā*.
In examples such as *rājapūjita* ("honored by the king"), however, there is a third-case compound with a word ending in the suffix *-kta* denoting the past tense (Pāṇini 2.2.13).
The genitive case is not compounded with a word ending in a *kta* suffix; for example:
*idam eṣām āsitam*, *gatam*, or *bhuktam*. (SK 708)
According to the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66), the genitive case that occurs when both [agent and object] are eligible [to take the sixth case] is not compounded; for example:
*āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful").
There is no compound with a word ending in the sixth case [denoting the object] together with words ending in the suffixes *tṛc* or *aka*, when they have the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The creator of the waters,
the wielder of the thunderbolt,
the cooker of the sacrificial rice.
What is the point of [using] the agentive suffix?
For example, *ikṣubhakṣikā* means "the eating of sugarcane.
However, in the case of the word *bhartṛ* when it has the sense of "husband," there is a compound with words such as *yājaka* (sacrificer), etc.
"In that case, how can there be a quarrel between the supporter of the earth (the potter) and the creator of the three worlds (Brahmā)?
Kaiyaṭa explains that this is a compound formed with a genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*)."
There is no compound of a genitive case ending in the sense of the agent with the suffix aka.

In this case, the genitive of the agent (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply after the word *śāyikā* when it is used with the word *tṛn*, because the agent is already expressed [by the suffix], and thus the genitive of the agent is absent in that construction.
In these two meanings, the genitive case is always compounded with one [of the two].
*Uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā* is a technical term for a specific type of game;
according to *Pāṇini’s Sūtra* 3.3.109 (*saṃjñāyām*), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied here in the sense of an action (*bhāve*).
In the case of livelihood, [the term] "dantalekhaka" (ivory-carver) is used;
there, since the prohibition "tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari" (Pāṇini 2.2.15) would have applied regarding play and conceptualization, this statement [is made] for the sake of livelihood.
"The terms 'east' (pūrva) and so forth are compounded with a whole (avayavin), provided that the whole is qualified by the number one."
This is an exception to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*):
"the front part of the body" is *pūrvakāyaḥ*, and "the rear part of the body" is *aparakāyaḥ*.
Why was it not previously stated by the proponent of a partial position that [the head] is a single locus of the body?
Why [is this asked]? Because it is a single locus.

Every single part of the word *pūrva* [denoting a direction] is compounded with a word denoting time of day (*ahna*) when referring to students, based on the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule: "A numeral and the word *vi* are compounded with words ending in *as*, as well as with *pūrva* and *apara* when they denote a direction, provided they do not signify a part of a whole" (Pāṇini 2.2.25).
"Midday" and "evening"— some, however, maintain that every single part [of the day] is compounded with "time," and not with "day" alone.
They say that because an indicator depends upon a general category,
by that [reasoning], it is established that "midnight," "ceased," and "having the latter part of the night as their domain" and so forth are proven.
The word *ardha*, when denoting an equal portion, is always neuter; it is treated as before [in compound].
The statement "there is no [application of the] term *upasarjana* when there is a single case-ending and not the sixth [genitive] case" refers to the domain of *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compounds);
by this, forms such as *pañcakhaṭvī* are established.
*ardhapippalī* (half of a *pippalī*) is used in the neuter; why is *grāmyārdhaḥ* (half of a village) [not so]?
Only when there is identity of substance [is it correct to say] "half of the pippalīs. (SK 714)
These [compounds] may optionally form a second [tatpuruṣa] with a word ending in the first case, as before; for example, *bhikṣāyā dvitīyam* becomes *dvitīyabhikṣā*.

According to the proponent of the *ekadeśin* view, why would there not be an optional sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*)— such as *bhikṣāyā bhikṣukaḥ*— by setting aside the prohibition [of compounds] stated in Pāṇini 2.2.11 (*pūraṇaguṇa-*) by virtue of the force of the mention of "one of the two" (*anyatarasyām*)?
With alms as his second [companion].

In this case, the compound *jīvikā-prāpta* (one who has obtained a livelihood) is formed by the rule *dvitīyā-śritātīta-patita-gata-atyasta-prāpta-āpanna-* (Pāṇini 2.1.24), which prescribes that a word in the accusative case may be compounded with words such as *śrita*. Thus, *jīvikām prāptaḥ* becomes *jīvikā-prāptaḥ*.
Similarly, *jīvikām prāpta-jīvikaḥ* is also formed.
In this sūtra, after splitting *āpannajīvikaḥ* as *jīvikāpannaḥ*, the vowel *a* is also prescribed by eliding the second vowel *ā*.
A woman who has obtained a livelihood by means of that is called *prāptajīvikā* or *āpannajīvikā*. (SK 716)
Time words are compounded with a nominal ending that expresses the object delimited by them; for example, "a month [has elapsed] since his birth" becomes *māsajātaḥ*.
"Born two days ago" (*dvyahajātaḥ*): the analysis of the compound is "he for whom there is a birth after a *dvyaha*, which is a combination of two days (*dvayoḥ ahnoḥ samāhāro dvyahaḥ*)."

For the sake of establishing *dvigu* compounds with a final member denoting a measure (*parimāṇin*), there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the rule for *tatpuruṣa* compounds regarding multiple [members]:
"one for whom two days have been born is *dvyahnajātaḥ*"; here, the substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan-* will be stated later by the rule *ahno'hna-*.
In the previous case, however, there is a prohibition [of the feminine suffix] for numerals and so forth in a collective compound (*samāhāra*), according to Pāṇini 2.4.1–2.

A word ending in the seventh case is optionally compounded with words such as *śauṇḍa*, as previously stated; for example, *akṣeṣu śauṇḍaḥ* becomes *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*. Here, the word *adhi* is also included in this list.
The suffix *kha* is applied according to *adhyuttarapadāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.60),
as in *īśvarādhīnaḥ* (dependent on the Lord).
With these [words], a word ending in the locative case forms a compound as before; for example, *sāṃkāśyasiddhaḥ*.
Dried in the sun,
cooked in a pot, and bound with a wheel.
A word ending in the locative case is compounded with a word denoting a crow (dhvāṅkṣa) when censure is intended.
Like a crow at a sacred bathing place, he is a "crow-at-the-tīrtha," a "crow-at-the-sacred-place" (tīrthadhvāṅkṣa).

A word ending in the locative case, when combined with words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, forms a compound as previously stated, provided it denotes something that must necessarily be done; for example, "a debt to be paid within a month."
The mention of "taking a loan" is intended as an illustration for "authorization" (niyoga);
this Sāman is to be chanted in the forenoon.
A word ending in the locative case is optionally compounded with a *sup*-ending word as previously stated, when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*).
Since a name cannot be understood through a loose syntactical expression (*vākya*), this is a compulsory compound (*nitya-samāsa*).
In the words *araṇyetilakāḥ* and *vanekaserukāḥ*,
there is no elision (*aluk*) of the seventh case ending according to the rule *haladantāt saptamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.9).
Parts of *ahan* (day) and *rātri* (night), ending in the locative case, [form a compound] with a word ending in a *kta* suffix, as previously stated.
What is the apprehension of parts performed in the forenoon or performed in the latter part of the night?
That which is seen during the day,
In this context, the word *tatra*, ending in the locative case, is joined with a past passive participle as before; thus:
*tatra bhuktam* (eaten there). (SK 724)
Pāṇini 2.1.47:
A word ending in the locative case may optionally form a compound with a word ending in the suffix *kta*, as previously described, when censure is intended; for example:
*avataptanakulasthitam ta etat* ("this conduct of yours is like that of a mongoose in a heated pan").
These are treated as irregular formations (nipātana) when used in the sense of censure (kṣepa).
Those who meet only at the time of eating are "pātresamitāḥ," but not those who assemble for business; likewise, one who is a hero only within his own home is a "geheśūraḥ."
*gehenardī* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*;
the particle *ca* is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
Therefore, they enter into other compounds as constituent members, but [the term] *parama* does not [enter], as in the case of *pātresamitāḥ*. (SK 726)

Although [the formation] is established by the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa* (Pāṇini 2.1.57), this sūtra is intended to restrict the position of the preceding member (*pūrvanipāta*) and to override the restriction [imposed by] the rule *ekaśabdasya diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.50).
Having first bathed and afterwards being anointed, he is "bathed-and-anointed" (snātānulipta);
he is the sole lord of all those who perform sacrifices.
The elder Naiyāyikas, the ancient Mīmāṃsakas, and the new students.
Those who are mere grammarians (kevalavaiyākaraṇāḥ).

The rule beginning with "with a word in apposition" (samānādhikaraṇena) is a restrictive rule (niyamārtha) governing everything up to the end of the chapter, intended to apply only when a name (saṃjñāyām) is being formed; for example:
*pūrveṣukāmaśamī*.
The seven seers are not here; the northern trees are not here.
The five Brahmins (SK 728; AS 2.1.51).

When the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is intended, when a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) follows, and when a collective compound (*samāhāra*) is to be expressed, the directional term and the numeral may optionally be treated as before; for example, "born in the eastern hall" (*pūrvasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*) becomes *paurvaśālaḥ*.
Once the compound is formed, the suffix *ñ* is applied by the rule *dikpūrvapadād asaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.107).
In all compound formations involving a pronominal stem, there is the substitution of the masculine form; thus,

in the three-membered *bahuvrīhi* "one for whom a former hall (*pūrvā śālā*) belonging to another (*āparaśāla*) is dear (*priyā*)," once the compound is formed, a *tatpuruṣa* occurs between the first two members with the word *priya* as the subsequent member.
Therefore, in the word *śālā*, the vowel *ā* is acute (*udātta*).
In the compound *pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ*, there is no collective formation (*samāhāra*) regarding the directions, because such a formation is not prescribed.
In the case of a numeral used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*),

as in "the offspring of six mothers" (*ṣāṇmāturaḥ*) or "one whose wealth consists of five cows," when a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed, there arises the possibility of an intermediate *tatpuruṣa* compound. This being the case, an option is presented.
(Vārttika): A rule stating that *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds are necessarily compound formations applies when the final member [of the compound] is a word [forming part of a larger compound].
The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied as a compound-final affix (*samāsānta*) after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *gont*, except when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix; for example:
*pañcagavadhanaḥ*. (SK 730)
Regarding the threefold [compound] mentioned in AS 2.1.52 (*taddhitārtha...*), it becomes a *dvigu* when preceded by a numeral (SK 731).
By the rule *dvigvarthaḥ samāhāra ekavad bhavati sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.1), the neuter gender [is applied].
The collection of five cows is "pañcagava" (a group of five cows).
Being reviled with insults as before, he was a "bad needle" among grammarians and a "badly grown" weed among Mīmāṃsakas.
An exception to the preceding rule.
Pāpanāpita was a potter of the Āṇaka clan.

In the example "ghanashyāmaḥ" (dark as a cloud), the word *ghana* (cloud) is used figuratively to mean something similar to it; thus, the word *iva* is employed in the popular analytical statement (*laukikavigraha*) to indicate that the first member of the compound is being used in a metaphorical sense.
The sūtra [Pāṇini 2.2.30] is for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding the obligatory prior placement [of certain words].

This sūtra provides for the prior placement of the substantive (viśeṣya) when the object of comparison (upameya) is joined with words such as *vyāghra* (tiger), provided that the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not employed as before; for example:
*puruṣavyāghraḥ* ("a tiger among men").
In the case of general application, what is the purpose of the *nṛsoma* group and the *vyāghrādi* group?
A man is like a tiger, a hero. (SK 736, AS 2.1.57)
A qualifier is frequently compounded with its coreferential qualificand as previously stated; for example, *nīlam utpalam* becomes *nīlotpalam*.
Because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulam*), in some cases the compound is obligatory.
The black cobra is not anywhere equal to Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
This [sūtra] is for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding the obligatory placement of the prior member.
In the case of *pūrvavaiyākaraṇa* and *aparādhyāpaka*,
the substitution of the fifth vowel (*pa*) for the second vowel (*a*) should be stated as an optional rule (*vā*).
Furthermore, regarding the compound *aparaś cāsau ardhaś ca* (the latter half), as in *paścārdhaḥ*, how could it be called *ekavīra*?
According to the rule *pūrvakāla-eka-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49), this would be set aside by the subsequent rule; thus, in this compound, it should rather be *vīraika*.
It will be so because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (bahula).

The rule regarding the sense of "becoming" (*cvyartha*) should be stated [to apply] to *śreṇi* and other such words: "Those who were not guilds (*aśreṇayaḥ*) have been made into guilds (*śreṇayaḥ*)" is expressed as *śreṇīkṛtāḥ*.
AS 2.1.60: A word ending in the suffix *kta* that does not have the negative particle *nañ* is compounded with another word ending in *kta* that is qualified by *nañ*;
for example, "done and not done" becomes *kṛtākṛtam*.
For the establishment of compounds such as *śākapārthiva* and others, there is the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) regarding the elision of the middle member:
one who is fond of vegetables and is a king is a *śākapārthiva*; a Brahmin devoted to the gods is a *devabrāhmaṇa*.
A good physician (SK 740; AS 2-1-61).
What is the purpose of being honored by those who are [already] great grammarians, when his greatness will be described hereafter?
The meaning is that the excellent bull has been pulled out from the mud.
*govṛndārakaḥ*.
