The supreme king, the overlord, the friend of Kṛṣṇa.
In the case of the suffix *ṭi*, there is elision (*lopa*), but not elsewhere.
The *uttamāha* sacrifice consists of two days; it is a *dvyaha* sacrificial session (*kratu*),
a *dvigu* compound formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

Regarding the rule *tamadhīṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.80), under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "dvigorvā" (Pāṇini 5.1.82), the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule *rātryahaḥsaṃvatsarācca* (Pāṇini 5.1.87).

Because the maxim concerning the inclusion of gender-qualified forms (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is not universally applicable (*anityatva*), the form *madrarājñī* (the queen of the Madras) does not occur here [as a *dvigu*].
For the word *ahan* following words beginning with *sarva*, the substitute *ahna* shall occur when a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) follows.
When the substitute *ahn* follows a *repha* (*r*) that is preceded by a dental (*adanta*) in the first member of a compound, the *n* of that substitute shall be changed to *ṇ*.
The entire day, the forenoon, and the counted day.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.11 (*kālāt ṭhañ*) to form a word meaning "occurring over two days" (*dvayahna-bhava*).
Then, by Pāṇini 4.1.88 (*dvigor lug-anapatye*), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ*.
In the feminine, *dvyahna* takes the suffix *ṭāp* because it ends in the letter *a*, resulting in *dvyahnā*.
One who does not like two days is *atyahnaḥ*.
AS 8.4.39: In these cases, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall not occur: *dīrghāhnī prāvṛṭ*.

And for this reason, the cumbersome effort of treating *ahnaḥ* as an imitation of a word ending in *a* need not be undertaken; for since the inclusion of [the word *ahnaḥ*] among the *kṣubhnādi* group is necessary to prevent the substitution of *ṇ* by Pāṇini 8.4.39 (*prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca*),
the mention of the suffix *tap* (in the rule *ahnaḥ*) indicates that it does not apply here.
The word *parāhṇaḥ* means "the latter part of the day" (*paragatamahaḥ*).
For a word beginning with a numeral that denotes a collective (samāhāra), there would be no substitution of *ahna* for *ahan*;
the phrase "beginning with a numeral" (*saṃkhyādeḥ*) is included for the sake of clarity.
Thus, the collective of two days is *dvyahaḥ*.
"tryahaḥ" [is formed by the elision of the middle member] according to Pāṇini 5.4.90.
From these two [words], there is the substitution of *ahna*;
the word *uttama* signifies the final [member], while the word *puṇya* denotes merit.
It would have been more appropriate to formulate the sūtra simply as "by means of the two, merit and [the day]," for *puṇyāha* is indeed *sudināha*.
The word *sudina* signifies "praiseworthy"; some maintain that the mention of "one day" (*ekāha*) is intended to include the penultimate [type] as well.
The days are counted.
The suffix *ṭac* should be applied [to form *aśvorasam*],
meaning "the foremost horse," like the chest (*uras*) of horses.
The suffix *ṭac* occurs when a genus is denoted, as well as when it is a proper name.
The upper stone is made of iron,
the lower stone is made of immovable rock.
"Maṇḍūkasarasam" is a generic term; "mahānasa" and "piṇḍāśma" are specific instances.
The designation "red iron" refers to a lake or pond.
AS 5-4-95: *grāmasya takṣā* (the carpenter of the village) becomes *grāmatakṣaḥ*; the meaning is "one who is common [to the village]."
*Kauṭa* means "one who exists in a hut" (*kuṭyām bhavaḥ*), and that same person is an independent carpenter; thus, he is a *kauṭatakṣa*. (SK 798, AS 5.4.96)
The boar is swifter than a horse; the army is swifter than a horse.
AS 5.4.97: The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the word *śvan*, when it expresses a comparison with something that is not a living being;
for example, *ākarṣaśvaḥ* ("a dog-like puller").
Or rather, among those without breath, is the monkey like a dog— a "dog-monkey"? (SK 800)
By virtue of the word "ca" (and), [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the word *saktha* when it follows a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
The deer-thigh,
the anterior thigh,
and the plank-like thigh are the *phalaka-sakthi*.
The suffix *ṭac* is applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *nau*, except when there is elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix.

He has come by two boats; [the compound] *dvināvarūpya* is formed because, in the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88), the word *aci* is understood to be drawn back [from the previous rule], so there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix after a consonant:
*pañcanāvapriyaḥ*.
Why does the rule state "when there is no elision of the taddhita suffix" (*ataddhitaluki*) in the cases of *dvināva* and *trināva*?
"Purchased for five ships" is *pañcanauḥ* [according to Pāṇini 5.4.100].
The suffix *avaṣṭac* is applied after the word *nau* [meaning "boat"] when it signifies "half";
thus, half of a boat is *ardhanāvam*.
The state of being a eunuch [is derived] from the world (loka).
After a *dvigu* compound and after the word *ardha*, the suffix *ṭa* (which becomes *ī*) shall optionally be applied to the word *khārī*; thus,
one has *dvikhāra* or *dvikhārī*.
Half a khāra is an ardhakhāra. (SK 804)
In a *dvigu* compound, the suffix *ṭac* may optionally be applied after the word *añjali*. Thus,
one says either *dvyañjali* or *dvyañjalika*.
The term *dvyañjali* [is formed] by the rule "ataddhitalukī" (Pāṇini 5.1.28); that which is purchased for two *añjali*s is called *dvyañjali*.
The suffix *ṭac* is added after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in "Brahman," provided that the compound as a whole denotes being a native of a country.
In the case of *surāṣṭra*, [the suffix] *brahma* is applied, forming *surāṣṭrabrahmaḥ*.
After these two [words], the suffix *ṭac* may optionally be applied to *brahman* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound; thus,
a contemptible Brahmin is *kubrahmaḥ* or *kubrahmā*.
Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.46:
When a word in grammatical apposition follows, the final phoneme of *mahat* is replaced by *ākār* (ā), provided that the subsequent word is either a *jātīya* suffix or another word in apposition.
Mahābrahmā, the Great Brahmā, Mahādeva.

Regarding the rule for the optional substitution of the long vowel in a compound with a word in grammatical apposition: what about "service to the great" (*mahat-sevā*)? [In this case, the substitution does not apply.]

If it is argued that, setting aside the technical (lākṣaṇika) rule, the specific prescription (pratipadokta) "sanmahat" (Pāṇini 2.1.61) should be understood as applying here, then the form *mahābāhuḥ* would not be possible; therefore, the paribhāṣā "between a technical rule and a specific prescription, the specific prescription prevails" does not apply here,
due to the force of the inclusion of the term "samānādhikaraṇa" (having a common substratum).
The substitution of *āt* occurs either by the rule of splitting (*yogavibhāga*) the sūtra beginning with *ātaḥ*, or by the indicative mention (*nirdeśa*) in the rule *prāgekādaśabhyaḥ*; thus,
[the forms] are *ekādaśa*.
When the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied to the word *mahatī* by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*, the substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel] occurs,
resulting in *mahājātīyā*.
Regarding the substitution of *ā* for *mahat* before the words *ghāsa*, *karin*, and *viśiṣṭa*, there is an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rule), as is the case with the masculine form.
This [rule] is for the sake of non-co-referentiality (asāmānādhikaraṇya):
*mahāghāsaḥ* means the food of a large [person] or a large amount of food;
*mahākaraḥ*.
The term *mahāviśiṣṭa* refers to that which is prepared on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) as an oblation (*havis*).

The meaning is that when the word *go* follows *yukta*, or when the word *gośabda* follows [a form of] *aṣṭan*, the substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan* must be stated if the sense of "yoked" (*yukta*) is to be understood; thus,
*aṣṭāgavaṃ śakaṭam*.

Regarding the rule *ac-praty-anv-ava-saṃ-darbhah* (Pāṇini 5.4.74), by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) following the word *ac*, the suffix *ac* is applied even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Thus, the collection of eight cows is *aṣṭagava*; because the cart is joined with that [collection], it is called *aṣṭāgava*. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows].
The augment *āT* shall be applied after [the verbal root] *as*.
Two and ten are twelve;
or, ten with two added is twenty-two.
Why [is it said] "not in a bahuvrīhi compound or when followed by aśīti"? [Examples: aṣṭādaśa (eighteen), aṣṭāviṃśatiḥ (twenty-eight).
It should be stated that "two or three" means "up to eighty-two before a hundred."
Here there are not two hundred nor two thousand.
In the aforementioned scope, the word *tri* shall be replaced by *traya*.
Thirteen and twenty-three;
however, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, "three tens" becomes *tridaśāḥ*.
The *bahuvrīhi* compound is used in the sense of "excellent" (*su-*);
however, for "eighty-three," it is *tryaśīti*,
because [the rule] specifies "prior to one hundred."
Three hundred and three thousand.
Before words beginning with "catvāriṃśat" (forty), the previously mentioned forms of *dvi*, *aṣṭan*, and *tri* may optionally be used;
thus, [the form] *dvicatvāriṃśat* (forty-two).
Forty-two,
forty-eight,
forty-eight.
Forty-three,
forty-three;
likewise fifty, sixty, seventy, and ninety.
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.76: A numeral beginning with *eka* shall remain in its original form when combined with the negative particle *nañ*, and the augment *ad-* is added to *eka*.

When *nañ* has been compounded with "twenty," it is then compounded with the word "one" (*eka*) by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) stating "with the third case. There is an optional nasalization (*anunāsika-vikalpa*). Thus, *ekena na viṃśatiḥ* becomes *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*.
"Ekānnaviṃśatiḥ" means nineteen;

it should be stated that the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the word "ṣaṣ" occurs before the words "datṛ," "daśan," and "dhā," and that the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the initial sound of the following word occurs optionally before the word "dhā."
Sixteen,
sixteen,
sixfold.
Sixfold.
The gender of these two [copulative compounds] would be like that of the final member: "this is a cock and a peahen" (kukkuṭamayūryau),
or "these are a peahen and a cock" (mayūrīkukkuṭau).
A prohibition must be stated regarding the compounds *ardhapippalī*, *dvigu*, *prāpta-apanna*, and *pūrva-gati* [compounds]. For example:
*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ pañcakapālaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake prepared in five potsherds").
One who has obtained a livelihood is *prāptajīvikaḥ*, one who has attained a livelihood is *āpannajīvikaḥ*;
one who is sufficient for a maiden is *alaṃkumāriḥ*.
For this very reason, based on the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), there is a compound:
*niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (SK 813).
AS 2.4.27: The dual number is not mandatory in the case of "horse and mare" (aśvavaḍavau).
Male and female horses with male and female horses.

According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.29, a *dvandva* or *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in these [two] words is masculine; because it follows immediately, this rule also sets aside the neuter gender of the collective (*samāhāra*) by virtue of its own posteriority.
Ahorātraḥ is a day and night; the former part of the night is pūrvarātraḥ,
and the former part of the day is pūrvāhṇaḥ.
*dvyahaḥ* (two days) is a neuter noun preceded by a numeral and followed by *rātraṃ*.
A two-night,
a three-night, or a multi-night [session].
It is indeed a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
But elsewhere, it is "apatha" (a pathless region);
because of the specific mention of the suffix *samāsānta*, "apanthāḥ" does not occur here.
Words such as *ardharca* and others may occur in both the masculine and the neuter genders.
Each half-verse is a banner.
Thus, [the Lord is called] Dhvaja, Tīrtha, Śarīra, Maṇḍa, Pīyūṣa, Deha, Aṅkuśa, Kalaśa, and so forth. (SK 817)
Even a single thing may take a plural form when it refers to many, as in "Brāhmaṇas are to be honored."
The Brāhmaṇa is worthy of honor. (SK 818; AS 1.2.59)
When singularity or duality is intended for the word "asmad," the plural may optionally be used; thus one says "vayaṃ brūmaḥ" (we speak), or alternatively,
"ahaṃ bravīmi" (I speak).
Or rather, there is a prohibition regarding that which has a qualifier, as in: "The two of us speak," or "I, being clever, speak."
In the case of duality, the grammatical operation conditioned by plurality may optionally take place.
The two Pūrva-phalgunīs are the Pūrvā-phalgunīs;
the two Pūrva-proṣṭhapadas [are the Pūrvā-proṣṭhapadas].
Are the Pūrvā-proṣṭhapadās the two Phalgunīs among the constellations, O young women?
Multiplicity is like duality.
Tiṣya and Punarvasu together are called Tiṣya-Punarvasū; why then is Viśākhā and Anurādhā called Tiṣya?
Regarding the term "constellation" (nakṣatra): what [is meant] by "the young brahmins Tiṣya and Punarvasu"? (SK 821)

AS 2.4.17: In the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), a *dvigu* compound and a *dvandva* compound shall be neuter; this is an exception to the rule regarding the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅga*).
A *dvigu* compound ending in the word *gava*,
*danta*, or *oṣṭha*,
with a vowel as its final member, is desired to be feminine (optionally).
Either the five roots ending in -ā or the five stools.
In a feminine dvigu compound, the word *khaṭvī* optionally becomes *khaṭvā*, and the final *n* of *anaḥ* is optionally elided; for example, *pañcakhaṭvī* or *pañcakhaṭvā*, and *pañcatakṣī*.
The term *pañcatakṣam* does not apply to anything from a bowl (*pātra*) onwards, nor does the term *pañcapātram*.
The three worlds and the four ages are [the measure of] a day;
by means of the two auspicious days, the neuter state is desired.
The word *puṇyāha* forms a tatpuruṣa compound with *sudināha*, as well as with words denoting a path, numerals, and indeclinables; [the final member may optionally take the neuter gender].
The meaning is that the word *patha*, when followed by a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and having taken a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), is neuter. For example:
the path of three is *tripatha*;
a deformed path is *vipatha*.
Because the term is taught with the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) already applied, *supanthāḥ* and *atipanthāḥ* do not occur here.
In the sense of a generic quality, it is neuter (optionally):
*mṛdu pacati* (he cooks softly),
*prātaḥ kamanīyam* (it is lovely in the morning).
This is a heading.
A Tatpuruṣa compound ending in *kanthā* shall be neuter, provided that it is a name for a ragged garment (*kanthā*) produced in the land of the Uśīnaras.
The descendants of Suśama are the Sauśamayas; their *kanthā* (a rag) is *sauśamikantham*.
Why [is the suffix] used in the sense of a name? [For example:
*vīraṇakanthā* (a rag made of vīraṇa grass).
What is Dākṣikaṇṭhā among the Uśīnaras?
SK 824

A Tatpuruṣa compound ending in *upajñā* or *upakrama* shall be neuter, provided that the beginning—that is, the priority—of those two things, namely the thing first known (*upajñāyamāna*) or the thing first undertaken (*upakramyamāṇa*), is intended to be expressed. Example:
*pāṇiner upajñā*, "the work first known by Pāṇini," which is *pāṇinyupajñaṃ granthaḥ*.
Droṇa [performed] the Nandopakrama [rite].
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *chāyā* (shadow) becomes neuter when there is an abundance of the meaning of the first member,
as in *ikṣucchāyam* (the shadow of sugarcane).
This is an exception to the optional rule stated in *vibhāṣā senā-* (Pāṇini 2.4.25).
In the phrase "seated in the shade of sugarcane," however, the prefix *ā* should be understood as meaning "on all sides" (*āsamantāt*), forming the compound *āśleṣa*.
A *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by a synonym of "king" (*rājan*) or preceded by a non-human term (*amanuṣya*), when used internally within a formal assembly (*sabhā*), shall be neuter:
*inasabham*,
*īśvarasabham*.
In this royal assembly, only a synonym is accepted.
The word *sabhā* (assembly) [in the compound] *candraguptasabhā* refers by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) to non-human beings such as *rakṣas* and *piśāca*; thus,
it means a "demon assembly" (*rakṣaḥ-sabham*).
A gathering of Piśācas (SK 827; AS 2-4-24).
A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *sabhā*, when it has the sense of a "congregation" (*saṅghāta*), is neuter; for example, *strīsabham*, meaning a "congregation of women."
Āśālā means a hall of Dharma; the meaning is a hall for the Dharma.
From this point up to the end [of the section], the *tatpuruṣa* compound may optionally be neuter.
Brāhmaṇasena, Brāhmaṇasenā, and Yavasura.
Yavasurā is the shadow of a wall, the shade of a wall.
Gośāla [dwelt] in Gośālā day and night.

Because of the continued application of the rule "śvaniśā tatpuruṣo'nañkarmadhārayaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.195), the word *dṛḍhasena* here [does not take the feminine suffix *ṅīp*] when it means "the king Dṛḍhasena."
"Without army" (*asenā*) and "supreme army" (*paramasenā*): this is the section on *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
Now begins the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds (SK 829; AS 2.2.23).
This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*):

the meaning is that the remainder (*śeṣa*)—that triad for which a specific compound has not been stated by rules such as *dvitīyā śritāt-* (Pāṇini 2.1.24)—consists of words ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*).
Multiple words ending in the nominative case, when functioning as the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*), may optionally be compounded; this is the *bahuvrīhi*.
It follows that a *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of a case other than the nominative, and that the constituent members must be in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
A village that has obtained water is called *prāptodaka*;
a bull that has drawn a chariot is called *ūḍharatha*; and Rudra is one to whom cattle have been offered as a sacrifice.
The pot from which the rice has been removed;
Hari wearing yellow garments;
a village whose men are heroes.
But in the sense of the nominative case, there is no [use of the locative]; nor is it used when the deity has not rained, even for words that have different substrata.
When preceded by *pra* and other such prefixes, the elision of the final member of a word derived from a verbal root (*dhātuj*) after the prefix is to be stated as optional;
for example, *prapatitaparṇaḥ* or *praparṇaḥ*.

In the case of words meaning "to exist" (*astyartha*) following the negative particle *nañ*, either the meaning [of the compound] is expressed, or there is the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). For example:
*avidyamānaputraḥ* becomes *aputraḥ*.
The word *asti* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that functions as a substitute for a case ending.
The cow has milk. (Pāṇini 5.2.94)
The term *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has no *ūṅ* [suffix] after a word that has been stated as masculine.

Due to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case-ending and elision (*luk*) of the sixth case-ending. When the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical, for a feminine-denoting word that follows a word previously stated as masculine and lacks the suffix *ūṅ*, the form shall be like that of the masculine-denoting word, provided the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is a feminine noun in grammatical apposition; however, this does not apply when a feminine ordinal number (*pūraṇī*) or a word such as *priya* follows.
By the rule *gostriyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), there is a short vowel [in the case of *go*]; thus,
from the colloquial analysis (*laukikavigraha*) "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*), the uncolloquial analysis (*alaukikavigraha*) is *citrā as go as*.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "one whose wife is beautiful" (*citraguḥ*), "one whose wife possesses form" (*rūpavadbhāryaḥ*), or "one whose brindled, aged cow is white" (*citrā jaratī gauryasya*), the term *bahuvrīhi* applies even to many [members] because it has been stated that there is no restriction to a few.
In this regard, some [use] *citrājaratīguḥ* or *jaratīcitraguḥ*.

In this way, in a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *dīrghātanvījaṅghaḥ* ("one with long and slender shanks") or *tanvīdīrghājaṅghaḥ* ("one with slender and long shanks"), the first member does not become masculine-like (*puṃvat*).
Because the second [member] is also separated from the first by the middle member, it does not become masculine either,
as it lacks the status of being a prior member (*pūrvapada*).
For they say that the word *uttarapada* is conventionally used for the final member of a compound, while the word *pūrvapada* is conventionally used for the first member; however,
in reality, the term *pūrvapada* is not implied here.
Just as in the rule *ānaṅ ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.98),
by that [rule], the penultimate vowel becomes masculine-like,
as in *citrājaradguḥ* and so forth.
For this very reason, even in a compound containing a *dvandva*— such as "one whose cows are variegated and old" (*citrā-jarad-guḥ*)— the *Bhāṣya* states *jarad-guḥ*; however,
when the first member is a *karmadhāraya*, both [words] undergo the masculine form, as in *jarat-citraguḥ*.

But when the final member of a *karmadhāraya* compound is feminine, [the rule does not apply]; for example: *citrajaradgavīkaḥ* ("one who has a brindled old cow"), *striyāḥ kim* ("why [is it] 'of a woman'?"—to show the necessity of the condition), *grāmaṇi kulaṃ dṛṣṭir asya* ("his view is that of a village headman"), resulting in *grāmaṇidṛṣṭiḥ*.
What is the purpose of the condition "having been previously used as a masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*)?
[Consider] *gaṅgābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is the Gaṅgā").
What is the purpose of the condition "not ending in the feminine suffix *ūṅ*" (*anūṅ*)? [Consider] *strībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a woman").
In "vāmorūbhāryaḥ," why is there a co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) compound? [Counter-example:
"kalyāṇyāḥ mātā" results in "kalyāṇīmātā."
What about in the feminine?
*kalyāṇīpradhānaḥ* means "one for whom a virtuous woman is the principal.
But in the case of a ordinal number (*pūraṇī*), [the rule does not apply].

The suffix *ap* shall be applied after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in a word formed with a suffix having the sense of a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), provided that the word is feminine, as well as after a Bahuvrīhi ending in a word denoting a measure (*pramāṇa*).
Those nights of which the fifth is auspicious are "kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ.
One for whom a woman is the authority is "strīpramāṇaḥ";
here, there is a prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) and the application of the suffix *ap*, provided that [the woman] is indeed the primary factor in the completion [of the task].
In the example cited, it is stated that the night must be expressed as "pūraṇī" (filling/completing); however, this is primary [only] in that specific case, whereas elsewhere it is otherwise.

After a bahuvrīhi compound whose final member is a feminine word ending in *nadi* or whose final member ends in long *ṛ*, the suffix *kap* is added, and there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).
When followed by *ke*, a short vowel shall take the place of *aṇ*.
This being the position reached, [the sūtra states]:
When followed by a word ending in *kap*, the short vowel of the preceding *aṇ* suffix would not occur [in this specific case],
as in *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ*; here, because the "fortnight" (*pakṣa*)— whose internal divisions are obscured— is the referent of the external compound, the "night" (*rātri*) is subordinate.
Since there are many agents [of harm], why is one who is fond of the virtuous not [likewise] fond of those who are unpleasant and so forth?
Beloved, charming, and auspicious.
Fortunate devotion and unfortunate devotion.
The minister, the sister, and the beloved wife.
Patient, even, and steady.
The daughter is lovely and weak.
The word *tanaya* is neuter when used in a general sense;
one whose devotion is firm is called *dṛḍhabhakti*.
But when there is an intention to express femininity, [the suffix ṅīṣ is applied], as in *dṛḍhābhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.4).
When suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending in *kṛtvasuc* follow, the feminine form should become like the masculine;
a specific enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made in order to avoid both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, or *caraṭ* and *jātīyar*, are optionally added after a word ending in *tra*.
The suffixes *kalpa*, *adeśīya*,
*rūpa*, *ppāśa*,
*praśasya*, and *thāl* [are applied after a word ending in the sixth case].
*tilthyanau* (or *vā*) [are used] in the sense of "in many" (*bahvīṣu*), "in many places" (*bahutra*), and "abundantly" (*bahutaḥ*).
In the rule "darśanīyatarā,

darśanīyatamā" (Pāṇini 6.3.43), the short vowel [of the feminine suffix] that is about to be mentioned supersedes the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) because it occurs later in the order of rules.
More acute, most acute, and of acute conduct.
Of a sharp nature, resembling those who are beautiful,
appearing as though they were beautiful.
Possessing forms that are now beautiful, with many enchanting snares for the sight.
*praśastā vṛkī* (an excellent she-wolf), *vṛkatiḥ*, and *ajābhyo hitā* (beneficial for goats) form *ajathyā*.
It should be stated that the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*) occurs when the sense of "much" or "little" is expressed.

Give much to those who are many, and give little to those who are few; [there is] optionally [the substitution of the long vowel for the final short vowel] of a word expressing a quality before the suffixes *tva* and *tal*.
The state of being white is "whiteness" (*śuklatvam*) or "the quality of being white" (*śuklatā*);
why [is this stated] regarding a word expressing a quality?
In cases such as *kartṛtva* ("the state of being an agent") and *śaratkṛtārthatā* ("the fulfillment of the purpose of autumn"), the neuter gender is used for the general abstract quality (*sāmānya*),
according to the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.149).
A collection of female elephants is called *hāstika*; what is it when [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied?
It is *rauhiṇeya*.
In this case, the suffix *ḍha* is understood from the rule *strībhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120),

whereas in the case of the suffix *ḍhak* from the rule *agnerḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33), there is simply *puṃvat* substitution. Thus, for a sacrificial oblation (*sthālīpāka*) whose deity is Agnāyī, the derivative form is *āgneya*.
The word *sapatnī* is derived in three ways:
first, from the word *sapatna*, which is a synonym for "enemy," with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule beginning with *śārṅgarava*;
second, from the analysis "she who has a common husband" (*samānaḥ patir yasyāḥ*), relying on the word *pati* as it is used in the context of marriage, and which is invariably feminine.

The third [type] is one whose gender has been expressed by the word *pati*, which is a synonym for *svāmin*; for the first two [types], the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.112, as in *sāpatnaḥ*, meaning "the offspring of a co-wife" (*sapatnī*).

But from the third [suffix], by the *paribhāṣā* regarding words qualified by gender, only the suffix *ṇya*— characterized by having *pati* as a subsequent member— is applied, and not *aṇ*, because in the *Śivādi* list only the two conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings are taken; thus, [the form] is *sāpatyaḥ*.
And after the words *bhavat* and *āśis*, [the suffixes] *ṭhak* and *chaś* optionally occur: *bhāvatkāḥ* and *bhavadīyāḥ*.

This Vārttika and the rule *ekataddhite ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.50) need not be formulated, because the intended meaning is already established by the statement of the Bhāṣyakāra: "In all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), there is the substitution of the masculine form for a pronoun. Thus, [the forms] such as *sarvamayaḥ* are accounted for.
One whose wife is Sarvikā, who desires everything, is called *sarvakabhārya*; likewise,
one who is dear to all is called *sarvapriya*, and so forth.
This [rule] applies only to the former [case],
based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *bhastraiṣājājñādvā* (Pāṇini 7.3.47);
therefore, it does not apply when the suffix *akac* is added or when a *ekaśeṣa* formation occurs.
All female [birds],
such as hens and others, [lay] their eggs and so forth.
A hen's egg,
a doe's footprint, a deer's footprint, and deer's milk.
A young crow.
After these two, [the feminine suffix] is treated like the masculine:
*etāyate* (she behaves like a female goat), *śyetāyate* (she behaves like a female hawk).
One who considers themselves beautiful thinks of a certain woman distinct from themselves as beautiful;
Caitra, who considers himself beautiful, thinks of a beautiful woman [as such].
AS 6.3.37: For a feminine stem having *k* as its penultimate letter, the masculine form is not applied [in a bahuvrīhi compound]; e.g., *pācikābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a cook").
The wife of Rasika acts like Madrikā, while she who considers herself Madrikā acts like [Rasika’s wife].
In the prohibition regarding the suffix *kopadha*, there is an inclusion of the *vu*-suffix (Vārttika); thus,
here [the rule does not apply],
as in "one whose wife is a cook" (*pākabhāryaḥ*).
For these two, there is no substitution of the masculine form.
In the case of *dattā-bhāryaḥ* and *dattā-māninī*,

because these are based on the act of giving (*dāna-kriyā-nimitta*) and function as designations for both a woman and a man, they possess the quality of having been previously used in the masculine (*bhāṣita-puṃskatva*).
One who has a fifth wife is bound by the noose of the fifth. (SK 840)

A feminine word ending in a taddhita suffix that causes a *vṛddhi* vowel by the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.118] *vṛddhir ādaic*, provided that suffix does not signify "dyed" (*rakta*) or "modification" (*vikāra*), does not become masculine-like (*puṃvat*). Example: *sraughnī-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is from Sraughna").
Does she who considers herself a native of Mathurā act like one from Mathurā because of the cause of her prosperity?
In the case of *madhyamabhāryaḥ*, [the suffix] *taddhita* is applied; what about *kāṇḍalāvabhāryaḥ*?
First, what is meant by the word "vṛddhi"? It refers to one whose wife is [so called]; however, he who possesses a saffron-colored patched garment is a *kāṣāyakantha*.
In the case of a derivative (*vikāra*), however, one who has a golden ring is called *haimamudrikaḥ*.

Because there is no presence of a result (*phalopadhāna*) with respect to the increase (*vṛddhi*) denoted by the word *vṛddhi*, the masculine form is applied here according to the rule of *puṃvat* [Pāṇini 6.3.34], as in the example *vaiyākaraṇabhāryaḥ*.
The word *sauvaśvabhāryaḥ* is formed according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.40.

A feminine word ending in the vowel *ī* that begins with a part of the body (*svāṅga*) does not take the masculine form [in a bahuvrīhi compound]; for example, *sukeśī-bhāryaḥ*. Why "beginning with a part of the body"? [To exclude cases like *citra-keśī-bhāryaḥ*, where the hair is not a part of the body].
Is the husband of Paṭu here? Is he the husband of Akeśa?
It should be stated as "amāninī" (not proud), or [alternatively] "sukeśamāninī" (priding herself on her beautiful hair).
SK 842
That which ends in a feminine suffix following a word denoting a genus (jāti) is not treated like the masculine,
as in the example *śūdrābhāryaḥ*.
This prohibition applies specifically to the word *sautra*;
therefore, in the case of *hāstikam* (a herd of female elephants), the rule *bhasyāḍhe* (Pāṇini 7.1.89) does indeed apply.
Indeclinables and other such words are compounded with a numeral whose meaning is that which is to be numbered; this compound is a *bahuvrīhi*.
Those who are near the ten are "upadaśāḥ," meaning nine or eleven;
the suffix *ḍac* is applied here according to the rule to be stated later: *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye* (Pāṇini 5.4.73).
In the word *viṃśati*, there is the elision of the syllable *ti* when followed by a suffix beginning with *ḍ*.
"Near-twenty" means close to twenty; likewise, "not far from thirty" means near thirty.
Forty-two or forty-three; two or three, i.e., two or three; repeated twice, i.e., ten or twenty.
The meaning is "twenty.
Regarding the names of the intermediate directions, as previously stated:
the intermediate space between the southern and eastern directions is called *dakṣiṇapūrvā* (southeast); however, this does not apply to those [names] that are etymological (*yaugika*).
The intermediate direction between the eastern and northern quarters.

When two words of identical form occur, one ending in the seventh case (locative) regarding the sense of "seizing" and the other ending in the third case (instrumental) regarding the sense of "weapon," they are compounded in the sense that "this battle has commenced," provided that the mutual exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*) is to be expressed; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and by the word "iti," this specific scope is obtained.
The suffix *ic* will be stated as the final member of the compound.
Because the suffix *ic* is taught in the list beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*, it possesses the status of an *avyayībhāva* compound and is therefore indeclinable (*avyaya*).
This is also seen in other cases: *dīrghaḥ keśeṣu* (the hair is long); having seized each other by the hair, this battle proceeded; hence *keśākeśi*.
Striking with staff after staff, this battle proceeded, blow against blow and fist against fist.
For a *bha*-stem ending in the vowel *u*, there shall be *guṇa* substitution before a *taddhita* suffix,
with the replacement of *u* by *av*.

Although one should have said *bāhubāhuvi* when expressing "arm-to-arm," the mention of the *guṇa* vowel is intended to indicate that "a rule conditioned by a specific technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (*anitya*).
By this, forms such as *svāyambhuvam* are established.
What is the meaning of "when they are of the same form"? [For example:
*halena mūsalena* (with a plow and with a pestle).
SK 848
The word *saha*, when used in the sense of equal conjunction, is compounded with a word ending in the third case, as previously stated.

AS 6.3.82: The word *saha*, when it is a constituent part of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, may optionally be replaced by *sa-*; for example, one who has come with his son is called either *saputraḥ* or *sahaputraḥ*.
The statement regarding "equal application" (tulyayoga) is general; for example, "he who has hair on his body also has hair on his arm."
In the sense of a benediction, the word *saha* shall remain in its original form (*prakṛti*).
"May there be well-being for the king, together with his sons, together with his ministers,
[and] with his cows and calves"— thus it should be said, or "with his cows."
Together with its calf and its rope,
The suffix *ḍac* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound that denotes a number (*saṃkhyeya*), as in *upadaśāḥ*.
Why [is it] not [formed] from *abahugaṇa*?
[Because] *upabahavaḥ* and *upagaṇāḥ* [are examples].
In this case, a specific accentuation for the number in a *tatpuruṣa* compound must be stated as an option:
*nirgataṃ triṃśato varṣāṇi caitrasya* = *nistriṃśāni varṣāṇi caitrasya*.
The word *nistriṃśaḥ* means a sword (*khaḍgaḥ*), derived from the sense of "having gone out from thirty fingers" (*nirgatastriṃśato'ṅgulibhyaḥ*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.113)
By way of an irregularity, the genitive case is used;
the suffix *ṣac* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *sakthi* or *akṣi* when they denote one's own limbs. Thus, one whose two thighs are long is called *dīrghasakthaḥ*.
Is a long-thighed cart a lotus-eyed woman from her own body?
A bamboo staff with thick joints [is used] because the joints are not visible to the eye;
thus [it is stated in] SK 853.

AS 5.4.114: The suffix *ṣac* is added after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *aṅguli* when the meaning is "wood"; for example, that wood which has five fingers [in length] is called *pañcāṅgulaṃ dāru*.

A wooden stick for scattering grain and other items, whose parts resemble fingers, is so called [by the term *aṅguli*]. Why [is this] stated by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound? [Because otherwise it would be confused with a *dvigu*:
"a staff (*yaṣṭi*) whose measure is two fingers" (*dvyaṅgulā*).
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the sense is that of a *taddhita* suffix, by the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.86), the suffix *ac* is applied; thus,
why would "a hand with five fingers" (*pañcāṅguli*) not refer to wood?
After these two [words], the word *mūrdhan* shall take the suffix *ṣ* when forming a bahuvrīhi compound.
The names Dvimūrdhaḥ and Trimūrdhaḥ should not be uttered when the leader is under the Nakṣatra constellation.
Those nights of which the deer is the leader are "deer-led" nights; [likewise] those led by Puṣya are "Puṣya-led.
After these two [words], when followed by *loman*, the suffix *ap* is optionally applied in a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for example, *antarlomaḥ*.
Having the hair pointing outward (bahirloma).
The suffix *ac* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *nāsikā*, and the word *nāsikā* becomes *nasa*; however, this does not apply when preceded by *sthūla*. (SK 857;

After a cause (nimitta) situated in the preceding member, the *n* of the following word becomes *ṇ* when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*), provided there is no intervention by the letter *g*. For example:
*druṇasaḥ* ("one whose nose is like a tree") and *kharaṇasaḥ* ("one with a harsh nose").

In the Bhāṣya, the word *aga* has been rejected on the grounds that it is unnecessary, since the form *ṛgayanam* (the study of the Ṛgveda) is derived from *ṛca* by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *ṛgayanam aṇṛgayanādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.72), which prescribes the absence of *ṇatva* (nasalization) through a specific nipātana (irregular derivation). Thus, the term *aga* is considered superfluous.
Is he thick-nosed because of his lack of bulk, or is it due to his two hooves?
The forms *khuraṇāḥ* and *kharaṇāḥ* are desired in the sense of "one who does not recite" (*ajapin*).
Those with deformed noses;
those with harsh noses.

AS 5.4.119: After a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *nāsikā* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *ac* is applied, and *nas* is substituted for *nāsikā*; this rule is stated to exclude cases where the term is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
One whose nose is elevated is "unnasa";
having set aside the rule *upasargādanotparaḥ*, the author of the Bhāṣya says [the following].
Following a cause situated in a prefix, the *n* of the root *nas* is optionally changed to *ṇ*;
for example, *praṇasaḥ*.
It should be stated as *vigra* or *vigraḥ*;
[alternatively], one whose nose (*nāsikā*) has departed is *vigraḥ*,
and *khyaḥ* is also [used].

How then is the word *vinaṣā* (noseless) in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*— where it describes one whose kinsmen have been slain— to be explained? It should be interpreted as being characterized by a nose that has departed (*vigatayā nāsikayā*).
AS 5.4.120: These [words] ending in the suffix *ac* are derived as irregular *bahuvrīhi* compounds.
His morning is auspicious: *suprātaḥ*;
his tomorrow is auspicious: *suśvaḥ*; his day is auspicious: *sudivaḥ*.
His belly is like that of a śāri bird, thus he is Śārikukṣa; his four corners are symmetrical, thus he is Caturaśra;
his feet are like those of an antelope, thus he is Eṇīpada.
A *proṣṭha* is a bull; one whose feet are like those of this [bull] is *proṣṭhapada*.
The suffix *ac* shall be applied [to form a bahuvrīhi compound] when it does not mean "a plough."
Without ribs,
without thighs,
without shanks.
Similarly, there is an alternative reading, "duḥsubhyāṃ śaktyoḥ," meaning "incapable."
Incapacity [to perform an action] (aśaktiḥ) [is a cause for the non-arising of a cognition].
By the rule *nañ-duḥ-subhyaḥ*, [the suffix *aC* is applied] after *nañ* and *duḥ*:
*aprajāḥ* (childless) and *duṣprajāḥ* (having bad offspring).
One with good offspring, one with intelligence, and one with poor intelligence.
Sumedhas (the wise) SK 863; AS 5.4.124.

The suffix *aṇic* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *dharma*, provided that the word *dharma* follows immediately after the first member [of the compound]. For example: *kalyāṇadharmā*. Why "immediately after"? [To exclude cases where it does not follow immediately.]

In the three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound "paramaḥ svo dharmaḥ yasya" (for whom the highest is his own duty), let there not be [the application of the rule] because here the word *sva-* is not merely a prior member (*pūrvapada*), but rather, being middle, it is relative; however,
in cases such as "saṃdigdhasādhyadharma" (having a doubtful property to be proven), it is a *bahuvrīhi* whose prior member is a *karmadhāraya*.
And thus, the term *paramasvadharma* is also quite correct— just like *nivṛttidharma* or *anucchittidharma*—
in which the preceding member is understood through an implied *bahuvrīhi* compound.
In the word *jambheti*, the form ending in the compound-affix (*samāsānta*) is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
*Jambha* refers to food and to a tooth; *sujambha* means one who has beautiful teeth, and *haritajambha* means one who has green teeth.
*Tṛṇajambha* means "one whose food is grass" or "one whose teeth are like grass"; *somajambha* means "one whose teeth are like the *soma* plant.
Why [is the suffix] *ka* not applied after these?
One whose jaw has fallen.
One who has a wound (*īrma*) on the right side is called *dakṣiṇermā*; the meaning is that the deer has a wound inflicted by a hunter.
After a *bahuvrīhi* compound expressing mutual action, the suffix *ic* shall be applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*), as in *keśākeśi*.
The *musalāmusali* compound [is formed by the elision of the middle term] according to Pāṇini 2.4.128.

This fourth case ending is used in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*); thus, this suffix *ic* occurs for the purpose of establishing these [compounds]. For example, a weapon in which there are two staffs is called *dvidaṇḍi-praharaṇa*.
With two pestles, with both hands,
with both arms.
When these two [words] precede, the word *jānu* is replaced by *jñu* in a bahuvrīhi compound.
One whose knees are well-developed is *prajñuḥ* (wise) and *saṃjñuḥ* (well-known).
SK 869
AS 5-4-130: *ūrdhvajñuḥ* and *ūrdhvajānuḥ*.
In a bahuvrīhi compound ending in *dhanus*, the substitution of *anaṅ* shall take place [for the final syllable].
The wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Śatadhanvā, Śatadhanuḥ (SK 872)
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *jāyā*, the substitute *niṅ* shall take the place of [the final phoneme].
AS 6.1.66: There shall be elision of the phonemes *v* and *y*, and there shall be the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), when followed by a consonant (*hal*).
The term *yuvajāni* refers to one whose wife (*jāyā*) is young (*yuvati*).
In place of the word *gandha* following these [words], the substitution of the single phoneme *ikāra* (i) shall occur:
*udgandhiḥ*, *pūtigandhiḥ*.
"Sugandhi" means "possessing a fragrant scent"; the addition of the suffix *it* in the sense of "having a smell" is for the purpose of restricting it to that specific meaning.
The meaning is that "solitude" (ekāntaḥ) is perceived as being indivisible, like a single location;
[the objects are] fragrant flowers, water,
and fragrant wind.
In this case, "excellent perfumes" refers to the substances belonging to a perfume merchant (sugandhāpaṇika).
That food in which there is even a trace of the smell of soup is called "sūpagandhi";
for the Viśva lexicon states: "gandha means smell, a trace, fragrance, pride, and relationship."
Like the fragrance of a lotus belongs to this, it is "lotus-scented" (padmagandhi).
In a bahuvrīhi compound, there is elision of the word *pāda* when it follows a word denoting a point of comparison, provided that the comparison is not with *hastin* and so forth.
This suffix added at the end of a compound is introduced by way of the word that occupies its place (sthānin);
for example, "vyāghrapāt" (tiger-footed), meaning one whose feet are like those of a tiger.
Why [is it said] "after words such as hasty"?
Hastipāda and Kusūlapāda (SK 878).
In the group of words beginning with *kumbhapadī*, the elision of *pāda* and the suffix *ṅīp* are prescribed as irregularities in the feminine;
[here] *pāda* becomes *pat*.
Why is *kumbhapadī* feminine, while *kumbhapādaḥ* is masculine?
In a Bahuvrīhi compound, there shall be elision of the word *pāda* as a suffix of the compound.
Two-footed, well-footed.
For the word *danta*, preceded by a numeral or the word *su*, the substitute *datṛ* shall occur when referring to age; for example, *dvidat*.
He has four teeth, six teeth, and sixteen beautiful teeth.
O fair-toothed one, why do you act like a two-tusked elephant in your youth?
Well-tamed (sudantaḥ) [is derived from] su + dantaḥ (Pāṇini 5.4.143).
After these [words], "danta" (tooth) becomes "datṛ" as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) in a *bahuvrīhi*; for example:
*ayodatī*, *phāladatī*.
In the case of *saṃjñā*, what is it that is equal?
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *danta-* may optionally be replaced by *datṛ-*; for example,
*śyāvadan*.
One with black teeth,
one who does not chew,
and one with teeth that do not chew.
After these [words], the word *danta-* optionally becomes *datṛ*.
One whose teeth are like the tips of flower buds (kuḍmalāgradanta).
SK 884
The words *ajātakakud* and *pūrṇakakud* [are used as names].
That which has three humps is *trikakud*.
This is the name of a particular mountain;
Trikakuda is another.
There shall be elision (lopa) of the *ut* and the *kaku*.
The palate is the elevated part of the mouth cavity.
*pūrṇakākut* becomes *pūrṇakākudaḥ*.
In the presence of the prefixes *su-* and *dur-*, the form *hṛt* is prescribed as a substitute for the word *hṛdaya*.
A friend is a friend; an enemy is a foe; elsewhere, there is one who is well-disposed.
durhṛdayaḥ SK 889 AS 5-4-151: "one who has a wicked heart" (an enemy).
The words *vyūḍhoraskaḥ*,
*priyasarpiṣkaḥ*,
*iha*, *pumān*, *anaḍvān*, *payaḥ*, *nau*, and *lakṣmīḥ* are recited as ending in the singular number.
However, after words ending in the dual or plural numbers, the suffix *kap* is optionally applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.154 (*śeṣād vibhāṣā*); thus, one may say *dvipumān* or *dvipuṃskaḥ*.
(ga) From the perspective of meaning, what is the purpose of the particle *nañ* being [treated as] meaningless? What is the purpose of *nañ*?
Meaningless and incoherent.
*bahudaṇḍikā nagarī*;
the mention of suffixes such as *an*, *ini*, *as*, and *man* applies the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) both when they have meaning and when they are meaningless.
Why is *bahuvāggmikā* used for a woman, but not *bahudaṇḍī*?
The village has many staff-bearers (or: many punishments).

The suffix *kap* may optionally be added to a *bahuvrīhi* compound that does not have a specifically prescribed *samāsānta* (compound-final suffix) and which falls under the scope of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) rule; for example:
*mahāyaśaskaḥ* or *mahāyaśāḥ*.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "anukta" (unspoken) and so forth: is it like a tiger’s footprint being fragrant?
Is "priyapatha" [the example] from the section on the remainder (śeṣādhikāra), or is it "upabahavaḥ"?
The northeast is for one with excellent sons;
by means of the Tantras and so forth, the word "remainder" (śeṣa) refers to two meanings.
In the case of a word ending in *kapyāsa*, the vowel may optionally be shortened.
*bahumālākaḥ* and *bahumālakaḥ* [occur] when the suffix *ka* is present; however, in the absence of *ka*, it is *bahumālaḥ*.
By the rule *śeṣāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.154), the suffix *kap* would have applied; however, it does not occur when [the compound] is a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
The Viśvedevas [are the deity] of this; [the suffix -aṇ] is applied [to form *vaiśvadeva*].

When the suffix *ka* is prohibited after a compound whose final member ends in *īyas*, as in *bahuśreyān* ("one who has many superiors"), the rule *go-striyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48) would require the shortening of the vowel. However, this is not the case. [The following applies: *SK-sandarbhah* 656. When the rule for shortening is about to apply...
It should be stated that [the suffix] *īyas* is not [retained] in a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
e.g., *bahuśreyasī* ("one who has many superiors"). Why "of a *bahuvrīhi*"? [Because in a non-*bahuvrīhi*, it would be *atiśreyasī*].
The suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied after a word denoting excellence (*atiśāyana*).

The *kap* suffix shall not be applied after a word ending in *bhrātṛ* when that word denotes something praised; for example, *praśasto bhrātā yasya* results in *prāstabhrātā*. However, the prohibition [of *kap*] stated in *pūjanāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.122) applies only to *bahuvrīhi* compounds prior to the rule *sakthyakṣṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.113), as will be explained later.
When she was saluted, [he asked], "Why do you have a foolish brother?
The suffix *kap* shall not be applied after a word ending in *nāḍī* or *tantrī* when these refer to one's own body parts; for example, *bahunāḍiḥ kāyaḥ*.
The neck has many sinews;
"sinew" (tantrī) here refers to a vessel (dhamanī),
and because it does not end in a feminine suffix, the vowel is not shortened.
What need is there for many channels in one's own body? A pillar has many beams; a lute has many strings.
In this case, the absence of the suffix *kap* is established as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
From the root *vye* preceded by *pra*,
the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to form *pravāṇī*, meaning "the shuttle of a weaver"; that which has its *pravāṇī* removed is called *niṣpravāṇi*, as in the case of a newly woven cloth.
*Samāptavānaḥ* means "new," according to *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.2.35.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) should be placed first; for example, *kaṇṭhekālaḥ*.
From this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that a *bahuvrīhi* may consist of words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇapada*).
The Vārttika states: "There should be an addition [to the rule] regarding pronouns and numerals [as the first members of a bahuvrīhi compound]; for example:
*sarvaśvetaḥ*."
In the compound *dviśuklaḥ*, the number is placed first because of the subsequent application of the rule regarding the priority of the word [in a compound] over the contrary rule; thus,
it is *dvyanyaḥ*.
When a smaller number is mentioned [in a compound], it may optionally come first; thus,
*dvitrāḥ* (two or three), even though it is a *dvandva* compound.
Or twelve [mouthfuls] for one who is dear; or [for one who] is fond of molasses.
In the case of *priyaguḍa*, the seventh case ending after words such as *gaḍu* is optionally retained; thus,
one says *gaḍukaṇṭhaḥ*.
In some cases, there is no flow of the breath.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix should stand first; for example,
*kṛtakṛtyaḥ*.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) should be stated as coming after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth; for example,
*sāraṅgajagdhi* (eaten by a deer) and *māsajātā* (born a month ago).
This is generally true for those born in happiness, provided they have undergone some hardship.
One who has drunk water.
*Āhitāgni* and *agnyāhita* belong to this class of words formed according to their general structure (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) and the locative case (*saptamī*) following words meaning "weapons" optionally [form a compound]; for example:
*abhyudyataḥ* or *daṇḍapāṇiḥ*.
In some places, [the rule] "not having an unsheathed sword" (*kvacinna vivṛtāsiḥ*) is an example of the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds.
Now begins the section on Dvandva compounds.
Multiple words ending in case-terminations (*subanta*) occurring in the sense of *ca* ("and") may be compounded; that is *dvandva*.
The meanings of *ca* are: conjunction (*samuccaya*), sequential mention (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective totality (*samāhāra*).
Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the connection of multiple things, each independent of the others, with a single [action or predicate].
When one [of two things] is secondary, it is *anvācaya*; when there is a connection of combined elements, it is *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction);
and when there is a collection, it is *samāhāra* (aggregation).

In these cases, there is no compound formation due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*): in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), as in "Worship both Īśvara and the Guru"; in the case of incidental mention (*anvācaya*), as in "Go for alms and bring the cow";
and in the case of a technical name and a rule (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣam*), as in "dhava and khadira."
Because they are mentioned as many, the Hotṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Udgātṛ form pairs two by two;
then, by forming a further pair, [the compound] is *hotāpotāneṣṭodgātāraḥ*.
Among these, that which is worthy of being placed first should be placed last;
for example, "the king of teeth" is *rājadantaḥ*.
Regarding dharma and the others, there is no fixed order;
[they may appear as] artha-dharma or dharma-artha.
Dampatī, jampatī,
jāyāpatī (husband and wife)
The substitution of *jam* or *dam* for the word *jāyā* is irregularly prescribed;

In a *dvandva* compound, that which is designated as *ghī* (ending in short *i* or *u*) shall stand first; for example,
*hariśca haraśca* becomes *hariharau*.
When multiple [deities] are applicable, there is a restriction to one; otherwise, there is no restriction. [Examples:
*hariguruharaḥ* or *hariharaguravaḥ*.
In a *dvandva* compound, this [the subsequent member] should be placed first.
Īśa and Kṛṣṇa [are the first two]; there is no fixed rule regarding the many; [the remaining] are Aśva, Ratha, and Indra.
In the case of *indrāśva-ratha* and others, [the rule] ending in a vowel beginning with *a* (i.e., *aja-ādi*) prevails over that ending in *yat* by way of a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*).
Thus, [we have] *indrāgnī*.
Śiva and Keśava (SK 905; AS 2-2-34)
According to the sequence of seasons and constellations with corresponding syllables,
winter, the cool season, and spring correspond to Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī.
Among those with equal syllables, which comes first: the summer or the spring? Is the light syllable [the first]?
And the Kuśa and Kāśa mountains, as well as the Tāpasa and Parvata mountains, are highly esteemed.
Or, according to the sequence of the castes, [they are] the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; or [according to seniority], those of the elder brother.
Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna.
The copulative compound (dvandva) of these [members] shall be treated as singular: for example, *pāṇipādam* (hand and foot) and *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* (the drummers and the lute-players).

Since the singular number is already established for a collective compound (*samāhāra*) by virtue of its being a single entity— such as "charioteers and horsemen"— this section is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) so that for parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and the like, the singular form occurs only in a collective compound.
A copulative compound of words denoting limbs [of the body] shall be treated as singular when used to refer to something already established.
It should be stated that [the suffix *luṅ* is used] after the roots *sthā* and *iṇ*:
"The Kaṭhas and Kālāpas have emerged [from their study]; the Kaṭhas and Kauthumas have stood firm [in their tradition]."
A dvandva compound consisting of words denoting sacrifices prescribed in the Yajurveda that are not neuter in gender shall be treated as a singular.
Are the Arkāśvamedha and the Adhvaryu-sacrifice [performed] by the Adhvaryu priest; and are the Iṣu and Vajra [sacrifices] prescribed in the Sāmaveda?
Why is it not neuter?
[Because] *rājasūya* and *vājapeya* belong to the *ardharcādi* group.
A dvandva compound consisting of those whose names are proximate [to each other] through study is treated as a singular.
The sequence of words and phrases (padakakramaka).
A copulative compound (dvandva) consisting of words denoting species of non-living things is singular;
for example, *dhānāśaṣkulī*.
However, for living beings, it is not so; for example, *viṭśūdrau*.
In this [world], color and taste belong only to those things that are of the nature of substances.
This singular treatment occurs precisely when the genus (*jāti*) is intended as the primary factor, as in the case of "going" and "contracting";
however, when there is an intention to express specific substances (*dravya*), one says "jujubes and myrobalans."
In a collective dvandva compound of words denoting villages, rivers, or regions that differ in gender, excluding those denoting villages, the compound shall be singular.
Uddhya and Irāvatī are "Uddhyerāvati";
Gaṅgā and Śoṇa are "Gaṅgāśoṇam";
and Kuravaḥ and Kurukṣetram are "Kurukurukṣetram."
What [is the rule] for those with different genders, such as Gaṅgā-Yamunā or Madraka-Ekayā?
Is Jambava not a village? Is Śālūkinī a village?
The *jāmbava* and *śālūkinī* [are two types of lotus].

In the collective compound (samāhāra-dvandva) of these, the dual form shall be treated as singular; small creatures beginning with lice and nit and ending with the mongoose (nakula) are considered "small animals" (kṣudrajantu).
For these, as before.
In cases such as *ahinakulam*,
*govyāghram*,
and *kākolūkam*, although the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga* (Pāṇini 2.4.12) would apply by virtue of its subsequent position, it is set aside by the particle *ca*.
For Śūdras who have not been excluded, it is as before.
The carpenter and the blacksmith are excluded from the company of those worthy of the alms-bowl; moreover, the Caṇḍāla and the Mṛtapā are likewise excluded.
Just as [words] are uttered, they are correct,
such as "gavāśvam" (cow-and-horse).
"Slaves, male and female," and so forth (SK 916;
There is a dvandva compound of the seven beginning with "tree" (vṛkṣa), as well as the three dvandvas beginning with "horse and mare" (aśvavaḍavā) and so forth; and as before,
in the case of "tree" and the others, only specific varieties are intended to be included, such as "plakṣa and nyagrodha."
Plakṣa and nyagrodha trees;
ruru and pṛṣata deer; ruru and pṛṣata deer.
Kuśa and kāśa grasses;
kuśa and kāśa grasses; rice and barley.
Rice and barley, curd and ghee; curd and ghee.
Cows and buffaloes;
cows and buffaloes; parrots and cranes.
Parrots and cranes; a horse and a mare; a horse and a mare.
Before and after,
in the before and after; below and above.

It should be stated as a rule (vārttika) that a *dvandva* compound consisting of many members—specifically those of the categories "low and high" (*adharottara*), fruits, army units, trees, wild animals, birds, small creatures, grains, and grasses—is treated as a singular entity. For example:
*badarāṇi cāmalakāni ca* ("jujubes and myrobalans") becomes *badarāmalakam*.
According to the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6), there is a singular formation; however, this is not the case here for "badara" and "āmalaka."

In the rule *vibhāṣāvṛkṣa-* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), the mention of those that are not living beings— such as "charioteers and horsemen" (*rathikāśvārohau*) and "plakṣa and nyagrodha trees" (*plakṣanyagrodhau*)— is intended to provide an option (*vikalpa*), since the rule *jātiraprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6) would otherwise have rendered such compounds obligatory.

The mention of "animals" (*paśu*) is for the purpose of restriction: since elephants, horses, and the like are necessarily included because they constitute parts of an army, the mention of "wild animals" (*mṛga*) and "birds" (*śakuni*) serves to restrict that wild animals must be paired only with wild animals and birds only with birds—forming a *dvandva* compound in both cases—whereas when these are combined with other [classes of beings], it is merely a *itaretarayoga* (copulative) compound. Thus, the inclusion of the terms "wild animals" and "birds" is for the sake of such a rule.
In this way, [the rule applies] to "pūrvāpara," "adhara-uttara," and so on.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *aśvavaḍavau* is for the sake of ensuring the neuter gender in certain instances;
otherwise, by virtue of its posteriority, it would result in the form *aśvavaḍavau* according to the rule *pūrvavadaśvavaḍavau* (Pāṇini 2.4.27).
A dvandva compound consisting of words with contradictory meanings that do not denote substances may optionally be singular.

In the compound *śītoṣṇam* (cold and heat), the formation of a collective dvandva by option (*vaikalpika*)—as prescribed by the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ samāhāraḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.29)—is subject to this restriction: if it occurs for words with contradictory meanings, then it applies only to those that do not denote substances (*adravyavācin*). This [present rule] is intended as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*) to that effect.
Therefore, for words denoting substances, there is only mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*); [for example,] "cold and heat exist in the waters.
What is contradictory?
In this case, "Nandaka and Pāñcajanya" is indeed a collective dvandva compound consisting of two members. (SK 918)
These two, curd and milk, should not exist in the same vessel.
In the words *idhmābarhiṣī* and *ṛksāme*, the vowel lengthening occurs by virtue of irregular grammatical derivation (*nipātana*).
Speech and mind.
If the number of substances were understood [as the primary meaning], there would be no restriction that it must be expressed in the singular, as in "ten teeth and lips" (daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ).
There may be a restriction of the form "only a collective [compound] occurs when there is a delimitation by proximity of the extent of the substratum," as in *upadaṃśam* or *dantoṣṭham*.
The compound *upadaśa* (meaning "nearly ten") is formed with the word *daśan* [as its final member],
according to Pāṇini 6.3.25.

In a *dvandva* compound, words ending in *ṛt* that denote a relationship through either learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*) shall take the substitute *ānaṅ* when followed by a subsequent member; for example:
*hotāpotārau*, *hotṛpotṛneṣṭodgātāraḥ*.
By the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkapluti) method, the word "son" (putra) is carried over from the rule "mātāpitarau putreṇa anyatarasyām," resulting in the compound "father and son" (pitāputrau).
In this context, when the subsequent member [of a compound] follows, *ānaṅ* is substituted [for the final vowel and consonant of the first member].
There is a prohibition against the use of the word *vāyu* when [the names of] Mitra and Varuṇa are employed; [alternatively,
it refers to] Agni and Vāyu.
The re-mention of *vāyu* and *agni* as a *dvandva* is for the purpose of including those whose association is well-known;
therefore, in cases such as *brahmaprajāpatī*, the suffix *anaṅ* does not apply.
For this [concomitance] is neither heard in scripture as a sharing of a single oblation, nor is it well-known in the world as such a coexistence (sāhacarya).
In the case of a dual compound of deities, [the first member retains its original accent] alone;
SK 924, Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.82.
In a compound, the *s* of these following words after *agni* becomes *ṣ*:
*agniṣṭut*, *agniṣṭoma*.
Agni and Soma;
Agni and Varuṇa.
SK 925
When the second member of a compound is a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel, the substitution of *it* for *agni* occurs in a *devatā-dvandva* (compound of deities);
[for example], that which has Agni and Marut as its deities is called *āgnimārutaṃ karma*.
Agni and Varuṇa are its deities;

thus, by the rule *devatādvandve ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.26), there is vr̥ddhi of both members [of the compound]. In the ungrammatical sentence (*alaukika-vākya*), having set aside the *ānaṅ* substitution and the substitution of *ī* for *i*, [the form is derived].
In the case of *vṛddhi*, why is there no *āgnendra*? [Because of the rule] "not when *indra* follows" (Pāṇini 7.3.21), there is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* of the final member.
Nor [is there] an offering to Agni and Viṣṇu in the case of Viṣṇu.
SK 926
In a dvandva compound of deities, when it occurs as the final member, [the form] dyāvābhūmī is used.
Heaven and earth.
The pronunciation of the vowel 'a' in the substitute *dyāvā* for *diva* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ru* for the letter *s*.
Heaven and earth are "divaspṛthivyau";
[the form] "dyāvāpṛthivyau" is according to the rule observed in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
In the passage "dyāvā cid asmai pṛthivī divaspṛthivyor aratim," the authors of the *padapāṭha* read the visarga [before "asmai"].
AS 6.3.31: In a dvandva compound of deities, the word *uṣas* is replaced by *uṣāsā*, as in *uṣāsāsūryam*.
Mother and father.
Why [is it] "mātāpitarau" according to the Northern Grammarians?
After a *dvandva* compound ending in a letter of the *ca*-class or in *da*, *ṣa*, or *ha*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). For example:
*vāk* and *tvak* form *vāktvacam*.
The bark-garland,
the *śamī* wood, the grindstone, speech, and splendor.
In the case of a collective compound (samāhāra), why is it not so for *chatropānaham* (umbrella and sandals), as it is for *prāvṛṭśaradau* (the rainy season and autumn)?
Thus ends the section on Dvandva compounds;
now begins the section on Ekaśeṣa (the retention of one).

AS 1.2.65: When there is a co-expression with a *yuvan* (youth), the *gotra* (lineage) term is retained, provided that the entire difference between the two consists solely of the *gotra* suffix and the *yuvan* suffix; for example, *gārgyaś ca gārgyāyaṇaś ca* = "Gārgya and Gārgyāyaṇa" [resulting in] *gārgyau*.
Is an elder [denoted] by *garga* or *gārgya*, or by *gārgyāyaṇa*? Is he [denoted] by the youth?
Are Garga and Gārgya characterized by that [same definition], or are they Bhāgavitti and Bhāgavittika?
What is the entirety [of this], O Gārgya and Vātsyāyana? SK 932

AS 1.2.66: When a feminine elder [term] is mentioned together with a masculine youth, the feminine is retained, and its meaning is treated like the masculine; for example, *gārgī* and *gārgyāyaṇau* become *gargāḥ*.

While the term *astriyām* (not feminine) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], by *yañañośca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64), there is elision (*luk*); thus, *dākṣī* and *dākṣāyaṇa* together form *dākṣī*. (Kāśikā 933)

AS 1.2.67: When there is a co-utterance with a feminine [noun], the masculine [noun] remains, provided that the distinction [between them] is based solely on their respective grammatical characteristics; for example, *haṃsī* (female swan) and *haṃsaḥ* (male swan) become *haṃsau* (the two swans).
A brother and a sister are [collectively called] *bhrātarau*.
The son and the daughter are "sons" (putrau).

When a non-eunuch (aklība) is mentioned together with a eunuch (klība), the eunuch remains [as the single form]; and that [remaining form] may optionally be treated as singular, provided the distinction between them is based solely on that characteristic:
for example, *śuklaḥ paṭaḥ* (a white cloth) and *śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment).
This cloth is white;
these [other things] are white.
When "mother" (mātṛ) is mentioned together with [a word for] "measure" (mātrā), "father" (pitṛ) may optionally remain as the residue.
Mother and father are "parents";
[the compound] *mātāpitarau* [is formed with the elision of the final vowel of the first member]. (SK 937)

When mentioned together with *śvaśrū* (mother-in-law), *śvaśura* (father-in-law) may optionally remain [as the single form], provided that the distinction between them is based on their common characteristics;
as in *śvaśrūś ca śvaśuraś ca* = *śvaśurau*.
Or [the forms] *śvaśrū* and *śvaśuraḥ* [are used]. (SK 938; AS 1.2.72)
When all [the pronouns] are mentioned together, those beginning with *tyad* are always retained; for example, "he and Devadatta" becomes *tau*.
When those beginning with *tyad* are mentioned together with one another, that which follows is optionally retained.
And he and he who— both of whom are seen as remnants of what precedes— this is the Bhāṣya; "sa ca yaśca" refers to those two.
When [the pronoun] *tyad* and so forth are used, the gender and number of the remaining [referents] follow those of the masculine or neuter;
thus: *sā ca devadattaś ca tau*, *tac ca devadattaś ca yajñadattā ca tāni*.

However, because the neuter gender takes precedence over both the masculine and the neuter, the neuter remains; and it should be stated as a supplementary rule (vārttika) that this applies except in the case of dvandva and tatpuruṣa compounds and their specific subtypes.
These two are a cock and a peahen;
these two are a peahen and a cock;
that and this are two half-pippalīs; those two are [the same].
In these cases, when there is a desire to express them together, the feminine form alone remains.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67).
[In the example] "these cows" (*imā gāvaḥ*), why is the word *grāmya* used?
These sounds— why do the Brahmins seek to capture the sacrificial animals?
What are these two cows among the assemblies?
What are they among those who are not young?
"O calves, these are among the animals with uncloven hoofs," or "these are horses"— thus it should be said.
In all these cases, once the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) has been applied, there is an absence of multiple *subanta* forms; therefore, a *dvandva* compound does not occur.

Consequently, in examples such as *śirasī*, *śirāṃsi*, and so forth, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) prescribed by the rule *samāsasya* does not apply, nor does the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) due to their being parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*).
Likewise, in examples such as *panthānau*, *panthānaḥ*, and so forth, the *samāsānta* suffix does not apply.
Thus ends the section on the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) compound;
now begins the section on the remainder of all compounds.

There are five types of derivative formations (*vṛtti*): primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), *ekaśeṣa*, and verbal roots with prefixes (*sanādyadhātu*).
"Vṛtti is the expression of the meaning for the sake of another;
a sentence that makes the meaning of the vṛtti understood is the vigraha. It is of two kinds:
worldly (laukika) and non-worldly (alaukika).
That which is grammatically established is correct and fit for worldly usage; that which is not so established is incorrect and unfit for worldly usage,
as in the example "the king’s man" (rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ).

O King, the expression *as puruṣaḥ su* is an *avigraha* (non-analytic) *nityasamāsa* (invariable compound); or rather, it is a case of the common saying that "compounds are of four kinds" being based on the analysis of their own constituent words (*svapadavigraha*).

Although they fall outside the specific governing rules (*adhikāra*) for *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and *dvandva* compounds, there is also a traditional saying among the ancients—representing their general intention—that this is because of the rule *saha supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4): that an *avyayībhāva* is dominated by the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārtha-pradhāna*), a *tatpuruṣa* is dominated by the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha-pradhāna*), a *bahuvrīhi* is dominated by the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha-pradhāna*), and a *dvandva* is dominated by the meanings of both members (*ubhayapadārtha-pradhāna*).

Since [the term *samāsa*] is absent in the avyayībhāva compounds such as *sūpaprati* and *unmattagaṅgam*, in the tatpuruṣa compounds such as *atimāla*, in the bahuvrīhi compounds such as *dvitrāḥ*, and in the dvandva compounds such as *danoṣṭham*,
the tatpuruṣa is a specific type [of compound], namely the karmadhāraya; and a specific type of that [karmadhāraya] is the dvigu.
It has been stated that the quality of having multiple words belongs only to *dvandva* and *bahuvrīhi* compounds, while for a *tatpuruṣa* it occurs only in certain cases;
furthermore:

It should be understood by the wise that there are six types of compounds: [those] of *sup* with *sup*, with a *giṅ* suffix, with a noun (*nāman*), with a verbal root (*dhātu*), of *tiṅ* with *tiṅ*, and of *tiṅ* with a word ending in *sup*.
An example of *sup* with *sup* is *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man).
By the verbal suffix (tiṅ), he adorned it with the name; by the root (dhātu), he was a potter (kumbhakāra); [and] by the prefix (kaṭaprū).
The continuous [series] of finite verbs with finite verbs: "drink and eat," "eat and rejoice."
The term *kṛntavicakṣaṇā* refers to that action in which [one] cuts (*kṛntati*) with skill (*vicakṣaṇa*).
It is a compound formed according to the rule "‘*ehīḍādayo ’nyapadārthe ca*’" (Pāṇini 2.2.19), because it is listed in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group.
Thus ends the section on all compound suffixes;
now begins the section on the suffixes for all compounds.
SK 940

AS 5.4.74: The analysis is *a-anakṣe* (not "in the case of *akṣa*"). For a compound ending in *ṛc* and so forth, the suffix *apratya* shall be the final member; however, it does not apply to that which ends in *dhur* when *akṣa* follows.

The term *ardharca* applies only to the reciter (*adhyetṛ*) when it does not refer to many verses (*anṛca*), as in the case of the *bahvṛca*; it does not apply here in the sense of [a specific] hymn (*ṛk*). Similarly, [the term] *sāman* [applies only to the reciter].
*Anuk-sāma*.
The *bahvṛca* hymn is Viṣṇu’s city; the neuter form [of the word] is *viṣṇupura*.
This is according to worldly usage.
A lake with pure water.

The form *apaḥ* is an imitation of a word ending in a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), used in the nominative case with the sense of the genitive; for these [words], the substitute *īt* shall take the place of *ap*.
That in which water has gone twice is a *dvīpa*; likewise,
an *antarīpa* and a *pratīpa*.
Regarding the term *samāpa* in the phrase *samāpo devayajanam*, it should be understood as "that in which the waters (*āpas*) are equal" (*samāḥ āpo yasmin*);
however, because the suffix *samāsānta* [ap] has been applied here, this [specific derivation] does not apply in this instance.
The suffix *svap* is applied after a verbal root ending in a vowel, optionally.
I prepared for the attainment of the highest goal.
parāpam SK 942 AS 6-3-98: [The suffix] *ap* is applied after the word *para*.
The *ap* following *anu* becomes *ūt* when referring to a region; thus,
"anūpa" means a marshy region (*rājadhurā*).
In the case of *akṣa*, however, [the forms] are *akṣadhūḥ*,
*dṛḍhadhurakṣaḥ*, and *sakhipathaḥ*.
A region with pleasant paths.
The suffix *ac* shall be applied after a compound ending in *sāma* preceded by *prati* or *anu*,
as in *pratisāmam* and *anusāmam*.
Without pause, in reverse order, and in direct order.
In descending order,
one will conquer the earth starting from the black, the watery, and the pale lands,
or [conquer] the black land.
A palace with two stories, having a white ground and a bright ground.
With a numeral, and with the words *nadī* and *godāvarī*, [the suffix *aṇ* is optionally applied] as in *pañcanadaṃ* and *saptagodāvaram*.
By means of a grammatical split (yogavibhāga) of the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.75], Padmanābha occurs elsewhere as well.
AS 5.4.76: After the word *akṣi*, when it does not follow a synonym of *cakṣus*, the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*).
For example, *gavām akṣīva* (like the eye of cows) becomes *gavākṣaḥ*.
These twenty-five [words] ending in the vowel *a* are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*).
The first three are bahuvrīhi compounds:
*avidyamānāni catvāry asya* results in *acaturaḥ*, and *vicatvāri* results in *vicaturaḥ*.
The very clever one conquered four [times] with three and two;
[thus] three and four.
The term *upacaturaḥ* means "near four";
from that, optionally, the dual form *strīpuṃsau* is used for a pair consisting of a female and a male.
The cow and the ox are the Ṛg and the Sāman; speech and mind.
The eyes and the eyebrows are "akṣibhruvam";
wives and cows are "dāragāvam";
and the thighs and the knee-joints are "ūrvaṣṭhīvam."

Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is elision of the suffix *ṭi*; thus, *pada-ṣṭhīva* [is formed], where by irregular derivation the word *pāda-* undergoes the substitution of *pad-* [for *pāda-*].
*Naktaṃ ca divā* means "by night and by day"; *naktandivam* means "by night and by day"; *rātrau ca divā* means "at night and during the day";
and *rātrindivam* means "night and day," where the final vowel of *rātri* is substituted as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
The term *ahardivam* is a dual compound (*dvandva*) prescribed by rule (*nipātita*) in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), meaning "day after day" (*ahanyahani*).
It is formed from *ahani* (locative) and *divā* (instrumental).
*Sarajasam* is an indeclinable *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "in its entirety";
however, in a *bahuvrīhi* [it would mean] "having pollen," as in *sarajaḥ paṅkajaḥ*.
*Niḥśreyasam* means "certainly the highest good" (*niścitaṃ śreyaḥ*).
In this world, the *tatpuruṣa* alone is not the person who has attained the highest good.
The lifespan of a person is *puruṣāyuṣa*;
from that, doubled,
it becomes *dvyāyuṣa*.
Then follows Tryāyuṣa, then the Dvandva, and then the Ṛgyajuṣa.
Then there are three types of *karmadhāraya* compounds:
*jātokṣaḥ* (a bull that has become large) and *mahokṣaḥ* (a large bull).
In the word *vṛddhokṣaḥ*,
when it occurs in proximity to *śvan* (forming *upaśunam*),
the elision of the suffix *ṭi* and the *samprasāraṇa* substitution are treated as irregularities (*nipātana*).
In the case of "goṣṭha," [the final vowel] becomes *a* when followed by "śvan" (dog), as in *goṣṭhaśvaḥ*.
May there be spiritual luster and the luster of an elephant.
And it should be stated that [the suffix -yañ] is applied after the words *palya* and *rāja*; thus, *palyavarcasam* and *rājavarcasam*.
*avatamasam* (a state of deep darkness).
It is called *andha* because it blinds with thick darkness; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the *pacādi* group.
Thus, *andham tamaḥ* becomes *andhatamasam*.
In SK 948,
AS 5.4.80 states that the word *vasu* signifies "praiseworthy"; from it, with the suffix *īyasun*, [the form] *vasīyaḥ* is derived.
The word *śvas* expresses the state of being an object of benediction for the praise of the meaning of the subsequent member;
it forms a compound with [the word *vasīyasa*] by virtue of belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group, resulting in *śvovasīyasam*.
May it be well with you tomorrow.
In secret,
in private,
in the heat of secrecy.
By the rule *urasi*, [the suffix *ṭhañ*] forms *pratyurasam*.
An *avyayībhāva* compound occurs in the sense of a case ending. (Pāṇini 2.1.6)
This [suffix] is elided when there is lengthening;
the compound "anugavam yānam" (a cart as long as a cow) is formed by the rule *yasya cāyāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.17).
The suffix *ac* is applied, the final syllable is elided (*pratyayalopa*), and the compound is formed as an irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
In rituals such as the Aśvamedha, the altar (vedi) is twice or thrice the size of the standard altar; it is in these cases that this specific grammatical formation applies. Why [is it not used] here:
