Consequently, from the word *gārgya*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṭhak* are applied; then, by *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the final vowel and its following consonant are elided, and by *āpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151), the *ya* is elided.
Those born in the land of Suvīra are called Sauvīras.
The suffix *ṭhak* is frequently applied after a word denoting a *vṛddha* (elder) belonging to the Sauvīra lineage to denote a *yuvan* (younger generation), provided there is contempt;
for example, from *bhāgavitti*, one forms *bhāgavittikaḥ*.
Optionally, the suffix *phak* may also be used.
The patronymic Bhāgavittāyana is formed by the suffix *phak* (āyana) according to Pāṇini 4.1.149.
The suffix *cha* and *ṭhak* are applied after a patronymic ending in *phiñ* that does not belong to the Sauvíra lineage, when contempt is to be implied; for example,
the descendant of Yamunda is Yāmundāyani, [formed] with *phiñ* from *tikādi*.
His descendant is Yāmundāyanīya or Yāmundāyanīka.

Why is the suffix used in the sense of censure? [Because otherwise] it would be Yāmundāyani, due to the elision (luk) of the general suffix *iṇ* by the rule "ṇyakṣatriyārṣañito yūni lugaṇiñoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.58).
Why [is the word] *sauvīra-* mentioned? [To exclude] *taikāyaniḥ*.

Regarding *sauvīreṣu na iha*, the author of the Vṛtti states that there is no application of "as many as the number" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) here, because of the grammatical indicator (*liṅga*) that the word with fewer syllables is placed last.
In the Bhāṣya, however, it is established that the correspondence is strictly according to the order of enumeration:
from Phāṇṭāhṛta comes Phāṇṭāhṛtāyani; from Maimata comes Maimatāyani.
[The suffix *yañ* is applied] in the sense of offspring (*apatye*).
The Kauravyas are eloquent Brahmins;
the Samrājs are Kṣatriyas.
The sovereign is other than the sovereignity.
By the rule *ebhyo ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.152),
which states that the suffix *ṇya* is applied after these [roots] when a name (*saṃjñā*) is formed, the *s* is changed to *ṣ*.
Hāriṣeṇya,
Lākṣaṇya,
Kāri, Śilpī, and Tāntuvāyya— therefore [these are] the [officiants].
The potter's son is a barber.
hāriṣeṇiḥ, lākṣaṇiḥ (AS 4-1-153)
From *tāntuvāya* and *kaumbhakāra*,
the suffix *phiñ* alone [is applied], because it follows after *nāpita*.
The addition of the suffix *aṇ* after *takṣan* [to form *tākṣṇaḥ*] is prescribed by Vārttika;
by Pāṇini 6.4.147 (*ṣapūrvah*), there is the elision of the vowel *a* of the suffix *an*.
The patronymic *tākṣṇyaḥ* is derived from *tākṣṇaḥ*.
The patronymic suffix *taikāyani* is applied [after the word *taka*, according to Pāṇini 4.1.154].
*phiñ* [is applied] for the sense of offspring;
it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ*.
This is held to be derived from the very root *paramaprakṛti*;
by virtue of its association with a suffix, the form of the root is substituted [as a nipātana]:
the offspring of one who is *kuśala* is *kauśalyāyaniḥ*.
The offspring of a *karmāra* is *kārmāryāyaṇi*;

For if this were an indicator of the etymological meaning of the compound (yoga), then it would not be observed in the absence of that [etymological sense].
Even a statement of the form "the meaning of the suffix is primary" is not to be taught;
why? Because the meaning is established from worldly usage alone.

The forests located near Mount Khalatika are called *khalatika-vanāni*.

Regarding the prohibition [of the suffix] when there is elision (*lub*) in the sense of "belonging to humans" (*manuṣya-lupi*): the meaning is that for qualifiers, the suffix does not apply when the sense of elision (*lub-artha*) pertains to a human characteristic, but it does apply to the word ending in the elided suffix itself.

AS 4.2.84: After the word *śarkarā*, these two suffixes [ṭhañ and ṭhak] occur when it belongs to the *kumuda* group or the *varāha* group; by virtue of its inclusion in those groups, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *kak* optionally occur as well.
By the force of the inclusion of the word "or" (vā), the general suffix *aṇ* applies optionally; its elision (*lub-vikalpa*) results in six forms:

AS 4-2-87: [The suffix *matup* is applied after the words] *kumuda* and *naḍa* to form *kumudvān* and *naḍvān*.

There is a country named Mahiṣmat.

The mention of *luk* is for the purpose of ensuring that only the suffix *chamātra* is elided, so that the suffix *kuk* is not removed; otherwise, by the principle of "those taught as a simultaneous injunction" (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭānām*), even *kuk* would be removed. Thus, the mention of *luk* serves to effect the elision of everything [pertaining to the suffix].
For there would be the elision of the *yam* portion;
thus ends the section on the fourfold suffixes (*cāturarthika*) within the governing heading of secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*).
Now begins the section on the remaining suffixes (*śaiṣika*) within the governing heading of secondary nominal derivatives.
Any meaning other than those beginning with "offspring" (apatya) and ending with the fourfold sense (caturarthī) is the "remainder" (śeṣa); in that case, the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* shall apply.
Visible form is grasped by the eye; sound is audible;
the person is known through the Upaniṣads.
Barley meal ground on a stone is *dārṣada*; barley meal ground in a mortar is *aulūkhala*; a wooden mortar is *aulūkhalo*;
a chariot drawn by horses is *āśvaḥ*.

"A cart (*śakaṭa*) is drawn by four [oxen] (*caturbhiḥ*)," "on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśyām*) the fourteen-fold (*cāturdaśa*) demon is seen," and "in the remainder (*śeṣe*)"— this is both the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the governing rule (*adhikāra*).
The section on the remainder (śeṣādhikāra) extends from this point up to SK 1514, "tasya vikāraḥ," according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.93.
From these two [words], *rāṣṭra* and *avārapāra*, the suffixes *gha* and *kha* respectively occur in the remaining cases; thus,

In this [section], the suffixes beginning with *gha* and ending with *aṣṭu*, *uṇ*, and *lyuṭ* are stated according to their specific bases (*prakṛti*). Their specific meanings, such as "born from" (*jāta*), and their governing case-endings (*samarthavibhakti*) will now be explained.

The *s* of a suffix beginning with *t* following a short vowel or the vowel *i* becomes *ṣ*, provided it is a *taddhita* suffix; for example, *niṣṭya* refers to those excluded from the [proper] castes and stages of life, such as Caṇḍālas and others.
[Alternatively, the suffix] *ṇa* is added after *araṇya*.

they are far-reaching.
From the northern side, one is "northerly" (auttarāhaḥ).

To prevent the substitution of *saṃjñābhūtā* for *prakṛti*,

Only [the rule] "from a word with a directional term as its prior member" applies.
According to the rule *diśo'madrāṇām* (Pāṇini 7.3.13), because the word *madra* is excluded, there is initial vṛddhi [of the first vowel of the following member]; thus,

That aggregate of vowels among which the first is *vṛddhi* shall be designated as *vṛddha*.

Āḍhakajambuka, Śākajambuka;
here there are no Malla-vāstus, [but] Māllavāstavas.

Kāmpilyaka [is derived from] SK 1346,
The suffix *vuñ* shall occur after words ending in these [prefixes] when they denote an increased measure (*vṛddha*); this is an exception to the suffix *cha*. Example: *mālāprasthakaḥ*.
The *nāndīpūraka* and the *pailūvāhaka* [are mentioned] for the purpose of including those at the edge of the city who have not yet arrived.

The suffix *vuñ* shall be applied after a word denoting a place name that begins with a *ra*-consonant, ends in long *ī*, and contains a *vṛddhi* vowel, provided it is not the word *geśa*; for example: *pāṭaliputrakaḥ* (from *pāṭaliputra*), *itaḥ* (from *iti*), and *kākandakaḥ* (from *kākandī*).
The suffix *vuñ* occurs after a word denoting a country (*janapada*) or its boundary (*tadavadhi*), provided that it is a *vṛddha* stem.

After a nominal stem denoting a country (*janapada*) or its boundary, provided it refers to the plural number and is either *avṛddha* (not having a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable) or *vṛddha* (having a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable), the suffix *vuñ* shall be applied;
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* after an *avṛddha* stem and to the suffix *cha* after a *vṛddha* stem.
From a non-vṛddha country: Āṅgaka;
from a non-vṛddha country up to the limit [of the suffix]: Ājamīḍhaka; from a vṛddha country: Dārvaka.
From the elders, up to the limit of the countryside; [the term] "Kālañjaraka" [is used]; why is there the mention of "region" (*viṣaya*)?
So that, by means of *ekaśeṣa*, it may not apply when there is plurality.
*vartanī*, *vartanī*, and *vartanī*—these are *vartanyaḥ*; that which exists in them is *vārtanaḥ*. (SK 1350;

Saindhuvaktraka and Bāhuvartaka (SK 1351).

The Brahmins of the city.

The path is forest-dwelling; the chapter, the logic, the monastery, the man, or the elephant [is forest-dwelling];

the mention of "uttarapada" (final member) in the case of *vṛkagartīya* is for the purpose of excluding those cases where *bahu* precedes.
The suffix *cha* shall be applied [after a word ending in *i* or *u*].

This [Vārttika] (*pārśvatīyam*) is intended to indicate that the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) after an indeclinable before a mere nominal stem (*bha*) is not invariably obligatory; furthermore,

Belonging to Devakī (ga),

What is the *kṛkaṇīya* and the *parṇīya* in the lineage of Bhāradvāja?
The *kārkaṇa* and the *pārṇa* [are types of medicinal herbs].
After the word *ca*, the suffix *cha* is applied in the alternative (*pakṣe*), and [the suffix] *aṇ* is also applied.
This belongs to you two or to you all; it is yours (yuṣmadīya) or ours (asmadīya).
AS 4.3.2: In place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, these two substitutes, *etado* and *adaso*, occur before the suffixes *khañ* and *aṇ*; [thus] *yauṣmākīṇaḥ*.
Our own;
yours; our own.
For the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when they denote a single referent (*ekārtha*), the substitutes *tavaka* and *mamaka* occur before the suffixes *khañ* and *aṇ*.
tāvakīnaḥ, tāvakaḥ, māmakīnaḥ: yours, belonging to you; mine, belonging to me.
But for me, it is indeed so.
For the two words ending in *map* that have a single referent, the substitutes *tvam* and *au* occur before an affix or a subsequent member [of a compound]; for example, *tvadīyaḥ*.
Belonging to me.
The recipient of the *arghya* offering.
The most excellent for the sake of the inferior, the lowest for the sake of the worthy.
The highest offering (uttamārghya) [is prescribed] in the Sūtra-kalpa (SK 1376),
according to the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra (AS 4.3.6).
And from this point, that which belongs to the first half is "pūrvārdhya."

AS 4.3.7: The suffixes *añ* and *ṭhañ* are applied after words ending in *ardha* that have a directional term (*dik*) as their prior member, provided those words denote a portion of a village or a portion of a country.
"These are the easterners of our village or district" (*paurvārdhāḥ paurvārdhikāḥ*);
[this is a compound] in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), meaning "those who exist in the eastern half of the village."
The mention of *ṭhañ* is for the sake of clarity; otherwise, if only *añ* were stated, it might be suspected that there is also an attraction (*anukarṣa*) from [the rule] *yataḥ*.
The intermediate [state] is [described in] AS 4-3-8;
[see also] SK 1379.

After the word *madhya*, the suffix *a* shall be applied in the sense of "present" (*sāmpratika*), [denoting] one who is devoid of excellence or deficiency; for example, a grammarian who is mediocre (*madhya vaiyākaraṇaḥ*).
The middle part of the wood is neither too short nor too long; this is the meaning. (SK 1380)
The suffix *yañ* is applied after the word *dvīpa* when it denotes a region located near the ocean; for example,
*dvaipyam*.
Dvaipyāḥ SK 1381 AS 4-3-11
The suffix *ṭhañ* shall be applied after words expressing time, as in *māsikam* (monthly) and *sāṃvatsarikam* (annual).

How, then, can it be both evening and morning, or recurring? For instance, Kālidāsa says, "to dispel the darkness of night," while Bhāravi says, "the glow of dawn not yet risen," and there are also expressions such as "simultaneous" and "prior in time."
The authoritative scholars maintain that these are indeed Apabhraṃśas;
this extends from the rule *tatra jātaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.25) up to the section on time (*kāla*) ending at Sūtra 4.3.11.
The suffix *ṭhañ* shall apply [after words denoting seasons], as an exception to the suffix *ṛtvaṇ*.
The autumnal ancestral rite (śrāddha).
Is the autumnal disease or the autumnal heat "śārada," or is it the curd derived from these two that is "śārada"?
Optionally, the suffix *ṭhañ* may be applied [to form a word denoting a place].
Pertaining to the night, nocturnal, belonging to the onset of night.
The evening twilight (prādoṣa).
After the word *śvas*, the suffix *ṭhañ* may optionally be applied, and there is the augment *tuṭ* added to it.

In the case of these words—*dvāra*, *svar*, *vyalkaśa*, *svasti*, *svara*, *sphyakṛt*, *svādu*, *mṛdu*, *śvas*, *śvan*, and *sva*—there is neither *vṛddhi* nor the substitution of *aij* [for *iK*] before the suffix *ṭhañ*. For example:
*śauvastikam*. (SK 1387)
From words such as *saṃdhivela* and others, from names of seasons (*ṛtu*), and from names of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) that denote time, the suffix *am* (forming adjectives) shall be applied.
For example, that which exists at the time of twilight (*saṃdhivela*) is *sāndhivelam*.
The summer solstice, the month of Taiṣa, the junction of seasons, twilight, the new moon day, the thirteenth day, the fourteenth day, the full moon day, and the first day of the lunar fortnight.
(ga) From the year, there is the fruit and the festival; that which pertains to the year is the annual fruit or festival, while the other is distinct.
SK 1388 AS 4-3-17 *prāvṛṣeṇyaḥ* (pertaining to the rainy season)
The garment suitable for the rainy season is called *vārṣika*. (SK 1389; AS 4.3.18)

"In the sense of 'properly' (sādhu), [the suffix *kha* is applied] when flowers bloom or fruits ripen according to their proper time" (Pāṇini 4.3.22). This refers to the meaning of "proper" (sādhu) [as stated in Pāṇini 5.1.97].

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after *hemanta*, with the elision of the *tal* (the final syllable), in both Vedic and worldly usage; by virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* optionally applies as well, resulting in *haimanam*.
haimantam SK 1391 AS 4-3-23: pertaining to winter; belonging to the winter season.

From the four indeclinables beginning with *sāyam* and from other words denoting time, the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* occur; moreover, there is the augment *tuṭ*, which is substituted before the initial portion of these two suffixes,
as indicated by the rule *anadyatane* (Pāṇini 4.2.105) and others.
In the words *sāyantanam* and *cirantam*,
the final vowel of the first members is substituted by *e* and *a* respectively, as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
prāhṇetana, pragetana,
doṣātanam.
The suffix *tana* should optionally be stated after *cira*, *parut*, and *parāri* to denote what occurred during the day;
[thus] *ciratna*.
The words *parutna* and *parāritna*,
when preceded by *agra* and so forth, optionally take the suffix *ḍimac*.
The foremost, the first, and the last.
And from the end, the final [syllable] (optionally). SK 1392
After these two [words], the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* optionally occur; furthermore, in one alternative, there is the augment *tuṭ*, and in another alternative, the suffix *ṭhañ*.
In the forms *pūrvāhṇetana* and *aparāhṇetana*,
there is no elision (*aluk*) according to Pāṇini’s rule *ghakālataneṣu*.
In the analysis of the compound *pūrvāhṇatanam* as "that which has endured the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇaḥ soḍho 'sya*), the form *paurvāhṇikam* [is derived]. Similarly, there is *aparāhṇatanam*.
The afternoon [meal] (āparāhṇika).
The suffixes beginning with *aṇ* and those beginning with *gha* occur after a word ending in the seventh case (locative), in the sense of "born there. For example:
one born in Sṛughna is *sraughna*; one born in Utśa is *autsa*.
"Rāṣṭriya," "avārapārīṇa," and so forth—
AS 4-3-26: An exception to [the suffix] eṇya;
that which is born in the rainy season is *prāvṛṣikaḥ*.
An exception to [the suffix] ṛtvaṇ.
The autumnal *darbha* grasses and specific types of mung beans.
This governing rule (adhikāra) extends from the sūtra *hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.36) up to [the sūtra] *SK 1397* (*AS 7.3.11*).

When a *taddhita* suffix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* follows, there shall be *vṛddhi* of the first vowel among the vowels of a second member that denotes a season, provided it is preceded by a first member denoting a part [of a year]. For example:
*pūrvavārṣikaḥ* (belonging to the first half of the rainy season) and *aparahaimanaḥ* (belonging to the latter half of winter).

Why [is the word] "avayavāt" [stated]? [Consider: "paurvavarṣikaḥ," meaning "one who exists in the preceding rains. Regarding the rule for the increase [of the suffix] after a season (*ṛtu*), there is an application of the *tadanta-vidhi* (the rule that the designation applies to the whole ending in that) in the preceding case. Or rather, [it is stated] "pūrvatra" (in the preceding).
But in this case, it is not so, because there is an absence of being a constituent part (avayavatva).
There is vṛddhi of the second member [of the compound], as in *supāñcālakaḥ*.

The suffix *vuñ* [is applied] after the words *sarva-pāñcālaka* and *ardha-pāñcālaka*, according to the rule: "After a country name and its derivative ending in *-vadhya-*, [the suffix *vuñ* is applied]. (Pāṇini 4.2.125).
The rule *susarvārdhadikśabdebhyo janapadasya* (Pāṇini 5.3.28) is interpreted as a *tadantavidhi* (a rule applying to words ending in those terms), according to the Vārttika (SK 1399, AS 7.3.13).
The *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs after a word denoting a direction that signifies a country, as in *pūrvapañcālakaḥ*; why [is it specified] "after a direction"?
This [person] belongs to the Eastern Pañcālas, thus he is a *paurvapañcāla*; [what about] one from among the Madras—
is he a *paurvamadra*?
The separation of the *yoga* rule is for the sake of what follows (SK 1400;
There is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final syllable of words denoting directions, words denoting cities, words denoting villages, and names of women. For example:
*pūrvaiṣukāmaśamaḥ*, meaning "one who resides in Pūrveṣukāmaśamī"; for a city: *pūrvapāṭaliputrakaḥ*.
*pūrvāhṇakaḥ* (one who belongs to the forenoon).
The afternoon meal consists of fresh ginger and radish.
Pradoṣaka is a refuse-heap.
Panthaka is one born on the road (pathi). (AS 4-3-29;
[The suffix -ka] forms *amāvāsyaka* and *āmāvāsya*.
The new moon day (amāvāsya). SK 1404 AS 4-3-31.
SK 1405 AS 4-3-32 sindhukaḥ (a type of salt)

When the suffix *aṇ* [denoted by] *kacchādyaṇ* and the suffix *vuñ* [denoted by] *manuṣyavuñ* would otherwise apply, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied instead]; when the general suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied instead].
They exist in sequence.
Saindhava is a benefactor.
After these words denoting lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), there shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffix expressing birth (*jāta*).
When there is elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix, there shall also be elision of a feminine suffix that is not a secondary member (*upasarjana*). [Example:
"Born under the *śraviṣṭhā* [nakṣatra]" becomes *śraviṣṭhaḥ*.
Regarding the rule beginning with *phalguna*,
there is an option (*vā*) to include the feminine forms of *citrā*, *revatī*, and *rohiṇī*:
one born under *citrā* is called *citrā*.
When the suffix *luk* is applied to *revatī* and *rohiṇī* by the rule *luktaddhitaluki*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added again because these words belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* known as *pippalyādi*.
After *phalgunī* and *aṣāḍhā*, the suffixes *ṭāp* and *an* should be stated [respectively];
[the rule] "in the feminine" (*striyām*) applies here as well,
thus [we have] *phalgunī*.
The suffix *chaṇ* should be applied after the words *aṣāḍhā* and *śraviṣṭhā*,
even when they do not denote a feminine gender.
The month of Śrāvaṇa; the month of Āṣāḍha.

In the word *proṣṭhapadā*, there is *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel at the beginning of the final member when followed by a suffix beginning with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* that denotes "born under" (*jātārtha*). Thus, one born under the *proṣṭhapadā* asterisms is *prauṣṭhapadaḥ*.
Because of the use of the plural number, the synonym Bhādrapada is also included.
After these [words], there shall be elision (luk) of the suffix expressing the sense of "born from" (jātārtha); for example, *goṣṭhānaḥ*.
In the case of *gośālaḥ*, *kharaśālaḥ*,
and *vibhāṣā senā* (Pāṇini 2.4.25), the short vowel is substituted when the word is in the neuter gender.
After these [words], there may optionally be elision (luk) of the suffix expressing the sense of "born from" (jāta).

In the sense of "born in," as in *vatsaśāle jātaḥ* ("born in Vatsaśāla"), the suffix *aṇ* is restated [after *vatsaśāla*] and should optionally be stated as having the augment *ḍit*, resulting in forms such as *vātsaśālaḥ*.
Śātabhiṣaḥ,
śātabhiṣajaḥ, śatabhiṣak.
In the sense of "born from" (jāta), there is frequently (bahulam) elision (luk) of the suffix (pratyaya).
Rohiṇa, Rauhiṇa. (SK 1413)
By the word *tatra* alone [the suffix -yañ is applied];
for example, one who has been made, obtained, purchased, or is skilled in Srughna is called *sraughna*.
In that case, it is simply "there. (SK 1414; AS 4-3-39)
One who generally or predominantly resides in Srughna is called *sraughna*.
Reaching up to the knees; reaching up to the ears; reaching up to the neck.
One who is born in Sṛghna is called *sraughna*.
Silk cloth.
That which is suitable for winter is *haimanta*, as in "a rampart (*prākāra*) [suitable for winter]."
In spring, the vernal kunda creepers flower;
in autumn, the autumnal rice crops ripen.
Barley that is sown in winter is called "winter barley" (haimanta).
This is an exception to the suffix *ṭhañ*.
Beans sown on the full moon day of Āśvayuja are called *āśvayujaka* beans.
In the alternative view, the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* [is applied].
The summer [rite],
the summer [rite], and the spring [rite].
The suffix *cha* (*ya*) is applied after the word *vāsanta*, provided that it does not denote a month.
A debt due monthly must be paid at the end of that very month.
That time during which peacocks possess their plumage is, by metaphorical usage, called "kalāpī"; a debt to be paid at that time is *kālapakam*.
The fruit of the *aśvattha* tree is *aśvattha*; the time associated with that [fruit] is also called *aśvattha*.
When the *aśvattha* trees bear fruit, there one should give the *aśvatthaka* offering;
when barley chaff arises, there one should give the *yavabusaka* offering.
A debt that is to be paid in the summer is "graiṣmaka"; it is equal to the [interest] for the interval between the seasons.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after a word ending in *ca*, when it denotes a collection.
Annual,
yearly, pertaining to the month of Āgrahāyaṇa.
The month of Āgrahāyaṇaka (SK 1426; AS 4-3-51).

The suffixes *aṇ* and others are applied after words denoting time ending in the locative case in the sense of "it cries out [at that time]"; if the one who cries out is a wild animal (*mṛga*), as in:
"it cries out at night," it is a *naiśa* or *naiśika* wild animal.
Only from [the word] *kāla*.
Study conducted during the night is "niśā-sahacara"; that which is endured during that [time] is "naiśa" (pertaining to the night) or "naiśika.
AS 4-3-53: That which exists in Sṛghna is *sraughna*; [the suffix] *rāṣṭriya* [is applied after the word *rāṣṭra*].
[The suffix -ya] is applied after a word denoting direction.
That which belongs to a class (vargya).
Tooth-paste for the ears.

In the region of the easterners, when the suffixes ñit, ṇit, or kit follow, there is the substitution of a vṛddhi vowel for the initial vowel of both the first and the second members of a compound ending in "nagara. For example:
*suhmanagare bhavaḥ* (born in the city of Suhma) becomes *sauhmanāgaraḥ*.
Is "paurvanāgara" used for those born in the eastern city, and "mānagara" for one born there in the northern direction?

For a stem ending in *jaṅgala* or similar words, when it is a prior member [of a compound], there is optionally the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the first vowel among the vowels of the subsequent member, provided that the subsequent member ends in a suffix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*.
Born in Kurujaṅgala is *kaurujaṅgalaja*; belonging to the Viśvedevas is *vaiśvadevanam* or *vaiśvadhainavam*.
Having a golden shaft and having golden feathers.
The word *dārteya* means "belonging to a sword" (*kaukṣeya*).
*Kalaśi* means a jar; that which is produced therein is *kālaśeya*. [Similarly,] *vāsteya* and *āsteya*.
This is not to be avoided.
And from *grīvā*, [the suffix] *ḍhañ* [is applied],
[forming] *graiveyam* and *graivam*.
That which exists in the profound is profundity (*gāmbhīrya*).
The addition of "pañcajana" [to the list of words for which the suffix -yaṇ is applied] is proposed [by some]; thus, [the word] is *pāñcajanya*.
*pārimukhyam* (that which exists around the face) is desired [only] after *parimukha* and similar words (or, according to some).
In this case,
*aupakūlaḥ* [is derived with the suffix *aṇ*].
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after an *avyayībhāva* compound, provided it ends in the word *veśman*; thus, *antarveśmam*.
In that context, the suffix -īya is desired [to express] "belonging to" (*bhava*), "internal" (*antarveśmika*), "belonging to the same group" (*āntargaṇika*), or "belonging to oneself" (*adhyātma*).
Internal existence is the internal [existence].
For these, there shall be vṛddhi substitution for both members of the compound when followed by a suffix marked with Ñ, Ṇ, or K:
*ādhidaivikam*, *ādhibhautikam*.
Aihalaukika, pāralaukika,
adhyātma, and so forth constitute a class of words based on their form (ākṛtigaṇa).
When these five [vowels] undergo *vṛddhi*, the substitute *āt* shall take the place of the vowel *a* before an affix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*.
*Dāvikā* refers to rice growing on the banks of the Devikā river;
*śāṃśapa* refers to a cup made from the modification of *śiṃśapā* wood.
From *palāśa* and other such words, the suffix *tyañ* is applied; thus,
from *dityauha* comes *dātyauha*,
and from *dīrghasatra* comes *dārghasatram*.
The word *bhava* becomes *śrāyasa* when it follows *śreyas*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* shall be applied after an *avyayībhāva* compound; thus,
[from *pari-grāma*] we have *pārigrāmikaḥ*.
ānugrāmikaḥ (one who belongs to a village) SK 1441 AS 4-3-62
The jihvāmūlīya and the upadhmānīya.
A letter belonging to the *ka*-group [is substituted] for [the final consonant of the preceding word].
According to the previous rule, the suffix *cha* is optionally applied; thus,
*madvargyaḥ*.
"Belonging to my group" (*madvargīṇaḥ*) and "belonging to my group" (*madvargīyaḥ*);
why [is the suffix] not used when there is no word [ending in a vowel]?
A letter belonging to the *ka*-group [is the substitute for the final of a word ending in a consonant].
A fillet for the forehead; a circlet.
The term *saupa* refers to a treatise that provides an exposition of the case endings (*sup*), and *taiṅa* refers to one that provides an exposition of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).
The suffix *kṛt* occurs after [stems ending in] case endings (*sup*),
and that which occurs after [stems ending in] case endings is called *sau-pa*.
The grammatical rule (*śāstra*) that prescribes the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṇ* is called *ṣatva-ṇatva*; that which explains it, or that which exists therein, is *ṣātvaṇatvika*.
In sacrifices to be accomplished by means of Soma, these two [terms] are well-known.
In that case, since the matter is established by the mention of either one, both are included here by virtue of the force of mentioning both; thus,
"pertaining to the Agniṣṭoma" (*āgniṣṭomika*) means either what is explained in the Agniṣṭoma or what occurs therein, and likewise for "pertaining to the Vājapeya" (*vājapeyika*).
The term *pākayajñika* does not include the *nāvayajñika*; the use of the plural number is for the purpose of excluding the injunction regarding the specific form [of the sacrifice].
This rule is formulated for the purpose of ensuring that the word has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after words denoting sages (*ṛṣi*)—which function as titles of texts to be explained—to form derivatives signifying either "belonging to" or "an exposition of" [that sage].
For example, a mantra seen by Vasiṣṭha is called *Vasiṣṭha*; an exposition of that, or something occurring therein, is a *Vāsiṣṭhika* chapter.
In the chapters, what is the Vāsiṣṭhī Ṛc?
A mantra associated with the *puroḍāśa* is called *puroḍāśa*; that very [mantra] is *pauroḍāśa*, from which the suffix *ṭhan* is applied.
The word *pauroḍāśikaḥ* [is formed by adding the suffix -ṭhak to *puroḍāśa-*] according to Pāṇini 4.3.71.
One who belongs to the Veda;
one who follows the Vedic rules.
A word consisting of two syllables [is used] in the sense of "pertaining to the iṣṭi."
The animal sacrifice and the Cāturhotṛka rite.
A Brāhmaṇika, an Ārcika, and so forth.
An exception to [the suffixes] beginning with ṭhañ.
A student of the Āraṇyakas, a student of the Upaniṣads, and a grammarian.
One who has come from Srughna is called *sraughna*.
One who has come from a customs house is called *śaulkaśālika*.
An exception to [the suffixes] -āyasthāna, -ṭhak, -cha, and so forth.
One who comes from a tavern is a *śauṇḍika*; one from *kārkaṇa* is a *kārkaṇa*;
one from *tīrtha* is a *tairtha*.
aupādhyāyakaḥ (SK 1456, AS 4.3.77) means "pertaining to a teacher."
The suffix -ka (kan) is applied after the word *pitāmaha* to form the sense of "belonging to" or "descended from.
(Pāṇini 4.3.79)
The exclusion of the *vuñ* suffix applies to words ending in *-pautra* and *-bhrātṛ*.
After [a word ending in] *ca*,
the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied [to form a derivative denoting "belonging to that"].
By the rule *rīṅ ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.27) and *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant],
resulting in *pitryam*.
Inherited from the father (paitṛka).
A descendant of Bida (Baida),
a descendant of Garga (Gārga), a descendant of Dakṣa (Dākṣa).
The state of being a descendant of Upagu (aupagavaka).

When a suffix beginning with the *ñ* or *ṇ* group follows, there is optionally the substitution of a *vṛddhi* vowel for the initial vowel of the five words beginning with *śuci*, provided that the preceding member ends in *su*; thus,
from *śuci*, we have both *āśaucam* and *aśaucam*.
Lack of mastery is non-mastery;
it is not the domain of the kṣetrajña.
Lack of skill regarding the knowledge of the senses is unskillfulness.
Lack of skill,
lack of proficiency.
That which has come together is of equal form; that which is not of equal form is of unequal form.
In the sense of "on the side," the suffix *cha* is applied because it belongs to the *gahādi* group; thus, we have *samīyam* and *viṣamīyam*.
Belonging to Devadatta: *devadattarūpyam*, *devadattīyam*,
*daivadattam*.
SK 1462 AS 4-3-82 samamayam: [The suffix -yaṅ is applied after the word *sama* to form a denominative verb meaning "to act like that which is equal to oneself."]
This is full of poison;
this is full of Devadatta.
AS 4-3-83: By the rule "tataḥ" (from that), [the suffix ṅīṣ is applied] after "himavat"; thus, the Gaṅgā originates from Himavat and is called Haimavatī.
A vaidūrya gem originates from Vidūra (SK 1464; AS 4.3.84).
*srughnaṃ gacchati* [means] "a path leading to Srughna" or "a messenger going to Srughna."
That very [word] "tat" (it).
The word *sraughna* is formed from *srughna* when it means "departing for" or "the gate of Kānyakubja belonging to Srughna.
The work composed concerning the *Śārīraka* itself is called *Śārīrakīya*;
however, it is termed the *Śārīraka-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Śārīraka) by way of metaphorical identification.
Pāṇini 4.3.88: *śiśukranda* is the crying of infants; a treatise composed concerning that is called *śiśukrandīya*.
The assembly hall of Yama is *yamasabha*; it is neuter due to irregular grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), and [one who belongs to] the assembly of Yama is *yamasabhīya*.

The *autsaṅgika* thief carries off [the goods] by means of his lap (AS 4.4.15).
In the rule *bhastrayā harati bhastrikaḥ*, because of the presence of the marker *ṣit*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
The bellows-like [breathing] (bhastrikī),
One who carries by means of a pole is a *vivadhika*;
alternatively, with the suffix *ṭhak*, it is *vaivadhika*.
Because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original], from *vīvadha* as well, by the suffix *ṣṭhan*,
we have *vīvadhikaḥ* (a carrier of loads) and *vīvadhikī* (a female carrier of loads).
The two words *vīvadha* and *vīvadha* refer to a wooden pole for carrying loads on the shoulder, with baskets tied to both ends.
*Kuṭilikā* is a specific gait of hunters; it is also iron used as an instrument for applying [deceitful] actions.
One who acts with *kuṭilikā*—whether a hunter or a blacksmith—carries away deer or charcoal by means of that crookedness.
Enmity arising from gambling with dice is called *ākṣadyūtika*.

After a word ending in the third case that has as its base a word ending in the three suffixes [taddhita-suffixes -aṇ, -ṭyaP, and -aK], the suffix *map* shall always be used in the sense of "produced from"; for example, *kṛtyā nirvṛttam* becomes *kṛtrimam*.
A word ending in a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) may optionally take the suffix *ima* when preceded by *paktrimam*; thus,
that which is produced by cooking is *pākimam*.
One who is generous (tyāgin).
*Āpamityaka* is derived from *apamitya*, a gerund (lyap-ending); it means "obtained by borrowing" or "that which is produced by what has been borrowed," i.e., something obtained through a loan.
*Yācitaka* is that which is produced by what has been requested (*yācita*).
*dādhikam* means "mixed with curd."
Apūpas mixed with powders are called *cūrṇinaḥ*.
Soup mixed with salt is "salted."
Salted vegetables.
Rice cooked with mung beans (maudga-odana).
The suffix *ṭhak* [is applied after the word *dadhi*] when it means "sprinkled with curd"; thus, *dādhika*.
One who acts with vigor (*ojas*) is *aujasika*; [this refers to] a hero and a reckless thief.
A fish in water.
The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after this word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) in the sense of "it proceeds from that";
since it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the second case is used:
"he proceeds against," *prātīpikaḥ*.
Following along,
acting in reverse order, and acting in opposition.
Conformable (ānukūlika) [is the name for the *anvaya* type of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference].
That which exists around the face is *pārimukhika*,
and it is also called *pāripārśvika*.
One who gives double for the sake of a double amount is a *dvaiguṇika*; one who gives triple is a *traiguṇika*.
It should be stated that the substitution of *vṛdhuṣi* for *vṛddhi* occurs [optionally]; thus, *vārdhuṣikaḥ*.
After these two [roots] which have the sense of "blameworthy," these two suffixes occur in the sense of "he gives";
*kusīda* means interest, and the substance for that purpose is *kusīda*; one who gives that is a *kusīdika*.

In the analysis of the compound *kusīdikī* as "eleven meanings" (*ekādaśārthatvāt*) and "those eleven are in fact ten" (*te ca te vastuto daśa*), the suffix *aka* is prescribed here by this very rule [Pāṇini 5.1.28] as the final member of the compound, resulting in *daśaikādaśikaḥ*.
In the expression *daśaikādaśikī*—
meaning "she gives eleven for ten"— it is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) alone who is the referent of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).
A *bādarika* is one who gathers jujube fruits by gleaning. (AS 4.4.32;
One who protects an assembly is a member of the assembly (sāmājika). (AS 4-4-33;
AS 4-4-34: One who makes a sound is called a *śābdika* (grammarian); one who makes the sound of a frog is called a *dārdurika*.
There is the apprehension of the essential nature (or its synonyms) and of the particulars.
In the sequence of fish,
the fisherman kills the fish itself; the fowler kills the bird.
A fowler, a fisherman, and a trapper.
A fowler, a hunter of deer, and a deer-trapper.
Sāraṅgika (the name of a person) SK 1586;

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after a word ending in the second case in the sense of "he stands" or "he strikes," with the exception of the word *panthān*. For example: one who stands obstructing the path is a *pāripanthika* thief;
one who strikes at the path is a *pāripanthika*.
A path that is straight like a staff is called a *daṇḍamātha*. (SK 1587; AS 4.4.37)
The pursuer of Daṇḍamātha runs after Daṇḍamātha; he is a foot-soldier,
one who follows in the footsteps.
From this [word], the suffix *ṭhañ* shall occur, and optionally *ṭhak*, in the sense of "running after."
One who runs toward a place of weeping for those in distress is called *ākrandika*.
One who takes the first member [of a compound] is called *paurvapadika*; one who takes the final member is called *auttarapadika*.
After these [words], the suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied in the sense of "grasping";
for example, *pratikaṇṭham gṛhṇāti* (he grasps by the throat) becomes *prātikaṇṭhikaḥ*.
ārthikaḥ (one who lives by wealth), lālāmikaḥ (one who lives by saliva).
It should be stated that he is righteous (dhārmika) because of his departure from unrighteousness (adharmāt), or else he is unrighteous (adhārmika).
One who goes along the road is a *prātipathika*.
Constituent member of a whole.
Pertaining to a group; collective.
One who belongs to an assembly is a member of the assembly (pāriṣadya).
The suffix *ṇya* may optionally occur, while *ṭhak* forms *sainyāḥ* and *sainikāḥ*.
A servant who watches the master’s brow is called *lālāṭika*.
By the word "kukkuṭī" (a hen's perch), a very small area suitable for her to alight upon is indicated; [thus] a "kaukkuṭika" is a monk.
The word *āpaṇika* denotes that which is lawful for a marketplace (*āpaṇa*).
The ritual duty pertaining to the mahiṣī is called māhiṣa; it belongs to the sacrificer.
The journey of a traveler is righteous when it is for the purpose of traveling.

And it should be stated that [the suffix *ya*] is added after the word *nara*; or rather, it should be stated that for the word *nara*, the feminine form is *nārī*, and that there is the elision of the *iṭ* augment and the addition of the suffix *añ* for the agent of the act of cutting (*viśasitṛ*).

The word *vaiśastra* is derived from *viśasitṛ* [meaning "one who slaughters"] with the suffix *dharmya*; alternatively, it should be stated that there is elision of the *ṇi* and the addition of *añ*. The word *vaibhājitra* is derived from *vibhājayitṛ* [meaning "one who distributes"] with the suffix *dharmya*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word ending in the sixth case (genitive) in the sense of "rent" or "hire."
The rent of a shop is the *āpaṇika*;
the substance to be taken by the king is the *avakraya*.
One whose merchandise consists of cakes is called *āpūpika*. (AS 4.4.51;
A seller of salt (lāvaṇika) [is derived from lavaṇa with the suffix -ika].
*kisara* is his merchandise; [the suffix] *ṭhan* is added, resulting in *kisarikaḥ*; because of the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
*Kisarikī*,
*kisara*, *uśīra*, *nalada*, and so forth—
all these terms denote specific fragrant substances.
In the alternative case, *ṣṭhan* or *ṭhak* [should be applied].
Śalāluka, śalālukī, and śālāluka.
Śālālukī and śalālu are specific types of fragrant substances.
One whose craft is the playing of the mṛdaṅga drum is called *mārdaṅgika*.
For one whose craft is the playing of the madduka drum, [the suffix ṭhak is applied], as in *māḍḍukaḥ* or *māḍḍukikaḥ*.
Jhārjhara and jhārjharika (SK 1607).
*tadasyeti* [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after [a word denoting a weapon];
*asiḥ praharaṇam asya* means "a sword is his weapon," resulting in *āsikaḥ*.
The word *dhānuṣka* [is formed by adding the suffix *kan*] after the word *dhanus*.
(Pāṇini 4.4.58)
One who wields a battle-axe is called *pāraśvadhikaḥ*.
(Pāṇini 4.4.59)
A spearman; a clubman.
*tadasyeti eva* means "one who has such a conviction as 'this world exists' and 'the other world exists' is an *āstika*."
He whose view is that "it does not exist" is not a nihilist;
he whose view is that "it is destiny" is a fatalist.
One whose habit is the eating of cakes is called *āpūpikaḥ*. (AS 4-4-61;
The word *chātra* refers to one whose habit (*śīla*) is to provide a covering (*āvaraṇa*) for the teacher’s faults (*gurordoṣāṇām*), namely an umbrella (*chatra*).

In the word *kārma*, the elision of the suffix *ṭi* is prescribed by nipātana when the suffix *ṇa* is added in the sense of habitual tendency (*tācchīlya*); thus, one whose nature is action (*karmaśīla*) is called *kārma*.

Since the result is already established by the rule *nastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144), the specific operation of *aṇ* is prescribed even for the *ṇa*-suffix used in the sense of habitual character (*tācchīlika*);
thus, forms such as *caurī* and *tāpasī* are established. [Question: Why is it specified "in the sense of habitual character"?
The kārmaṇa [body] is [the cause of] the [subsequent] body.

The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after a word ending in the nominative case to express the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), provided that the action denoted by the nominative is one undertaken for the purpose of study. For example, *aikānyikaḥ*:
he who, having engaged in study, committed a single error at the time of examination consisting of a wrong pronunciation.
In the domain of what precedes [the rule], SK 1615 / AS 4.4.64.

The meaning is: "He has twelve other [instances of] actions occurring during his study; he is one for whom there are twelve 'anyikas' (miscarriages), i.e., twelve errors in recitation have occurred. (SK 1616)
*apūpabhakṣaṇam* (the eating of cakes) is beneficial for him; thus, he is called *āpūpikaḥ*.
One to whom the first portion of food is invariably given is called *āgrabhojanikaḥ*.
*śrāṇikaḥ* and *śrāṇikī* mean "one to whom boiled gruel (*śrāṇā*) is given as a regular portion."
The inclusion of "meat-rice" (māṃsaudana) is for the purpose of including both compounded and uncompounded meanings; thus,
one who deals in meat-rice is a *māṃsaudanika*, and one who deals in meat is a *māṃsika*.
One who eats rice; a rice-eater (odanika).
Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.4.68: *odanādibhyo ṭhañ*.
In this sense, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied: *bhaktaḥ* means "to whom food is assigned," while *bhāktikaḥ* means "one who receives food."
One appointed to a mine is an *ākarika*.
One appointed to a temple is a *devāgārika*.
According to Pāṇini 4.3.71,
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word denoting a prohibited place or time when it refers to one who studies [there or at that time].
One who studies in a cremation ground is a *śmāśānika*;
one who studies on the fourteenth day is a *cāturdaśika*.
By the rule *tatra ity eva vaṃśakaṭhine vyavaharati vāṃśakaṭhinikaḥ*, one who deals in bamboo and leather is called a *vāṃśakaṭhinika*.

The meaning is that in whatever region there are bamboos (*vaṃśa*) and reeds (*veṇu*) that are hard— that is, in a region characterized by such hardness (*vaṃśakaṭhina*)— he performs exactly in that manner whatever action is to be performed in that region;
he is thus a "prāstārika" (one who follows local customs) and a "sāṃsthānika" (one who conforms to established institutions).
A monk who stays nearby (a *naikaṭika* bhikṣu).
One who dwells in a lodging is an *āvasathika*.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after [a word ending in] *śit*, as in *āvasathikī*;
it is also optionally applied after words beginning with *ākarṣa* and *parpa*, after words beginning with *bhastrā*, and after the word *kusīda*.

"From *āvasatha*, *kisara*, and so forth, [the suffix] *ṣit*": this means that these six [suffixes] are prescribed by the six sūtras [beginning with Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.75] under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *ṭhak*.
"Six" refers to those established by the group of six sūtras.
The seven suffixes beginning with *pratyaya* have been explained; the limit for *ṭhak* is thus concluded.
This concludes the section on the *ṭhak* suffix within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*).
Now, within the section on secondary derivatives (taddhita), the section beginning with "prāg-dhita" [SK 1626; Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.4.75].
That which is governed [by the rule] from *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5) up to before *SK Sandarbhaḥ 1665* is [governed by] *yad adhikriyate* (Pāṇini 4.4.76).
That which draws the chariot is the *rathya*;
that which is yoked at the time of training the calves is the *yugya*; and the piece of wood placed upon the shoulder is the *prāsaṅga*.
The draft-animal carries that [load] by means of the yoke-pole. (Pāṇini 4.4.77)
When the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.69) would otherwise require the substitution of a long vowel, [the following applies]:
There should not be lengthening of the penultimate vowel of *kurchura* and *bhṛśa*;
[examples are] *dhuryaḥ* and *dhaureyaḥ*.
One who carries every burden is called *sarvadhurīṇa*.
That which carries a single burden is *ekadhurīṇa*.
One who bears a single yoke.
A cart-pulling ox is called a *śākaṭa*.
The plowman, the son of a Sairandhri, drives the oxen.
The word *janya* refers to those who carry or bring the bride (*janī*, *vadhū*) [to the groom's house].
According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.4.83,
the suffix *yat* is applied after a word ending in the accusative case in the sense of "pierces," provided that a bow is not the instrument; for example,
*padyāḥ śarkarāḥ*, "pebbles that pierce the feet."
This [word] ends in the suffix *tṛn*. (SK 1636; AS 4.4.84)
Having obtained wealth, he is fortunate; having obtained a multitude, he is counted among the eminent.
Having obtained food, he is called "Anna" (the eater).
*Vaśya* means one who follows the will of another (AS 4-4-86);
*padya* refers to mud that is not completely dry; this is the meaning.
*Ābarhaṇa* means *ābarha*, which is uprooting; that which possesses this is called *ābarhin*.
Those for whom the root is removed are "mūlyāḥ," as in the case of mung beans.

The augment *ṣuk* and the suffix *ya* are irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*) for the word *dhenu* in its own sense when it forms a technical name (*saṃjñā*); thus, *dhenuṣyā* means "a cow pledged as collateral. (SK 1642)
AS 4.4.90: The householder is the sacrificer; the Gārhapatya fire is that which is connected with him.
That which is to be crossed by a boat is *nāvya*; one who is equal in age is *vayasya*.
That which is obtainable by means of dharma is *dharmyam*;
one who is to be killed by poison is *viṣyaḥ*; that which is to be bent down by means of a root is *mūlyam*.
"Equal in value to the root [price] is *mūlya*; a field measured by the furrow is *sītya*;
that which is measured by a balance is *tulya*."
That which does not deviate from dharma is *dharmya*.
wholesome, meaningful, and just.
That which is composed in the Vedic meters is called *chandasya*.
The meaning is "done by desire" (icchayā kṛtam).
Furthermore, a son produced from the chest (uras) is called *aurasa*,
*aurasya*, or *urasya*.
A region dear to the heart (hṛdya).
By the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.50), there is the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya*;
this is stated in SK 1648 and AS 4.4.96.
From the word *hṛdaya* ending in the genitive case, the suffix *yat* occurs when "binding" is to be expressed in the Veda;
thus, *hradyo vaśīkaraṇamantraḥ* means "a spell for subjugation that binds the heart.
The word *mata* means knowledge; its instrument (*karaṇa*), state (*bhāva*), or means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is *matya*.
The speech of a person is *janya*.
The suffix *ya* is applied after the word *hala* to form *halya*, meaning "ploughable.
*agre sādhuḥ* becomes *agryaḥ*;
*sāmasu sādhuḥ* becomes *sāmanyaḥ*.
By the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāvaḥ*).
Capable of action and a source of refuge.
*pratijanam* [becomes] *prātijanīnaḥ*;
*sāṃyugīnaḥ*.
Belonging to all people;
belonging to all mankind.
The term *bhākta* refers to those things which are fit for consumption; for example, rice grains.
According to Pāṇini 4.4.101, *pāripadyaḥ* is derived from *pariṣad* by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*), which also allows for the suffix *ṇya*.
The reading "pariṣadaḥ parṣadaḥ" [is explained as] "pārṣadaḥ."
One who is skilled in discourse is called *kāthika*.
Sugarcane that is good for molasses is called *gauḍika*.
Barley grains that have been parched are called *sāktuka*.

That which is suitable for the road is *pātheya* (provisions for a journey); that which is suitable for a guest is *ātitheya* (hospitality); that which is suitable for clothing is *vasana*; and the night suitable for dwelling there is *vāsateyī*.
svāpateyam means wealth.
A member of an assembly (sabhyah) [is so called] when he possesses the qualities mentioned in Pāṇini 4.4.107.
One who has desisted from improper conduct is a *sādhu*;
one who dwells [with another] is a *vāsī*;
and one who dwells with a teacher at the same sacred site (*tīrtha*) is a *satīrthya*.
One who has lain or stayed in the same womb is a uterine brother (samānodarya).
SK 1660 AS 4-4-109 sodaryaḥ (a uterine brother)
The meaning is as before;
thus, within the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), this concludes the section on *prāgghitīya* suffixes.
Now begins the section on the application of the suffixes *-cha* and *-ya* in the sense of "worth" (*ārhīya*) within the section on secondary derivatives.
From SK 1661 (AS 5-1-1 *tena krītam*) up until *SKsandarbhaḥ* 1702, the suffix *cha* is governed.
"Only [the rule] prior to krīta," thus [it is stated].
The suffix *yat* shall apply after words ending in *u* and after *go* and so forth; this is an exception to [the application of] *cha*.
(Gaṇasūtra) Furthermore, *nābhi* becomes *nabha-*; thus, *nabhya-* refers to an axle.
Just as there is the insertion of the *mañjana* [nasal] in the case of the *nābhi* of a chariot wheel,
so too here there is the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *śu* [of *śvan*], and optionally the lengthening of the vowel.
The word *śūnya* is repeated (*śūnyam śūnyam*);
[the suffix] *naṅ* is substituted for the final vowel of *ūdhas*.
That which is conducive to prosperity.
What is the purpose of the technical term *kambalya* when it refers to one hundred palas of wool?
Wool belonging to a blanket-maker.
The curd is for the *āmikṣā*;
the rice grains are for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Pertaining to the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), pertaining to the cakes (apūpa).
The cowherd who is beneficial to the calves is called *vatsīya*.
Śaṅkavya refers to wood suitable for a stake; gavya refers to that which is fit for an oblation.
Dental.
That which is for the nose is *nasya*, [administered] from the throat or from the nose.
The suffix *nābhi* is applied [to form a bahuvrīhi compound] when it denotes the navel; Pāṇini 5.4.92.
When a taddhita suffix follows, the word *śiras* shall undergo the substitution *śīrṣan*; as in *śīrṣaṇyaḥ*.
Why "when a taddhita suffix follows"?
One desires the head (*śiras*) or acts for the sake of the head (*śirasyati*) with respect to the hair; thus,
the hair is called *śīrṣaṇyāḥ* or *śirasyāḥ*.
It should be stated that "aci śīrṣa" [is the rule]; when a taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel follows, *śiras* is replaced by *śīrṣa*.
Thus, for *sthaulaśiras*, the derivative form is *sthaulaśīrṣam*.
That which is beneficial for a threshing floor is called *khalyam*.
Barley, beans, and sesame.
It is aphrodisiac, beneficial to Brahmins,
and not to be used on a chariot path.
Not belonging to the herd, like one not born of the herd.
Non-delusion (avithyā) [is the cause of knowledge],
according to Sūtra 5.1.9.
These two [suffixes] occur by virtue of their inherent nature (*kheprakṛtyā*).
The term *ātmanīna* means "beneficial for oneself," while *viśvajanīna* means "beneficial for all people"; these two forms are desired only when derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The suffix *cha* alone is applied after a genitive tatpuruṣa compound and after a bahuvrīhi compound; furthermore, there is an extension [of this rule] for the word *pañcajana*. (Vārttika)
From *pañcajana*,
the suffixes *aṇ* and *khaś* are added [to form] *sārvajana*;
[with the suffix *iKa*], it becomes *sārvajanika*.
Known by all people;
[the suffix] *aṭṭhañ* (or *ika*) after *mahājana*:
*māhājanika*.
Enjoyed by the mother,
enjoyed by the father, enjoyed by the king.
(ga) And from "ācārya" there is the suffix -aṇ [with the elision of the final syllable],
as in *ācāryabhogīnaḥ*.
AS 5.1.10: It should be stated that "sarva" may optionally take the suffix "aṇ"; [thus] "sārva" means "beneficial for all."
Because of the usage by the author of the Bhāṣya in the passage "sarvīyam purūṣādvadhavikārasamūhatekṛteṣu," the word *tena* is inserted in the middle of the dvandva compound.
The killing of a person (*puruṣa*) is *pauruṣeya*; when the suffix *aṇ* [denoting "belonging to this"] would have applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*,
[it is instead] *pauruṣeya* meaning "a modification of a person" (*puruṣasya vikāraḥ*).

Regarding the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.116), the suffix *añ* would have applied [to words like *paura*]; however, since the suffix *aṇ* also applies to denote a collection (*samūha*), Māgha uses the phrase *ekākino'pi paritaḥ pauruṣeyavṛtā iva*.

Thus, the distinction is as follows: the suffix *aṇ* would apply to a work composed by him (*tena kṛte granthe*), whereas it does not apply at all to non-literary things such as palaces (*prāsādādau*).
That which is beneficial for a young boy is *māṇavīna*.
The term *cārakīṇam* [is formed by adding the suffix *khañ*] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.12.
The suffix *cha* shall be applied after a word ending in the dative case that denotes a modification, when the material cause (*prakṛti*) intended for that purpose is to be expressed; for example,
these are "aṅgārīyāṇi" (wooden sticks) for the sake of embers, or "prākārīyāḥ" (bricks) for the sake of a rampart.
Wood fit for a stake.
The word *chādiṣeya* refers to grasses; the word *bāleya* refers to rice grains; [in these cases] the suffix *ya* is desired in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
It is called *upadhi* because it is placed upon (*upadhīyate*); it is a component of a chariot, and that very thing is the *auṣadheya*.
The disparagement of a horse is [the comparison] to a calf fit for a bull; [the disparagement] of sandals is [the comparison] to *muñja* grass.
In the case of *carman* as well, by this same prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the form is *aupānahyam carma*.
The suffix *añ* shall be applied after a word denoting a modification of leather;
for example, this leather for a shield is called *vārdhra*.
A shield made of leather.

The wall of these bricks would be *prākāra*; the bricks belonging to the wall would be *prākārīyā* bricks; the wood for the palace would be *prāsādīya*; the region in which there is a wall would be *prākārīya*.
The word "iti" follows the worldly intention [of the speaker]; therefore, in this context, it does not mean "there would be a palace belonging to Devadatta."
Enclosed land.
The limit for the suffixes *cha* and *ya* has been reached;

as in: *yathāmukhaṃ darśanaḥ* becomes *yathāmukhīnaḥ*, meaning "one who shows the face of everyone," and *saṃmukhīnaḥ*, meaning "facing toward."
After a word beginning with *sarva* and ending in *pathin*, provided it is in the accusative case, the suffix *kha* shall be applied.
It pervades all paths; it is all-pervasive, extending to all limbs, and effective in all actions.
One who possesses all vessels;
one who is worthy of all vessels.
*Prapada* is the tip of the foot; a garment that extends as far as that limit is called *āprapadam* or *āprapadīna*.
The prefix *anu* is used in the sense of extension (*āyāma*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*).
A sandal whose straps are bound along the length and which has no heel-strap eats all kinds of food; a monk who eats all kinds of food is called *sarvānnīna*.
A particular place for driving back and forth is called *ayānaya*; a shuttle that moves back and forth over it is called *āyānayīna*.
He who experiences both the higher and the lower is called *parovarīṇa*.
The substitution of *u* for the final vowel of *avara* is prescribed by nipātana;
it experiences the subsequent and the further [stages], hence it is called *paramparīṇa*.
The state of being a succession (*paramparabhāva*) is prescribed by nipātana from the base *prakṛti*.

One experiences sons and grandsons; the word *putrapautrīṇaḥ* is a distinct, unanalyzed (avyutpanna) feminine noun. From that very word, by adding the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (*svārthe*), one obtains *pāramparyam*.
How is it that it is like *pārovarya*?
This [form] is indeed incorrect,
because the form *parovara* is established by nipātana (irregular derivation) specifically in connection with the suffix *kha*.
*avārapāraṃ gāmī* (one who goes from this shore to the other), *avāraparīṇaḥ*, and *avārīṇaḥ*.

Pārīṇa means one who has reached the further shore; pārāvārīṇa means one who goes from this shore to the other; atyantagāmī means one who goes to the end; and atyantīna means one who goes to the very limit.
The meaning is "one who goes excessively"; *anukāmīnaḥ* means "one who goes according to desire," that is,
one who goes as he pleases.
The elision of *ya* and the non-elision (*aluk*) of the remaining case-ending in the preceding member are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*).

The word *samāṃsamīnā* refers to a cow that calves every year; it is formed from the sense of "calving every year" (*prativarṣam prasūyate*). It should be stated that when the suffix *kha* does not arise, there is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of the *yaṇ*.
She gives birth every year, or every year.
*adyaśvīnā* means "she will give birth today or tomorrow"; that is, a mare (*vaḍavā*) whose delivery is imminent.
Some, however, do not follow the reading "vijāyate" (is born),
but rather interpret it as "adyaśvīnam," meaning that death is imminent.
The suffix *kha* is prescribed as a substitute for the word *go* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, when it denotes a laborer.
One who performs work until the return of the cow is called *āgavīna*.
The cowherd who follows after the cow, going as far as it goes, is called *anugavīna*.
One who goes a sufficient distance on a road is called *adhvanya* or *adhvanīna*;
[the suffix *khañ* is also used] after words meaning "non-existence" (*abhāva*) and "action" (*karman*). (Pāṇini 5.2.16)
By the two rules "ātman" (Pāṇini 6.4.141) and "adhvānaḥ khe" (Pāṇini 6.3.96), there is the absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* [sandhi] (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.126).
From the roots *cādi* and *khu*,
[the forms] *abhyamitrīya* and *abhyamitrya* [are derived].
*Abhyamitrīṇaḥ* means one who goes well toward the enemy; that is the meaning.
A place where cows formerly grazed is called *gauṣṭhīna*.
That which is traversed in one day is called *ekāhagama*, such as a horse-drawn journey (*āśvīna*) over a certain distance.
One who deserves entry into the hall is *śālīna*, meaning modest or unassuming.
The word *kaupīna* denotes sin, as it deserves to fall into a well (*kūpa-patana*);
likewise, by virtue of being its instrument, or because it must be concealed like that [sin], it refers to the male organ;
and by association with that, it also refers to the garment that covers it.
One who lives by means of a *vrāta*—
that is,
through physical exertion and not through the power of the intellect— is a *vrātīna*.
That which is obtained by seven steps is called *sāptapadīna*.

In the rule Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.23 (*hyogodohasya hiyaṅgurādeśaḥ khañ ca*), *hiyaṅgu* is substituted for *hyogodoha*, and the suffix *khañ* is also prescribed in the sense of a derivative product (*vikāra*).
That which is milked is "doha" (the milk); for butter made from yesterday's cow-milk (*hyogodoha*) is a derivative product (*vikāra*), namely *haiyaṅgavīna*, which is fresh butter (*navanīta*).
*pālukuṇaḥ* [is derived from] *pīlūnāṃ pākaḥ* (the ripening of Pilu fruits); *karṇajāham* [is derived from] *karṇasya mūlam* (the root of the ear).
In [Pāṇini] 5.2.25,
only the mention of the word "root" (mūla) is carried over.
The root of a wing is the *pakṣati*.
The letter *ya* is indicated as elided at the beginning of the two suffixes; therefore, the *ca* [of the root] does not receive the designation *it*. Thus:
*vidyayā vittaḥ* becomes *vidyācuñcuḥ* or *vidyācaṇaḥ*.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.27:
The suffixes [tasil and śas] occur in their own sense after words expressing the meaning of "separation" (asaha) or "distinctness" (pṛthagbhāva).
Without variety,
[The suffix *vistṛta*] occurs in its own sense after a word denoting a means qualified by an action.
Vast and expansive.
The narrow and the manifest.
And for *utkaṭa* and *advikaṭa*,
there is an addition of the suffix *raja* after *alābu*, *tila*, *ūma*, and *abhaṅga*. (Vārttika)
The suffix *kaṭa* is added after the word *alābu* when it means "dust," as in *alābukata*;
and the suffixes *ja*, etc., are added after animal names to denote their place of origin and so forth, as in *tilakaṭa* and *goṣṭhaja*. (Or optionally.)
The word *goṣṭha* is used in the sense of a collection of cows; by the rule that *kaṭac* is optionally added after such words, *avikaṭaḥ* denotes a collection of sheep.
In the case of width, [the suffix] *paṭac* (or *avipaṭa*) is used;
in the case of duality, [the suffix] *goyugac* (or *go-yuga*).
Two camels are a "pair of camels" (*uṣṭrayuga*);
six cows are a "six-cow herd" (*ṣaḍgava*), as are six horses (*aśvaṣaḍgava*).
Among oils,
sesame oil or mustard oil [is used].
In the case of a field of cultivated plants, [the terms] *śākaṭa* and *śākina* [are used]; for a field of sugarcane, [the terms] *ikṣuśākaṭa* and *ikṣuśākina*.
From the word *cat*, the suffix *kaṭac* is applied [to form a word denoting a place where something abounds].
*Avācīna*, *avakuṭāra*, and *avakaṭa* mean hanging down or turned downwards.
Bending is not [the same as] that which has already been bent.
The depression of the nose is called avaṭīṭa,
avanīṭa, or avabhraṭa.
Through connection with that [nose], the nose is depressed; likewise, a person is also said to be "depressed-nosed" (avaṭīṭa).
*nibiḍa* and *nibirīsa* [mean "dense" or "thick"].
Only when preceded by *ni*.

When the word *nata* meaning "nose" is the object to be expressed, the suffixes *inac* and *piṭac* are to be prescribed [after it], as well as the substitutes *cik* and *ci* for the base, and the suffix *kap* with the substitute *cik*; [alternatively], *vācīnakam*.
The nose is flattened and moist,
and his eyes are squinting and swollen.
His eyes are moist; he is *cillaḥ*, *pillaḥ*, or *cul* (or *cu*).
Culla [is used] in the sense of "small" (SK 1835;
The term "in the case of *saṃjñā*" (as a proper name) continues to apply here. A place near a mountain is called *upatyakā*; a place situated above it is called *adhityakā*.
That which acts (ghaṭate) is called a pot (ghaṭaḥ).
The suffix *ac* is applied after roots beginning with *pac*, and the suffix *kha* is applied in the sense of the object; thus, a person who is capable of performing work is called *karmaṭha*.
*tārakitaṃ nabhaḥ* (the sky has become starred);
this is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
In [Pāṇini] Sūtra 5.2.37,
the phrase "tad asya" (that belongs to this) is understood to carry over from the previous rule.
"Ūrupramāṇa" means its measure is the thighs; "ūrūdvayasa" means reaching as high as the thighs; "ūrūdaghná" means thigh-high; "ūrumātra" means merely the length of the thighs.
In the case of measurement, the suffix *la* denotes the agent, as in *śama-* and *diṣṭi-*.
A *vitasti* is always [the measure] of two *yugas*; that which has two *śamas* as its measure is *dviśama*.
When there is doubt regarding measure, quantity, or even number, the suffix *mātra* should be stated [as an alternative]; for example:
*śamamātram* (a mere handful) or *prasthamātram* (a mere prastha).
The suffixes *dvayasaC* and *mātraC* are frequently applied (*bahulam*) after a word ending in *vat* in the sense of the base itself; thus,
from *tāvat*, one forms *tāvaddvayasa*.
Only that much. (SK 1839;
The measure of this is a man; it is man-sized,
measuring two men, as large as an elephant.
The measure of two *hastas* [is called] *dvihastika*.
Whatever its measure may be, as much as it is, so much is this.
From these two [words], the suffix *vatup* is applied, and the *va* of that suffix is replaced by *gha*.
How much is this?
After the word "ca," the suffix vatup is applied; furthermore, the *va* of that [suffix] is replaced by *gha*.
What is their number? Those [things] whose number they are are called "how many" (kati) or "how much" (kiyantaḥ).
That which has five parts is "fivefold" (pañcatayam), such as wood (dāru). SK 1844.
dvayam and dvitayam mean "a pair" or "two."
The triad,
the threefold set.
After the word *ubha*, the suffix *tayap* is replaced by *ayac*, which is acute-accented on its first syllable;
[the resulting form is] *ubhayam*.
Thus ends the section on the fifth case (pāñcamika) within the governing heading of secondary derivatives (taddhita).
Now begins the section on possessive suffixes (matvarthīya) within the governing heading of secondary derivatives.
AS 5.2.45: When eleven are added to it, it is called *ekādaśam*; this is desired only in the case of a hundred or a thousand (according to the Vārttika).
In this [section],
eleven [sūtras] are added; it is intended that [the rule applies] only when the base and the suffix denote things of the same class within these twenty [sūtras].
In this hundred gold coins, there are eleven *māṣas* in excess. (SK 1847)
AS 5-2-46: The suffix *ḍa* is applied in the sense already mentioned; for example, "one hundred in which thirty are added" is *triṃśaṃ śatam*.
The twenty [is the number].
The suffix *mayaṭ* shall be applied in the sense of the genitive case after a word denoting a number ending in the nominative case when it signifies a portion (*bhāga*) that serves as the price;
for example, *dvimayam udaśvid yavānām* ("two parts of curdled milk are the price of this portion of barley").
Why [is there the condition] "of a quality" (*guṇasya*)?
Two measures of rice and barley are the measure for this whey;
regarding the measure, what [is the ratio]?
Two parts of milk and one part of oil—milk twice the amount of oil is cooked with the oil.
That which completes eleven is "ekādaśa" (the eleventh).
The augment *maṭ* shall be added after the suffix *ḍaṭ*.
The fifth is that which completes the five; why [is it not so] in the case of "viṃśa" (twenty)? It is because it does not end in the letter "n".
Why is the suffix -tama (forming ordinals) not applied to words such as *asaṃkhya* and others?
Before the suffix *ḍaṭ*, the augment *thuk* is added to these [words]; thus, "the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhaḥ*) means "the completer of six" (*ṣaṇṇāṃ pūraṇaḥ*).
Although the word *katipaya* is not a numeral, by this very indicative rule (*jñāpaka*), the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to form *katipayathaḥ*, meaning "the how-many-th."
The fourth [suffix] is *cha*, *iya*, or *taya*; there is also the elision of the initial syllable, optionally,
resulting in *turīya*.
The fourth [state] (turya).
The suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to the words *pūga* and *saṅgha*, even though they are not numerals; for this very reason, forms such as *bahutitha* are derived.
[The suffix] ḍaṭ alone [is applied].
The ordinal number [is formed] from whatever [number].
The suffix *ḍaṭ* is an exception [to the previous rule];
that which completes two is *dvitīya*.
AS 5-2-55: The third [is established];
After these [words], the augment *tamaṭ* may optionally be added to the suffix *ḍaṭ*;
[thus] *viṃśatitamaḥ*.
The twentieth,
the twenty-first, the twenty-one-fold.
That which completes a hundred is "śatatamaḥ" (the hundredth).
The hundred-and-first [month] is therefore expressed as *māsatamaḥ* by the suffix *ḍaṭ*.
SK 1858 AS 5-2-58 Sixtieth [Sūtra]
But in the case of numbers such as twenty and so forth, according to the rule *viṃśatyādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.2.56], there is indeed an option; thus,
one is called both *ekaṣaṣṭaḥ* and *ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ*.
Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.59 (SK 1859):
The suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
The word *acchāvāka* exists in this [hymn], thus it is the *acchāvākīya* hymn;
the *vāravantīya* is a *sāman*.
By this very [sūtra] being an indicator (jñāpaka), the suffix *cha* occurs there in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
And by virtue of the power of the rule itself, there is optionally elision (*luk*):
*gardabhāṇḍaḥ* or *gardabhāṇḍīyaḥ*.
In the sense of possession, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied to denote an *adhyāya* or an *anuvāka*.
In this [treatise], there exists the word *vaimukta*,
meaning "pertaining to the Daivas and Asuras.
The suffix *ka* is added after the words *adhyāya* and *anuvāka* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), as in *goṣadaka*.
The suffix *tvak* occurs after the word *iṣ* [in the sense of "desiring"].
A traveler on the road may be skilled in the way.
In the rule *ākarṣe kuśalaḥ* (AS 5.2.64), the primary reading is *ākaṣādibhya�*, which is devoid of the letter *r*. Thus, the word is *ākarṣakaḥ*.
Ākaṣa means a touchstone.
Kāma is desire for wealth; Dhanaka was the Hiranyaka of Devadatta.
One who is attached to hair is called *keśakaḥ*.
The meaning is that he is intent upon its arrangement (SK 1867;
The suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied when there is no desire to act; it is an exception to *kan*.
One who is excessively tormented by hunger and intent upon the stomach is called *audarika*.
Regarding "ādyūna": what is meant by *udaraka*?
It means one who is intent on such things as rubbing the belly.
the suffix *kan* is prescribed, but not *ṭhak*.
The word *sasya* denotes a quality (*guṇa*) and not grain (*dhānya*).
There is an alternative reading, *śasyena*; [in that case], *sasyaka* means "well-bred" (*sādhu*), being thoroughly produced or connected with the quality of excellence (*sasyena guṇena*).
Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.69: The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *hṛ* when preceded by *ā*, in the sense of necessity (*avaśyaka*).
For this very reason, when used in conjunction with that [word], the genitive case is not employed; [as in the example:
"an heir to a share" (aṃśako dāyādaḥ). (SK 1870)
A cloth woven from a single thread.
The meaning is "fresh" (pratyagra).
A country where Brāhmaṇas live by means of weapons is called *brāhmaṇaka*;
a gruel (*yavāgū*) that contains little food is called *uṣṇikā*,
as the word *anna* is irregularly substituted by *uṣṇa*.
One who says "I do" [but does not] is called *śītaka*, meaning lazy.
One who acts quickly is called *uṣṇaka*, according to the rule "the word *uṣṇa* [forms a suffix] when meaning 'he makes hot'" (SK 1873; AS 5.2.73).
The suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in *adhyārūḍha*, and there is the elision of the final member of the compound (Pāṇini 5.2.74).
The suffix *kan* is applied after the roots *anv* and *abhi*; there is optionally a lengthening of the vowel for the root *abh*, as in *anukaḥ*, meaning "one who desires."
One who desires intensely is *abhikaḥ* or *ābhīkaḥ*.
*pārśvaka* refers to one who seeks [something] by means of a crooked method (*anṛjur upāyaḥ*).
*āyaḥśūla* means a sharp means; one who seeks [his goal] by that is *āyaḥśūlikaḥ*—one who acts with rashness. *Daṇḍājina* means hypocrisy; one who seeks [his goal] by that is *dāṇḍājinikaḥ*.
The suffix *kan* may optionally be applied [to a word ending in a feminine suffix], and there is also optional elision (*luk*) of a ordinal number suffix.

The second *dvika* refers to the apprehension of Devadatta by means of a second form; that is to say, the sense is "he apprehends him by the *n*-th [form]. In this case, the suffix *-kan* should be stated [after the ordinal], and there is always elision (*luk*) of it.
In its sixth form, it grasps; Devadatta is sixfold or fivefold. (SK 1878)
AS 5-2-78: Those for whom Devadatta is the chief are *devadattakāḥ*; those for whom you are the chief are *tvatkāḥ*.
The suffix *mat* [is applied after a word denoting a part of the body] when the sense is "possessing that" (SK 1879;
The word *śṛṅkhalaka* [is used] for a young camel (*karabha*).
From the word *ud* (up) combined with the prefix *ut*, the suffix *kan* is applied in its own sense (*svarthe*), resulting in *utkaḥ*, meaning "eager" or "longing.

AS 5.2.81: The suffix *kan* occurs after words expressing time and after words expressing a purpose, when referring to a disease; for example, a fever that occurs on the second day is called *dvitīyaka-jvaraḥ*.
*Prayojana* means the cause or the fruit of a disease;
*viṣapuṣpaka* is that which is produced by poison-flowers; *uṣṇaka* is that whose effect is hot.
Is this the second day of his illness?

The suffix *kan* shall be applied after a word ending in the nominative case to express the sense of the locative case, provided that the nominative-ending word refers to food and signifies "mostly. For example:
*guḍāpūpikā paurṇamāsī*, meaning "the full-moon day on which sweetmeat balls (*guḍāpūpa*) constitute the principal food."
The suffix *ini* may optionally be applied after the word *vaṭaka*,
forming *vaṭakinī*. (SK 1883)
AS 5-2-83: *Kulmāṣāḥ prāyeṇānnam asyām* [forms] *kaulmāṣī*.
The term *śrotriyaḥ* [is used here] because the word *vā* (or) is understood from the preceding rule, and thus it follows the Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
SK 1885 AS 5-2-85 śrāddhī (one who performs the śrāddha rite)
śrāddhikaḥ (one who performs a śrāddha rite) SK 1886 AS 5-2-86
"By him, the former [deed] was performed previously. (SK 1887; AS 5.2.87)
One who has previously performed [an action]. (Pāṇini 5.2.88)
He has sacrificed; he is a sacrificer.
He has studied; he is a student.
But in common worldly usage, the word *paripanthin* is not etymologically justified. (AS 5.2.89;
*anupada* [forms the suffix] *in* when meaning "a seeker," as in *anupadī gavām* ("one who seeks the tracks of cows").
AS 5-2-91: A witness is one who perceives directly (sākṣād-draṣṭā).
AS 5-2-92: *Kṣetriya* refers to a disease that must be treated in another body; the meaning is that it is incurable [in the present life].
Indra is the self; his existence is inferred from the instrument by means of the agent.
The word "iti" has the sense of "kind" or "manner"; [it refers to] the faculty that is difficult for Indra to conquer (durjaya).

AS 5.2.94: The suffix *matup* is applied after the word *go* ("cow") when it signifies that [the person or place] possesses cows, provided that the sense is abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, or excellence. (The suffix may optionally be applied.)
When there is a desire to express association (*saṃsarga*), the suffixes *matup* and others are employed [according to Pāṇini 5.2.94–95].
The form *matup* [is used] for the purpose of excluding other suffixes having the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
Taste, form, color, smell, touch, sound, and viscidity (ga)— from these qualities (ga), [the suffix] ekāc [is applied].
Possessing its own [specific] qualities, it is the qualifier of taste and the other [objects], such as sweetness and so forth.
When a suffix denoting possession (*matvartha*) follows, the forms ending in *tān* and *sān* are designated as *bha*;
furthermore, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel in *vasu*.
The suffix *matup* is generally elided after words expressing qualities;
thus, "that which has whiteness as its quality" is called a "white cloth."
Kṛṣṇa is [the one who] acts (karoti).

The *m* of the suffix *mat* is replaced by *v* when it follows a word ending in a labial (*ma*-varṇa) or a nasal (*a-varṇa*), provided that the preceding vowel is a labial or a nasal (*upadhā*) and the word is not among those beginning with *yava*. For example:
*kiṃvān*, *jñānavān*.
Possessed of knowledge, possessed of fortune, and possessed of fame.
But from the word *yava* (barley) and others,
there is the suffix *mān*, as in *bhūmimān* (possessing land).
After a word ending in a *jhay* consonant, the *m* of the suffix *matup* may optionally become *v*.
Because it is at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the substitution of *jaś* does not apply; thus, [the form] is *vidyutvān*. (SK 1899)
In the word *mat*, the *m* may optionally become *v*,
as in *ahīvatī*.
In the case of *munīvatī* and those beginning with *śarā*, there is lengthening [of the penultimate vowel], according to *Sārasvata-kaumudī* 1042 and *Sārasvata-prakriyā* 1900.
These six are irregularly formed (nipātita) for the purpose of naming; [specifically] the word *āsana* undergoes the change to *āsandī*.
The village is called Āsandīvat because it possesses seats; elsewhere, the word *asthi* (bone) undergoes the change to *aṣṭhī*.
The sage named Aṣṭhīvān means "possessing bones"; elsewhere, however, there is the transformation of the word *cakra* into *cakrī*.
The word *cakrīvat* means "possessing a wheel"; elsewhere, [the term] *cakravat* refers to a girth-rope, where there is a vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel.
The sage named Kakṣīvān means "possessing a girth-band"; elsewhere, the word *lavaṇa* undergoes a change to *rumaṇ*.
The mountain named Rumaṇvat;
elsewhere [the suffix] lavaṇa-vat,
where there is no elision of the *c* in *carman* and the substitution of *ṇ*.
The river named Carmaṇvatī is elsewhere called Carmavatī. (SK 1901)
The substitution of *udan* for *udaka* is prescribed before the suffix *matau* and in the name *udadhi*;
thus, *udanvān* refers to the ocean and also to a seer (*ṛṣi*).
The earth is possessed of a king.
The suffix *vati* occurs after a word ending in *rājan*, except in other cases [i.e., when it does not mean "king"].
(Pāṇini 5.2.96)
*cūḍālaḥ* means "one who has a crest" (*cūḍavān*);
[the suffix *lac* is applied] because it refers to something residing on a living being.
If a lamp has a flame, why does it not have hands?
Or rather, in this case, the wise one [derives it] only from a limb of a living being.

Since the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is already established by the accent of the suffix itself, the particle *ca* in Pāṇini 5.2.97 (*cūḍālo'sītyādau svarito vānudātte padādau*) is intended to override the circumflex (*svarita*) accent prescribed by that rule.
One who has *lāja* (scab) is called *sidhmala* or *sidhmavat*.
The inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of adding the suffix *matup*, and not for the purpose of providing an option between suffixes;
therefore, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* do not apply after words ending in *ā*.

aikadhyam (being together)

After these two [words], the suffix *dhamuñ* may optionally replace the word *dhā*, as in *dvaidham* or *dvidhā*.

On the path, there are two kinds of grasses. (SK 1992; AS 5.3.46)
twofold, threefold SK 1993

The second part is "dvitīya" (second);
