after a word ending in *tīya*, the suffix *īkak* may optionally be used in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). For example:
*dvaitīyīkaḥ*.
The second,
the third,
the third.
There is no second or third [form] of knowledge.
"Knowledge" indeed—
The suffix *an* is applied after a word ending in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇa-pratyaya*) to denote a part, as in "the fourth" (*caturthaḥ*) and "the eighth" (*aṣṭamaḥ*).
*cādan* (the suffix *an* is applied after a verb root denoting an action that causes someone to move).

the sixth.

If it is a part of an animal, the eighth part [is used]; for the word *ña*, there is either the substitution of *ana* or elision (*luk*), and by the force of the particle *ca*, it is also as otherwise prescribed.
Sixth, sixtieth, eighth.
The eighth [point]:
although [the elision] is established by the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the explicit statement of elision (*lugvacana*) indicates that in the preceding cases, the suffixes *ñ* and *an* are obligatory (*nitya*).
AS 5.3.52: After the word *ca*, the suffixes *kan* and its elision (*luk*) may optionally be applied; [the resulting form] is *eka*.
Alone, solitary.
AS 5.3.53: One who was formerly wealthy is called *āḍhyacara*.
According to Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.53–54,
the suffixes *rūpya* and *caraṭ* are applied after a word ending in the genitive case when the sense is "formerly being such."
In the expression *kṛṣṇasya bhūtapūrvo gaur* ("a cow that was formerly black"),
the forms *kṛṣṇarūpyaḥ* and *kṛṣṇacaraḥ* do not undergo masculine substitution (*puṃvat*) because the suffix *rūpya-* is not included in the list of suffixes beginning with *tasil*.

The word *śubhrāya* (the son of Śubhrā) is formed by the rule *śubhrādibhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.123), which prescribes the suffix *yañ* after the base *śubhra*. However, according to the Vārttika *śubhrādīnāṃ cārupyaḥ* (Vt. 5 on Pāṇini 6.1.157), the *yañ* suffix is replaced by *arupya* when it follows a word belonging to the *śubhra* group. Thus, the form *śubhrārūpyaḥ* is derived. The term *bhūtapūrvaḥ* means "one who was formerly [called] Śubhrā. This refers to a person who was previously the daughter of Śubhrā but has since married and changed her status. The rule *śubhrāyā bhūtapūrvaḥ śubhrārūpyaḥ* indicates that the specific designation *śubhrārūpya* applies to one who was formerly the daughter of Śubhrā. SK 2001 corresponds to Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.55: *śubhrādibhyaś ca*, which prescribes the patronymic suffix *yañ*. AS 5-3-55 corresponds to the Vārttika *śubhrādīnāṃ cārupyaḥ*, which prescribes the substitution of *arupya* for *yañ* after words of the *śubhra* class.
These two suffixes occur in their own sense when applied to a word denoting an object qualified by excellence:
"this one is the wealthiest among these," *āḍhyatamaḥ*.
The lightest of the light (laghutama) is the most minute (laghiṣṭha). (Pāṇini 5.3.56)
When the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*) is to be expressed after a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), the suffix *tamap* shall be applied; this is Sūtra 1.1.22 of the Aṣṭādhyāyī.
These two [suffixes] have the designation *gha*.
(SK 2004; Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.11)

The suffix *ām* is added after a word ending in the interrogative pronoun *kim* (when it functions as a particle) or after an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that ends in the suffix *gha*; however, this does not apply when there is an intensification of a substance,
as in *kiṃtamām* or *prāhṇetamām*.
In the case of excellence regarding substance, however, "the tree is most tall" [is used] for that which is exceedingly tall.

When two things are to be distinguished, and one of them is superior, these two suffixes [īyasun and īyan] occur after a word ending in a nominal suffix (sup) or a verbal suffix (tiṅ), provided that such a word is used as an *upapada*.
This is an exception to the two preceding [rules]; it is more light than these two, exceedingly light, most light.
The northerners are more proficient and more skillful than the easterners.
AS 5.3.58: The suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* occur only after words expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*); they do not occur here [after the following].
A better cooker; a best cooker.
The suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* are applied after words ending in *tṛn* and *tṛc*.
There is elision of the sound *tṛ* when the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, or *īyasun* follow. [Example: *atiśayena kartā* (one who is most a doer) becomes *kariṣṭhaḥ*.
The word *dohīyasī* is [substituted for] *dhenuḥ*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.60)
In place of this [suffix], there shall be the substitution of *śra*, except when it is followed by a vowel or the letter *j*.
In the superlative and comparative suffixes, a monosyllabic base remains in its original form; thus, *śreṣṭhaḥ* and *śreyān*.
In place of *praśasya* (praiseworthy), there shall be the substitute *jya* before the suffixes *iṣṭha* and *īyas*.

[The substitute] takes the place of that which follows; this is more authoritative. (Pāṇini 1.1.54) This is superior.
The substitute *jya* shall take the place [of *jyā*] before vowels and the word *jyeṣṭha*. Thus: *jyeṣṭhaḥ*.
The elder [is designated first].
The nearest among goats and others; nearer.
Most excellent,
more excellent.

In these [words], that which follows the *yaṇ* (semivowel) and so forth is elided, and there is *guṇa* substitution for the preceding [vowel], in the case of the suffixes beginning with *iṣṭha*; for example, *sthaviṣṭhaḥ*.
The most distant,
the youngest,
the smallest.
The superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* is used after [a stem ending in] *kṣipra*,
*kṣudra*,
and so forth.
Because *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra* belong to the group beginning with *pṛthu*, the forms are *hrasimā*,
*kṣepimā*, and *kṣodimā*.
In the case of *iṣṭhan* and other suffixes, the words beginning with *pra* are respectively substituted for the words beginning with *pray*.
In the case of *preṣṭha* and so forth: *preṣṭhaḥ*, *stheṣṭhaḥ*.
Most excellent, most eminent, most abundant.
The most weighty, the highest, the most formidable.
*drāghiṣṭhaḥ* and *vṛndiṣṭhaḥ* are formed thus with the suffix *īyasun*.

The word *preman* and so forth are derived from the root *prī* by adding the suffix *iman* according to the rule beginning with *pṛthv-ādi*. Thus, it is formed from *priya*, *uru*, *bahu*, *guru*, and *dīrgha*.
Therefore, *preman* means "one who is very dear" (*preyān*).
When the suffixes *imanic* and *īyasun* follow the word *bahu*, there is elision (*lopa*) of these two suffixes, and the substitute *bhū* is applied to *bahu*.

The *iṣṭhan* suffix following *bahu* undergoes elision, and there is the augment *yiṭ*; thus,

According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.64, the substitution of *kan* may optionally occur for these two [suffixes] *iṣṭha* and *iyas*.

AS 5.3.65: There shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *vin* and of *matup* before the superlative suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. [Example: *sragvī* (one who possesses a garland) becomes *srajiṣṭhaḥ* (most garlanded).

AS 5.3.83: In this section, when a suffix beginning with *ya* or a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) follows, everything after the second vowel of the base is elided. Thus, "Devadatta who is pitied" becomes *devikaḥ*.
Devīyaḥ, Devilaḥ, Devadattakaḥ.

the elision of either the preceding or the following member may be stated even without a suffix (*pratyaya*).

After a word ending in *u*, the suffix *la* is added [to form a patronymic], and the *i* of the suffix may optionally be replaced by *la*;

there is elision of the fourth letter (*ṛ*) when followed by a vowel other than *a*, as well as elision of the preceding member; likewise, this is desired before the suffix *apratyaya*, and [there is optionally] elision of *i* after a vowel ending in *u*.
The designation *la* signifies elision (*lopa*) according to the Eastern grammarians; Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.62.

and also that which is otherwise applicable.

Upika, Upiya, Upila.

AS 5.3.81: Following the rule "of a human name" (manuṣyanāmnaḥ),
the suffix *kan* is added after a word denoting a genus that is also a human name, in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*) and in the sense of a policy (*nīti*).
The lion, the śarabha, and the donkey.
If it is a diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*) as the second [member], then the elision of the first [member] should be stated (optionally):
*anukampitaḥ kahoḍaḥ* becomes *kahikaḥ*.

Thus, *anukampitaḥ śevaladattaḥ* becomes *śevalikaḥ*.
Śevaliya, Sevalila, and Suparika.
The Viśālika, the Varuṇika, and the Aryamika.

Vyāghrājina, Vyāghraka, and Siṃhaka were shown compassion. (SK 2040)
A small amount of oil is called *tailaka*.

The mention of "yatama" and "tatama" is for the purpose of excluding the *akac* suffix.
The suffixes *yaka* and *saka* [are applied] according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
That which [is formed] from *kim* in this context also takes the suffix *-atarac* optionally.
Which one?

"one of these two is Maitra" (*anayor ekataraḥ maitraḥ*) and "one of these many" (*eṣām ekatamaḥ*).
One who is proud because of grammar is called *vyākaraṇakaḥ*.

however, in the case of something already inherently censurable, [the rule] applies to the word *kutsite* (in the sense of "censured"), as per the rule *svataḥ kutsite tu kutsite* (Pāṇini 5.3.74). Now begins the section on suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) within the governing heading of secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*).
What could be the suffix *ka* in the sense of "like a horse"? It is *aśvakaḥ*; what is it used for in the sense of a likeness?
Like a cow is a gavaya.

The suffix *kan* may be applied in the sense of "like" (*iva*), provided that the resulting whole is understood as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). This rule is commenced to prevent [the application of *kan*] in the sense of a mere likeness; thus, it is the name for something resembling a horse.
Aśvaka and Uṣṭraka.

Why do you sell elephant cubs, which are not for sale?

*Haṃsapatha* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class of words). (SK 2056)
"iva" continues to apply,

After a compound whose sense is that of *iva*, the suffix *cha* shall be applied; for example, *kākatālīyo devadattasya vadhaḥ* ("Devadatta's death was like the fall of a palm fruit upon a crow").

As *śārkara* is derived from *śarkarā*.

After the word *ekaśālā* and others, when the sense is "like that," the suffix *ṭhac* is optionally applied; alternatively, *ṭhak* is applied.

Aikaśālikaḥ (one who eats only once a day) — Pāṇini 5.3.110.
A white horse is *karka*; like that, *kārkīka* refers to red crystal (*lauhityaka-sphaṭika*). (SK 2066)
The sense of *iva* has ceased [to apply].

The suffix *ñya* shall be applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after words denoting *pūgas*—which are associations of various kinds, with indefinite membership, and primarily concerned with wealth and pleasure.

The suffix *cha* (forming *lauhitya*) is applied after *lohita* when it means "having a red banner," provided it does not refer to a feminine; [the suffix] *cphañ* is applied after *vrāta* when it does not refer to a feminine.

why is "a weapon" mentioned?

Dāmanaya was the son of Aulapi; Aulapi was the son of Aulapi.
Trigarta, Kauṇḍoparathīya, and Dāṇḍakīya.
Pāṇini 4.3.117: After these [names] denoting guilds of those who live by arms, the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* respectively are applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
pārśavaḥ,
pārśavau,
parśavaḥ
A Yaudheya, two Yaudheyas, [many] Yaudheyas.
The suffix *yañ* shall be applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after words such as *abhijit* that end in the suffix *aṇ*.
The descendant of Abhijit was Ābhijitya;
[his son] was Vaidabhṛtya; [his son] was Śalāvatya.
The Śaikhāvatyas, the Śāmīvatyas, and the Aurṇāvatyas.
The feminine forms are *śrāmatī*, *śrāmatyau*, *śrāmatyaḥ*.
(Pāṇini 4.1.6)

Starting from *pūgāñ-yaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.127), those [suffixes] mentioned [in the following rules] shall bear this designation (*saṃjñā*). Consequently, when used in the plural for non-feminine [nouns], there is elision (*luk*); for example, *lohitadhvajāḥ*.
The Kapotapākās, the Kauñjāyanas, the Brādhnāyanas, and so forth.
The statement regarding elision (lopa) is for the purpose of showing that it is not caused by anything else.
Therefore, by the rule *na sthānivat* (Pāṇini 1.1.56),
when the compound is formed according to *pādaḥ pat* (Pāṇini 6.4.130) and *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), the suffix [is applied].
When it is uttered with reference to a woman alone,
one gives two feet at a time— that is, two hundred [paṇas]— which constitutes a "two-footed" (dvipadikā) fine.
The mention of "a hundred pādas" is purposeless, because it is seen elsewhere as well; [as in the expression] "two modakas. (Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.1.58) SK 2074.
The suffix *vuñ* shall be applied [after a word denoting a part of the body];
this is for the purpose of excluding the sense of distributive repetition (*avīpsā*).
He who has been punished with two pādas pays a fine of two pādas, that is, two hundred [paṇas]; this is the meaning.
The suffix *jātīyar* is an exception [to the preceding rules].
The words *sthūlaka* and *aṇuka* [are formed with the suffix *kan*]; there is also the addition of *cañcat*, *bṛhat*, and *urū* [to this rule].
Cañcatka and bṛhatka are [names] for the snake of wine.
The snake Surāvarṇa is indeed Suraka;
Cut, broken, and unbroken.
When a word synonymous with *sāmi* (half) is used as a co-occurring term (*upapada*), the suffix *kan* is not added after a word ending in the suffix *kta*.
Since the words *sāmikṛta* and *ardhakṛta* denote a state that is not final (*anatyantagati*), the suffix *kan* is not obtained by the preceding rule due to the very nature of their expression.
This very prohibitive sūtra also indicates that the suffix *kan* is extremely frequent even when used in its own primary sense.
There may be two, namely the *prāvāra* and the *uttarāsaṅga*, which are equal; likewise, there is the *bṛhatikā*.
Regarding clothing, what is the *bṛhatī* meter?
A mantra that is not *aṣaḍakṣīṇa* is used in its own primary sense.
The meaning is that it is formed by two [suffixes] alone; *āśitaṅgavīnam* refers to a forest in which cows have been fed (*āśitā gāvo 'smin*),
where the augment *mum* is applied to the preceding part due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*).
Adequate for action; fit for action;
fit for a man;
dependent on the Lord.
This suffix *kha* is compulsory; because of the mention of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) in the subsequent sūtra,
it is understood that some other svārthika suffixes are also intended to be compulsory.
The suffixes beginning with *tamap* and ending before *kan*,
those beginning with *ñya* and ending before *vun*, and those beginning with *ām* and ending before *mayaṭ* [are called *avyayībhāva*].
"Compounds ending in *bṛhatī* and *jāti*, as well as those with compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), [are feminine]," so says the Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 5.4.8.
The suffix *kha* may optionally be added in its own sense (*svārthe*) after a nominal stem ending in *añc*, provided it does not denote a cardinal direction; for example:
*prācīnam*, *pratyañcam*, and *pratīcīnam*.
*Avāk* and *avācīna* mean low, base, inferior, vile, contemptible, or wretched.
*Arvāk* and *arvācīna* derive from "that which goes toward the horse" (*arvantam añcati*).
Regarding the first woman, is she the eastern direction or the northern direction?
What is the purpose of mentioning the direction?
What is the purpose of mentioning the Brāhmaṇa woman?
The mango trees are to the east of the village.
O kinsman of the brahmin caste, is the brahmin caste auspicious?
Substance is the manifester of genus and the relative.
The meaning is that if it is equal in its sixfold basis, it is meaningful up to the end of its locus; thus,
one who stands in the place of a father is "father-like" (pitṛsthāna).
What is the location of a cow by means of its six locations?
One who follows behind is an *anugādī*; that very person is [called] *ānugādikaḥ*.
The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied [in this case].
[Vaisāriṇaḥ] means "fish"; why [is it not used here]? Devadatta is a wanderer (visārī).
Repeated occurrence is birth.
The suffix *kṛtvasuc* shall be added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*) after a numeral word that functions by counting the occurrence of an action;
for example, *pañcakṛtvo bhuṅkte*.
Why [is it said] "after a numeral"?
He eats many times.
This is an exception to the suffix *kṛtvasuc*:
he eats twice; he eats thrice.
The collection of the Rātsa [mantra], SK Sandarbha 280;
four, SK 2087.
AS 5.4.19: *sakṛt* and so forth are substitutes [for the word *kṛtvas*]; furthermore, by the addition of *ca*, the suffix *suc* is also applied: *sakṛdbhuṅkte*.
By the rule *saṃyogāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.23), there is the elision of the suffix *su*, and not by the rule *halṅyāp* (Pāṇini 6.1.68);
for in the case of *abhaitsīt*, just as with the suffix *sic*, the same [elision] does not apply to *su*. (Kāśikā 2088)
One who is not remote, that is, one who is near,
eats many times during the day.
When the time [of death] is near, how many times does he eat in a month?

AS 5.4.21: *prācuryeṇa prastutam* means that which is introduced or treated as predominant; *tasya vacanam* is its expression or exposition, [the suffix] *lyuṭ* being applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
In the first case, the food under discussion consists of cakes,
flour-cakes, or gruel.
In the second [month], the sacrifice consists of food; the festival consists of cakes. (SK 2090)
Collective suffixes are extended [by analogy], as in *cānmayaṭ*; when *modaka* is the base, *maudakika* is formed.
The *śaṣkulikā* consists of *modakas*,
and the *śaṣkulī* consists of *śaṣkulikās*.
In the second sense,
a *maudakika* sacrifice consists of sweetmeats (*modaka*).
The infinite itself is infinity.
The word *āvasathya* refers to that which belongs to a dwelling (*āvasatha*); the phrase *itiheti* is a collection of particles meaning tradition (*aitihya*).
*bheṣaja* itself is *bhaiṣajya*. (SK 2092; AS 5.4.24)
*Tādarthya* means "being for that purpose"; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense [to form the word *tādarthya*].
For example, "this is for the deity Agni" is *agnidevatyam*.
That which has the ancestors as its deity.

The word *pādya* means water for the feet; *arghya* [is formed from *arha*] with the substitution of *nava* for *nu*; and it should be stated that the suffixes *tṛ*, *ta*, *na*, *p*, and *khāś* are also applicable.
fresh,
new, recent.
And [the suffix] *na* should be stated after the word *pra*, when it occurs in the sense of "ancient" (*purāṇa*), as in *praṇa*; furthermore,
the previously mentioned [suffixes] should also be applied.
Ancient,
far-reaching, and pleasing.
The suffix *dheya* is applied after words meaning "portion," "form," and "name" [to form the names of sacrificial offerings], as in *bhāgadheya*,
*rūpadheya*, and *nāmadheya*.
The name [of the shed] is derived from *āgnīdhra* with the suffix *añ*, which is common to both [the shed and the priest]; thus it is called *āgnīdhra*.
The common feminine suffix is *ṅīp*, as in *āgnīdhrī*.
Common to all (sādhāraṇī) SK 2094 AS 5-4-26.
By the rule "tādarthye" (in the sense of being for that purpose), [the suffix yañ is applied];
thus, *ātithyam* means "this is for the guest.
The deity itself is the divinity. (AS 5.4.27;
A ewe is indeed a sheep; a ram is indeed a sheep. (AS 5.4.28;
*yāva* itself is *yāvaka*;
[the suffix] *maṇika*.
Just as a red gem is called "red" (lohitaka).
"He is red with anger."
Or rather, there is a sublation of the gender [of the base] by the suffix *lohitāt*:
*lohitikā* and *lohinikā* when expressing anger.
AS 5.4.32: From the word *lohita* when it denotes something dyed with lac and so forth, the suffix *kan* is applied,
and there is either the sublation of gender or [the formation of a feminine stem].
A red garment, a crimson garment.
The two [terms] "varṇe" (in the case of color) and "anītye rakte" (in the case of an impermanent red) recur; for example:
"kālakaṃ mukham" (a dark face due to embarrassment) and "kālakaḥ paṭaḥ" (a dark cloth).
A black garment (kālikā śāṭī) [is permitted] according to Sūtra 2102 of the *Śāṭī* section,
Pāṇini 5.4.34.
The discipline itself is the means for training; it is conventional and possesses brevity.
Aupayika (suitable, expedient) [is formed by adding the suffix -ika to aupāya according to Pāṇini 5.4.35].

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of the word itself after the word *vāk* when it is present in the phrase *saṃdiṣṭārthāyāṃ vāci* (a speech containing a message); thus, *saṃdeśavāk* becomes *vācikam*. (SK 2104)
*Kārmaṇa* is indeed action;
the meaning is that it is action performed after hearing [an instruction], whether verbal or otherwise.
The suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
Does one drink medicine when it has not yet arisen? Are medicinal herbs not grown in the field?
The wise one is indeed the conscious one.
A wise woman is a divinity and a kinsman.
*mṛd* itself is *mṛttikā*.
*rūpapa* is an exception [to the preceding rule].
*Praśasta* (praiseworthy), *mṛt*, *mṛtsā*, and *mṛtsnā* [are formed with the suffix *kan*];
because the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is not included in the subsequent sūtra, this [application of the suffix] is obligatory.
*bahuśas* means "he gives many times."
"Few," "in small measure," "many," "few," "much," "little"— these words [denoting quantity], as well as expressions of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, do not apply here.
He gives much to those who are unworthy,
and he gives little to those who are exalted.
He gives two by two; he gives bean by bean, i.e., in groups of beans.
Since words denoting measure, such as *prastha*, have precisely one meaning in their application [to a substance],
why [is the rule] stated as "from a numeral and a singular"?
"He gives pot after pot"—in this case, what is the meaning of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)?
[Answer: He gives two.
By the rule "from a kāraka," [the suffix] applies only to two by two as the owner.

AS 5.4.44: When used in conjunction with *prati* as a *karmapravacanīya*, the suffix *tasi* shall be applied after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) that has been prescribed; for example, *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇataḥ prati*.
An addition [to the rule] should be made for words beginning with "ādi" and so forth:
*ādau*, *āditaḥ*,
*madhyataḥ*.
"Behind," "on the side"—
this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).
By means of the tone, according to the accent and the phoneme.

The suffix *tasi* shall be applied after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) when that fifth case denotes the *apādāna* (ablative); for example, *grāmād āgacchati* ("he comes from the village").
Why is there no [substitution] for *ah* and *īyar* after *grāma*,
as in *svargād dhīyate*?
He descends from the mountain.
The suffix *tasi* may optionally occur after a word ending in the third case when it does not denote the agent; thus,
*atigrahaḥ* means "grasping beyond" or "surpassing," as in "he is surpassed by his conduct."
It is surpassed by conduct; the meaning is that it exists without overstepping conduct. "Unwavering" means being motionless.
He does not waver from his conduct; he does not waver from his conduct; the meaning is that he does not deviate from his conduct.
Censured by his conduct,
he was cast out because of his conduct.
The meaning is "blamed for his conduct.
Why is it stated "not when [the agent] is not the actor"? [Consider:
*devadattena kṣiptaḥ* ("thrown by Devadatta").
The suffix *tasi* is optionally used after a word ending in the third case that denotes the agent, provided it is joined with a word meaning "inferior" (*hīyamāna*) or "sinful" (*pāpa*).
By conduct one falls away; by conduct the wicked man [is defined].
This [rule] applies when the sense of "scorning" (kṣepa) is not intended to be expressed; however, when scorn is intended, it is already established by the preceding rule.
Why [is it stated] "not in the sense of an agent" (akartari)?
[The action] is abandoned by Devadatta. (Pāṇini 1.4.29)
The suffix *tasi* may optionally occur after a word ending in the sixth case when there is recourse to different sides; for example:
"the gods were on Arjuna's side" (*arjunataḥ*) and "the Ādityas were on Karṇa's side" (*karṇataḥ*).
The meaning is "on Arjuna's side"; [as for] "in a case of mutual dependence," what [is the relation] of a tree to its branch?
The suffix *tasi* is optionally added after a word denoting a disease in the genitive case when the sense is "medical treatment."
The meaning is: "O Kuru, provide a remedy for this dysentery. In what sense does [the suffix] express removal?
It causes the provocation of dysentery.
It should be stated that [the suffix *cvi* is used] in the sense of "becoming what it was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāva*).

Alternatively, when the material cause (*prakṛti*) attains the nature of a modification (*vikārātmatā*), the suffix *cvi* may optionally be applied after a word denoting that modification in its own sense (*svārthe*), provided it is used in conjunction with verbs such as *karoti*. (Pāṇini 5.4.50)
In the presence of the suffix *cv-* (the marker of the cvi-derivation), the vowel *a* is replaced by *ī*, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*).
Due to the suffix *cvi*, there is the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*): "He who was not black becomes black" (*akṛṣṇaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ saṃpadyate*), "he makes him so" (*taṃ karoti kṛṣṇīkaroti*),
[and] "he becomes Brahman" (*brahmībhavati*).
It should be stated as a Vārttika that the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of *gaṅgā* does not occur when the indeclinable *avyaya* is followed by *cvī*:
*doṣābhūtam ahaḥ*.
"The night became day," and this [expression] was stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *avyayībhāvaśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.18).
There is elision of the *ya* of an affix denoting descent (*apatya*) when it follows a consonant, provided that *kyac* or *cvī* follows;
for example, *gārgībhavati*.
When *cv* follows, there shall be a long vowel for the preceding [element].
Some say that the suffix *paṭu* becomes *śuci* and that there is no lengthening of the vowel in the indeclinable; however, that is without foundation.

If it is argued that [the form] *svastīsyāt* is established by the *Mahāvibhāṣā* because of the absence of the *cv-* suffix [in such cases], so that it may occur even in the alternative view where one says "may there be well-being," then let it be so; however,
if this is not desired, then let it be that the *cv-* suffix simply does not arise due to the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*).
He makes [them] forget their mother.
AS 5.4.51: There shall be the elision (lopa) of these [suffixes], and the suffix *cvi* [is applied];
for example, *arūkaroti*.
From the state beyond the mind (unmanī), it causes one to look upward and causes one to become conscious.
It causes separation; it causes disfigurement.
In the domain of cvi, sāti may optionally be used to express completeness.
According to Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.111,
the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* should not occur in the case of *sasya*; for example,
in *dadhi siñcati*.
The entire weapon becomes fire; it is reduced to fire, it turns into fire;
according to the *mahāvibhāṣā*, this may also be expressed as a full sentence.
If [whiteness] exists in its entirety, how can a cloth become white by means of only one part?
In connection with *saṃpad*, as well as with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, the suffix *sāti* may optionally be used when there is pervasion (*vyāpti*);
in the alternative case of connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, the suffix *cvi* is used.
But by means of the *saṃpat* [method], the very sentence itself is reduced to fire; the sacrificial implement becomes fire;
it turns into fire.
It becomes water, that is, it turns into water like salt;
however, "pervasion" (abhividhi) refers to the transformation of a single manifest entity across the limitation of all its constituent parts.
The suffix *sāti* occurs in connection with the verbs *kṛ*, *bhū*, *as*, and the noun *saṃpad*; for example:
*rājasātkaroti*.
"From the *rājasa* [nature] one becomes a king"; the meaning is that one is dependent upon the *rāja*. (SK 2126)

When that which is to be given is dependent on someone, the suffixes *trā* and *sāti* may be used after a word ending in the sixth case, provided it is in construction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and others;
for example, *viprādhīnaṃ deyaṃ karoti* (he makes the gift dependent on the Brahmin) becomes *vipratrā karoti*.
What is the point of bestowing [a gift] upon a Brahmin who is distracted, or making him the master of what is to be given?
The kingdom arises from the quality of passion (rājasa).

The suffix *trā* may be added after these words when they end in the second or seventh case; as in *devatrā* (I salute or I delight in the gods), because of the frequentative statement (*bahulokteḥ*), it occurs elsewhere as well.
The mind of a living being wanders in many places.

The suffix *ḍāc* shall be applied after a nominal stem consisting of two syllables as a minimum— meaning it must not have fewer than two syllables, that is, it must have more than one syllable— as its first member, provided that such a stem ends in the word *ardha*, when used in conjunction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*.
When *ḍāc* is intended to be expressed, it should be stated that [the substitution] occurs diversely (*bahulam*) or invariably (*nityam*) when there is a reduplication (*āmreḍita*).
When a reduplication follows *ḍāc*, the single substitute form of the subsequent sound (*pararūpa*) shall take the place of both the preceding and following phonemes (*pūrvapara-varṇa*).
Thus, between the letters *ta* and *pa*, the letter *pa* [is substituted]; as in *paṭapaṭākaroti*,
following the rule for the imitation of indistinct sounds (*avyaktānukaraṇa*).
Does he make it into stone? [He asks] "kim" (what) after a word ending in two or more syllables; does he make it into sacred scripture (*śruti*)?
"Avareti"— why does it produce the sound *kharaṭakharaṭā* and the sound *trapaṭatrapaṭā*?
It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as *anekāca*;

for in this way, when there is doubling, it can be easily stated that the locative case in *ḍāci* is indeed a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). [Question: What is the purpose of excluding *ni* and *tau*?
He makes a clapping sound.

The suffix *ḍāc* is applied after words beginning with *dvitīya*, provided they are used in conjunction with the verb *kṛ* (to do) in the sense of "plowing," due to the frequent occurrence [of this rule]. Because of the mention of "frequently" (*bahula*), there is no reduplication for anything other than an unexpressed imitation of sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) when *ḍāc* is applied.
Thus: *dvitīyam tṛtīyam karṣaṇam karoti* becomes *dvitīyākaroti*.
The third [type] is *śambākaroti*;
the word *śamba* means "against the grain":
when a field that was plowed with the grain has been plowed again against the grain, one says *śambākaroti*.
One ploughs together with the seed; one sows the seed. (Pāṇini 5.4.59)
In connection with the root *kṛ* (to do/make), when used with the word *kṛṣi* (plowing), the suffix *ḍāc* shall be applied;
as in *dviguṇākaroti kṣetram*, which means "he performs a double plowing of the field," that is, he performs the work of plowing the field twice over.
The word "in *kṛṣ*" has ceased to apply.
When used in conjunction with the root *kṛ*, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied; for example, *samayākaroti*, which means "he passes the time."
He equips the deer with feathers.

The meaning is that by causing the arrow with its feathers to enter, one makes it "with-feathered" (*sapatra*); [the prefix *ni-*] in *niṣpattra-karoti* is used in the sense of excessive piercing. What is the purpose?
He makes the surface of the earth either with leaves or without leaves.

*niṣkulākaroti dāḍimam* ("He desegregates the pomegranate"): [the suffix] *ḍāc* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *kula*, provided that the *kula* (group) has departed from it— that is, the collection of internal parts has been removed— SK 2134.
He makes the teacher happy; he makes the teacher dear.
The meaning is that one gladdens [the other] by acting in a favorable manner. (SK 2135; AS 5.4.64)
It causes suffering to the master;
the meaning is that it afflicts him. (SK 2136)
AS 5.4.65: *śūlākaroti māṃsam* means "he cooks the meat with a spit."
A merchant makes merchandise true-to-weight (or authenticates it).
The meaning is that he makes it true by saying "it must be bought";
however, in the case of an oath, the Brahmin makes it true [by saying] "I swear.
The word *madra* signifies auspiciousness;
*parivāpaṇa* means shaving.
The meaning is that he makes [the child] auspicious (*madra*) by means of a consecratory tonsure (*māṅgalyamuṇḍana*);
it should be stated [as an addition to the rule]: "and after *bhadra*" (Vārttika).
Does the word *bhadrā* perform the same function as before in the case of *parivāpaṇa*? What is the point?
"It brings welfare; it brings prosperity"—
this concludes the section on suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) within the governing rule for secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).
Now begins the section on repetition (dvirukta-prakaraṇa),
Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.1.
With reference to this,
[it is said] in Sāṃkhyakārikā 21 and Yogasūtra 8.1.4.
When frequency or repetition is to be indicated, a word is reduplicated;
frequency occurs in the case of verbal endings (tiṅanta) and words ending in kṛt suffixes that are designated as indeclinables (avyaya),
as in *pacati pacati*.
Having eaten repeatedly— [the repetition indicates frequency]— he waters tree after tree.
Every village is delightful.
"From all sides, the god has rained for the Vaṅgas"—
the meaning is "having excluded the Vaṅgas";
[this is because] there is an option regarding the exclusion [indicated by] *pari*.
From the Vaṅgas, [protect us].
"Uparyupari grāmam" means above the village, that is to say, in a place near the top of the village; "adhyadhi sukham" [means] upon happiness.
The meaning is that suffering occurs immediately after happiness;
"below, below" means in a region close to the bottom of the world.
[The suffix *kvip* is applied] in the sense of censure (*asūyā*).
O handsome one, O handsome one, your beauty is in vain; O god, O god, you are to be honored when pleased,
but when angry, O ill-behaved one, O ill-behaved one, now you shall know!
In cases of contempt: "O archer, O archer, your bow is useless"; in cases of reproach: "Thief, thief, I shall have you executed.

The word *eka*, when repeated, shall function like a *bahuvrīhi* compound; by this rule, there is the elision of the case-ending (*sub-lopa*) and the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), as in the expression *ekaikam akṣaram*.

In this case, when the *sup* suffixes of both words have been elided, the status of the whole as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) arises precisely through the application of the *bahuvrīhivadbhāva* rule; consequently, the *sup* suffix is added to the aggregate.
Here, in the first part, due to the *puvadbhāva*, there is a specific distinction regarding the *avagraha*.

Regarding the phrase "na bahuvrīhau" (Pāṇini 1.1.29), the ancient grammarians maintain that the repetition of the term *bahuvrīhi* there is for the purpose of securing the primary (*mukhya*) *bahuvrīhi*;
therefore, they hold that the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) indeed exists in the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) *bahuvrīhi*.
However, in reality, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, this [repetition] has been rejected.

Even according to the Sūtra system, since the prohibition applies to the non-ordinary analytical statement (alaukika-vigraha) which serves as the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi*, there is no possibility of extending that rule to the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself; thus, one should say:
"Give to each one" (*ekaikasmai dehi*).
When affliction is to be indicated, two [words] are used, and it is treated like a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for example, *gatagataḥ*.
This is the utterance of one being tormented by separation; the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) occurs because of the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [resulting in the form] *gatagatā*.
In this case, there is the substitution of the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) [according to Pāṇini 7.1.74].
In these subsequent instances of reduplication, the operation is like that of a *karmadhāraya* compound;
the purpose [of this treatment] is the elision of the case-ending (*sublopa*), the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), and the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*).
(Vārttika 2147)

When similarity (*sādṛśya*) is to be expressed, there is reduplication of a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*); and that [reduplicated form] is treated like a *karmadhāraya*, because of the governing rule (adhikāra) "it is like a *karmadhāraya* in the subsequent [rules]" (Pāṇini 8.1.11).

By that [rule], there is the substitution of the masculine form for the prior member, and by the rule *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223), the final syllable is acute; thus we have *paṭupaṭvī* and *paṭupaṭuḥ*.
"Similar to 'clever' (paṭu)" means "slightly clever";
here, both words denoting a substance with a quality as a subordinate element and those denoting a quality alone are included.
"White-white color," "white-white cloth"—
these two [expressions] are to be stated in succession (or as an option).
At each root, the form is *sthūla*;
when used with haste, its application is manifold as desired, established by grammatical rule (*vā*):
*sarpa sarpa*, *budhyasva budhyasva*.

"Sarpa, sarpa, sarpa; budhyasva, budhyasva, budhyasva"—this is for the sake of expressing intensity (*bhṛśārtha*), since [the reduplication] is already established by the rule "for repetition and pervasion" (*nityavīpsayoḥ*) when there is the frequent repetition of an action (*akriyāsamabhihāra*), as in "He cuts, he cuts" (*lunīhi lunīhītyevāyaṃ lunāti*). This [rule] is intended to ensure reduplication even in the sense of intensity.

Even in the sense of repetition, when used together with the *loṭ* [imperative] to express that meaning, or in the case of mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*), two forms of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) are to be stated; and "optionally like a compound" (*samāsavacca bahulam*).
Because of the mention of "optionally" (*bahula*), it is not like a compound in the cases of "other" (*anya*) and "subsequent" (*para*).

However, since the word *itara* always functions as if it were not part of a compound (*asamāsavadbhāva*), it should be stated that the case-ending (*sup*) of the preceding member is replaced by *su*;
thus: *anyonyaṃ viprā namanti* (the Brahmins bow to one another), *anyonyau*.
"By one another," "done by one another," "given to one another," and so forth.
"Touching one another with their lotuses," so says Māgha;
thus,
here, due to the *kaskādi* group, the visarga is replaced by *s*.

In compounds such as *itaretaram* and *itaretareṇa*, the substitution of *ām* for the case-ending of the second member (*uttarapada*)— provided it belongs to the feminine or neuter gender— is optionally (*vā*) to be stated.
*anyonyām*, *anyonyam*, *parasparām*, *parasparam*, *itaretarām*, or *itaretaram*.
"These two Brahmin women feed [the guests] in the family";
in this case, some hold that the second case ending alone is used for the object.

Because it has been illustrated in that very manner in the Bhāṣya and other works, they say that for feminine and neuter [bases] as well, in the third case and those following, the form is exactly like the masculine; others, however, maintain that since the illustration is merely indicative (diṅmātra), the substitution applies to all case-endings.

The absence of the *ṭāp* suffix in both [masculine and neuter] genders, the absence of *adḍ* in the neuter after [the word *dvi*] in the dual number, and the elision (*luk*) of the *su* and *am* case-endings in a compound—all three of these are established by way of irregularity (*bāhulaka*), as follows: [The verse: "By the power of the Great Lord, the *ṭāp* is absent in both genders; in the neuter, there is the absence of *adḍ* in the dual; and in a compound, there is the elision of *su* and *am*—these three are established through irregularity. [The commentary: In the case of the word *dvaya*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is not applied in either the masculine or neuter gender. In the neuter dual, the suffix *adḍ* is not applied. Furthermore, when this word occurs in a compound, the case-endings *su* (nominative singular) and *am* (accusative singular) undergo elision. All three of these features are accomplished by means of the principle of irregularity (*bāhulaka*). To explain further: 1. **Absence of *ṭāp*:** By the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.4), the suffix *ṭāp* is prescribed for feminine nouns ending in short *a*. However, due to irregularity, it is not applied here, resulting in the forms *dvayaḥ* (masculine plural) and *dvaye* (neuter locative plural). 2. **Absence of *adḍ*:** By the rule *ṅeprathamayoram* (Pāṇini 7.1.28), the suffix *am* is substituted for the dual endings *au* and *śas* after neuter nouns ending in *a*. However, due to irregularity, this substitution does not occur, resulting in the form *dvaye* (neuter dual). 3. **Elision of *su* and *am* in a compound:** When the word *dvaya* is part of a compound, the case-endings *su* and *am* are elided. For example, in the compound *dvayaputraḥ* ("one who has two sons"), the nominative singular *su* is elided. Similarly, in *dvayaputram* ("two sons"), the accusative singular *am* is elided. Thus, these three grammatical phenomena are justified through the principle of irregularity (*bāhulaka*). This principle allows for exceptions to general rules, thereby accounting for forms that would otherwise appear anomalous. It is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Irregularity (*bāhulaka*) is the resort for all cases where a desired form is not obtained through the application of specific rules. This ensures that the linguistic system remains comprehensive and capable of accounting for the vast diversity of attested usage.
In the case of *anyonyaṃ* and *parasparam*, the suffix *ṭāp* would be applicable in both members of the compound;
nor does the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre* (or *vā*) apply here to effect the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).
Since the status of being like a compound does not apply to either of the other two [types of *vṛtti*],
repetition (*dvirvacana*) alone cannot be considered *vṛtti*,
because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "whichever [woman] the lover gazed upon, she, she [was struck with fear], O timid-eyed one."

Regarding the forms "anyonyam" and "itaretaram," the suffix *adḍ* (which would result in *anyad-am* and *itarad-am*) is prescribed by the rule *adḍḍatarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.25). Furthermore, in examples such as "anyonya-saṃsaktamahastriyāmam" (days and nights joined with one another), "anyonyāśrayaḥ" (mutual dependence), "parasparākṣisādṛśyam" (similarity of each other's eyes), and "aparasparaiḥ," the elision (*luk*) of the nominative case ending (*su*) is also prescribed. All of these [irregularities] are to be resolved by the force of the term *bāhulaka* (diversity/irregularity).

The example from the *Vārttika* and *Bhāṣya* on the present topic is found in the rule *striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.3), where the *Bhāṣya* states: "But this [would result in] mutual dependence. This is the authority here (SK 2148, AS 8.1.13).
One gives out of affection for what is dear,
or one gives out of love for happiness.

Alternatively, because of the application of the *karmadhārayavat* rule when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*), even after the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*), that same number of syllables remains;
thus the meaning is that it bestows even a most beloved object without effort.
In the rule *yathāsvam* (SK 2149, AS 8-1-14), the term *yathāsvam* is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

In the expression "that which is this self and that which is one's own," the word *yathā* is used twice, its neuter gender is prescribed, and it is thus formed as *yathāyatham*, meaning "one who knows each thing according to its own nature."
The meaning is "according to their own nature," or "according to what belongs to each.

In these senses, the reduplication of the word *dvi*, the substitution of *ambh-* for the first member (*pūrvapada*), the substitution of *at* for the second member (*uttarapada*), and the neuter gender are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*). Among these, the secret (*rahasya*) is that it is the meaning of the word *dvandva*.
The others, being the objects [of the conversation],
deliberate in pairs; that is to say, they consult in secret.
The non-transgression of the established order:
for even among these animals, pairing occurs until the fourth generation;
a mother even enters into union with her son.
"Having transgressed the bounds," meaning having gone beyond even the grandson and great-grandson; "separated," meaning existing apart;
"divided into pairs," meaning situated separately due to their connection with two groups.
He joins the sacrificial vessels in pairs;
the meaning is that Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva are manifested as a pair through their association.
By means of the separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*), a *dvandva* compound is also desired in other instances; thus ends the section on reduplicated forms.
Now begins the section on the *bhū*-class of roots ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*).
Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.123:
*vartamānakriyāvṛtter dhātor laṭ syāt*— the suffix *laṭ* shall be used after a verbal root that denotes an action occurring in the present time.
The roots √aṭ and √avit [take the suffix *kvip*] when expressing the sense of "wandering.
(Pāṇini 3.2.172)

The *lakāra*s [verbal suffixes] following transitive roots occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*); those following intransitive roots occur in the sense of the state of being (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). (Pāṇini 3.4.69–70)
This is a governing rule (adhikāra).
These eighteen substitutes shall take the place of the l-sounds and the ṛ-sounds.
The substitutes for *la* shall be designated as *parasmaipada*. (Pāṇini 1.4.99–100)
The pratyāhāra *taṅ*, as well as *śānac* and *kānac*, shall have this designation; it is an exception to the preceding designation.
For a root that is marked with an indicatory letter *ṅ* in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), or for a root ending in such a letter, the *ātmanepada* endings shall take the place of *la*.

The *ātmanepada* affixes shall be used after a verbal root that has a *svarita* accent on its first vowel or is marked with the mute letter *ñ*, when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. (Pāṇini 1.3.72)
In the sense of the agent, *parasmaipada* endings shall occur after a verbal root that lacks the causes for the *ātmanepada* endings.
AS 1.4.101: Of the two words [in a compound], the three triplets of verbal suffixes (tiṅ) belonging to each shall, respectively, receive these technical names (saṃjñā).
AS 1.4.102: Those which have received the designations *prathamā* and so forth, namely the three triplets of *tiṅ* suffixes, shall each receive the designations *ekavacana* (singular) and so forth.

AS 1.4.105: When *yuṣmad* (the second person pronoun), which denotes a grammatical participant (*kāraka*) expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), is used—or even when it is not used—the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) shall be employed.

When a verbal root has *manya* as its subordinate element (*upapada*), and that [root] serves as the base (*prakṛti*), the second person (*madhyama*) shall be used if derision (*parihāsa*) is implied; however, for the root *manya*, the first person (*uttama*) shall be used, and it [the first person] shall denote a single agent.
In that same way, when [the speaker] is in such a state, the first person (uttama) shall be used for the word "we" (asmad).
In the absence of the scope for the middle and highest persons, the first person shall be used.
1. *bhū* in the sense of existence.
When the agent is intended to be expressed, the form *bhū* is established as *bhūti* (Pāṇini 3.4.113).
The suffixes *tiṅ* and *śit*, as well as those mentioned under the heading of "dhātu" (verbal roots), shall receive this designation (*saṃjñā*).
(SK 2167; Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.68)
When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix denoting the agent follows, the affix *śap* shall be added after the verbal root; by the rule of *śap-āvitau*, [the *śap*] is elided.
When these two [suffixes] follow, there shall be *guṇa* substitution for a stem ending in a long vowel, and the replacement of *i* by *av*.
It exists for you.
An *antādeśa* (final substitute) of *jha* should occur for that which is a member of a suffix, when followed by *at*, due to the rule of *guṇa*. (SK 191)
They are;
you are;
you two are.
Be!
(Second person plural imperative)
Therefore, there shall be lengthening of the stem when followed by a sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with *yañ* (i.e., *ya*, *yā*, *yās*, etc.), as in *bhavāmi* and *bhavāvaḥ*.
We are;
he is;
those two are.

come, I think you will eat rice," he said; but that [rice] was eaten by the guests. "Come both of you, I think you two will eat rice."
you will eat,
I will eat,
we two will eat.
"We shall eat," you think; "you think [so]."
The meaning of *manyadhve* and so forth is governed by the rule *yuṣmadyupapade* (Pāṇini 1.4.105) and subsequent rules which continue to apply.
Therefore, let your honor not think, "I shall eat rice," for that [rice] has already been eaten by the guests;
what laughter is there in this?

In the case of speaking according to the facts, let there not be [the fault of contradiction], as in: "Come, you think 'I shall eat rice,' but it has already been eaten by the guests," and so forth. (SK 2171)

*Liṭ* shall be substituted for *la*, when the verbal root (*dhātu*) has as its meaning an action that occurred in the past, not belonging to the current day, and was not witnessed by the speaker; *ti* and the other substitutes of *la* shall take its place.
A substitute for *liṅ* that is a *tiṅ* affix should have the designation *ārdhadhātuka* only, and not the designation *sārvadhātuka*.
Therefore, *śa* and the others [are not substitutes] by Pāṇini 3.4.82.
For the nine suffixes beginning with *ti* of the *liṭ* [perfect], nine substitutes beginning with *ṇal* shall occur; thus,
when *bhū a* is established,
The augment *vuk* is added to the root *bhū* before the suffixes *luṅ* and *liṭ*, provided they are followed by a vowel;
because it is mandatory (*nitya*), *vuk* overrides both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
With reference to AS 6.1.2,
[it is stated in] SK 2177.

When *liṭ* follows, there is reduplication of the first monosyllabic (*ekāc*) portion of the verbal root (*dhātu*), which is the first part [of the reduplicated stem]; however, for that which follows the initial vowel, it is the second [monosyllabic] portion that is reduplicated.
Thus, when *bhū-bhū-a* is established:
In this context, of the two [operations] that are prescribed, the former shall be designated as "repetition" (abhyāsa).
In the case of a reduplication, the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable is retained; the other consonants are elided.
Thus, there is the elision of *v* [by Pāṇini 6.1.66].
In the reduplication (abhyāsa), a vowel shall be short. (Pāṇini 7.4.59)
In place of the reduplicated root *bhū*, the substitute *a* shall occur before the suffix *liṭ*.
In reduplication (*abhyāsa*), *jhal* sounds become *car* sounds, and *jhaś* sounds become *jaś* sounds; furthermore, among those, *khay* sounds become *car* sounds.

Moreover, there is a distinction such that *prakṛti-jaś* sounds become *prakṛti-jaś* sounds and *prakṛti-car* sounds become *prakṛti-car* sounds, due to the principle of closest similarity (*āntaratamya*).
From this point onward, until the conclusion of the chapter, [the section] is called Ābhīya.
Since that [substitution] must be applied when the common locus [of the two sounds] exists, it would be unestablished;
therefore, because the *vuk* augment is unestablished, *uvaṅ* would apply.
Thus, it must be stated that *vuk* and *yuṭ* are established in relation to *uvaṅ* and *ayaṇ* respectively.
He became,
they two became, they all became.
According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.35, the augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix following roots beginning with *val*.
You became,

we two became, we all became.
In the sense of the future not belonging to the current day, the suffix *luṭ* shall occur after a verbal root.
The term *lṛ* is used to denote both *lṛṅ* (the conditional mood) and *lṛṭ* (the periphrastic future).

The suffixes *syat* and *tāsī* occur after a verbal root when followed by the markers of the *lṛṭ* (future) and *luṭ* (periphrastic future); they are exceptions to [the application of] *śa* and the other [verbal suffixes].
A suffix prescribed by the rule *tiṅśidbhyo 'nyo dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.91) as being other than a *tiṅ* or a *śit* shall bear this designation (*iṭ*).
In the neuter gender,
the suffixes ḍā, rau, and ras occur respectively [in place of su, au, and jas].
By virtue of the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is elision of the final syllable even for that which is not *bha*.
(SK 2189; Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.86)

In a verbal root (*dhātu*) and in a stem (*aṅga*) having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), there shall be *guṇa* substitution for the single vowel (*eka*) before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. According to the authority of this rule, even when there is an intervention by that which does not cause separation, [the substitution applies];
therefore, in forms such as *bhinatti*, there is no *guṇa* for the single vowel that is separated by multiple [intervening elements].
In this case, one [of the two] becomes [the predominant factor] when a quality is attained.
AS 1.2.6: For the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, and for the augment *iṭ*, neither *guṇa* nor *vṛddhi* substitutions occur;
[thus, the form is] *bhavitā*.
In the presence of an affix beginning with *s*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final syllable of both *dāsa* and *īśa*.
Before an affix beginning with *ra*, it is as previously stated.
bhavitārau, bhavitāraḥ,
bhavitāsi

After a verbal root expressing a future meaning, the suffix *lṛṭ* shall occur when there is an action for the sake of that [future] action, whether such [purposeful] action exists or does not exist; [the augment] *iṭ* shall also occur.
he will be, they two will be, they will be; he will become, they two will become, they will become.

we all shall be.
In the senses of injunction and so forth, the suffix *loṭ* shall be applied after a verbal root.
According to Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.86,
the vowel *i* of the imperative (*loṭ*) is replaced by *u*; thus,
[the form] becomes *bhavatu*.
In the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), *tātaṅ* may optionally be substituted for *hi* and *tu*.
Because it consists of more than one *al* (phoneme), it is a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*).

Although this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) by virtue of the rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53), it has already fulfilled its purpose regarding elements like *anaṅ* which have a *ṅit* marker for no other reason; thus, when encountering the *tātaṅ* replacement where the *ṅakāra* serves purposes such as the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* or *saṃprasāraṇa*, it proceeds sluggishly and is superseded by the subsequent rule, because here even a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) possess equal force.
May it be for you.
The operations of the *loṭ* [imperative] should be like those of the *laṅ* [imperfect]; therefore, the suffixes *tām* and so forth [should apply], as well as the elision of the *s*.
For it is thus:
For the four [conjugational] endings marked with ṅ, *tām* and the others shall apply in their respective order.
In the case of a final *s* belonging to the first person plural ending (*uttama*) which has an indicatory *ṅ*, there shall always be elision (*lopa*).
By the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final *s*,
resulting in *bhavatām* and *bhavantu*.
In place of the *s* of the imperative (*loṭ*), *hi* shall be substituted; that [substitute] is also marked with the *p*-marker.
After this [suffix], there shall be elision (luk) of the following *hi*.

may you all be.

In place of the imperative suffix *loṭ*, *mer* shall be substituted.
(SK 2204; Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.92)

The augment *āṭ* shall be added to the first person of the imperative (*loṭ*), and it is also *pit*; furthermore, there is no substitution of *u* for the *i* of *hi* and *ni*, due to the force of the vocalization of the letter *i* [in the rule],
as in *bhavāni*.

*laṅ* shall be used after a verbal root (*dhātu*) that functions with reference to a past time not belonging to the current day (*anadyatana-bhūta*).
When these [suffixes] follow, the augment *aṭ* is added to the base (*aṅga*), and it is acute (*udātta*).

When these meanings are to be indicated (dyotya) or expressed (vācya), the optative suffix (liṅ) shall be used;
"injunction" (vidhi) means the instigation of a subordinate person, such as a servant.
*Nimantraṇa* is the act of assigning a duty; *āmantraṇa* is the instigation of a daughter's son or others to perform necessary acts such as a *śrāddha* meal;
*adhīṣṭa* is the granting of permission for one’s own conduct, consisting of an activity preceded by formal respect.
It would be quite easy to say simply that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) [expresses] instigation;
the separate mention of the four [suffixes] is for the sake of elaboration.
According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.103,
the augment *yāsuṭ* is added to the *parasmaipada* endings of the optative (*liṅ*). Since this [augment] is marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ* (udātta),

it is understood from the mention of its *ṅit*-status that the prohibition "even in the case of an operation dependent on an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), provided it is not an operation concerning a phoneme (*analvidhi*)" applies in some instances.
The fact that the substitute *śānac* for *śnā* is marked with the *śit* designation is also an indicator here [of this rule],
The augment *suṭ* should be applied to the *takāra* and *thakāra* of the *liṅ*;
*yāsuṭ* is not superseded by *suṭ*, because their spheres of application differ: *yāsuṭ* belongs to the *liṅ* [in general], whereas *suṭ* belongs specifically to the *takāra* and *thakāra*.
In a *sārvadhātuka* affix and in the *liṅ* (optative) affix, there shall be elision (*lopa*) of the non-final *s*.
Thus, there is the disappearance of both *s* sounds,
yet the hearing of the *suṭ* augment occurs more clearly in the āśīr-liṅ (precative) mood, and even more so there in the ātmanepada.
In place of the *y* belonging to a portion of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that follows *at*, *iy* shall be substituted.
The elision of *y* would be a secondary quality (*guṇa*).

In the case of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, what would [the rule] intend to do? For, according to the maxim that an exception (*apavāda*) sublates [only] that which precedes it, only the elision of the final vowel (*ato lopa*) would be sublated.
But in cases such as *bhavet*, the long vowel would occur by virtue of its higher priority [in the order of rules]; thus, *bhavetām*.
In place of the *jhi* of the *liṅ*, *jus* shall be substituted;
[the *j* of *jus*] is elided.
When *uṣ* follows an *a*-vowel that does not occur at the end of a word, the single substitute shall be the form of the subsequent sound (*pararūpa*).
This being the case, the ancient teachers [state]: "Because it is subsequent and because it is eternal, *iy* [replaces *yās*]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.80).
Although, by virtue of being internal (*antaraṅga*), the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) would be more logical, nevertheless, it should be explained that *iy* replaces *yās*.
In this way, however, the sandhi is archaic;
[the forms] would be *bhaveyuḥ* and *bhaveḥ*.

may you be;

Because those [roots] denote action in general, while the verbal bases (*prakṛti*) of the *ām* suffix denote specific actions, there is a relation of non-difference between their respective meanings;

however, although *saṃpad* is included within the pratyāhāra, it is not employed because its meaning is not compatible [with the context]. As for *kṛ*, when the fruit of the action accrues to another, the *parasmaipada* would have been expected to occur.
In the rule *ām pratyayo yasmāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.93), the compound is a *bahuvrīhi* of the type where the qualities of the members are not included in the referent (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).

Therefore, even when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings do not occur in examples such as *indāñcakāra*, according to Pāṇini 3.4.81.

In place of the *ta* and *jha* suffixes of the *liṅ* (optative), *eś* and *irec* respectively are substituted. SK 2439 AS 7-2-77 SK 2440: In the case of a word ending in *ṣat*, when it is followed by a word beginning with *a* or *ā*, the elision of the final vowel of the first word and the initial vowel of the second word is optional. SK 2440: When a word ending in *ṣat* is followed by a word beginning with *r*, the elision of the final vowel of the first word and the initial *r* of the second word is obligatory. Thus, from *ṣaṭ + rathaḥ*, one derives *ṣaḍrathaḥ*. SK 2441: When a word ending in *ṣat* is followed by a word beginning with *l*, the elision of the final vowel of the first word and the initial *l* of the second word is obligatory. Thus, from *ṣaṭ + lakṣāṇi*, one derives *ṣaḷlakṣāṇi*. SK 2442: When a word ending in *ṣat* is followed by a word beginning with *v*, the elision of the final vowel of the first word and the initial *v* of the second word is obligatory. SK 2443: When a word ending in *ṣat* is followed by a word beginning with *s*, the elision of the final vowel of the first word and the initial *s* of the second word is obligatory. Thus, from *ṣaṭ + sahasrāṇi*, one derives *ṣaṭsahasrāṇi*. SK 2444: When a word ending in *ṣat* is followed by a word beginning with *y*, the elision of the final vowel of the first word and the initial *y* of the second word is obligatory.
