In *ruditaḥ*, because it is followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant (*paratvāt*), there is no substitution of *dhi* for *hi* when the suffix begins with *iṭ*. Thus,
*rudihi*.
After a verbal root beginning with *hal*, the augment *īṭ* shall be added to a following *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix that consists of a single phoneme (*apṛkta*).
He wept; he was weeping.
Not having wept,
you did not weep; you wept— you did weep.

Because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the augment *aṭ* and the suffix *iṭ*, which depend respectively on the specific base (*prakṛti*) and the specific suffix (*pratyaya*), the *yāsuṭ* augment should be applied; thus,
[the form] is *arudat*.
He wept.
1068. The root √śvas means "to sleep";
he sleeps (svapiti).
He slept;
they two slept.
They slept;
you two slept; you all slept.
After these [prefixes], the *s* of the initial element of a *sup* [suffix] shall become *ṣ*;
first, the verbal root is joined with the prefix.

In the case of the *liṭ* suffix, because the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the *ṣatva* [substitutions] apply by virtue of being subsequent rules, reduplication occurs; however, according to the principle that "what is established as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it does not cause reduplication," we have *suṣuṣupatuḥ*.
In the case of *suṣuṣupuḥ*, since the reduplication occurs before the suffix *akit*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable;
because the substitution of *ṣ* (by *ṣatvam*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* applies prior to that.
Because it is eternal, and because of the absence of the form *suṣi*, there is no *ṣ* in *susuṣvāpa*.
He slept well; he slept; he slept.
He may sleep, he may sleep, he may sleep soundly.
He slept (asvāpsīt).
1069. *Śvas* (to breathe): he breathes (*śvasiti*).
He breathed, he has breathed,
he was breathing; they two would breathe.
By the rule *śvasyāstām-hmyant-kṣaṇa* (Pāṇini 7.2.64), there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution]; thus,
it becomes *aśvasīt*.
And here,
breathing in is *āna*.
not led, led, led down;
not brought, brought, brought down; not bent, bent, bent down.
After a cause situated in a prefix, the *n* of the root *ani* shall be replaced by *ṇ*.
prāṇiti (1071); jakṣa in the sense of eating and laughing; jakṣiti.
Eaten (jakṣitaḥ) [is derived from the root *ghas*] by Pāṇini 6.1.45, Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.4.
The substitution of *at* for the root *jha* (*ad*) is an exception to the rule concerning final sounds; thus,
we have *jakṣati*.
Regarding the rule *sijabhyasta-saṃyogād yaj-ah* (Pāṇini 3.4.109), which prescribes *jus* for the suffix *jhi*,
Ujjvaladatta erroneously claimed that *ajakṣuḥ* begins with a semivowel (*antasthādi*).
The five roots beginning with *rud* have been completed (1072).
*Jāgṛ*, meaning "to wake from sleep," forms *jāgarti*.
"Those who are awake wake up," as stated in the Uṣavid-saṃdarbha (verse 2341).
He remained awake; he was vigilant.
AS 7.3.85: *jāgarti* shall undergo *guṇa* substitution in place of *viciṇṇalṅit*, except in the domain of *vṛddhi* and in the domain of prohibition;
[thus] *jajāgaratuḥ*.
*ajāgar*, *ajāgṛtām*:
because it is a reduplicated (abhyasta) stem, the suffix takes the form *jus*.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.83:
*ajādau jusīgantāṅgasya guṇaḥ syāt*— the *guṇa* substitute shall take the place of the final vowel of a stem ending in *i* or *u* when followed by the suffix *jus* beginning with a non-*j* vowel.
They did not wake; [if it were] *ajādi*, would they have woken? (*jāgṛyuḥ*)
In the sense of a blessing (āśis), however: jāgaryāt,
jāgaryāstām, jāgaryāsuḥ.

In the case of *ajāgarīt* from the root *jāgṛ*, the *yaṇ* substitution is first applicable; that is superseded by the *guṇa* of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix; that is superseded by the *vṛddhi* in the *sic* affix; and that is superseded by the *guṇa* of the root *jāgṛ*. When that has been applied, the *vṛddhi* conditioned by the root ending in a consonant (*hal*) becomes applicable, but it is prohibited by the rule *neṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.4). Subsequently, the rule *ato halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) is set aside, and the rule *ato lrāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.2) becomes applicable, but it is prohibited by the rule *hmyanta* (Pāṇini 7.2.5).
Regarding this, they say: "Guṇa, Vṛddhi, Guṇa, Vṛddhi, prohibition, option, again prohibition of Vṛddhi; therefore, there are nine applications [of rules] preceded by *yaṇ*. (Pāṇini 6.4.145–154).
*Daridrā* means in a miserable state.
The root *daridrā* (to be poor) [takes the suffix *śyan*] according to Pāṇini 3.1.68 and Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.114.
The vowel *i* is substituted for the root *daridrāti* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has the markers *k* or *ṅ*. Thus:
*daridrataḥ*. (SK 2483)
For these two [roots], there is the elision of the long *ā* before a *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with *k* or *ṅ*.
[The root] *daridrāti* [is one such].

Regarding the rule *anekāctvādām daridrāṃcakāra āta au ṇalaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.125), although the form would have been established by simply [stating] *o*, the prescription of *au* is for the purpose of ensuring its audibility when the *ā* of the root *daridrāti* has been elided.
For this very reason, based on the indicative [evidence], some maintain that the form *āmnat* occurs in cases such as *dadaridrau*, *dadaridruḥ*, and so forth.
As for the form *dadaridra* with the suffix *ṇal*, that is entirely without foundation; rather,
it should be stated as an option (*vā*) that there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ā* of the root *daridrā* when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is intended,
or optionally (*vā*) in the *luṅ* tense.
When the suffixes *san*, *ṇvul*, and *lyuṭ* follow, [the substitution] does not optionally apply to the root *daridrā*: *adaridritā* / *adaridrāt*.
They have not made her poor; may they not cause her to become poor.
From poverty, one becomes wealthy; [the suffixes] iṭ and sakau [are applied].
*adaridrāsīt* (he was not poor) 1074;
*cakāsṛ* in the sense of shining:
*cakāsti* (he shines).
For the root √jhas, *at* is substituted [before *liṭ*];
[thus] *cakāsati*, *cakāsāṃcakāra*.
According to some, the elision of *s* in *dhica* (Pāṇini 6.4.100) applies only to the suffix *sic*; however, because of the word *ca*,
the Bhāṣya states that it occurs as *cakādhi* and *cakādhī*.
In the context of the tip-pratyaya, a *s* at the end of a word becomes *d*, except in the case of the root *as*.
acakāt, acakāt, acakāsuḥ (SK 2485)
AS 8.2.74: For the *s* of a verbal root at the end of a word, *r* is substituted optionally; in the alternative case, by the rule of *jaś*-substitution, *d* is substituted.
acakāḥ, acakāt (1075) √śās in the sense of instruction.
He instructs. (Pāṇini 1.4.52)

In place of the penultimate vowel of the root *śās*, there shall be *it* (i) before the suffix *aṅ* and before *kṅit* suffixes beginning with a consonant; by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.60), the *ṣ* is substituted [for the *ś*]. Thus, *śiṣṭaḥ*.
He instructs, he has instructed; from the one who has instructed.
They two instructed the remaining [disciples].
According to Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.35,

the substitution of *śā* for the root *śās* occurs when the suffix *dhvam* follows; however, because this substitution is *abhīya* (belonging to the subsequent rule), it is considered asiddha (non-existent) for the purposes of the preceding rule, which results in the change of *hi* to *dhi*.
Teach the untaught; instruct those who have not been instructed.
He has commanded; he has commanded; he has commanded.
From the root *śās* (to instruct), by [Pāṇini 3.1.56] *sarti-śāsti-sūty-edh-ty-ūṭhsu aṅ*,
the form *aśiṣat* is derived.
*aśāsiṣyat* (1076).
*dīdhīṅ* [is used] in the senses of shining and playing; these five roots beginning with it are Vedic (*chāndasa*). [Example: *dīdhīte*.
By the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82), the *yaṇ* substitution occurs in *dīdhyāte* (SK 2488).

By the rule *AS 7.4.53*, "there is elision of the final [sound] of these two when followed by *y* or an *i*-vowel," one might expect elision; however, this is set aside by the substitution of *ai* for *ṭā*, as that rule is obligatory (*nitya*).
By the rule *dīdhye dīdhīvevīṭām*, there is a prohibition of *guṇa* [substitution]; thus,
[the form] is *dīdhyāñcakre*.
The root *dīdhī* (to shine) will be used in the same sense as *vevīṅ* (to go).
By the word "vī" (gone), the meaning is that it functions in a sense equivalent [to the preceding].
Now, there are three roots that take the *parasmaipada* endings:
1078. *ṣasa*, 1079. *ṣasti*, both meaning "sleep."
They lie down; he has lain down; they have lain down.
He has taught; they two have taught; let him teach.

Because of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1), the substitution of *sa* for *śa* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); therefore, by the rule *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105), the elision (*luk*) does not occur.
May they sit;
may he be; may it be.
From *sasyāt* arose *asāsīt* and *asasīt*.

When *santi* is followed by *id* (the augment *it*), and the suffix *anum* has been applied, the form becomes *saṃstas*. At this stage, by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), the *s* is elided; then, by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), there is optionally the elision of the *t* sound, resulting in *santaḥ*.

Since it is accepted that the technical term "conjunction" (saṃyoga) applies only when two [consonants] meet and not when many are gathered together, there is no elision by the rule *skoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), and thus [the form] is *saṃsti*.
Some say it is *saṃstaḥ*;
1080; *vaśa* means "desire," and desire is longing.
The one who has grown desires; they desire.
The bull has bellowed;
he has lowed.
May she, the mistress, will; may she desire.
Fly up from the camel!
Descend into the pit!
avaḍ, auṣṭām, auśan.
May they two desire him against his will; may they two desire him.
1081. And the *carkarīta* [intensive] should be understood as belonging to the *adādi* class when in its *yaṅ-luk* form.
1082. *hnuṅ* in the sense of removing.
he has hidden,
he has concealed, he may hide or conceal.
*ahnoṣīṣṭa*, *ahnoṣṭa*,
and so forth, belong to the adādi (second) class.
Thus ends the section on the *tiṅ* suffixes beginning with *ad*.
Now begins the section on the *tiṅ* suffixes beginning with *hujo* (the *juhotyādi* class):
1083. *Hu*, in the sense of giving and eating.
"Also in taking," and "also in satisfying," says the Bhāṣya;
and here, "giving" (dāna) means casting [into the fire].
And that [offering] is obtained by its very nature as being upon a Vaidha receptacle;
thus, from this [root], there are four [forms] in the *parasmaipada*.
In the case of the suffix *śap*, there shall be *ślu* substitution.
AS 6.1.10: Two [occurrences] of a verbal root are used [in reduplication],
as in *juhoti*.
In the case of *juhutaḥ*, by [Pāṇini 6.1.18] *adabhyastāt* and [Pāṇini 6.1.77] *huśnuvoḥ*, the *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs.
They offer oblations.
After these [roots], there may optionally be *ām* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), and the grammatical operations regarding *ślau* apply as if it were *ām*:
*juhavāṃcakāra*,
*juhāva*.
The Hotṛ shall offer; let him offer.
Sacrifice! Offer! Sacrifice!
Perform the oblation! Offer the oblation! Perform the oblation! Offer the oblation!
By virtue of its subsequent position, *guṇa* [is applied];
by virtue of its subsequent position, *juṣi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.83) [prescribes] *guṇa*.
They sacrificed; he should sacrifice; he would sacrifice.
He sacrificed;
[the root] *ñibhī* means fear;
he fears.
The substitution of *ik* (i) shall take place before an affix beginning with a consonant that is marked with *k* or *ṅ*, provided it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
Fearing,
fearing, they are afraid.
He was afraid;
he feared; he is one who will fear.
1085 *hrī* in the sense of modesty: *jihreti*, *jihrītaḥ* (he is ashamed).
He was ashamed; he became ashamed;
he felt shame.
1086 *pṝ* in the senses of protecting and filling;
In the case of *ślau*, the short vowel *i* shall be the substitute for the final sound of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). (SK 2494; Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.60)
The *ṛ* at the end of a stem that begins with a labial consonant (*uṣṭhya*) preceded by a semivowel (*aṅgāvayava*) shall be replaced by *ut*; however, because of its subsequent status,
this rule is superseded by the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*,
as in *piparti*.
The long vowel [ā] is substituted [for the short *u*] by the rule *utvaṃ raparatvaṃ hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73).
He has filled,
he fills,
he has filled full.
When *liṭ* follows, the substitution of *guṇa* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 7.4.12) would apply to the roots *ṛ*, *ṛcchati*, and *ṝ*. However,
[this is prevented by the following rule].
In the case of these roots, when the *liṭ* suffix follows, there may optionally be a short vowel; alternatively, there is *guṇa*, as in *papratuḥ*.
They filled, they two filled,
they all filled.
Thoroughly surrounded,
you have drunk deeply.
May he fill up the hollows;
may he fill up the joints; may he fill them full.
May he fill;
he has filled; they two have filled.
Some say that this [root] ends in a short vowel,
as in *piparti* and *pipṛtaḥ*.
They have granted;
may they grant;
may he grant for the sake of a blessing.
In the system of Pāṇini, however, he has excluded [this root]; in cases such as *pipṛtam* in the verse *taṃ rodasī pipṛtam*, one must take refuge in its being Vedic (*chāndasatva*).
(1087) The root *ḍubhṛñ* means "to support" and "to nourish."
For these three roots— *bhṛñ*, *māṅ*, and *ohāṅ*— the *it* (indicatory letter) shall be substituted for the reduplication when *ślau* (the suffix *liṭ*) follows.
He bears,
you two bear, you all bear.
By virtue of the substitution of *ślu*, there is reduplication;
[the forms] are *bibharāmāsa* and *babhāra*.
You bore; he bore; bear!
May I bear; you have borne; they two have borne.
They bore; he may bear; he shall be borne.
bhṛṣīṣṭa,
abhārṣīt, abhṛta
The root *māṅ* is used in the senses of measuring (*māna*) and sound (*śabda*).

The long vowel *ā* of the roots *śnā* and those with a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) is elided before a *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with a consonant that has the markers *k* or *ṅ*, but not for a root designated as *ghu*; thus,
in *mimīte*,
there is elision of the *ā* by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112).
They measure,
they fashion,
and the foundation has been laid.
1089 ohāṅ in the sense of "going": jihīte, jihāte.
He is being abandoned, he has abandoned, he is an abandoner.
hāsyate 1090: the root √ohāk, meaning "to abandon," belongs to the *parasmaipada* voice.
he abandons SK 2498 AS 6-4-116
Before a sārvadhātuka affix beginning with *ha* that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*, there is optionally the substitution of *ī* for the vowel [of the root]; thus,
*jahitaḥ*.
He was abandoning, he abandons, he abandoned.
In the presence of the suffix *ha*, the root *jahāti* becomes *jahā*; furthermore, when followed by vowels beginning with *a* or *i*, it becomes *jahī*.
leave it, you will leave it, you shall leave it.
He abandoned; they abandoned.
In the case of the root *jahāti*, there shall be elision of the letter *ā* before an affix beginning with *ya* that is a *sārvadhātuka*; thus, [the form] is *jahyāt*.
In the Erliṅi (Erliṅi SKsandarbhaḥ 2374),
it was lost from the *heya*.
1091. The root *ḍudāñ* means "to give";
[in the present tense] one gives (*praṇidadāti*), and [in the past participle] it is "given" (*dattaḥ*).
He gives, he gave, he has given.
By the rule *ghvasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.119), there is the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication; thus,
*dehi* and *adadāt*.
One should give what has not been given.
may he give,
he gave, they two gave; may he give, he gave, they two gave.
adu (1092) and ḍudhāñ (1093), meaning "to hold" and "to nourish."
Some also apply their minds toward generosity.

For the reduplicated root *dhāñ* ending in a *jhaṣ* consonant, a *bhaṣ* sound shall replace a *baś* sound when followed by *t*, *th*, *s*, or *dhv*; because of the force of the explicit statement [in the sūtra], the elision of *ā* is not treated as *sthānivadbhāva*—so state Vāmana and Mādhava.
In reality, however, with respect to what is not established in the preceding [rule], there is no substitution of the original form; thus, one says *dhattaḥ* and *dadhati*.
dhatthaḥ, dadhvaḥ,
dhatte
dhatse dhaddhve dhehi
Now, three roots beginning with *svar* have the svarita accent (1093):
*ṇijir* in the sense of purification and nourishing.
In the case of the suffix ślu, there shall be guna substitution for the reduplicated syllable of the roots √ṇij, √vij, and √viṣ.
He washes; they two wash; he washes (causative).
The one who has washed away [impurity] will not look [at it] again.
Wash it; wash it thoroughly.
AS 7.3.87: The guṇa substitution for a light penultimate vowel shall not take place [in the case of the desiderative form] *nenijāni*.
They made her who was not straight out to be straight.
He should cleanse; he should purify;
he purified.
anaikṣīt, anikta (1094) —
the root *vij* means "to become separate."
He separates, he has separated, you have separated.
In this context, the designation *ṅit* [of the root] is not applicable by the rule *vija iṭ* (Pāṇini 1.2.2), because the root *ovijī* is what is intended there; furthermore,
*ṇij* and *vijī* also belong to the *rudhādi* class.
1095 viṣlṛ, in the sense of pervading: veveṣṭi (active), veviṣṭe (middle).
Because it is marked with *lṛdit*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied; [the result is] *aviṣat* in the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) voice, with the suffix *ksa*.
By the rule *ajādau kṣasyāci* (Pāṇini 6.1.115), there is elision of the *a* [of the suffix *kṣa*] before a vowel beginning with a non-j letter; thus:
*avikṣata*, *avikṣātām*.
Now, those ending in the suffix -āna are *ātmanepada* roots, as well as Vedic ones;
[the root] *ghṛ*, meaning "to flow" and "to shine," is number 1096.
"I sprinkle the foremost one with the oblation of clarified butter"—
here, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.103), the substitution of *i* for *ī* occurs;
[the root] *hṛ* is used in the sense of "doing forcibly."

This *sruva* ladle offers the oblations (*abhijiharti*). Although [the form] is already established by the rule "In the Vedic language, [the roots] *sṛ*, *gatau* [and others take *i*]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.44), this [form *jiharti*] occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*) due to the prescription of *it* by the rule "And for the roots *ṛ* and *piparti*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.77).
By the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78), the substitution *iyAṄ* is applied, resulting in *iyarti* and *iyṛtaḥ*.
He goes;
he has gone.
By the rule *iḍattyarti-* (Pāṇini 7.2.71), the augment *iṭ* is obligatory; thus,
the forms are *āritha* and *artā*.
He will harm these others.
They two went; they went; he would go.
From the noble one,
he has ceased from the course.
The root *bhas* (1100) means "to threaten" and "to shine.
In the form *babhasti*,
the penultimate vowel is elided according to Pāṇini 6.4.100 (*ghasibhasorhalica*).
By the rule *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26), there is the elision of the *s*; thus, [the forms] are *babdhaḥ* and *bapsati*.
1101. *ki* (to know) in the sense of cognition; 1102. *tura* (to hasten) in the sense of speed.
He has tormented; he has tormented repeatedly; he torments.
1103 *dhiṣ* in the sense of sound: *didheṣṭi*, *didhiṣṭaḥ*.
Bestowing wealth and grain,
they bestow them.
The people offer [oblations] in the place of birth.

For these [roots], the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel occurs before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant followed by *san*, and before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*.
He has been born;
he is being born; you have been born.
He has been born;
may he be born;
may he be born.
From *janyāt* [comes] *jāyāt* (1106); *gā* is used in the sense of praise (*stuti*).
Seeking favor, he goes toward the gods; having conquered, he goes forth as a conqueror.
Thus ends the section on the *juhoty-ādi* (third) class of verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*.
Now begins the section on the *div-ādi* (fourth) class of verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*.
1107. The root *divu* is used in the senses of playing, desiring victory, dealing, shining, praising, rejoicing, intoxication, sleeping, beauty, and motion.
The roots beginning with *jhṛṣ* are *parasmaipada*.
(SK 2505; Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.69)
The long vowel [substitution] by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.71) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *śap* [affix]; [thus,
the form is] *dīvyati*.
They have played,
they are playing,
and they will play.
May he play;
he played;
he should play.
May he play;
he played; he would play.
1108. *Ṣivu* (in the sense of "sewing together" or "continuous stringing"):
*pariṣīvyati*, *pariṣiṣeva*.
nyapevīt, nyasevīt (1109) √sriv, in the senses of moving and drying.
1110. *ṣṭhivu* (to spit) in the sense of ejecting;
some do not read this root here.
1111. *ṣṇusu* (to eat).
Some say "grasping," others say "non-seeing";
thus he weeps.
suṣṇosa 1112: the root √ṣṇasu means "to cast out"; one casts out (snasyati).
*sasnāma* 1113; *knasu* [is used] in the senses of crookedness (*hvaraṇa*) and shining (*dīpti*); *hvaraṇa* means crookedness (*kauṭilya*).
The root *caknāsa* (1114) means "to burn";
it has the form *vuvyoṣa*.
1115 *pluṣ* (to burn);
1116 *nṛtī* (to move the limbs),

The roots beginning with *vṛt*, *puṣ*, and *div* have been conjugated.
However, some hold that the formation of *vṛt* is solely for the purpose of completing the *puṣādi* group;
whereas *div* and others belong to the *bhvādi* class as an unformed (*ākṛta*) group,
and thus [the root] *kṣi* is included [therein].
They say that [the forms] beginning with *mṛgyati* are established;
thus ends the section on the *div*-class (*divādi*) of verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*.
Now begins the section on verbal roots beginning with *su* (tiṅanta-svādi-prakaraṇam).
1248. The root *ṣuñ* (in the sense of pressing) forms *abhiṣavaḥ*, which denotes sprinkling, bathing, pressing, ritual ablution, and the fermentation of liquor.
In that context, the verb "to bathe" (snāti) is intransitive (akarmaka) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.73.
By the rule "sunoti sunutaḥ huśnuvoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.87), the *yaṇ* substitute [i.e., *u*] is applied.
They press,
you two press, you all press.

he has pressed.
Sītā gave birth to a son.
I shall press; let me press; one should press.
By the rule "sūyāt-stu-su-dhū-bhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.44), the augment *iṭ* is applied,
resulting in *asāvīt*.
He pressed; he is pressing; he has pressed.
He pressed [the Soma].
(Pāṇini 8.3.117)

The augment *iṭ* may optionally be applied after the roots *vṛ* and *vṛñ*, as well as after those ending in long *ṝ*, before the suffixes *liṅ* and *sic* when followed by the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) terminations.
In the case of the root *vṛ*, there shall not be lengthening of the augment *iṭ* in the optative;
[thus] *variṣīṣṭa* and *vṛṣīṣṭa*.
He has covered; they have covered; you have covered.
*avṛta* 1256: *dhuñ* in the sense of shaking; *dhunoti*.
He shook off; he has shaken off; he will shake off.
This [root] also ends in a long vowel:
*dhū* (to shake) takes the forms *dhūnoti* and *dhūnute*.
By the rule *svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied; thus,
[the forms] are *dudhavitha* and *dudhotha*.
In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix, however, setting aside the prohibition by the rule *śryukaḥ...* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), the augment *iṭ* is obligatory due to the restriction by the *krādi* group;
furthermore, the augment *iṭ* is obligatory after the roots *du*, *dhū*, *stu*, and *dhūñ* by the rule *stusudhūñbhyaḥ...* (Pāṇini 7.2.72). Thus, [the forms] *dudhuviva* and so on are established.

It has been stated that here too the rule from another grammatical system (vyākaraṇāntara), "the *liṭ* [affix] of the roots *śranth*, *granth*, *dambh*, and *svañj* is optionally *kit*," is adopted. Since that [elision] is considered non-established (*asiddha*) because it belongs to the *ābhīya* class, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not apply.

thus: *debhatuḥ*, *dadambhatuḥ*.

From the root *chur* (1374), meaning "to blossom clearly," [the form] *sphuṭati* [is derived].

*khuḍa*, *chuḍa*— thus say some.

jugure (root) guritā 1398, meaning "to praise" (ṇū stavane).

nuvati, anuvīt 1399; dhū [is used] in the sense of shaking.

He has heard from a short limb;
they two have heard.
aguṣuḥ 1401; [the root] dhru [is used] in the senses of motion and steadiness; *dhruva* is an alternative reading.

Kaiyaṭa and others hold that [the suffix] has a long final vowel, as in *kuvīt* and *akuvīṣṭa*.
Why does the author of the Nyāsa say "ending in a short vowel"? It is not so.
The roots beginning with *vṛt* have been explained; now, 1403.
*pṛṅ* (to exert oneself).
Generally, when preceded by *vi* or *ā*, the substitution of *riṅ* and *iyaṅ* occurs.
He is occupied;
he has been occupied; they have been occupied.

he was occupied; they two were occupied.

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes are applied after the root *mṛ*, which is the base for the optative (*liṅ*) and imperative (*loṭ*), as well as for the *śit* (present indicative), and not elsewhere; its *ṅit*-character is for the sake of the accent,
as in *mriyate*.
I died, I am dead, I have died.
You shall die; he will die; may he forgive.
Now, the seven roots ending in *am* that take the *parasmaipada* endings:
1405 *ri*, 1406 *pi*, meaning "to go."
Because it is internal, *iyaṅ* [replaces the vowel] in the forms *riyati* and *piyati*.
*retā* and *petā* [are roots];

O singer!

*ādriyete*

Now, there are sixteen roots that take the *parasmaipada* endings.
1414. *pracch* (to ask) in the sense of desiring to know: *pṛcchati*.

The augment *am* is applied by the rule "sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti" (Pāṇini 6.1.58), which states that the augment *am* is added after the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś* before a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant, provided the suffix does not have *kit* as its marker. you have bathed,
you have immersed yourself,
you will bathe.
He will smear; he smeared;
they two smeared.

mṛdnāti,

thus, [the form] is *eṣitā*.
In reality, however, the optionality of *iṭ* is appropriate even for the root *iṣ*;
and thus the *Vārttika* states:
"There is a prohibition [of *iṭ*] after the suffix *śyan* when there is the substitution of *takāra* for the root *iṣ*. (Vā.)
In the absence of poison,
it expands and envelops.

Some say that this [world] has been vomited out by the Knower.

AS 6.4.19: For the *ch* and *v* of a root that contains a *t*, there are respectively the substitutes *cha* and *ūṭh* when followed by an affix beginning with a nasal (*anunāsika*) or a consonant (*jhal*) that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*, provided it is not an ārdhadhātuka affix; for example, *khauṇāti*.

The causative form *cakhāva* is derived from the root *khā* with the suffix *śānac*; because the substitution of *ūṭh* occurs by virtue of its higher priority (*paratva*), the suffix *śānac* is not applied due to the absence of a final consonant (*halantatva*). [Pāṇini 6.4.67] *heṭha* and [the following].
For it effects the state of being *ṣṭu* [in the root *hiṭhṇāti*, 1534]; *graha* means "taking up."
The root *grah* (to seize), being marked with the svarita accent, takes the *samprasāraṇa* substitution [of its semivowel] before the suffixes beginning with *jyā*, as in *gṛhṇāti*.
He grasps.

The long vowel is substituted for the augment *iṭ* prescribed after the root *grah*, provided it consists of a single vowel; however, this does not apply in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, as in *grahītā*;
but in the *liṭ* tense, [the form] is *jagrahitha*.
By the rule *gṛhyāt grahīṣīṣṭa hmyanta...* (Pāṇini 7.2.37), there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution].
He took;
they two took;

*agrahīṣātām*, *agrahīṣata*: the section on the *tiṅ*-endings of the *kriyādi* (the first class of roots).

The root *cur* (to steal) [is used with the genitive case of the object],

One who steals shall be stolen from; may he be stolen from.

Some consider this indicative [sūtra] to be dependent on the general rule;

For this very reason, there is no redundancy in [the rule] *ādhṛṣādvā* (Pāṇini 1.4.35); for when there is a restriction (*saṃkoca*),

*dolayati*, *dolayāmāsa* (he swings/took up and down).

*campati* (1621) [is used] in the sense of patience (*kṣānti*); [it is conjugated as] *kṣampayati*.

The prohibition of the *mittva* designation for the root *nī* (meaning "to lead") applies only when it is not preceded by another [prefix], as in the form *śamayate*; [the root] *kuts*, meaning "to revile," is [treated similarly]. 1698. *kuts* in the sense of throwing down.

The binding of power is the capacity for procreation, and this binding of power increases through the union of intoxication and satisfaction. 1706. Madatṛptiyoge.
mādayate (1707) means "to rejoice"; divu (1708) means "to coo" or "to warble"; gṛ (1709) means "to perceive" or "to understand."
The root *gār* (in the sense of censuring) is conjugated as *gārayate*.
The root *vid* (in the senses of perceiving,
telling, and dwelling) is conjugated as *vedayate*.
The root *vid* takes the suffix *śyan*, *luk*, or *śnam* respectively in the senses of "attaining" (prāpti) and "measuring" (māna); in the sense of "stubbornness" (stambha),

1711. *yu* in the sense of disgust (*jugupsā*): *yāvayate* (Gaṇapāṭha).
1712. *kusma* as a name (*nāman*). Or [it may be used] optionally.
The root *kusm* occurs in the sense of contemptuous smiling;
[its forms are] *kusmayate*,
*acukusmata*.
Alternatively, *kusma* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); from that, the suffix *ṇic* expresses the meaning of the verbal root, and thus [the roots] beginning with *ā-kusmīya* [are formed].
1713. *carca* in the sense of "reciting" (*adhyayana*).
1714. *Bhūṣaṇe* (in the sense of ornamenting). 1715. *Śabda* (sound) and *upasargāt āviṣkāre ca* (and after a prefix, in the sense of manifestation), and also in the sense of ornamenting (*bhūṣaṇe*).

jambhayati, jambhati (1718); ṣūda, in the sense of flowing.
sūdayati,

The prohibition "not others [are] measured" (*nānye mitaḥ*) applies to the root *am*,

meaning "to go" and so forth, when followed by the suffix *śap*; because it has undergone the causative suffix *ṇic*, the prohibition "not for roots ending in *kam*, *yam*, or *cam*" (*na kamyamicamām*) applies.
The roots *āmayati* (1722),
*caṭa* (1723), and *sphuṭa* mean "breaking" and "expanding"; it is stated that [the latter] takes the forms *sphuṭati* and *sphoṭate*.

1724. *Ghaṭ* [is used] in the sense of "striking together" (*saṅghāta*); it forms *ghāṭayati*. The phrase "and those having the meaning of 'to kill'" (*hantyarthāśca*) means that even those roots not included in the ninth class (*navagaṇya*), provided they have the meaning of "to kill," take the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in their own sense (*svārthe*). 1725. *Div* [is used] in the sense of "crushing" (*mardana*).
By virtue of being [a root] beginning with *ud*, it is also [used] in the sense of "to cross over" (tīr); furthermore,
*arj* is used in the sense of "exertion" (*pratiyatna*),
and this [root] is also used in other meanings.
He acquires wealth;
[the root] *ghuṣ* in the sense of proclaiming means he proclaims.

In the rule *ghuṣir aviśabde* (Dhātupāṭha 3063), the negative particle *a-* in the word *avi-* serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) for this root is not mandatory; thus, one may optionally form *ghoṣati*, or, because it is marked with the indicatory letter *iṭ*, the suffix *aṅ*.
*aghuṣat* and *aghoṣīt* [are the forms]; however, for the causative (*ṇyanta*), it is *ajūghuṣat*.

The root *krand*, belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa, is stated to mean "calling out" (*āhvāna*) and so forth; when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, that very same root takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "continuity" (*sātatya*).
Others, however, say that the root *ghuṣ* preceded by the prefix *ā-* means "to cry out," as in the expression *ākrandayati*; thus,
one says *āghoṣayati*.
1729 *lasa* in the sense of artistic skill; 1730 *tasi*; 1731 *bhūṣa* in the sense of adorning:
*avataṃsayati*.
*Avataṃsati* means "to adorn"; *arha* is used in the sense of "worship."
1733. *Jñā* in the sense of commanding means "he commands. 1734. *Bhaja* in the sense of bestowing means "he bestows."
1735. The root *śṛdh* (meaning "to mock" or "to laugh at") forms *aśaśardhat* and *aśīśṛdhat*.
1736. *yata* in the sense of humiliation (*nikāra*) and adornment (*upaskāra*).
1737. *raka*. 1738. *laga* in the sense of tasting (*āsvādane*); some say [it means] moving (*ragha*).
Others say that *rañja* means "to color";
*añc* means "to distinguish," as in *añcayati*.
The status of being *uditt* is for the purpose of the optional application of *iṭ*;
for this very reason, the causative suffix *ṇic* is optionally applied after the root *añc*.
In this same manner, it should be understood for *śṛdhuj* and others as well.
1740. The root *ligi*, meaning "to mark" or "to characterize," forms *liṅgayati*.
The root *liṅg* (numbered 1741) means "to mix"; it causes the barley meal (*saktu*) to be mixed with ghee (*ghṛta*).
1742. *tras* means "to hold" according to some; others say it means "to ward off."
1743. Regarding *udhraṣa* in the sense of "gleaning": some say that the letter *u* is a constituent part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), while others say it is not.
He causes to fall;
he falls; he causes to rise up.
1744 *muc* in the senses of releasing and gladdening;
1745 *vas* in the senses of affection, cutting, and taking away;
1746 *car* in the sense of doubt.
Some say that it causes [the mind] to fall away from both sorrow and laughter.
The root *cyu* (in the form *cyuṣ*) means "to fall" (*cyavate*);
with the prefix *ava*, it means "to calculate" (*avakalkane*).
1748. *bhuvaḥ* [is used] in the sense of "calculating."
Some say that *avakalkana* is mixing; others say it is reflection; [the root] *bhū* means "he brings about."

And from the root *kṛp* (in the sense of "to devise" or "to prepare"), [the suffix] *kalpa* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ā*, provided that the object is coreferential with the agent (*svakarmakāt*). For example: *āsvadakaḷpa*.
The causative suffix *ṇic* occurs after roots that can take an object, provided that the action extends to the agent's own enjoyment (*svadi*); for example, from the root *gras* (to swallow),
one says *grāsayati* (he causes to swallow) the fruit.
1751. *puṣ* in the sense of supporting; it supports an ornament (*ābharaṇa*). 1752. *dal* in the sense of splitting.

1753. *dālayati* (to split) 1754. *paṭa* (to split) 1755. *puṭa* (to fold or envelop) 1756. *luṭa* (to roll or toss) 1757. *tuji* (to strike) 1758. *miji* (to crush) 1759. *piji* (to press) 1760. *luji* (to break) 1761. *bhaji* (to break or divide) 1762. *laghi* (to move quickly) 1763. *trasi* (to tremble) 1764. *pisi* (to grind) 1765. *kusi* (to tear) 1766. *daśi* (to bite) 1767. *kuśi* (to tear) 1768. *ghaṭa* (to join or strive) 1769. *ghaṭi* (to join or strive) 1770. *bṛhi* (to grow or speak) 1771. *barha* (to pluck or tear) 1772. *valha* (to pluck or tear) 1773. *gup* (to protect or hide) 1774. *dhūp* (to fumigate or perfume) 1775. *viccha* (to shine or spread) 1776. *cīva* (to sew or weave) 1777. *putha* (to strike or kill) 1778. *lokṛ* (to see or look at) 1779. *locṛ* (to see or look at) 1780. *ṇada* (to sound) 1781. *kupa* (to be angry) 1782. *tarka* (to reason or infer) 1783. *vṛtu* (to choose) 1784. *vṛdhu* (to increase) These [roots] have the sense of speaking (*bhāṣārtha*). [The causative form] *pāṭayati* (causes to split).
He strikes,
he tosses, he beats.
He weaves; thus he causes others to strive.
He causes to ring.

In the case of a causative suffix (*ṇic*) that elides a portion of the root (*aglopin*), as well as for roots marked with *ṛ* (*ṛdit*), there shall be no shortening of the penultimate vowel when followed by a *caṅ* (the reduplication of the aorist) suffix; thus,
*alulokat* and *alulocat*.
It causes to turn and it causes to increase; because it is marked with *ud*, it turns by itself.

vardhati (1784), ruṭa (1785), laji (1786), aji (1787), dasi (1788), bhṛśi (1789), ruśi (1790), śīka (1791), rusi (1792), naṭa (1793), puṭi (1794), ji (1795), ci (1796), raghi (1797), laghi (1798), ahi (1799), rahi (1800), mahi— these have the meaning of speaking (bhāṣārtha). Laḍi (1802), taḍa (1803), nala— these have the meaning of speaking (bhāṣārtha).

In the root *pūrī* (meaning "to fill"), the quality of being *īdit* is for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *iṭ* after the *niṣṭhā* suffix; for this very reason, the causative suffix *ṇic* is optional.
*pūrayati* and *pūrati* (1805) [mean] to fill;
*ruj* (1806) [means] to injure or harm.
1806. The root *ṣvad* means "to taste"; some say it is *svad*.
The form *asiṣvadat* [is derived from it].
Because the long vowel [in *āsvadat*] is taught by Tvaṣṭṛ, the forms such as *asisvadat* belong to the *āsvadīya* class.
(ga) From *ā dhṛṣādvā* onwards, up to and including the root *dhṛṣ*, the suffix *ṇic* is optional. 1807. *yuj* and 1808. *pṛc* [take *ṇic*] in the sense of restraining.
He yokes; he has yoked; he yoked.
He causes to cook;
he cooks; he will have cooked.
1809. *arca* in the sense of worship;
1810. *ṣaha* in the sense of endurance.
That very same elephant endures the insults from young elephants; it assists him [in this].
(1811) *īr* [is used] in the sense of casting away.
1812 *lī* in the sense of liquefying: *lāpayati*, *layati*.
In the year 1813, in the sense of "avoiding" (vṛjī varjane),
[the root] varjayati [is used].
He avoids;
[the root] *vṛñ* in the sense of covering, he wards off (*vārayati*).
He restrains, he restrains,
he has restrained.
*varītā* (1815);
*jṛ* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohāni*), as in *jārayati*.
He grows old;
he is one who has grown old;
he is one who will grow old.
1816. And *jri* causes to hasten (*jrāyayati*) and hastens (*jrayati*).
*jretā* (1817): *ric* [is used] in the senses of separation and purifying; it forms *recayati*.
The root *rec* (reca-ti) means "to evacuate" (*rektā*), [occurring] in the sense of not being suitable for all purposes (*asarvopayoge*).
1818. *śiṣa*. *Śiṣ* [is used] when there is no application for everything.
He leaves over,
he leaves remaining;
she will leave over.
He learned that this root *tap*, preceded by the prefix *vi-*, signifies "to burn" in the sense of excellence.
1819. *tapa* (means) burning.
It heats, it burns, it is heated.
1820. *tṛp* in the sense of satisfaction;
some say [it means] inflaming;
[the form] *tarpayati*.
*Tarpati* (when caused) means "is satisfied"; *chṛdī* (the root) means "inflammation" or "burning."
He vomits, he spits out; [the one] who has vomited.
Regarding the rule *chardiṣyati śeṣici* (Pāṇini 6.1.59), the option [of the substitution of *iṭ*] does not apply because,
due to association (*sāhacarya*), only the root belonging to the *raudhādika* class is understood there.
Some say that *cṛpa*, *chṛpa*, *tṛpa*, and *dṛpa* mean "to inflame"; thus, one says *carpayati* or *charpayati*.
1822. The root *dṛbh* means "to fear"; it forms *darbhayati* and *darbhati*.
*darbhitā* (1823): the root *dṛbh*, meaning "to weave," belongs to the *tudādi* class and is marked with the *īṭ* augment.
1824. *Mokṣa* (to release);
some say [it means] injury.
The roots *māyayati*, *mayati*, and *metā* (1826) mean "to bind."
*granthayati* and *grathati* (1827) [mean] to tie;
*śīka* (1828) [means] to endure;
and *cīka* (1829) likewise.
1829 *ard* in the sense of "to afflict," is marked with the svarita accent; [it is conjugated as] *ardayati*.
*ardati*,
*ardate* (1830); *hiṃs* in the sense of injury.
It means "he injures," "he harms," or "he destroys"; thus it is explained with the *śnam* suffix.
1831. *Arh* (to be worthy) in the sense of worship;
1832. after the prefix *āṅ*, *sad* (to sit) in the sense of "attaining" [is replaced by] *āsādayati*.
By the rule *āsīdati pāghrā-* (Pāṇini 7.3.78), there is the substitution of *sīd* for *ās*; thus,
[the form] is *āsattā*.
He sat down;
[the root] *śundh* is used in the sense of the act of purification,
[and its past participle is] *śundhita*.
aśundhīt, aśundhiṣṭām 1834; chada in the sense of covering.
The root *juṣ* (marked with the svarita accent) is used in the sense of *paritarkaṇa*;
*paritarkaṇa* means either deliberation (*ūha*) or injury (*hiṃsā*).
Others say "paritarpaṇa" means "complete satiation"; [the root] *juṣ* causes one to perform the act of complete satiation.
The root *juṣ* (joṣati) means "to please" and "to serve"; it is listed as *juṣate* in the *tudādi* class (1836).
The root *dhūñ* means "to shake."
With reference to the [roots] beginning with *ṇau*,
it should be stated that the augment *nuk* is applied after the roots *dhūñ* and *prīñ*:
*dhūnayati*.
Some read "dhūñ prīṇoḥ" [in the Dhātupāṭha] and, on account of its association with the root *prī*, claim that the augment *nuk* applies only to the root *dhū*.
This [root] *dhāv* occurs in the *svādi*, *kryādi*, and *tudādi* [classes],
and in the *svādi* and *kryādi* [classes].
In the case of the *svādi* [group of roots], there is also a short vowel;
likewise, in the *Kavirahasya*, it is stated:
"He shakes the groves of campaka, he shakes the aśoka, he shakes the mango, and he shakes the blossoming atimuktikā."
In the forest, the wind stirs up the pollen of the campaka flowers and causes the clusters of sandalwood blossoms to dance;
it gladdens and satisfies all.
However, according to the reading stated by Haradatta as "dhūñ-prīṇoḥ," [the forms] are *prāyayati* and *prayati*.
*prath* (1838), *śranth* (1839), *granth* (1840) in the sense of composition; *āplṛ* in the sense of obtaining.
He causes to obtain; he caused to obtain; he obtains.
Some say that this [term] *āpa* is *svarita* when it is *āpta*.
In the year 1841, there was a deficiency in both faith and the necessary requisites,
and even due to the presence of adverse conditions, there was a lack of long-term endurance.
It extends, it stretches out, it spreads.
Some say that it spreads out, destroys faith,
and brings [them] together.
*canati* (1842): in the sense of speaking or sending a message, it means "he speaks" or "he sends."
The verb *vad* (to speak) is marked with the svarita accent;
it is conjugated as *vadati* (in the parasmaipada) and *vadate* (in the ātmanepada).
According to some, [the root] *vad* is anudātta; thus they say *vavadatuḥ* and *vavaditha*.
vavade vadyāt 1843 vaca paribhāṣaṇe (to speak)
He causes to speak, he speaks, [he is] a speaker.
The root √mān (avākṣīt) is used in the sense of honoring;
it forms mānayati.
The root *mān* in the sense of "to honor" belongs to the *bhūvādi* class and is always accompanied by the suffix *san*.
The roots beginning with *stambh* (as in *stambhe mānayate*) belong to the Ākusmīya group;
*man* (as in *manyate*) belongs to the Divādi group.
"Manute" belongs to the *tan* class (DhP 8.1). Furthermore,
the root *bhū*, meaning "to attain," is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) as *bhāvayate*.
Some say that the ātmanepada ending occurs for the root *bhū* only by virtue of its connection with the suffix *ṇic*.
1846 *garh* in the sense of censuring; 1847 *mārg* in the sense of seeking;
1848 *kaṭh* in the sense of grieving.
The prefix *ud* is used here in the sense of longing (*utkaṇṭhā*).
The root *kaṇṭh*, meaning "to long for," has been listed [in the Dhatupatha] as taking the *ātmanepada* suffixes (1849).
The root *mṛj* means "purification" and "adornment."
He cleanses,
he cleanses, [she] has cleansed.
The root *mṛṣ* (mārṣṭā), meaning "to endure" (*titikṣāyām*),
is marked with the *svarita* accent.
He endures,
he forgives,
he patiently accepts.
*mṛṣyati* and *mṛṣyate* belong to the *divādi* class; with the suffix *śap*, they mean "to sprinkle" (*secane*), as in *marṣati*.
(1851) *dhṛṣ* means "to laugh at" (*prahasane*).
The *ādhṛṣīya* [verbal roots] are those such as *dharṣayati* and *dharṣati*.

Now, those ending in vowels: 1852. In the case of *kath* in the sense of "composition of speech," there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] because of the status as a *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision (*alopa*).
He says that because it is aglopi (having lost its penultimate vowel), there is neither lengthening nor the treatment as *saṇvat*,
[as in] *acakathat*.
1853. *Var* in the sense of desire;
it has been explained that [the root] means "he chooses" (*varayati*) or "he wards off" (*vārayati*).
1854. *gaṇa* in the sense of counting: *gaṇayati* (SK 2573).

AS 7.4.97: The vowel *ī* shall be substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of the root *gaṇ*, and this substitution also occurs when followed by a *ṇi*-affix that is itself followed by *caṅ*;
[as in] *ajīgaṇat*.
*ajagaṇat* (1855); *śaṭha* (1856) and *śvaṭha* (1857) mean "to speak correctly";
*paṭha* (1858) and *vaṭha* (1859) mean "to bind."
1859 *raha* in the sense of abandonment;
1860 *ararahat*; 1861 *stana* and *gadī* in the sense of the word for "god."
It thunders, it roars, it has thundered;
or [it denotes] the motion of a bird.
Or [the root] is causative (*ṇijanta*), or according to some it ends in *a* (*adanta*);
in the first case [it is as follows].
He causes to fall, he falls, he has caused to fall.
Having fallen [into the first], one causes another to fall.
*apīpatat* (1863): [the root] *paṣa* [takes the suffix *nic*] after a prefix,
only in the sense of "motion."
paṣayati (1864); in the sense of throwing the voice, svarayati.
1865. *rac* in the sense of effort (*pratiyatna*): *racayati*.
1866. *kal* in the senses of moving (*gati*) and counting (*saṃkhyāna*).
1867. *cah* in the sense of plotting; plotting means hypocrisy and deceit. 1868. *mah* in the sense of worship.
The root *mah* with the suffix *śap* means "to increase" or "to be great" (1869). The roots *sāra*, *kṛpa*, and *śratha* mean "weakness" (1870–1871).
It causes to flow,
it softens, it loosens.
1872 *spr̥h* (to desire);
1873 *bhām* (in the sense of anger),
as in *ababhāmat*.
1874. Regarding the root *sūca* in the sense of "backbiting" (*paiśunya*): it is *sūcayati*.
Because it is not taught with an initial *ṣ* (*aṣopadeśatvāt*), there is no substitution of *ṣ*.
*asūsucat* (1875) [is used] in the sense of "eating food"; some say [it is used] with a word ending in the third case.
Others say *khoṭa* [means] "to deceive" (1876); *kṣoṭa* [means] "in destruction" (1877); *goma* [means] "in smearing."
In 1878, he played with the princes; he sported with the princes.
1879. *Upadhāraṇa* in the sense of maintaining moral conduct (*śīla*); *upadhāraṇa* means practice (*abhyāsa*).
1880. *Sāma* in the sense of employing conciliation (*sāntva*).
*sasāma* [is used] in the sense of conciliation (*sāntvana*); *asīṣamat*, however, refers to the past;
*velā* [is used] in the instruction of time (*kāla*).
Some say that because it measures time (*velayati*), it is a separate element (*dhātu*);
it causes [things] to pass through time (*kālayati*).
1882. *palyūla* in the sense of cutting and winnowing; 1883. *vāta* in the sense of blowing and pleasant service;
[the root] *vātayati*.
In the year 1884 of the *avavāta* era,
he searched for and sought out Ajagava.
1885. *vāsa* in the sense of service; 1886. *nivāsa* in the sense of clothing; [the suffix] *anin* in the sense of dwelling.
1887. *Bhāja* is used in the sense of dividing or separating (*pṛthakkarmaṇi*). 1888. *Sabhāja* is used in the sense of affection and looking upon;
others say it means affection and service (*prītisevanayoḥ*).
He honors; 1889; in the sense of diminishing, he diminishes.

In the rule *oḥ puyaṇji* (Pāṇini 7.4.80), although it would have been sufficient to state *payayoḥ*, the inclusion of the term *vargapratyāhāraja* (the class-consonants and the semi-vowels) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that an *ādeśa* (substitute) for the vowel *a* should not take effect when a reduplication (*dvitva*) is to be performed.

This prohibition applies only where, upon reduplication, the first vowel of the subsequent portion of the reduplicated stem is found to be an *avarṇa* (a, ā) either in the process of derivation (*prakriyā*) or in the final established form (*pariniṣṭhita*).
This is because an indicator (*jñāpaka*) operates with respect to its own kind (*sajātīyāpekṣatvāt*).

By that, it is established that [the rule] "tenācikīrtat" applies; however, in the present case, there is reduplication of the root *naś*, followed by the elision of the vowel *a* in the subsequent portion,
resulting in *aunanat*.
Do not be silent;
[he] made a sound, he did not remain silent.
1891 *kūṭa* means "to torment" or "to burn," according to others; 1892 *saṅketa*, 1893 *grāma*, 1894 *kuṇa*, and 1895 *guṇa* mean "to summon."
Furthermore, even a peak (kūṭa) deceives (kūṭayati),
that is, it signals (saṅketayati).
He causes to sound, he causes to bend, he causes to string.
An alternative reading (pāṭhāntara) [states]:
"In the month of Śrāvaṇa, he invites [them] at the invitation."
The roots *kuṇ* and *guṇ* take the suffix *abhi-ket-ya-ti* in the sense of addressing (*cāmantraṇe*); by the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), the root *ket* is also included.
1897 *kūṇa* means contraction;
1898 *stena* means theft, as in *atiṣṭenat*.
Up to the root *gurv*, these roots are *ātmanepada*;
the root *pad* (in the sense of "going") is conjugated as *padayate*.
In the case of the word *gṛha* being used with the prefix *apa*, it is understood as "one who seizes."
1901. *mṛg* (to search for game): *mṛgayate*, *mṛgyati*—this belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* group.
1902 *kuha* in the sense of deceiving; 1903 *śūra*; 1904 *vīra* in the sense of valor; 1905 *sthūla* in the sense of increasing.
*sthūlayate* means "to become gross" (*atusthūlatā*) [in the sense of] requesting a means for a purpose (*arthopāyāñcāyām*). 1906.
*arthayate* (the form *ārthayata*) is used in the sense of performing a continuous action (*santānakriyā*). 1907.
Because it has multiple vowels (*anekāctvāt*), *asasatra* is not an *ṣopadeśa* [root]; thus,
[in the desiderative] one forms *sisatrayiṣate*.
In the case of the root *garva* (meaning "to be proud"),
by virtue of its being cited as ending in a short vowel (*adanta*), there is an option regarding the suffix *ṇic*.
The final vowel of the root *dhā* is acute in the *liṭ* [perfect] and in the case of *ām*; such is the result here and likewise in what follows—
thus say the followers of Āgastya.
1909. The root √sūtr, meaning "to wind thread," forms *sūtrayati* (he threads) and *asusūtrat* (he threaded).
he urinated while urinating in a stream of urine.
1911 *rūkṣa* in the sense of harshness; 1912 *pāra*; 1913 *tīra* in the sense of the completion of an action; *apapāra*.
In the sense of "joining leaf-cups," [the root *puṭ*] becomes *puṭayati*.
Some say that from the year 1915 onwards,
he showed [this] repeatedly;
in 1916, there was a relaxation of his efforts.
Some also say it is *katrayati*, *katri*, or *kartṛ*.

The suffix *ṇic* is added to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the sense of verbal action (*dhātvartha*), and it is applied diversely (*bahulam*), as well as taking the effects of the suffix *iṣṭhan*. Examples include *kartayati* and *kartati*.

The suffix *ṇic* should be applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the sense of verbal action (*dhātvartha*), when the desiderative suffix *iṣṭhan* is intended; as the nominal stem undergoes masculine conversion (*puṃvadbhāva*), elision of *ra*, elision of *ṭi*, elision of *vin* or *matup*, elision of *yaṇ* and so forth, the substitution of *prastha*, *sphā* and others, and the designation of *bha*, these same operations should also occur before *ṇic*. For example: *paṭum ācaṣṭe* becomes *paṭayati*;
because it is subsequent, once *vṛddhi* has occurred, there is elision of *ṭi*.
In the Bhāṣya on the rule *apīpaṭat ṇau caṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.31), however, it is established that "elision is stronger than vṛddhi," and thus [the form] is *apapaṭat*.
(ga) "He does that" and "he describes that" are an elaboration of the preceding [rule];
in the forms *karoti* and *ācaṣṭe*, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is merely the meaning of the verbal root itself.
But the meaning of the desiderative suffix (*laṭ*) is not intended [here];
therefore, from *atikrāmati*,
*aśvena atikrāmati*, and *aśvayati* [the same form arises].
In the case of *hastinātikrāmati*, it becomes *hastayati*;
the form of the verbal root (*dhāturūpa*) assumes the form of the root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
The word *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated;
thus, the Vārttika says:

"From a verbal derivative (*ākhyāna*), one expresses that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix; there is elision of the *kṛt* suffix and restoration of the original base and its suffix; and the case-role (*kāraka*) is as it was in the original base. (Vārttika).
In the case of *kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe* ("he tells the killing of Kaṃsa"), which results in *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("he causes Kaṃsa to be killed")— here, the form *kaṃsaṃ han* being present (SK 2574)—
By Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.32, the letter *t* is substituted for the final [letter] of the root *han* before an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, excluding *ciṇ* and *ṇi*.
Now, in this case, would not the designation of *aṅga* (stem) and the designation of *dhātu* (root) apply to that which is qualified by *kaṃsa*?
Consequently, there would be the fault of [applying] the *aṭ* augment and doubling;
furthermore, *kutva* and *tatva* would not occur,
because when a verbal root is mentioned by its own form (*svarūpa*), it is understood that the operation applies to a suffix attached to that root.
In the phrase "satyam prakṛtivat," the word "ca" (and) is displaced; it connects both the "agent" (kāraka) and, by virtue of the "ca," the "effect" (kārya).

The meaning is that in the case of a *ṇic* suffix added for the sake of causality (*hetumaṇṇic*), whatever *kāraka*—which was not included within the verbal root (*dhātu*)—belonged to the base root such as *han*, and which appeared in the accusative case, and whatever grammatical operation occurred, such as the substitution of *ku* for *k* or *t* for *n*, those same things apply here as well; thus, one says *kaṃsam ajīghatat*.
[This is taught] under the rule *kartṛ-karaṇāddhātvarthe*.

The meaning is that an instrument is that which serves the purpose of the agent's operation, and not merely the eye and so forth; [as in] "he kills with a sword" (*asinā hanti*) or "he causes to kill" (*asayati*). [The root] *valka* means "seeing. (1917)
In 1918, *citra* means "making a picture," that is, the act of painting; or sometimes it means "seeing."
The root *cit* takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "wonderful appearance," as in *citrayati*; the root *aṃs* [takes it] in the sense of "striking."
1920. *vaṭ* in the sense of dividing; 1921. *laj* in the sense of manifesting;
some say [the roots] are *vaṭi* and *laji*.
Some say that because [the root] is listed among the *adanta* (ending in *a*) roots by virtue of its appearance in the *pāṭha*, there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] for those ending in *a*.
[The rule] *vaṇṭāpayati* and *lañjāpayati* [is formed];
however, Śākaṭāyana states that the suffix *puk* is added to all [roots], including *kath* and others.
In his opinion, [the roots] *kathāpayati*, *gaṇāpayati*, and so forth belong to the *miśra* (mixing) class, meaning "to mix" or "to combine. 1922. *Miśra* = contact.
In the year 1923, during the battle,
because this [root] is anudātta and due to the elision of the vowel *a*,
he did not fight.
1924. *stoma* is used in the sense of praise (*ślāghā*), but not when it means a hymn (*atustoma*). 1925. *chidra* is used in the sense of piercing the ear (*karṇabheda*).
Some say [the root] *karaṇa* means "piercing";
others say *karṇa* is a different verbal root (dhātu). 1926. *Andha* [is used] in the sense of impairment of vision.
Others say that *upasaṃhāra* means "placing down," as in the phrase *daṇḍa-daṇḍanipātane* (in the striking down of the staff).
In 1928, regarding the word *pada* and its definition,
[the root] *añc* was conjugated; in 1929, [the suffix] *aṅga* [was applied].
*āñjagat* (1930) [is used] in the sense of happiness (1931) and suffering; *tatkriyāyām* (1932) [is used] in the sense of that action; *rasa* [is used] in the senses of tasting and moisture.
1933 *vyaya* means expenditure or the giving away of wealth; 1934 *rūpa* means form or the act of making a form.
The seeing or making of form is the action of form; [the root] *chid* means "to split" or "to divide," as in *acicchedat* ("he cut").
1936. *Chad* means concealment, according to some; [it] covers. 1937. *Lābha* means incitement.

1938 *vraṇa* [is used] in the sense of powdering a wound on the body; 1939 *varṇa* [is used] in the senses of coloring, spreading, and describing qualities; "coloring" (*varṇakriyā*) means the act of making color.
"Suvarṇam varṇayati" means he describes the story; that is, he elaborates upon it.
"He describes Hari" means "he praises him"; this illustration is manifold.
The meaning is "a demonstration of the adamantine element";
other [forms] should also be understood according to the principle of predominance (*bāhulaka*),
as follows:
1940. *parṇa* in the sense of being green: *apaparṇat*. 1941. *viṣka* in the sense of seeing.
1942 *kṣip* in the sense of impelling; 1943 *vas* in the sense of dwelling; 1944 *tutth* in the sense of covering.
Thus he swings, oscillates, and mimics.
Regarding the phrase "it causes to tremble" (*adhīrayati*) and so forth,

others say that the reading of the ten groups (*daśagaṇī*) is extensive (*bahulam*); therefore, even those not included in the [standard] recitation— whether from the Sūtras, common usage, or the Vedas— are to be understood.

Others, however, say that the reading "bahulam" (variously) applies to the nine groups [of suffixes]; therefore, the causative suffix *ṇic* occurs even after roots not included in those groups, as in the case of *rāmaḥ* [from *ram*], where the meaning is "he causes to delight. Others, again, maintain that the form *ṇij* [is used] in this sense.
All these views are established in the treatises of the ancients:
(Ga) after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a limb (*aṅga*), the suffix *ṇiṅ* shall be applied in the sense of "expelling" (*nirasana*).

He throws away his hands; he acts with his hands, acts with his feet. [The suffix *yat* is applied] after the words *śvetāśva*, *aśvatara*, *gāloḍita*, and *āhvaraka*; furthermore, there is the elision of the parts *-aśva-*, *-tara-*, and *-eta-* [in those respective compounds].
In the case of the four roots beginning with *śvetāśva*, the suffixes *aśva* and so forth are elided, and the affix *ṇiṅ* is applied in the sense of the verbal root itself;
thus, from *śvetāśva* and the others, one either surpasses [another] or expresses [him], as in *śvetayati* or *aśvayate*.
*Gāloḍitam* means the deliberation of words; that which performs this is *gāloḍayate* or *āhvarayate*.
However, some maintain that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) alone applies; according to their view, the verb also takes the *parasmaipada* (active) voice.
(ga) Regarding [the roots] such as *pṛcch*, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is already established;
therefore, let the ātmanepada ending arise from the causative (*ṇijanta*) itself by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacana*).
There is no need for the specific prescription of the affix *ṇiṅ* in the rule *pṛcchi-bhāṇḍa-* (Pāṇini 3.1.26).

The word *siddha* at the end of the treatise is for the purpose of auspiciousness. Thus ends the section on the *curādi* [roots] ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Now begins the section on the causative (*ṇic*) endings.
An instigator of an agent shall be designated as both a *hetu* (cause) and a *kartṛ* (agent).
Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.26: When the operation of an instigator (*prayojaka*), such as commanding (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth, is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇic* shall be added to the verbal root (*dhātu*).

The suffix *ṇic* [is applied] in the sense of "he impels" or "he causes to cultivate"; by the rule *bhāvayate* (Pāṇini 1.3.72), the *ātmanepada* ending is used when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. Thus, he says *bhāvayate*.
He cultivated [it].

When the suffix *san* follows, there shall be the substitution of *i* for the vowel *u* of the reduplicated syllable of that base, provided that *pa*, *yaṇ*, or *ja*— followed by a non-*a* vowel (*avarṇa*)— follows;
as in *abībhavat* and *apīpavat*.
He has caused the seed to swell;
he has caused it to flow.
Like the sound of an enemy,
like the sound of a bee,
like the sound of a goat.

For these [roots], when followed by the suffix *san* with the augment *iṭ*, there may optionally be the substitution of *i* for the vowel *a* of *asū* (to throw), provided that a letter of the *avaṇ* class follows the root-vowel.
In the forms *asisravat* and *asusravat*, there is no shortening [of the vowel], according to *SK-sandarbhah* 2572.
He ruled;
he approached; he shone brightly.
According to another opinion,
*acacakāsat* will be cited as an example under the section on roots ending in *n* in the rule regarding *aglopi*.
In the case of a root ending in *ṇi*,
the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*)— by virtue of either a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) or because it is an exception (*apavāda*)— prevents the *vṛddhi* substitution, as in *corayati*.

By the rule *ṇau caṅi* (Pāṇini 7.4.1), there is shortening; by *dīrgho laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94), there is lengthening. Nor is it the case that both [operations] are impossible because the root would be *aglopi* (one whose penultimate vowel is elided), because the reference is made to the generic form (*ākṛti*) of the suffix *ṇi*.
He stole.
In the presence of the affix *caṅ* or the affix *ṇi* that follows *caṅ*, there may optionally be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *śvi*.
According to the rule "vocalization and the grammatical operation dependent upon it are stronger," there is vocalization; by the rule for the formation of the single substitute [P.
6.1.102], the result is *aśūśuvat*.
Because it is not light, it did not lengthen;
[the root] *śvi* was not applied.
Following a cause situated in a prefix, the *s* of these [roots] does not become *ṣ*, except in the case of *caṅ*;
e.g., *avātastambhat*.
He caused to flow around; he caused to settle down; he pecked repeatedly.
The shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*), although it is an external factor (*bahiraṅga*), occurs even before reduplication,
as indicated by the fact that the root *oṇ* is marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter.
Let there not be *vṛddhi* here for [the root] *dhā* following *ejādi* when preceded by *pra*, because it is prescribed [only] after [a prefix] ending in *i*;
thus, "mā bhavān predidhat."
According to the rule *na ndrāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3), there is no doubling of the letters *n*, *d*, or *r*; thus,
[the forms] are *aundidat* and *āḍḍiḍat*.
The root *ārcicat* means "to straighten" or "to set upright";
it has the letter *d* as its penultimate when used in the sense of instruction.

In the rule *bhujanyubjau pāṇyupatāpayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.56), the substitution of *va* for *da* occurs by way of a specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*). Although this substitution is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), it takes effect only after the reduplication of the syllable *ji* has occurred—due to the prohibition in *na ndrāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3)—and not before;
this is because of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the explicit utterance of the letter *da*.
The rule *ajāder* (beginning with a vowel) applies here; therefore,
it does not apply in this case.
He caused to sleep.
The augment *num* shall be applied after a root beginning with a vowel, provided it is followed by a vowel, but not before the suffixes *śa* (present indicative) or *liṭ* (perfect).
In the rule *ararambhat alalambhat heracaṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.12), because it is stated "not when *aṅ* follows," the substitution of *ku* (the *kutva* change) does not take place.
The roots √ajihayat,
√atsmṛd, √ṛtvara, √prathamrad, √astṝ, and √spaś take the suffix *am* (indicating the past tense).
He remembered.
By the force of the *tapara* designation, there is no long vowel for the short vowel here;
[this is] SK 2583.
AS 7.4.96: When followed by *caṅ* (the aorist marker), the reduplication may optionally take the vowel *ā*;
[as in] *avaveṣṭat*.
he enveloped;
he moved;
he exerted himself.
By the rule *bhrājabhās-* (Pāṇini 3.2.177), there is shortening of the penultimate vowel;
thus: *abibhrajat*, *ababhrājat*.
It should be stated that "or *kāṇi* and so forth" applies;
the six roots *kaṇ*, *raṇ*, *bhaṇ*, *śraṇ*, *lup*, and *heṭh* with the causative suffix *ṇic* are mentioned as *kāṇyādi* in the Bhāṣya.
In the Nyāsa, four more are added: *hvāyi*, *vāṇi*, *loṭi*, and *lop*.
Vāṇiloṭhī also spoke thus elsewhere;
in this way, he uttered twelve [verses].
He desired to act.
There shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the causative form of the root *svap* when followed by the suffix *caṅ*;
[as in] *asūṣupat*. (SK 2585)
[The substitution of] *puK* is set aside when *ṇi* follows.
He causes to lie down;
he causes to call.
When followed by a *ṇi* suffix that is itself followed by *san* or *caṅ*, there shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *hve*; [as in] *ajūhavat*.
He caused to sacrifice.
There shall be elision of the penultimate vowel of the root *pā* (to drink), and the substitution of *ī* for its reduplicated syllable, when followed by a *ṇi*-affix that is itself followed by *caṅ*;
[the augment] *puK* is added by the rule *arti-hrī-* etc. (Pāṇini 7.3.36). Thus: *apīpyat*.
He causes to offer,
he causes to feel shame,
he causes to feel loathing.
It repays;
it moistens.
He causes [them] to ask for forgiveness and establishes [them].
When followed by *caṅ* (the reduplication of *ṇic*), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is replaced by *i*; [as in] *atiṣṭhipat*.
He caused [him] to smell repeatedly.
He caused [him] to smell;
he caused [him] to act.
He proclaimed, he revealed,
he turned.
He wiped;
he cleansed.
Regarding the root *pā* (to drink), it should be stated that there is elision [of the *ṇi*] when the suffix *ṇic* follows.
The refutation of the objection protects [the position].
The suffix *juk* is optionally applied after the root *vāti* when it means "to shake," provided that the suffix *ṇi* follows;
thus, *vājayati*.
In the sense of "shaking," does one cause the hair to fall out?
[The rule] *vibhāṣā līyateḥ* [applies]. (SK 2509)

In the sense of "becoming oily" (*snehadrave*), the augment *nuṭ* is optionally applied after the root *lī*, and the augment *luk* is optionally applied after the root *lā*, respectively, when followed by a causative suffix (*ṇau*).
He causes to melt, he causes to dissolve, he causes to liquefy.
Or does it mean "it causes the ghee to liquefy"?

Since there is an elision (praśleṣa) of the vowel *ī* in the form *lī-ī*, according to the alternative view (*ātvapakṣa*) where *ā* is substituted for *i*, why would the augment *nuk* not apply in the case of a viscous liquid?
It melts the metal; it causes it to melt.

Regarding the roots *li* (to deceive), *li* (to overcome), and *lī* (to honor), it should be stated that the suffix *ātmanepada* is always applied when these meanings are expressed. Alternatively, it should be stated that the suffix *ā* is added [before the suffixes beginning with *ś*].

The *ātmanepada* ending shall occur after the roots *lī* and *līṅ* when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), even if the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent, provided the meaning is that of honoring, overcoming, or deceiving.
The meaning is that he causes the matted locks to utter praise;
it is like a hawk causing a bird to cry out.
The meaning is "he overcomes";
the meaning of "he makes the fool prattle" is that he deceives him.
After the root *bhī*, there shall be substitution of *ā* for *e*, provided that the fear arises from an instigator (*prayojaka*).
After these two roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*, the Ātmanepada endings shall be used, provided that fear (*bhaya*) and pride (*smaya*) are the causes.
In the sūtra, the mention of *bhaya* (fear) is an illustration for the general sense of the verbal root; as in the example:
*muṇḍo bhāpayate* ("the shaven-headed man causes fear").
The vowel *ī* is elided [from the root *bhī*]; for the root *bhi*, ending in *ī*, the augment *ṣuk* shall be applied before the causative suffix *ṇi* when fear is caused by a specific cause.
The root *bhī* (to fear) takes the suffix *ṇic* when it means "to frighten."

The substitution of *āt* for the root vowel of *smi* (to smile) occurs invariably before the causative suffix *ṇic*. However, this does not apply here because of the rule stating that the causative of *smi* is used when the cause of the smiling is fear or wonder (*bhaya-smayau*), as in the case of "the matted-hair ascetic causes wonder. Since there is no such cause here, the substitution does not take place.
He terrifies and astonishes [the listener] with this key;
how then is it said, "astonishing, he is astonished at his own conduct"?
For it is precisely because of the mention of the *karaṇa* (instrument) in the phrase "in human speech" (*manuṣyavācā*) that pride (*smaya*) arises there;
otherwise, even the suffix *śānac* would have to apply— this is true.

The traditionalists maintain that the reading should be *vismāyayan* (causing amazement). Alternatively, it may be explained as follows: human speech is the indirect agent (*prayojyakartṛ*); by means of that speech, the lion causes amazement. Thus, it is to be analyzed as the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the causative form (*ṇyantāt*) of the root *ṇau*.
In the case of the causative suffix *ṇiC*, [the substitution of *guṇa* for the penultimate vowel of the root occurs]. (Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.41)
sphāvayati (SK 2598;

In the causative (*ṇic*) of the root *śad*, there shall be the substitution of *t* for the final letter, but not in the sense of "going"; [this applies] when it means "to cause to fall," but not when it means "to go.
*Śātayati* [is used] in the sense of going.
Govinda causes the cows to lie down;
the meaning is that he makes them go [to rest]. (SK 2599)
In the case of the causative suffix *ṇi*,
[the root *ru* becomes] *ropaya-ti*.
It causes to grow.
For these very roots, there shall be substitution of *ā* before the causative suffix *ṇi*:
*krāpayati*, *adhyāpayati*.
The causative form *jāpayati* [is used when the agent causes another to perform the action denoted by the root] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.51.
Before an affix marked with Ñ or Ṅ that follows either *caṅ* (the aorist marker) or *ṇi* (the causative marker), the root *iṅ* may optionally be replaced by *gāṅ*. Thus:
*adhyajīgapat* or *adhyāpipat*.

In the case of the root *sidh* meaning "to accomplish" with respect to a worldly object (*aihaukika*), when it is present [as a verbal root], its *eC* vowel is replaced by *āT* before the causal suffix *ṇi*.
It means that he prepares or accomplishes food;
[the question is] "in what regard to the next world?"
The ascetic accomplishes;
he ascertains the reality;
it impels him; it establishes the ascetic through austerity.
In the sense of "procreation," the substitution of *ā* for this [root] may optionally occur before the suffix *ṇi*.
The forms *vāpayati* or *vāyayati* mean "the east wind causes the cows to conceive" (*garbhaṃ grāhayati*);
[this is according to] Pāṇini 6.4.89: *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*.
The suffix *ṇiC* is applied after the root *guh* (to hide) when the sense is that of hiding.
It is easy to say "duṣaḥ" [as the root],
because by the rule "the penultimate vowel of the root duṣ- becomes ūt before the causative suffix ṇiC," one forms "dūṣayati."
Dispassion is the state of being displeased.
Desire corrupts or defiles the mind;
the term *mita* is short,
as it is stated to belong to both the *bhvādi* and *curādi* classes of roots.
The roots *janī* and *jṛṣ* form [the present stem] as *janayati*.
From the root *jṛṇāti* comes *jarayati*,
but from [the causative] it is *jārayati*.
In the case of the root *rañj* with the suffix *ṇic*, the elision of *na* should be stated when it means "the sporting of deer" (*mṛgaramaṇa*).
Hunting is the sporting of deer;
[thus, one] causes the deer to sport.
Why does the deer delight the birds?
It delights them with nothing other than mating; it delights the deer by providing grass.
In the *curādi* group, it is stated that for roots beginning with *jñap*, as well as *ci* and *cisphur*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied, resulting in forms such as *capayati* and *cayayati*.
From the root *ci*,
one forms *cāpayati* and *cāyayati*.
He expands, he causes to expand, he expanded.
It burst forth.
In the case of the verb *an* when accompanied by a prefix, both *n* sounds undergo the change to *ṇ*, provided the necessary cause is present,
as in *prāṇiṇat*.
In the context of the causative suffix *ṇic*, the root *iṇ* (to go) shall be replaced by *gam*.
Thus, [from *iṇ*] one forms *gamayati*.
But in the sense of causing to understand,
it is like the root *iṇ* (according to the Vārttika):
*adhigamayati*.
By the rules *hanas-to'ciṇ-ṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.32) and *ho hanteḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.54), there is the substitution of *ku* [i.e., *gh*],
resulting in *ghātayati*.
It should be stated that *īrṣyayati* and *īrṣyate* [apply] to the third [consonant]; or rather,
the meaning is that it applies to the third consonant and to monosyllabic roots ending in the third [consonant].

In the first case, this [rule] is intended to prevent the doubling of the letter *ṣ*; however, in the second case, it operates within the domain of the desiderative (*sannanta*) as an exception to the rule "the second [consonant] of a root beginning with a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), as in *airṣyiyat*.
In the second explanation, it will be shown that when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied and then followed by *caṅ*, only the letter *ṣ* is heard in the reduplication,
because of the rule "the remainder [is retained] when the root begins with a consonant."
Duality, however, belongs to the second [agent] alone; because there is no third, the present Vārttika does not apply.
When the causative suffix *ṇic* is added to a root from which the sense of "sending" has been withdrawn, the meaning is identical to that of the simple [root].

Therefore, it is established that [the verb] *prārthayati* (he desires) is used with the beloved woman who has risen from bed, and so forth; in this manner, it should be inferred for all transitive verbs.
Thus ends the section on the *ṇic* suffix in verbal forms (*tiṅanta*).
Now begins the section on the *tiṅ* and *saN* suffixes (Pāṇini 3.1.7).

The suffix *san* may optionally occur after a verbal root that has the same agent as the action denoted by the desiderative (*iṣi-karman*) when desire is expressed; because it is prescribed after a verbal root, *san* here is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix,
and [the augment] *iṭ* is applied.
One who desires to recite the *dvitva* (doubling) of the *saṃyanta* (consonant cluster ending in *s*) [as taught in] the *Sārasvatasandarbha* 2317 says *pipaṭhiṣati*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "by means of an action" (*karmaṇaḥ*)?
[It is so that] it may not apply when there is a desire expressed by a verbal root (*gamanena icchati*),
lest [the suffix *san*] arise from a root having the same agent (*samānakartṛkātkim*).
The teacher desires that "the students should recite";
because of the inclusion of the word *vā* (or), the sentence is also [an option] in this case.
By the rule *luṅsanoḥ ghasḷ* [Pāṇini 2.4.37], and by the rule *ekāca upadeśe...* [Pāṇini 7.2.10], the augment *iṭ* is not applied.

He wishes to eat that grain; [the form] *jighatsati* is derived from the root *ad* with the desiderative suffix *san*, while *īrṣyati* is derived from the root *īrs*, which undergoes reduplication according to the rule "of the third [root] and of *yis*."
īrṣyayiṣati, īrṣyiṣiṣati (SK 2609)
AS 1.2.8: After these [roots], the suffixes *san* and *ktvā* are *kit*. Example:
*rurudiṣati*.
He desires to know;
he desires to liberate himself.

According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.12 (*graher guher ugantāc ca sana iṇ na syāt*), there shall not be the augment *iṭ* after the root *grah*, nor after *guh*, nor after a root ending in a long vowel (*u*-class), when followed by the suffix *san*; furthermore, by Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.16 (*grahijyā-*), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
Because the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is considered *asiddha*, the *bhaṣ*-substitution occurs:
*jighṛkṣati*,
*suṣupsati*.
Pāṇini 7.2.75: The augment *iṭ* shall be applied after the suffix *san* following the roots *kṝ*, *gṝ*, *dṛṅ*, *dhṛṅ*, and *pracch*.
He desires to ask;
he desires to do;
he desires to swallow.
In *jigaliṣati*,
the lengthening of the vowel is not desired; [likewise],
in *didariṣate*.
Understand that *didhariṣate* and *uddidhīrṣuḥ* are derived from the roots *dhṛ* and *dhṛñ*, which belong to the *bhūvādika* class.
A *san* suffix beginning with a consonant (*jhal*) shall be marked with the *kit* designation after a verbal root ending in a vowel (*iganta*).
He desires to be;
he wishes to give *dīṅ*; he desires to cause to give.
Because this [root] does not fall within the scope of that [rule], there is no substitution of *ā* according to the rule *mīnāti-minoti-* (Pāṇini 6.1.50);
for this very reason, in the sūtra *sani mīmā-* (Pāṇini 7.4.54), the root *mī* is mentioned separately from the root *mā*.
A *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant that follows a *hal* (consonant) immediately after *īkṣa* shall be treated as *kit*,
as in the case of *guhū*.
Why [is it that] one who desires to conceal and one who desires to break [are called] *ika*?
He desires to sacrifice;
he desires to increase his strength.
The mention of the suffix *hal* refers to the class [of consonants]; [thus] from the root *tṛh*, we have *titṛkṣati*.
he desires to satisfy his thirst; he wishes to quench his thirst.

A long vowel is substituted for the final vowel of roots ending in a vowel—specifically for *han* and for *gam*, which undergoes substitution for *aj*—before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant followed by a *san* suffix; likewise, a long vowel is substituted for *ji* before *san* and *liṭ*.
(Pāṇini 6.4.16–18) He desires to conquer (*jigīṣati*). (Pāṇini 6.1.31) And [a long vowel is optionally substituted] for *ci* before *san*. (Pāṇini 6.1.32) He desires to accumulate (*cikīṣati*).
He desires to pile up;
he desires to kill.
For the root *iṇ*, *gam* shall be substituted when followed by the suffix *san*, except in the sense of "knowing";
[thus], *jigamiṣati*.
In the sense of "desiring to awaken," the root *iṇ* is optionally treated like *adhi-i* (as in *adhijigamiṣati*).

Because it is stated that the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings occur in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), there is no augment *iṭ*; furthermore, by the rule "there is lengthening before a *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant," the vowel is lengthened.

Because it is stated that [the rule applies] to the substitute *aja*, there is no lengthening for the root *gam*; thus, [the form] is *jigaṃsyate*. *Jigāṃsyate* and *adhijigāṃsyate* [are derived accordingly].
The root *sañjigams* [is used] in the sense of "desiring to go" (SK 2616;
The root *gam* may replace *iṅ* before the suffix *san*:
[as in] *adhijigāṃsate*.
