AS 1.2.26: After a root beginning with a consonant and ending in *r* or *l*, provided it has *u* and *i* as its penultimate letters (*upadhā*), the suffixes *ktvā* and *san* are optionally treated as *kit* when followed by a *seṭ* (suffix containing an *iṭ* augment).
In the case of the roots *dyuti* and *svāpi*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
He desires to shine;
he desires to shine intensely; he desires to blaze.
Does he wish to shine? He wishes to write.
What is *ralaḥ*?
In *dideviṣati*,
[the substitution of *i* for *e* occurs] because of the intervening vowel; why does it not occur in *vivartiṣate*?
In the case of *halādi* (a root beginning with a consonant),
as in *eṣiṣiṣati*,
even though doubling (*dvitva*) is obligatory here, it is superseded by the *guṇa* substitution.
For the operation caused by the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is stronger because it depends on duality;
this is because the introduction of the *ṛt* designation for the root *oṇ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on a general expectation.

According to Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.49, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after roots ending in *iva* and after *ṛdhu* and others; in the absence of *iṭ*, there is *kitva* (the status of being a *k*-suffix) due to the rule "halantācca" (Pāṇini 1.2.10).
By the rule *chvoḥ śūḍ anunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), *v* is replaced by *ūṭh*; after the *yaṇ* substitution, there is reduplication, resulting in *dudyūṣati*.
Due to the forthcoming restriction— "dideviṣati [is formed] from the roots √div and √stu only"— there is no substitution of *ṣ* in *susyūṣati*.
He desires to serve.
For these [roots], there may be *it* before a suffix beginning with *s*, when *san* follows;
(Pāṇini 7.4.58).
Beginning with *sanimīmā-* (Pāṇini 7.4.54), that which was stated therein is as follows: there would be the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *abhyāsa* (reduplication);
[for example], one who desires to obtain is *īpsati*, and one who desires to increase is *ardhitum icchati*.
The substitution of *ra* for *la*, and the substitution of *ca* for *ja*, as in *īrtsati*.
He desires to cause to suffer;
he desires to shine forth;
he desires to bear.
He wishes to break;
he desires to scatter.

In the case of the root *dambh*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *s* and having the *san* marker, the vowel *a* is replaced by *it*, the letter *i* is added, and there is elision of the reduplicated syllable.

In the rule *halantācca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10), it has been stated that the mention of *hal* refers to the class (*jāti*). Consequently, due to the *kittva* of the suffix *san*, there is elision of the nasal (*nalopa*),
as in *dhīpsati*.
He desires to deceive; he desires to deceive; he desires to resort to.
In *śiśrayiṣati*, by Pāṇini 7.1.102 (*udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*), [the substitution of *ū* for *u* occurs]; thus, *susvūrṣati*.
He desires to sharpen; he desires to separate; he desires to strive.
He desires to cover;
he will desire to cover; he will desire to cover.
Nor should it be argued that because the substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occurs due to their being subsequent [rules], the letter *u* would not be heard in the reduplicated syllable;

for by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), when reduplication is to be performed, there is either the extension (*atideśa*) of the form of the original base (*sthānin*) or the non-prohibition of the substitute (*ādeśa*).
Furthermore, it should not be asked how the causative suffix (*sannanta*) can serve as a cause (*nimitta*) with respect to reduplication while itself being the object of the operation (*kāryin*).
For an agent who is experiencing an action is not accepted as the cause [of that action], yet one who is not experiencing it is not [the cause] either;
and here, while existing, he does not experience duality, nor does he desire to become.
The root *jñap* (to make known), being puganta and having the letter *p* as its final, belongs to the curādigaṇa;
in the absence of the augment *iṭ*, there is no guṇa substitution because of the *kit* designation according to Pāṇini 1.2.5 (*iko jhal*).

In the case of *ajjhan-*, the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.12] prescribing lengthening is superseded by the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 6.4.51] for the elision of *ṇi*; thus, by [Pāṇini 7.4.55], the vowel becomes long:
*jñīpsati*.
But when one wishes to cause another to know immeasurably,
one uses *jijñāpayiṣati*.
By the rule *janasana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.42), there is the substitution of *ā* [for the root vowel];
thus: *siṣāsati*, *sisaniṣati*.
After the roots *tan*, *pat*, *daridra*, and *āta*, the suffix *san* may optionally take the augment *iṭ*.
(Pāṇini 6.4.17)
The long vowel may optionally replace the penultimate [vowel] of this [root] before an affix beginning with *jhal* when followed by *san*; thus,
*titāṃsati* or *titaṃsati*.
The suffix *san* should be stated [after a root] when there is a sense of apprehension; for example, *titaniṣati* ("he fears he might die") and *mumūrṣati* ("he fears he might die").
The bank wishes to fall.

For these [roots], when followed by a suffix beginning with *s* and preceded by *san*, there would be the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), and by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), there would be the elision of the *s*.
he desires to make poor,
he wishes to make poor,
he intends to make poor.

From the two roots *ḍumiñ* and *mīñ*, the suffix *san* is applied; and because there is no distinction in their having the form *mī*, even for the root *minoti*, the substitution of *s* for *si* occurs by the rule "saḥ si" (Pāṇini 8.3.106). Thus, *taḥ* [is derived].
He desires to give; he wishes to bestow.
Today he desires to give.
The root *dheṭ* [is used] in the sense of "wishing to give" (*ditsati*, *ditsate*).
He wishes to place;
he wishes to maintain.
He intends to place, he intends to injure, he intends to take.
The root *śak* (in the form *śikṣati*) means "to endure" (*marṣaṇa*); it belongs to the *divādi* class.
The [verb] marked with the svarita accent takes both parasmaipada and ātmanepada endings:
*śikṣati* and *śikṣate*.
*pitsate* is used in the sense of injury; *sanīs* is to be mentioned as an alternative [suffix],
as in *ritsati*.
In the case of violence, what does he desire to accomplish?
AS 7.4.57: When the suffix *san* begins with *sa*, there is elision of the reduplication.
The calf either seeks liberation or desires to be liberated by itself;
how can Kṛṣṇa desire to liberate the calf, since [liberation] is not an object of action?
The substitution of *vṛddhi* does not occur after the four roots beginning with *vṛ* when the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes follow; however, it does occur in the case of *vivṛtsati*.
By the rule "vivartiṣate se'sici" (Pāṇini 7.2.49), there is optionally the augment iṭ; thus:
ninartiṣati.
He desires to dance.
After the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, as well as after a root ending in long *ṝ*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied to the suffix *san*; thus,
one forms either *titariṣati* or *titarīṣati*.
He wishes to cross over; he wishes to open; he wishes to reveal.
He wishes to choose; he desires to choose.
He wishes to open;
he wishes to shake.
AS 7.2.74: After the roots √smi, √pūṅ, √ṛ, √añj, and √aś, the augment iṭ shall be added to the desiderative suffix san; [as in] sismayiṣate.
In *pipaviṣate* and *aririṣati*, there is reduplication of the root *riṣ*.

Since the element *san* is a constituent part [of a verbal root] and thus occupies the status of an effect (*kāryin*), it cannot serve as a cause (*nimitta*) for itself; therefore, the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59) does not apply,
as in the forms *añjijiṣati* and *aśiśiṣate*.
Both [forms] with the suffix *sābhyāsa* (reduplicated) are: *prāṇiṇiṣati* and *ucchestuk*.
By the rule *cutvaṃ pūrvatrāsiddham advirvacane*, the doubling of the *iṭ* together with the *c* and *ch* occurs; then,
by *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, all other consonants are elided.
One might argue that "when the cause (nimitta) disappears, the effect (naimittika) also disappears" is not a universal rule,
because of the inclusion of the augment *tuK* in the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Or, by virtue of the rules *prakṛtipratyāpattivacanāt* and *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30 and 6.1.31), the substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ* and the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *śvi* may optionally occur,
as in *adhijigāpayiṣati*.
He desires to cause [him] to study;
he desires to cause [the child] to cry; he desires to cause [the child] to grow.

Regarding *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.32): in *juhāvayiṣati*, because it has been stated that there is no substitution of *ā* for the vowel before reduplication when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) follows, the reduplication occurs of the *u*. [Likewise], in *pusphārayiṣati*.
In *cukṣāyayiṣati*, by [Pāṇini 6.1.31] *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*, [the substitution of vṛddhi occurs]. In *pipāvayiṣati*...
Does one wish to cause to manifest,
wish to cause to be born,
or wish to purify? What?
Now he wishes to cause others to speak; what does he wish to become?
By the rule *sravati*— *Sārasvata-Kaumudī-Sandarbha* 2578— the substitution of *i* optionally occurs, as in *sisrāvayiṣati*,
*susrāvayiṣati*, and so forth.
Another indeed desires to hear [the teaching].

In the case of reduplication, the *s* of a following root that ends in *stu* or a causative (*ṇyanta*) shall become *ṣ*, provided that the suffix *san* itself becomes *ṣ*; but not for any other [root], as in *tuṣṭūṣati*.
By the rule *dyutisvāpyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.19), the substitution of *u* occurs; thus,
one forms *suṣvāpayiṣati* and *siṣādhayiṣati*.
In the case of *stauti* and *ṇyanta* roots,
[the rule] "after a prefix, in the case of *sthā* and others, as well as with the reduplication" (Pāṇini 8.3.65) applies the substitution of *ṣ*. Thus, we have *sisikṣati*.
When you desire to sprinkle [it] around, why do you stand still?
Because it is stated that "one desires to sleep through repetition," there is no prohibition here of the suffix *iṇ*.
He will wish to lie down;
he will wish to study.

In the case of these roots ending in a causative suffix (ṇic), when there is repetition (abhyāsa), the *s* of the subsequent [reduplicated syllable] remains *s* and does not become *ṣ*, even when followed by the suffix *ṣaṇ*.
sisvedayiṣati, sisvādayiṣati, sisāhayiṣati
Because of the restriction "in the case of *sthā* and so forth, by means of repetition," there is no [application] here in the following:
*abhisusūṣati*,
*śaiṣikāt matubarthīyāt śaiṣikaḥ*, and *matubarthikāt*.
A suffix with the same form [as its base] is not desired; it will not be applied after a base ending in *san*.
(From the Bhāṣya:
A secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) with the same form as another secondary derivative is not [permitted]; therefore, for "existing in Śālīya," only the sentence itself is used.

But why is it that a suffix beginning with *ch* following a suffix ending in *ch* is not considered identical in form (*sarūpa*), as in the case of *āhicchatra*, which means "originating from Ahicchatra"?
That which exists in Āhicchatra is *āhicchatrīyaḥ*;
[this is formed] with the suffix *cha* after a word ending in *aṇ*.
Likewise, that which has the form *sap* is not [formed] from a word denoting possession (*matvartha*).
In this context, the word *dhanavān* exists as one ending in the suffix *matup*; however,
it would indeed be of a different form [if derived] from *matup*.
The phrase "the hall possessing staff-bearers" (*daṇḍimatī śālā*) is connected with the word "similar" (*sarūpa*);
its meaning is a similarity by way of the object.
Therefore, [the suffix] *san* occurs after a desiderative (*icchā-sannanta*) ending in *san*,
but it certainly occurs after a *san* used in its own sense (*svārtha-sannanta*), as in *jugupsiṣate*.

The section on desiderative suffixes (*saN*) ending in verbal terminations, following the section on desiderative suffixes; now begins the section on intensive suffixes (*yaṄ*) ending in verbal terminations.
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.22:
*paunaḥpunyam* (repetition), *bhṛśārthaḥ* (intensity), and *kriyāsamabhihāraḥ* (frequency of action)— when these are to be expressed, the suffix *yaṅ* shall be applied.
The reduplication (abhyāsa) should take the *guṇa* substitute when followed by the suffix *yaṅ*, as well as when *yaṅ* is elided (*yaṅluk*).
By the rule *sanādyantāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), these [forms] possess the nature of verbal roots (*dhātu*); thus, the *laṭ* and other suffixes are applied.
Because they end in a *saN* affix that is marked with the indicatory letter *Ṅ*, the *ātmanepada* endings are used.
It occurs repeatedly or with intensity as *bobhūyate*.
*bobhūyāṃcakre* and *abobhūyiṣṭa*:
why [is this] from the verbal root (*dhātu*)?
So that the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* may apply, [the rule] "bruvo vaciḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.53) and so forth [is stated]; [in this context],
what is the purpose of the term "ekācaḥ" (of a monosyllabic root)?
Why does she wake again and again, and gaze intently at the plowshare and other implements?

Regarding the statement "it shines intensely" (*bhṛśaṃ rocate śobhate*), the *Bhāṣya* says that the *yaṅ* suffix applies here; however, in the sense of repetition (*punaḥpunye*), the form would indeed be *rorucyate*.
The suffix *yaṅ* should be stated after the roots *śośubhi*, *sūci*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭi*, *arti*, and *śūrṇoti*.
The first three of these belong to the *curādi* class and are *adanta* (ending in -a).
It is indicated (sosūcyate) and formulated (sosūtryate); because it is not an upadeśa with multiple consonants (anekāctvena), there is no substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
The root *mūtr* (to urinate) takes the suffix *yaṅ*.

In the rule "yasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.148), there is a reference to a composite form; it means that the *ya* sound following a consonant (*hal*) is elided before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, according to the principle that "the substitute takes the place of the initial [element] of what follows."
Therefore, there is elision [of the *yaṅ* suffix]. *Sosūcāñcakre*, *sosūcitā*.
They are well-expounded and well-explained.
In the case of a root beginning with a vowel, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable when the suffix *yaṅ* is present or when it is elided (*yaṅluk*); e.g., *aṭāṭyate*.
In the case of the root *ṛ*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant and having *yaṅ* as its marker, there shall be *guṇa* substitution for the *ṛ*.
There is no prohibition of doubling for the *repha* that follows the letter *ya*, because of the example given in the Bhāṣya: *arāryate*;
[thus we have] *arāritā*.
The wool is spun out and repeatedly split.
Because of the status of the substitute as the original (sthānivadbhāva) for the elision (allopasya), there is no guṇa substitution for the penultimate vowel (nopadhāguṇaḥ) in *bebhiditā*.
The suffix *yaṅ* occurs after a root meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) only when there is crookedness (*kauṭilya*), and not when there is repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). Example:
*kuṭilaṃ vrajati* (he walks crookedly) becomes *vāvrajyate*.
After these [roots], the suffix *yaṅ* shall occur only when there is censure (*garhā*) regarding the meaning of the verbal root.
It destroys what is censurable, it plunders, and it devours.
AS 7.4.87: For these two [roots], *nuK* shall be substituted for the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) when the suffix *yaṅ* or its elision (*yaṅluk*) occurs;
by the term *nuk*, the anusvāra is indicated.
And that [final *m*] should be stated as being like the end of a word (*padāntavat*), so that the rule *vā padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.59) may apply.

By the rule *AS 7.4.88* (*caraphalorabhyāsātparasyāta utsyādyaṅyaṅlukoḥ hali ca*), there is lengthening [of the vowel] when the suffixes *yaṅ* and its elision (*yaṅluk*) follow, and also before a consonant (*hal*).
He moves about,
he wanders about, he flutters about.
It blooms.
The suffix *nu* may occur after these [roots] in the sense of repetition (*abhyāsa*) when the suffixes *yaṅ* or *yaṅluk* follow; for example,
*jañjapyate* (he mutters repeatedly in a censurable manner), and so forth.
In the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix, the letter *r* of the root *gṛ* becomes *l*.
The word *gilati* (he swallows) is derived from the root *gṛ*, which is considered contemptible;
the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs according to the rule *ghumāsthā...* (Pāṇini 6.4.66).
The quality is given away;
it is drunk repeatedly.
The root *śvi* optionally takes the suffix *seṣīya*; [thus] *śośūyate*.
In the intensive (yaṅ) formation, the root *smṛ* becomes *śeśvīyate*. It is thus remembered (*sāsmaryate*).
The reduplicated form of *rīṅ* (from the root *ri*) takes the suffix *suṭ*.
It is purchased together.
(Pāṇini 8.3.112)
The substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of *sic* would not occur in the *yaṅ* [intensive] formation; thus, [the form] is *nisesicyate*.
AS 7.4.63: The substitution of *c* for the reduplication of the root *kavati* does not occur before the suffix *yaṅ*;
thus, *kokūyate*.
But from the roots *kauti* and *kuvatī*, the form *cokūyate* is derived [by Pāṇini 7.4.84].

In the case of the repetition (abhyāsa) of these [roots], there is the augment *nīg* in the *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk* formations; because it is stated that this applies "except for *akit*," there is no lengthening, and there is elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).
"It is repeatedly drawn back; it is completely cast away," and so forth (SK 2643).
AS 7.4.85: For a stem ending in an *anunāsika*, the augment *nuk* shall be applied to that which is its penultimate vowel;
it has been stated that by the augment *nuk*, the *anusvāra* is indicated.
By the force of the rule *taparaḥ*, even that which was previously long (*bhūtapūrva-dīrgha*) is not [included] when it is doubled as *ya~yyamyate* or *yaṃyamyate*.
The root *bhām* means "anger";
it is conjugated as *bābhāmyate*, according to the rule *vibhāṣā*. (Vārttika 2319)

The forms *jājāyate* and *jañjanyate* are derived from the root *han*, meaning "to kill" or "to injure," with the intensive suffix *yaṅ*; it should be stated that the substitution of *ghnī* occurs [in place of *han*].
For *jehnīyate* is used in the sense of harming; [is it] *jaṅghanyate*?
Pāṇini 7.4.90: For a root having *ṛ* as its penultimate letter, the augment *rīk* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) when the suffixes *yaṅ* or *yaṅluk* follow.
*varīvṛtyate* [is formed] with *ṇa*-substitution due to its inclusion in the *kṣubh*-class;
*narīnṛtyate*.
The substitution of *l* occurs in both cases: *jarīgṛhyate* and *calīklṛpyate*.
It should be stated that [the forms] *rīgṛtvataḥ* [occur]; [alternatively,
it is said that] *varīvṛścyate* and *parīpṛcchyate* [occur].
There shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) before the suffix *yaṅ*.
He is about to fall asleep,
he shivers,
he trembles.
vāvaśyate (he desires repeatedly)
He shines intensely.
He smells. (SK 2648, AS 7.4.31) *jighrīyate*
It is blown upon.
The substitution of *ayaṅ* for the root *śīṅ* occurs when followed by an affix beginning with *ya* that has the markers *k* or *ṅ*;
[in this case], there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable: *śāśayyate*.
Then the quality is brought near and sharpened.
Thus ends the section on the *yaṅ* affix for verbal roots;
now begins the section on the elision (*luṅ*) of the *yaṅ* affix for verbal roots.
AS 2.4.74: There shall be elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix when followed by the suffix *ac*; due to the word "and" (*ca*), there is also frequently elision even without that [suffix].
This [elision] is unconditional; because it is an internal operation (*antaranga*), it occurs first.
Then, by the characteristic of the suffix, because it ends in *yaṅ*, there is reduplication as the operation on the abhyāsa;
and because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*), the *laṭ* and other suffixes are applied.
The *parasmaipada* [ending] applies by the rule *śeṣāt kartari* (Pāṇini 1.3.78),

whereas the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12) does not apply because the property of being *ṅit* is common to both suffixes and non-suffixes, and thus the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle does not operate here.

For where the unique (asādhāraṇa) form of a suffix is relied upon, [the rule applies] only there; for this very reason, in the case of *sudṛṣat-prāsāda*, the lengthening [prescribed by] Pāṇini 6.4.14 (*atvasantasya ca yatrām*),
does not apply, nor does it apply even to those [roots] such as *spardh* and *śīṅ* which are marked with an indicatory *ṅ* and are anudātta.
Because of the mention of the indicatory letters (anubandhas) in the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* (Pāṇini 1.3.12), and because there [in that context] the suffixes *śtip* and *śap* [are used].
Because of this prohibition,
for that very reason, *śyan* and the others are not included by reference to the [Dhātu] list.
However, because *śev-* and *carkarītam* are recited at the beginning of the *ad-ādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix [by Pāṇini 2.4.72].
According to Pāṇini 7.3.94, the augment *īṭ* may optionally be added to a *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with a consonant that follows a stem ending in *yaṅ*;
however, the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution prescribed by Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.85 (*bhusuvoḥ*) does not apply when there is *yaṅluk* in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
The form *bobhūtu* is established by the Vedic irregularity (*nipātana*) in *taitikte* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.65);
for this very reason, it is also established in the secular language (*bhāṣā*) in the absence of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*).
Nor should it be argued that the absence of *guṇa* is merely prescribed as an irregularity where it was not otherwise applicable in the case of *yaṅluk*.

Because the inclusion of the *prakṛti* (the base form) includes that which ends in *yaṅluk*, it follows from the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "doubling is the repetition [of the base], according to Pāṇini 6.1.1" that *bobhavīti* is formed.
He becomes;
he has become; they become.
He has become repeatedly; he will become repeatedly; he became.
abobhot, abobhūtām, abobhavuḥ
bobhūyāt, bobhūyātām, bobhūyāstām
By the rule *gāti-sthā-* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*;

and in the alternative case where the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *yaṅo vā-* (Pāṇini 7.3.94), the augment *vuk* is inserted by virtue of its being obligatory (*nityatva*), thereby overriding the *guṇa* substitution, resulting in *abobhūvīt*.
*abobhot*,
*abobhūtām*:
the suffix *jus* occurs when there is a reduplicated base (*abhyasta*).
Because it is eternal, [the forms] *aruk*,
*abobhūvuḥ*,
*abobhaviṣyat*, and so forth, [are derived].
pāspardhīti,
pāspardhi, pāspardhaḥ
The root *pṛ* (to fill) substitutes *dhi* for *hi* after roots ending in *h*, *jhal*, or *b*. (Pāṇini 6.4.101) *pāspardhati*; *pāsparsi*. (Kāśikā 2425)
He vied; he vied less.
In the alternative where *r* is substituted by *apāspard-r-ṣi* according to *sipi daśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.74), [the form] becomes *apāspāḥ* by *ro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14).
For you have awakened from sleep; you have awakened; you have caused [them] to awaken.
In the alternative view where *sip* is replaced by *rut*,
[the forms] *ajāghāḥ* and *nāthṛ* [are derived].
He bestows manifoldness upon manifoldness.
You have given, you give, you have caused to be given.
He gave;
they two gave; you two gave.
In the *luṅ* [aorist] tense, [the forms] are *adāt* and *adādhiṣṭa*.
He gave;
they indeed kiss.
They have shaken, they have shaken (feminine),
they have shaken (masculine).
He rejoiced, he was delighted, he exulted.
She was delighted, she was not delighted, she was not unmoved.
O you who are not un-joyful, O you who are not un-joyful, O you who are not un-joyful!
In the case of *amomuḥ* and *amomot*, there is *guṇa* substitution in the *luṅ* tense.
He rejoiced,
and he leaped up, and he leaped about.
In the imperfect (laṅ): acokūtat,
acokūrdīt.
In the matter of their craft,
they were not agitated and not disturbed.
He has gone;
he deceives as one who deceives,
he practices deception.
vanīvakti; vanīvacati;
avanīvañcīt.
The earth moves as it were, and they move upon it.
By the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), there is the elision of the nasal [in *jaṅghan*]; thus,
from *jaṅghantaḥ*,
we derive *jaṅghanti*.
And from the root *mvoś*, [the forms] *jaṅganmi* and *jaṅganvaḥ*.

Because it has already been stated by the mention of *ekāj*, there is no prohibition of *iṭ*. Furthermore, because the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is *asiddha* according to the rule of *abhīya*, there is no elision of *hi*.
The root *jaṅgh* is not [included] because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*). In the form *ajaṅghan*, because of the mention of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*), *aṅ* is substituted for *cli*.
By the rule *hmyanta-śamāṃ dīrgho 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.95), there is no *vṛddhi*; thus:
*ajaṅgamīt*, *ajaṅgamiṣṭām*.

Although the substitution of *k* for *h* (kutva) in *han* is prescribed by the rule *hanteryuṅluk abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.54)— which follows the word *hanter* from the preceding rule *ho hanteḥ* (7.3.54)— nevertheless, the author of the Nyāsa states that it indeed occurs even in the case of *yaṅluk*, [as indicated] by the mention of *śtip* and *śap*.

The sense is that the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *yaṅlukoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.4) is not universal (*anitya*), because of the general indicator (*jñāpaka*) [implied by the rule] *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.82). Thus,
one forms *jaṅghanīti* and *jaṅghanti*.
From the shanks,
he strikes; [he is] one who will strike.
Because of the instruction [in the sūtra] using the form *śtip*, the substitute *j* does not occur; thus,
[the forms] are *ajaṅghāt* and *ajaṅghanīt*.
In the sense of "one who has struck," it is *ajaṅghan*;
however, in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*), it is *jaṅghanyāt*.
*vadhyāt*,
*avadhīt*,
*avadhiṣṭām*, and so forth.
However, doubling does not occur for the substitute of *vadh*,

because of the prohibition "not when it is a non-reduplicated [root] by virtue of being a *sthānivṛt*" (*anabhyāsasya*); for that [prohibition] is a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in apposition with it.
By the force of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, however,
the *ātmanepada* ending is applied according to the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28),
as in forms such as *ājaṅghate*.
By the rule *utparasya...* (Pāṇini 1.1.47), there is no *guṇa* substitution because of the mention of *ta* (the *tapara* designation); however,
by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77), a long vowel (*dīrgha*) would indeed occur, since that [long vowel] cannot be prevented by the *tapara* designation due to its being *asiddha*.
"Cañcurī" means one who moves about, "cañcūrti" means moving about, and "cañcūrtaḥ" means one who has moved about.
He moves about; he did not move about; he has not moved about.
In the word *caṅkhanī*, the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel] occurs according to the rule *caṅkhaṇi caṅkhaṇte janasana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.41).
By the rule *caṅkha-taḥ gama-hana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.98), there is elision of the penultimate vowel; thus,
*caṅkhnati*.
With conchs,
he sounded the conchs; he did not sound them falsely.
They did not walk about, they did not walk about, they did not walk about.
Those who expound the Vibhāṣā [should know that] from *caṅkhāyāt* [comes] *caṅkhanyāt*.
In the case of *acaṅkhanīt* and *acaṅkhānīt*,
because of the continued application of the rule *nābhyastasya* [Pāṇini 7.1.4], there is no vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) after the syllable *u*.
yoyoti, yoyavīti, ayoyavīt
In the case of *ayoyot* and *yoyuyāt*,
the vowel is long in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).
He has caused to go;
he has gone; he causes to sound repeatedly.
He binds,
he causes to sacrifice,
he abandons.

The following five rules do not apply here: 1. *ī halyaghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.66) 2. *jāhītaḥ* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.4.66) 3. *āca hau* (Pāṇini 6.4.117) 4. *lopo yi* (Pāṇini 6.4.118) 5. *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisāmaliṅi* (Pāṇini 6.4.66) and *erliṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.45).
Because it is taught with the *śtip* affix,
[the forms] are *jāhati* and *jāhāsi*.
you may abandon,
you two may abandon,
you all may abandon
He goes; he went; he has gone.
He abandoned; they two abandoned; they would have abandoned.
When the suffix is elided (*luk*), because there is an absence of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇābhāvāt*), the substitution of *u* (as in *svapisyami*) does not occur; furthermore,
because it is specified in the list [of roots] beginning with *rud* (*rudādibhyaḥ*), the augment *iṇ* does not apply, as in *sāsvapīti*.
He desires to sleep;
he has slept; he sleeps.
He slept;
he slept; may he sleep.
But in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), by the rule *vacisvapi-* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel; thus,
from the root *svap*,
one forms *asāsvāpīt*.
asāsvapīt SK 2652 AS 7-4-91: [the augment iṭ] is not applied after the root *svap* when followed by the suffix *ktvā*.
When there is elision of *yaṅ*, the augmentments *ruk*, *rik*, and *rīk* are added to the reduplicated syllable of a verbal root that has a short vowel as its penultimate letter. (SK 2653; AS 7.4.92)
Likewise, from a verbal root ending in ṛ,
one forms *varvṛtīti* and *varivṛtīti*.
He turns repeatedly, he revolves, he moves about.
He revolves repeatedly; he has revolved; he revolves. 3 times each.
The form *varvartāmāsa* occurs;
because it is specified as belonging to the class [of roots] beginning with *vṛt*, the rule *na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.59) does not apply.
He will roll about; he rolled about; he rolled about.
In the alternative where *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) applies by the rule *sipi ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.74), the form becomes *avarvāḥ* by the rule *ro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14);
because it is specifically mentioned in the *gaṇa*, the augment *aṅ* does not apply.
He has rolled down;
he resounds repeatedly; he resounds.
carikarti, carīkarti, carkṛtaḥ (3)
He performs repeatedly; he has performed repeatedly; he will perform repeatedly.
acarkarīt, acarkaḥ; carkṛyāt.
In the sense of a benediction: *riṅ carkriyāt* (may he celebrate repeatedly),
*acarkārīt* (he celebrated repeatedly).

And because of the rule *ṛtaśca* (Pāṇini 7.4.10) [which specifies the vowel *ṛ*], due to the inclusion of the long vowel by the *tapara* marker, the root *kṝ* in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepe*) is not included here; thus, it does not become *cākarti*.
He crosses over; he has crossed over; he causes [others] to cross over.
For he, the father, has indeed caused those fathers to cross over.
They have not crossed; they have not crossed over; they have not crossed across.

In forms such as *atātārīt* and *atātāriṣṭām*, when there is *yaṅ*-luṅ (elision of *yaṅ*) after the root *ṛ*, following reduplication, the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs, followed by the substitution of *ra* for that *u*.

By the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60), all but the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable are elided; then, by the rule *ruk-rig-ṛkārāṇām tu abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 7.4.92), the vowel *i* of the reduplicated syllable is replaced by *iyaṅ*.
Ararti, ariyarti, ariyarti.
He moves, he moves hither;
he has moved.
The vowel *ṛ* is substituted for *ar* and *ṝ*.
By the rule *ruko rori* (Pāṇini 8.3.17), there is elision; and in the application of that [elision], there is no status as a *sthānivadbhāva* for the *yaṇ*,
because that [status] is prohibited regarding what is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it.
In the case of *ārati* and *ariyati*,
because of the mention [of the roots] with the *śtip* affix in the *liṅ* [optative], there is no *guṇa* substitution according to the rule "guṇo'rti— " (Pāṇini 7.3.99). Thus, there is no *guṇa*.
When a long vowel is elided, it is treated as long.
From the noble one, from the noble one, he has gone away.
The root *gṛh* (to seize) in the Āryā meter is *jargṛhīti*. 3.
He swallows repeatedly; they swallow repeatedly; he swallows repeatedly.
*ajarghaṭat* [is formed] from *ghaṭ*,
while *jāgrahīti* is from *grah*.

In forms such as *jāgrāt*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) caused by the suffix *ṅi* is not present in *naruk* and similar words, because that [suffix] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being *bahiraṅga*.
You have awakened; you awaken; you will awaken.
In the luṭ (periphrastic future) after the root *jāgr*,
the form is *jāgriṣyati*.

Regarding the rule *graho'liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.37), the lengthening [of the vowel] does not occur there because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition *ekācaḥ* (a one-syllable root). Mādhava, however, asserts that the lengthening does occur; this contradicts the Bhāṣya.
The root *gṛdh* is used in the sense of longing;
[the reduplicated forms are] *jargṛdhīti*, *jargṛdhīti*, *jargarddhi*, *jargarddhi*.
jargṛddhaḥ 3, jargṛdhati 3, jargṛdhīṣi 3.
*jargharṣi* 3, *ajargṛdhīt* 3; in the absence of *īṭ*, there is *guṇa*.
Elision of the *hal* and *dyat* etc., substitution of the *bhaṣ* sound, and the *jaś* and *cart* substitutions.

In *ajarghatar* (3) and *ajargṛddhām* (3), there is optionally the substitution of *r* by [Pāṇini 8.2.74], which states: "In place of *d*, *r* is substituted before the suffix *sip*. Thus, in one alternative, there is the substitution of *r*.
ajarghāḥ 3, ajargardhīt 3, ajargardhiṣṭām 3.
In *pāpraṣṭi* (from the root *prach*),
the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) does not occur before suffixes beginning with *t* and so on, according to Pāṇini 6.1.16 (*grahijyā-va-yayi-vip-pracchi-śvi-dām ca*).

Because of the instruction with the *śtip* affix; [the substitution of] *śū* for *ch* and *v* according to Pāṇini 6.4.19 (*cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*), and the substitution of *ṣ* according to Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraśca-*) etc.
I have asked, I am asking, I ask.
Regarding *pāpraccha* and *pāpraśma*,
it was indicated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19) that there is no *yaṅluk* for roots ending in *y* or *v* that undergo the substitution of *ūṭh*.

And Kaiyaṭa has clarified this: the [rule] *cchvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19) pertains to those cases where *ūṭh* is applied by *jvaratvara-* (Pāṇini 6.4.20); however, for the roots *sṛ* and *mṛ* which undergo *ūṭh*, the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) certainly exists—this is the logical conclusion and is supported by Mādhava and others.
In the case of *mavya* in the sense of binding,
this [root] undergoes the substitution of *ūṭh*;
furthermore, *tevṛ*, *devṛ*, *devane*, and so forth, end in *vānt*.
The root *haya* means "to go"; thus, *jāhayīti* becomes *jāhati*.
He causes to go away; you cause to go away.
When *ya* and so forth are elided after *jāh*, there is a long vowel; thus, *jāhāmi*.
*jāhāvaḥ* and *jāhāmaḥ* [are forms] of the root *hary*, meaning "to move" and "to desire."
He seizes; he seizes; they two seize.
In the imperative (loṭ),
[the form] is jāharhi.
They have not brought;
they have not brought away;
they have not carried off.
The suffix *maP* is applied after the root *bandh* [to form the present participle].

The augment *ūṭh* is applied after the roots *jvar* and others when followed by the suffixes *upadhā* and *kār*, provided that the suffix *kvip* follows and begins with a *jhal* consonant and a nasal;
here, the condition *kṅiti* does not apply, as is seen from the form *otus* derived from the root *av* with the suffix *tun*.
The mention of *anunāsika* continues [from the previous rule],

because we see the form *om* when the suffix *man* is added to the root *ava* with the elision of the *ṭi* portion; and in the absence of *īṭ*, when *ūṭh* occurs before a *pit* suffix, there is *guṇa*.
He attains me, he protects me, he has protected me.
Protect me; you protect me; I am yours.
Protect me;
protect me well; protect me thoroughly.
I have reached me; I have attained me; we two have attained me.
We bow down; we have bowed down; we have bowed down completely.
The root *turv* means "to injure"; [the form] *totūrvī* is derived from it.
According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.21, there is elision (lopa) of *ch* and *v* following the letter *r*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant or an *anunāsika* nasal;
thus, there is elision of the *v*.
The *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel.
(Pāṇini 7.3.86)

The prohibition— that when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur for an *ik* vowel that is caused by the elision of a portion of a verbal root (*dhātvaṃśalopa*)— does not apply here,
because *tiP* and the other suffixes are not *ārdhadhātuka*; thus, [the form] is *totorti*.
By the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), there is lengthening:
*totūrtaḥ*, *totūrvati*.
To-tho-rti do-do-rti do-dh-or-ti.
*Murchā* means *momūrcchī*,
which is *momorti*.
In forms such as *momūrtaḥ* and *momūrchati*,
the term *ārdhadhātuke* functions as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).
Therefore, when the *yaṅ* [intensive suffix] is intended to be expressed, *aj* becomes *vī*,
resulting in *vevīyate*;
for this root, there is no *yaṅ-luk* (elision of the *yaṅ*).

Because the elision (*luk*) does not trigger the substitution of *vī* due to the absence of the required object, [the section on] the elision of *yaṅ* in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta-yaṅluk-prakaraṇa*) concludes.
Now begins the section on nominal roots (*nāmadhātu-prakaraṇa*) ending in verbal suffixes.

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.8 (SK 2657): The suffix *kyac* may optionally be applied after a word ending in a case-suffix that denotes an object of desire and is related to a desirer, in the sense of "desiring."
There is elision of the case-ending (*sub*) because it is a part of a nominal stem (*dhātu*).
(SK 2658; Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.33)
The affix *kyac* is applied after this [root] when one desires a son for oneself; thus, from the root *putra*, one forms *putrīyati* (he desires a son) when the suffix *yi* follows. (Pāṇini 3.1.8)
"But [the rule] 'gavyati nāvyati lopaḥ śākalyasya' (Pāṇini 8.3.19) does not apply here."
Because it is not at the end of a word; for thus [it is said] in SK 2659.
In the presence of *kyac* and *kyaṅ*, only a word ending in *-n* shall be [the base]; no other [word ending in *-n*] shall be so.
By the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *y* of *kyac* does not occur.
He made [them] desirous of cattle;
he did not make [them] desirous of ships.
In the case of the suffix *nāvyat*, there is no elision of the letter *n*; for example, *rājīyati*.
And [the substitution of *at* for *tvad* and *mad* occurs] before a suffix beginning with a consonant and before a word as a subsequent member of a compound:
*tvadyati*,
*madyati*.
The rule "when they have the same referent" applies here as well:
*yuṣmad-yati*,
*asmad-yati*.
And after the root *hali*,
[the suffix *ya* is applied]: it is swallowed (*gīryati*) and it is filled (*pūryati*).
By the rule "of the verbal root" (dhātoḥ), one does not desire [the application of] *div* here.
"Mādhava has stated that [the word *pura*] means 'it shines here' (*divyati iha*), 'it desires' (*icchati*), or 'it fills' (*puryati*); this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) should be considered,
because *pūḥ* and *gīḥ* are identical."
The form *dīrgha* [derived from the root] *div* meaning "to play" is merely a careless error of the Easterners;
[the correct form is *adasyati* according to the rule] *rīṅ ṛtaḥ*.
In the case of the suffixes *kyac* and *kyaṅ*, [the final vowel of the base is replaced by its Guṇa substitute]; thus, from *garga*, one forms *gargīyati*.
By the rule *vācyati-akṛt-sarva-* (Pāṇini 6.4.54), there is lengthening [of the vowel],
as in *kavīyati*.
He kindles.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.49)
The elision (lopa) of the suffixes *kyac* and *kyaṅ* following a consonant (*hal*) may optionally occur before an *ārdhadhātuka* affix; [furthermore],
by the rule "the elision of the initial [vowel] of the subsequent [element]" (*ato lopaḥ*), the vowel *a* is elided.
Because it is treated as the substitute (sthānivadbhāva), the guna substitution of the light penultimate vowel does not occur;
thus [the forms are] *samidhitā* and *samidhyitā*.
The suffix *kyac* is not applied after a nominal stem ending in the suffix *mān*, nor after an indeclinable (*avyaya*). [Examples:
*kim icchati*, *idam icchati*.
One desires one's own [happiness].
Derivatives ending in *kyac* are irregularly formed as follows:
*aśanāyati*, *udanyati*.
In cases such as hunger, one desires food; why then does one not desire to eat?
It behaves like water; it behaves like wealth.
AS 7.1.51: Before the suffix *kyac*, the augment *asuk* is added to these [words], and to *aśva* and *vṛṣa* when there is a desire for sexual intercourse (*maithuna*). (Or rather, it is optional.)
The verb *aśvasyati* is used when a mare desires a stallion,
and *vṛṣasyati* when a cow longs for milk or salt. Alternatively, these may be used in the sense of intense longing (*lālasā*).
A child desires milk (*kṣīrasyati*); a camel desires salt (*lavaṇasyati*).
After all nominal stems, when the suffix *kyac* is added in the sense of longing (*lālasā*), the augment *suk* (or *su*) is optionally applied.
He will desire curd;
he will desire honey; he will desire mead.
It determines the middle.
The suffix *kāmyac* occurs in the sense mentioned above;
for example, "he desires a son for himself" is expressed as *putrakāmyati*. Here, by the rule *yasya halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.49), the elision [of the final vowel and consonant] does not take place.
Because it would otherwise be meaningless,
it has been stated that the mention of the compound [in the rule] refers to the whole; thus, one who desires fame is called *yaśaskāmyati*.
This [suffix] should indeed occur even after words ending in *m* and indeclinables; for example,
*kiṃkāmyati*.
He desires heaven.
(Pāṇini 3.1.8)
The suffix *kyac* is applied after a word ending in a case-suffix that functions as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), in the sense of behaving like that; for example:
*putrīyati chātram* (he behaves toward the pupil as if toward a son), *viṣṇūyati dvijam* (he behaves toward the twice-born as if toward Viṣṇu).
And it should be stated that [the suffix *ya*] is applied after a locative case ending:
"The monk finds pleasure in a hut" (*kuṭyāṃ prāsādīyati*) or "he finds pleasure in a palace" (*prasāde kuṭīyati*).
After a noun ending in a case-suffix that functions as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the suffix *kyaṅ* may optionally be added to express the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*).
Since it is stated that for a word ending in *s* which denotes an agent, there may either be elision (*lopa*) or the suffix *kyaṅ*, in one alternative there is a sentence; however,
the elision of the final *s* is prescribed as being conditioned by the occurrence of *kyaṅ*.
And he is established [in this state] through vigor (*ojas*) and celestial nymphs (*apsaras*); for others, it is optional (*vibhāṣā*).
He acts like Kṛṣṇa; he behaves as Kṛṣṇa does (*kṛṣṇāyate*).
The word *ojas* [functions] in the scope of its derivative usage (*vṛtti*) to denote that which possesses it; thus,
one says *ojāyate* and *apsarāyate*.
He acts like one famous, he acts like one seeking fame, he acts like one learned.
He is known,
he is praised, and he is intoxicated.
But when there is a plurality of referents, [the suffix] *kyaṅ* is applied after words for "you" (*yuṣmad*) and "I" (*asmad*),
as well as after words denoting those who possess pride (*mānin*).
She acts like a maiden, she behaves like a maiden;
she acts like a doe.
She acts like a green thing; she acts like a heavy thing; she acts like a rival wife.
He acts like a rival wife; he acts like a co-wife; he acts like a young woman toward a youth.
The suffix *kyac* is applied after a word ending in the letter *k*, provided that the penultimate vowel is not long, as if it were *paṭu* (clever) or *mṛdu* (soft); for example,
*pācikāyate*.
Regarding the sense of "conduct" (*ācāra*), the suffix *kvip* may optionally be prescribed after the words *avagalbha*, *klība*, and *hoḍa*.
Because of the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is also applicable.
The words *avagalbha* and the others end in the suffix *ac* (i.e., they are derived from verbal roots with the addition of *ac*).
By the application of the suffix *kvip*, it is declared that the *ac*-suffix [of the root] is both unaccented (*anudātta*) and nasalized (*anunāsika*);
therefore,
*agalbhate* takes the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings.
The suffix *ām* is applied after a word ending in more than one vowel that ends in *klība* or *hoḍa*, even when these words refer to what was previously [so].
By the very power of undertaking this Vārttika,
the establishment of forms such as *na cāgalbhate* is its result,
because even in the case of simple roots (*kevala*), the occurrence of the suffix is possible.
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, "avagalbhāñcakre" means "he made [himself] a eunuch."

Mādhava and others maintain that because the root *vṛt* is taught with the prefix *ava-* (in the form *avavartate*), the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs only after this specific form, as well as after the simple root and after other prefixes; however,
it is more appropriate to hold that the *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* endings) do not occur.
The suffix *kvip* should be stated as optional after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

However, the previous Vārttika was intended for the purpose of attaching an indicatory letter (*anubandha*); there, *kvip* is restated, and because of the mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), the term "sup" [from the preceding rule] is not connected here.
Therefore, it does not undergo the grammatical operation pertaining to a *pada* like the root *kṛṣṇ*; rather,
from the rule "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) together with the suffix *śap*.

Because [the rule] "a ivācarati" (Pāṇini 3.1.12) mentions the suffixes *ati*, *ataḥ*, and *anti*, and because of the statement that [the substitute] applies when there is more than one vowel (*anekāc*), [the term] "nāman" is understood.
The two have gone;
O! (or: He has gone.)
From this, there is doubling [of the consonant];
then, by the rule *ata ādeḥ*, there is lengthening of the initial vowel.
In the case of *ṇal* and *au*, there is *vṛddhi*;
however, in the case of *atus* and so forth, as well as before *iṭ*, there is elision of the long *ā* according to *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64). Thus, "he acts like a garland" becomes *mālāti*.

Either by the *paribhāṣā* regarding gender-distinction (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) or because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the end of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*), the suffix *kvip* occurs; thus, [the form] *mālāṃcakāra* is derived in the *laṅ* tense.
In *amālāt*,
there is no elision according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* because, by association with *ṅī*, the elision of *āp* is also prescribed only before the case-ending *su*.
The two dice made the dice-board their garland; like a poet, they composed poetry.

In the rule *āśīrliṅi kavīyāt sicirvṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that there is no *vṛddhi* for a nominal root (*nāmadhātu*), because the word "root" (*dhātu*) is understood from the previous context and is interpreted as "that which is a root. Thus,
[the form] is *akavayīt*.
Like a weaver, he weaves;
he has woven;
they two have woven.
It has flowed, it has flowed like glory.
He has resorted; he resorted; they two have resorted.
Like a father, he protects;
in his blessing,
may he extend us long life.
In this case, the rules "gāti-sthā-ghu-pā-bhū-māsyati-tyate-ti-kiti" (Pāṇini 6.4.66), "bhuvo vuk" (Pāṇini 6.4.88), and "bhavateraḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.73) do not apply,
because only that which exists in the Dhātupāṭha is understood there due to its being explicitly manifested.
He has become; he has perished; he runs like a tree.
And by the rule "niśri—SKsandarbhaḥ 2312," the *caṅ* [affix] does not cause reduplication; thus, it did not sound repeatedly (adrāvīt).

AS 6.4.15: A long vowel shall be substituted for the penultimate (upadhā) of a word ending in a nasal (anunāsika), when followed by the suffix *kvip* or by an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*. [Thus:
*idam ivācarati* becomes *idām ati*.
Like a king he rules over kings; like a path he leads to paths and leads to the goal.
Regarding *ṛbhukṣīṇa*,
Mādhava says it means "shining like the sky" (*dyaur-iva-dyavatī*); however, in this case, *ūṭh* having been applied, it would be more appropriate to say *dyavatī*.
Haradatta asks, "Who is it and how many *cakas* are there?
Mādhava, however, states that because of the rule "ṇyallopau," the elision of the *a* (ato lopaḥ) prevails over the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] in the *ṇal* suffix, resulting in the form *cakaḥ*.
He has breathed forth like his own self; he has breathed forth.
As for the statement that "the master causes his own [action] to be done," that is indeed without a source (anākara).

The suffix *kyaṅ* shall be applied after words such as *bhṛśa*, which denote the state of becoming what one was not, in the sense of "becoming"; furthermore, there is elision (*lopa*) of these [words] when they end in a consonant.

From the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not *ac*" (*acveḥ*), it is understood that this refers to the state of becoming what one was not (*abhūtatadbhāva*). [Examples: One who was not intense becomes intense: *bhṛśāyate*.

Therefore, the meaning here is that those things which are intense at night, such as the stars and so forth, do not exist anywhere during the day; and those which are intense during the day do not exist anywhere at night.
The word *sumanas* undergoes elision of its final vowel when the suffix *āya* is added:
*sumanāyate*.
In the *curādi* class, the root *saṃgrām* is recited in the sense of "fighting"; therein, *saṃgrāma* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
From that, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is established by the rule *tat karoti*. In connection with that [suffix], the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is attached.

Even though the word *grāma* is mentioned in the rule for *yuddhe yaḥ*, since the word *saṃgrāma* is understood by implication, the specific recitation (*viśiṣṭapāṭha*) indicates that a preceding member which has the same form as a prefix is separated when a suffix that triggers the designation of a verbal root (*dhātusaṃjñā*) is intended to be applied;
therefore, the augment *aṭ* is inserted before the word *manas*.
He was with mind; he became beyond mind; he transcended the state of being beyond mind.
In this way, it should be understood that even in examples such as *avāgalbhata* and *avāgalbhiṣṭa*, there is a separation of the prefix *ava-* [from the root].
And the indicator (*jñāpaka*) applies to cases of the same class;
therefore, the separation occurs only where the entire form of the prefix is heard and has not been replaced by a substitute.
Thus, in forms such as *ā-ūḍhaḥ*, *oḍhaḥ*, and *sa ivācarya oḍhāyitvā*, the suffix *lyap* does not occur (as it would in *atra unmanāyya* or *avagalbhyet*).
This is because the evidence (*jñāpaka*) [of the rule] applies only to specific cases; in this regard, the sixth-century *Vārttika* and its commentary (*bhāṣya*) serve as the authority.
For instance,
*usyomāṅkṣvāṭaḥ* is a prohibition; its meaning is that when *usi*, *om*, or *āṅ* follow, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for *āṭ* does not take place.
He desired a cow;
he performed the *ausrīya* sacrifice and the *auṅkārīya* sacrifice.

It is established in the *Ṣaṣṭha-adhyāya* (Pāṇini 6.1.89) that this [form] is accomplished because the rule "auḍhīyat āṭaśca" (Pāṇini 7.3.34) prescribes *vṛddhi* again by means of the word "ca" (and).
According to AS 3.1.13, the suffix *kyaṣ* occurs in the sense of "becoming" after words beginning with *lohita* and after those ending in *ḍāc*.
AS 1.3.90: After a verbal base ending in *kyaṣ*, the *parasmaipada* endings may optionally occur;
as in *lohitāyati* or *lohitāyate*.

Here, by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "from *ac*," the status of being a domain of "the becoming of that which was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is obtained; and this qualifies the word *lohita* alone, because it is impossible for it to apply to the suffix *ḍāc*,
nor to those [words] included under the term "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Because of that rejection,
the Vārttika likewise states:
"The rule for *kyaṣ* after words ending in *lohita* and *ḍāj* [is established], while the others [are included] among the *bhṛśādi* group."
Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of its power of enunciation (*uccāraṇa-sāmarthya*), the *k* of *kyaṣ* would likewise be heard [as a separate phoneme], as is the case with *kāmyac*;
for that [distinction] too has been rejected in the Bhāṣya,
as in the example *paṭapaṭāyati*.
In this context, the suffix *ḍāc* occurs even without connection to the roots *kṛ*,
*bhū*, or *as*, because of the force of the rule prescribing *kyap* after a word ending in *ḍāc*.
That which consists of redness, blackness, and suffering; joy, pride, and pleasure;
fainting, sleep, compassion, and smoke—these are the constant skins of compassion.

Having read this, some cite two forms even for *śyāmā* and others when *kyaṣ* is applied; however, that contradicts the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika. Therefore, only *kyaṅ* applies after them, as in *śyāmāyate*.
Terms such as *duḥkha* (suffering) and others apply to the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) by virtue of their application to that which possesses it; thus,
by the rule regarding gender-distinction (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), the suffix *kyap* is also applied after the word *lohinī*, resulting in *lohinīyati*.
It is made red (lohinīyate).

The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after the word *kaṣṭa* ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*) in the sense of "endeavoring" (*utsāha*). For example: *kaṣṭāya kramate* (he endeavors toward hardship), meaning he strives to perform an evil deed.
It should be stated that [the suffix *kha*] is applied after the words *satra*, *kakṣa*, *kaṣṭa*, *kṛcchra*, and *gahana* when there is a desire to do something wicked (*kaṇvacikīrṣā*).
In this context, *kaṇva* means "evil," and *satra* and the others have the sense of "evil" within the scope of their derivative usage (*vṛtti*).
From those words ending in the second case, when there is a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied; thus,
"he desires to do evil" (*pāpaṃ cikīrṣati*) is expressed as *satrāyate*, which does not involve a separate analysis of its constituent parts (*asvapadavigraha*).
"It acts as an armpit," and so forth (SK 2671;

The suffix *kyaṅ* may be applied after the roots *vṛt* and *car* when preceded by *romantha* and *tapas* respectively, provided they function as the object (*karman*). Thus, *romantham vartayati* becomes *romanthāyate*;
it should be stated [as a rule] that this applies when there is movement of the jaw (*hanucalana*).
The meaning is "chewing again what has already been chewed and drawn out"; here [the term] *romantha* does not refer to a worm performing rumination,
but rather to the substance that has emerged from the region of the anus.

Kaiyaṭa states that the meaning is "he eats it," while the author of the Nyāsa and Haradatta state that the meaning is "he makes it round"; furthermore, there is an option for the *parasmaipada* ending after the root *tapas*.
He performs austerity; he practices asceticism. (Pāṇini 3.1.16)
The suffix *kyaṅ* may be applied after these two verbal roots: *bāṣpa* (steam) and *ūṣman* (heat). Thus, "he emits steam" becomes *bāṣpāyate*, and "he emits heat" becomes *ūṣmāyate*.
And it should be stated that [the suffix *kyac* is applied] after the word *phena*:
*phenāyate* (it foams). (SK 2673)
After these objects, the suffix *kyaṅ* may be used in the sense of "to do";
for example, *śabdam karoti* becomes *śabdāyate*.

According to one view, the suffix *ṇic* is also accepted in the sense of "he causes that to be done"; thus, the *Nyāsa* states: "[the suffix ṇic is applied] after the words *sudina*, *durdina*, and *nīhāra*, or optionally."
It becomes a fair day.

The suffix *kyaṅ* may be applied after words such as *sukha* when they function as objects of the action of feeling (*vedanā*), provided that the *sukha* and so forth belong to the very same agent who performs the feeling. [For example:
"he feels pleasure" (*sukhaṃ vedayate*).
Why is the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) necessary?
One experiences the happiness of another. (SK 2675; AS 3.1.19)

Since the term "in the sense of the instrument" (*karaṇe*) is understood from the previous context, [the suffix *ṇic*] is applied to specific actions such as worship (*pūjā*), service (*paricaryā*), and wonder (*āścarya*);
thus, "he pays homage to the gods" (*namasyati devān*) means "he worships them."
"Varivasyati" means he serves his gurus; that is the meaning.
"Citrīyate" [means he treats them with wonder].
The meaning is "he causes wonder";
others say it means "he causes [others] to wonder.
*pucchād ud-asane vyasane paryasane ca* (or not).
*Vyasana* means lifting up in various ways or in a contrary manner.
He asks, he asks back, he asks thoroughly.
In the sense of gathering together from a container,
*saṃbhāṇḍayate* means he gathers the goods together.
The meaning is that he piles them up; he has gathered the robes for the purpose of acquisition and wearing.
The meaning is that a monk "procures robes" (saṃcīvarayate) means he acquires or puts on robes.
[The suffix *kṛtya*] is used in the sense of the root *kṛ* (to do).
He makes [someone] shave [his head]; he causes [him] to shave, because of the vow regarding eating or abstaining from it;
he takes milk or the food of a Śūdra as his vow.
In the sense of covering with a garment, [the suffix ṇic is used]; or,
in the sense of taking from a field and so forth, [the suffix ṇic is used].
The fact that *hali* and *kali* end in the letter *a* is also established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
Thus, "he seizes the plough" or "he seizes the strife" is expressed as *halayati*.

Hali effects the elision of the heavy syllable (mahaddhalaṃ) because it is subsequent; even though the substitution of vṛddhi has occurred, by virtue of the treatment as if it were iṣṭhan, only the suffix *ac* is elided.
Therefore, because of the absence of the *sanvadbhāva* and the lengthening [of the vowel],
*acakalat* does not lose its original form.
He takes what has been made; he makes it;
he removes the husks; he husks.
Some say "tūṣṭa" means hair;
others say it means matted hair;
others say it means evil.
It is more appropriate to read *muṇḍa* and the others in the very rule *satyāpapāśa-* (Pāṇini 3.1.25),

because the sense of the verbal root is already established from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The inclusion of some of them is for the sake of adding the causative suffix (*ṇic*) even after words that require a complement,
as in *muṇḍayati māṇavakam* ("he causes the boy to be shorn").
"He mixes the food,
softens the cloth,
and seasons the condiment."
The suffix *apuk* is added to *satya* for the sake of making *halika* and *kalika* end in *a*,
while for some it is added merely for the sake of verbal elaboration (*prapañca*).
One makes true or declares as true, thus *satyāpayati*;
the suffix *āpuk* should also be stated [after the roots] *artha* and *vid*,
as in *arthāpayati*.
He causes the snare to be known;
he releases it; he unbinds it;
he sees form; he forms it.

The meaning is that he sings to the accompaniment of a lute, plays the lute, combs [the hair] with cotton, combs it following the grain of the cotton, and touches the tip of a blade of grass with cotton.
He praises with verses (*upaślokayati*),
he approaches with an army (*abhiṣeṇayati*);
[the substitution of] *ṣ* occurs by the rule "after a prefix, before *su*" (Pāṇini 8.3.65).
By the rule *abhyaṣeṇayat prāksitāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.65), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs; thus,
[the form] is *abhiṣiṣeṇayiṣati*.
And by the rule "sthādiṣv abhyāsena ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.64), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs;
he strokes the hairs (*lomāni anumārṣṭi*), that is, he makes them smooth (*anulomayati*).
[The root] *tvaca* is used in the sense of covering (*saṃvaraṇe*), with the suffix *gha*.
He takes the skin; he skins it. He equips with armor; he armors it. He takes the color; he colors it.
With *cūrṇaiḥ*, one scatters or covers;
because of the extension [of rules] by the term *iṣṭhavad*, there is masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) and so forth. One who causes *enī* (a brindled cow) to be expressed becomes *etayati*.

He speaks of *darada*; [the denominative] *dāradayati* means "he makes broad" or "he expands," provided that there is an increase [in size], or else there is the elision of the suffix *ṭi* at the beginning.
He spread it out; he spread it wide; he softens what is soft.
It causes one who is already extremely emaciated to become even more severely weakened.
He emaciates,
he strengthens, he did not fall away.
He looked upon it; he made it firm; he encompassed it.
It stated that doubling (*dvitva*) is taught for the *ūḍhi* [suffix], but it was said that the rule "that which is not established in the preceding context does not apply to doubling" is non-eternal;
others, however, say that doubling applies to the element *ḍhi*.
auḍiḍhat means "he spoke having carried"; aujaḍhat means "he made stiff."

In the rule *auḍadhat oḥ puyaṇjyapare* (Pāṇini 7.4.80), the inclusion of the class-consonant (*varga*) and the semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) as well as the letter *ja* is an indicator (*liṅga*) that when a doubling (*dvitva*) is to be performed, the substitute for *ṇi* does not take place; this was stated in the commentary on the root *ūnayati*.
By virtue of being a single syllable by nature, there is *vṛddhi* and *puṅ*;
[thus] he causes [him] to sleep (*svāpayati*).
He causes one to speak of you or me; [the forms] *tvāpayati* and *māpayati* are derived from the stems *tvad* and *mad*, ending in *map*.
Because it is eternal, the elision of the *ṭi* occurs before the substitution of the subsequent form; thus, *vṛddhi*, the augment *puK*, and so forth,
are more logical in the forms *tvādayati* and *mādayati*.
Because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), when the *pararūpa* (single-substitute form) has been applied, the status of the original base (*prakṛtibhāva*) applies by the rule *prakṛtyaikāc*.
One should not fall into the error of thinking that this *prakṛtibhāva* was rejected in the Bhāṣya;
for the Bhāṣya merely intends to show an alternative derivation (*anyathāsiddhi*) regarding specific examples such as *proṣṭha*.
He says "you two" or "us two" regarding you or us;
he says "dog" regarding a dog: *śāvayati*.
By the rule *nastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144), there is elision of the *ṭi* portion;

Furthermore, due to its status as a *bha*-stem, there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
Others, however,
hold that *na ṣṭar ddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.153) is not extended here [to the suffix *iṣṭhan*], because that [substitution] is not observed in the case of *iṣṭhan*.

Regarding *vidāvayati*, others hold that after the *saṃprasāraṇa*, the *vṛddhi* [substitution], and the substitution of *āv*, [the rule applies]; however, because it is obligatory (*nitya*), the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs prior to the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel),
and due to its being an *antaraṅga* operation, the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) [of the preceding and following vowels] takes effect first.

He speaks correctly; he causes to come together; he caused to come together. He speaks crosswise; he causes to stretch across.

Even in the case of an elision [of the *ṭi*] due to the violation of the desired operation (*añceṣṭilopa*), [the elision of the first *ṭi*] is not established because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) and thus considered non-existent (*asiddha*). By the rule "it is as if non-existent here" (*asiddhavad atra*), according to the logic of the *ciṇ* and *luṅ* [affixes], the elision of the first *ṭi* is non-existent; therefore, there is no further elision of the *ṭi*. Thus, *tiras* becomes *tiriḥ*.

Alternatively, by the *paribhāṣā* "a rule concerning the operation of a constituent element does not apply when that element has been elided," the penultimate vowel is not shortened in *atitirāyat* because the *caṅ* suffix is *aglopi*.
He speaks toward one who is turned together; he causes him to go together; he caused him to go together; [he speaks] toward one who is turned in all directions.
He has entered; he flows toward the gods; he causes it to flow toward the gods;
he has flowed toward the gods.
He has driven him away from here; he has driven him away from there.
He causes to swell; he has caused him to swell,
bending toward that [person].
He causes [him] to cause [him] to go about repeatedly;
[the periphrastic form is] āmumuāyayat.
He causes the earth to become;
he made it not-become.
He causes the eyebrow to become; he made it not-become.

he has driven forth the cow;
he has sent forth wealth.
Like a ship that does not sink, possessing good horses and good reins, it possesses the light of heaven.
In the case of indeclinables, there is elision of the suffix *ṭi* when followed by a mere *bha*-affix (Vārttika);
[as in] *svayati* from *asasvat*.
In the word *asisvat*, it causes many [things] to become; others say it means "it multiplies," with the suffix *vin* dropped according to the rule *vinmatorluk*.

He caused the milch cows to yield milk;
he makes them yield milk.
In this case, there is no substitution of *ṭi* for the penultimate vowel, because the elision (*luk*), which is an exception to that rule, has already taken effect; thus,
one causes the large to become small (*sthūlam sthavayati*).
How then does it cause [the sun] to go far away? It causes it to go far when the sun has set; or rather, it extends from afar, or it moves from afar.

The meaning is "making [them] distant. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *kan*, as in the rule "for *yuvan* and *alpa*" (Pāṇini 5.3.64), which forms *yavayati* or *kanayati* [meaning "he makes young" or "he diminishes"].
It brings near what is distant;
it thoroughly accomplishes what is excellent; it renders praiseworthy that which is already praiseworthy.
In this case,

It rains down what is dear, it causes one to obtain it, and it expands it extensively.
It chooses the wide, wards it off, and increases it abundantly.
He makes the heavy light; he protects the distressed; he lengthens the short.
The section on nominal roots ending in verbal suffixes, namely *vṛndayati* derived from *vṛndāraka*;
now begins the section on nominal roots beginning with *kaṇḍū*.

for the *kaṇḍvādi* group is twofold: they are both verbal roots and nominal stems.

furthermore, *valgu* is used in the senses of "worship" (*pūjā*) and "sweetness" (*mādhurya*).
valgūyati 1948; [the root] asu [is used] in the sense of afflicting (upatāpa); [the form] asū.
Some say "asūn" because he throws [them].
The roots *asūyati* and *asūyate* (1949) are used in the sense of envy (*leṭ* 1950), while [the root] in the sense of theft (*loṭ*) is used in the sense of prior existence and dreaming.

loṭyati, loṭitā; 1951 lela, in the sense of blazing.

By the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), there is lengthening:

1955. *uṣas* in the sense of dawn; 1956. *veda* in the sense of theft and sleep; 1957. *medhā* in the sense of quick apprehension.
medhāyati 1958; kuṣubha, in the sense of throwing away, kuṣubhyati.

Now begins the section on the series of *tiṅanta* suffixes.

When the suffix *san* is applied to the root *kaṇḍūyati*, the doubling of the first monosyllable would [otherwise] occur by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*; however, it should be stated as an exception (*vārttika*) that for roots beginning with *kaṇḍū*, the third syllable is doubled. Thus:
*kaṇḍūyiyiṣati*.
The meaning is that after a root ending in *kyac*, the suffix *san* is applied as desired;
among the first three [types of verbal roots], any one may undergo reduplication, whereas for those beginning with *a*, it is the second syllable [that is reduplicated].
*puputrīyiṣati*, *putitrīyiṣati*, *putrīyiyiṣati*,
*aśiśvīyiṣati*, *aśvīyiyiṣati*.
The prohibition of doubling applies only to that which follows a vowel when it is part of a conjunct consonant consisting of *n*, *d*, or *r*.
From the root *indriy*, with the suffix *san*, there is reduplication of either the syllable *drī* or the syllable *yi*;
thus: *indidrīyiṣati* or *indrīyiyiṣati*.
He desires to cause [someone] to wish to speak of what is dear: *cicandrīyiṣati*, *candidrīyiṣati*, *candrīyiyiṣati*; or he desires to incite one who is speaking of what is dear:
*piprāpayiṣati*, *prāpipayiṣati*, *prāpayiyiṣati*; he desires to cause [something] wide to be opened: *vivārayiṣati*, *vārirayiṣati*, *vārayiyiṣati*.
The three forms beginning with *bāḍhaṃ sisādhayiṣati* exist, but the form with *ṣatva* does not, because [the rule] "a *san* following a *yaṅ* or a causative (*ṇi*) stem" does not apply here.
*bobhūyiṣayiṣati* is formed by adding *ṇic* after the forms ending in *yaṅ*, *ṇic*, and *san*;
[thus] *bobhūyayiṣati*, and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the series of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta-pratyaya-mālā*).

Cracking of the feet, chilblains, and the riverbank splitting apart;
there is no prohibition against [the use of] substances that act upon other parts of the body. (Vārttika)
The ants open the mouth of the moth. (SK 2687; AS 1.3.21)
And [the suffix *ya* is applied] after roots beginning with *ad* and *āṅ*,
as in: *anukrīḍate*, *saṃkrīḍate*,
*parikrīḍate*.
The word *ākrīḍate* is derived from the preverb *anu* used as a *karmapravacanīya*; it does not form a compound with the preverb *na*, due to its association with [other] preverbs (*upasarga*).

"When *āṅ* is used, [the *taṅ* ending applies] after the roots *nṛt* and *pracch*. (Vārttika).

Regarding the rule "the fifth case [is used] after a word ending in *lyap*": this refers to cases where the meaning of that suffix is understood even without a form ending in *lyap*, such as in the example "to break" (*bhettum*), or where there is an ellipsis of a form ending in *tumun*,

Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.67:

The Ātmanepada suffix shall be used after a root ending in the causative marker *ṇic*, provided that the action expressed by the non-causative (*aṇau*) is the very same as that expressed by the causative (*ṇyantena*), and the factor that was the object (*karma-kāraka*) in the non-causative becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative; however, this does not apply in the case of the act of remembering (*anādhyāne*).

Since the rule *ṇicaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74) already establishes this, the present rule is for the purpose of [indicating] when the result does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). However, when the result benefits the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), the option provided by *vibhāṣopapadena* (Pāṇini 1.3.77) applies; and since *aṇāvakarmakāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.88) would apply subsequently to prescribe the *parasmaipada* ending, this very [present rule] is desired by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
Examples are verbs whose state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) and those whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*).
For thus they behold existence; the meaning is that the devotees make it an object of visual cognition.
The meaning is that when the impelling aspect is abandoned, existence is seen as becoming an object.
Therefore, they show the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense that "devotees see existence" (*bhavaṃ paśyanti*).
Furthermore, when the meaning of the reflexive (*nyartha*) is not intended to be expressed, as in "Bhava shows himself" (*darśate bhavaḥ*),
the meaning is identical in the first and third stages and in the second and fourth stages;
however, in that third stage, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings do not occur.
Even though the action is the same, because the *karmakāraka* (the object) in the *aṇ* [denominative base] lacks the status of being the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇi*-derived [causative] form,

In the first [case], because of being the agent of the action and of existence here,

The meaning is that the verb *bhavati* causes one to see, while *ārohati* (the elephant) causes one to mount; thus, it impels both the observer and the rider.
Then, even when the two causative suffixes (*ṇic* and *śānac*) and their respective bases are abandoned along with the two acts of instigation (*preṣaṇa*),
the examples *darśayate* and *ārohayate* have the same meaning as before.

In this view, in the second stage [of the argument], the suffix *taṅ* (the ātmanepada marker) does not apply because there is an absence of "identity of action" (*samānakriyatva*), due to the addition of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij*). [Objection:
Why is it said "except in the sense of 'thinking' (*anādhyāne*)"?

After the roots *vṛt* and others, when followed by the suffixes *syat* (the future) or *san* (the desiderative), [the substitution of *iṭ* is optional]. Examples:

Now begins the section on verbal endings for the impersonal (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*) voices.
Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.67: The suffix *yak* shall be added to a verbal root when a *sārvadhātuka* affix denoting the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) follows.

*Bhāva* (being) is *bhāvanā* (the creative force); it is an act of production, and as such, it is denotable by all verbal roots (*dhātu*). It is restated by means of a verbal suffix (*lakāra*) whose meaning is *bhāva*. Because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the first person is used.
Since the *bhāvanā* expressed by the verbal suffix is non-substantial (*asattvarūpa*), duality and other numbers are not perceived; therefore, dual and plural endings do not occur.
However, since the singular number alone is the default (autsargika) for that [agent], it does not depend on [any other] number; thus,
when the agent has not been expressed, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is employed.
By you, by me, and by others, it is being and it has been.

When *syat* and other suffixes follow, expressing the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or passive (*karman*), there may optionally be an application of the stem-operation as if it were *ciṇ* (the *ciṇ* augment) for those roots ending in *ac* taught in the *upadeśa*, as well as for *han* and others; furthermore, the *iṭ* augment is applied to these *syat* suffixes.
Since this *iṭ* is prescribed in conjunction with the *ciṇvadbhāva*, it does not occur in its absence.
Here, the term *ārdhadhātuka* is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*) and serves as a qualifier for *sīyuṭ*, but not for the others, because there is no deviation [in their application].
Due to the *ciṇvadbhāva* [treatment], there is *vṛddhi*: *bhāvitā*.
It will become; it will be brought into being;
it will come to be.
May it be;
it was; may it be.

resulting in *āritā*.
The object remembered is the rememberer.
In this case, because it has been stated that the term *nitya* (invariably) is understood from the rule *guṇo’rti-ŚK-sandarbhah 2380*, no *guṇa* substitution is applied here; rather,
by the rule *aniditām-ŚK-sandarbhah 415*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *n*.
The root *sras* takes the augment *it*,
while *nand* undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
The root *ij* (to sacrifice) takes the suffix *yaṅ* when followed by a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*,
as in *śayyate*.
The substitute *ā* may optionally take the place of the final [phoneme].
That which is protected and extended is called *vibhāṣā*.
It is born; it is produced. (SK 2760)
The affix *ciṇ* shall not occur after the root *tap* when it follows *cala*, in the sense of the object becoming the agent (*karmakartṛ*), nor in the sense of repentance;
e.g., *anvatapta pāpena*.
The meaning is that he has been struck by that evil-doer; [this is expressed] in the passive voice using the *luṅ* suffix.
Alternatively, the meaning is "it was grieved by" (aśoci) the sinful agent; thus,
by the rule *ghumāsthā...* [Pāṇini 6.4.66], the substitution of *i* (*itvam*) is applied,
resulting in *dīyate*.

In the rule *dhīyate ādecaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), the phrase *aśiti* is a *karmadhāraya* compound; thus, there is a prohibition regarding that which begins with a *ś* bearing the technical designation *it*.
Since this [root] lacks an initial *ś* (*ādi-śit*), the substitution of *āt* does not occur before it.
He should fast for three days.
For roots ending in *ā*, the augment *yuk* is inserted before a *ciṇ* affix, as well as before affixes marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, and before *kṛt* affixes; thus,
[the forms] *dāyitā* and *dātā*.
It should have been given;
it was given;
it was given.
*adāyiṣātām* (from *sthā-ghvoricca*); *adiṣātām*.
They two were placed;
they two were sat upon;
they two did not become weary.
In *aglāsātām*,
by the rule *ityate aciṇṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.36), it is stated that there is no substitution of *t* for *h* in the case of *han*.
By the rule *ho hanteḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.54), there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *gh*), resulting in *ghānitā* and *hantā*.
In the benedictive (āśīrliṅ) [mood], the substitution of *vadh* is superseded by the treatment as if having the suffix *ciṇ* (ciṇvadbhāva), which results in the forms *dhāniṣyate* and *haniṣyate*.
Because [the suffix] *sīyuṭ* is specifically prescribed for the *ārdhadhātuka* [context], one says *ghāniṣīṣṭa* in one alternative and *vadhiṣīṣṭa* in the other.
They have sinned; they two have sinned; they have committed sin.
In the [perfect] stem, there is the substitution of *vadh* for [the root]; thus:
*avadhi*, *avadhiṣātām*.

It should not be argued that [the root] would have been *aghāniṣyata* or *ahaniṣyata*, because by the extension rule (*atideśa*) "as if *ciṇ*" (*ciṇvat*), the substitute *vadh* would apply before the suffixes *iṣ* and so on.
Because of the governing rule *aṅgasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.1) [in the sūtra *ciṇvad aṅgasya*], since the designation applies only to the *aṅga*,
the lengthening does not apply to the *iṭ* augment of the *ciṇvat* substitute.
Since the long vowel is prescribed by the rule *aliṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.35) for the *iṭ* augment characterized as having *val* etc.,
[the forms] are *grāhitā* and *grahītā*.
He will grasp;
he will seize; may he grasp.
He would have grasped;
he grasped; they two grasped.
They two would have grasped; it is seen; it was seen.
*adarśiṣātām* [is derived from the root *dṛś*];
because the suffix *sic* is *kit*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *r* to *ṛ*,
resulting in *adṛkṣātām*.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) after the root *gṛ*, when the suffix *dhvam* is applied, there are one hundred and four forms; for it has been stated that the long vowel does not occur for the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment, as in *agāridhvam*.
But in the second [person], by the rule *iṭi vṛto vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.38), there is optionally a long vowel:
*agarīdhvam* or *agaridhvam*.
Among these three, there are five optional [alternatives]: the substitution of *l* for *r*, the substitution of *ḍh* for *dh*, and the triplication [of the consonant].
Thus, there are ninety-six [possibilities].
Since the suffix *liṭ* is optional according to *liṅsicor ātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 1.2.11), when the augment *iṭ* is absent, the suffix is *kit* by virtue of *uśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.12).
By the rule *raparatvaṃ hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), there is lengthening;
by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃ-luṅ-liṭāṃ dho 'ṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.78), there is obligatory substitution of *ḍha* for *dha*, resulting in *aśīḍhvam*.
When the eight possibilities for the doubling of the *ḍh* sound are added to the previously stated ninety-six, the total number mentioned is reached;
