[the factors involved are]: the substitution of *iṅ* for *i*, the long vowel, the augment *iṭ* as in *ciṇ*, the substitution of *l*, the substitution of *ḍh*, and likewise the triad of doublings.
Thus, by combining these eight options, there are one hundred and four [forms];
the suffix *la* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*) after a causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) verbal root, with the addition of *yak*.
Delusion, which is known as the disappearance of [true] knowledge, is destroyed by Mukunda.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.93: When *ciṇ* follows, and when *ṇi* followed by *ṇamul* follows, there is optionally a lengthening of the penultimate vowel of roots marked with the marker *mit*;
however, the previously established shortening for *mit* roots is not itself made optional. (SKsandarbhaḥ 2568) Indeed, it is not made optional.
Because the optionality of shortening (*hrasva-vikalpa*) is not established when *ṇic* follows a root ending in *ṇi*,
the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is successfully realized by the rule for long vowels— since the elision of *ṇic* is not considered a substitute (*na sthānivat*)—
but in the case of a rule for shortening, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*) is unavoidable.

In the Bhāṣya, however, by relying on the principle that "what is not established in what precedes it does not behave like its original" (pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat), the rules concerning reduplication, homogeneous vowels, anusvāra, lengthening, and the substitution of *jhal* for *car* are rejected;
the intention there is that the mention of *ṇau* refers to the class (*jāti*) and that the explicit inclusion of the term "lengthening" (*dīrgha*) need not be made.
The one who has calmed, the one who is calming, the one who causes to calm.
It will be calmed; it will be pacified; it will be brought to rest.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied after a root ending in *yaṅ*; [the forms are] *śaṃśamyate* and *śaṃśāmitā*.
The forms *śaṃśamitā* and *śaṃśamayitā* are likewise derived from the *yaṅ*-luṅ (*yaṅluk*) stem followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
According to the Bhāṣya view, however, the distinction is that there is no long vowel when the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment follows a reduplicated stem (*yaṅanta*);
thus, in the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it is praised by the Sage [as being correct].
There shall be no *vṛddhi* substitution for the penultimate vowel of the root *upadhā* before a *ciṇ* affix, or before an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, or before a *kṛt* affix; e.g., *aśami*.
In the rule "of one who teaches the udātta," why [is it said] "he went"?
What was said regarding that which ends in *m*?
What [is the rule] for anything other than *ācam-*?
It should be stated that [the substitution of] *ā* occurs for the roots *ācam*,
*anācam*, *kam*, *iv*, *mī*, and *nām* in the *ciṇ* affix; this is because of the rule "In the *ciṇ* affix, the *āya* and others [are applied]" (*āyādayaḥ*) when the *ṇiṅ* affix is absent.
Even so, though I am free from desire, I do not attain it.
In the sense of killing or injury, the root *vadh* ends in *hal*; by the rule "there is no *vṛddhi* in the case of *jan* and *vadh*" (Pāṇini 1.1.59), there is no *vṛddhi*.
Because of the rule "avadhi-jāgro 'viciṇ-ṅitsu" (Pāṇini 7.3.85), there is no *guṇa* substitution; thus,
[the form] is *ajāgāri*.
The elision of *n* may optionally take place.
It was divided;
it was broken.
The augment *num* may optionally be added after the root *labh*. Example:
*alambhi*.
Because of the persistence of conceptual construction, he did not obtain [the goal], yet because of the constant presence of mindfulness, he attained it.

However, for verbs with two objects—such as *duh* (to milk) and others—the [agent] is the locus of the action (*kartṛ*) with respect to the secondary object; for *nī*, *hṛ*, and *kṛṣ*, it is the primary object;
for verbs meaning "to know" (*budh*) or "to eat" (*bhakṣ*), and for those having sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), it is according to one's own wish.
For other roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*, the *l*-affixes (*la-kṛt* suffixes) are considered to denote the indirect object (*prayojya-karman*); for example:
*gaur duhyate payaḥ* ("the cow is milked for its milk") and *ajā grāmaṃ nīyate* ("the goat is led to the village").
It is carried away, dragged, and borne along.
The Dharma is being taught to the young brahmin,
or [it is said] "the Dharma [is taught] to the young brahmin," or Devadatta is going to the village.
For intransitive verbs and for those that have time and the like as their objects, the *lakāra* (verbal suffixes) is desired in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the abstract state (*bhāva*);
for example, *māso māsaṃ vā āsyate devadattena* ("a month is sat through by Devadatta").
However, from a causative (*ṇijanta*) verb, the suffix is applied in the sense of the instigator (*prayojya*).
"The boy sits for a month" (*māsam āsyate māṇavakaḥ*).
This concludes the section on verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) concerning the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*);
now begins the section on verbal suffixes concerning the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*).
An agent who performs an action similar to that which resides in the object shall be treated like the object.
This is an extension of the operation; therefore, the *yaka*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the *ciṇ*, and the *iṭ* of *ciṇvadbhāva* shall apply,
and because the agent is expressed, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used.
The rice is being cooked; the wood is splitting; it was cooked.
If it is argued that, since the *bhāva* (action) is expressed by the *lakāra*, the agent (*kartṛ*) should take the second case ending due to this extended application (*atideśa*), we say no;
for it is only the agent denoted by the *lakāra* itself who is treated like the object (*karmavat*).
Because of the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85) and because of the rule *liṅyāśiṣy aṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.86), where the suffix *la* is understood from the word *dvi-lakāraka*,
there is no presentation of the agent (*kartṛ*) when the suffix denotes the state (*bhāva*).
For this very reason, the suffixes *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khal* do not occur in the case of the "agent-as-object" (*karmakartṛ*).

Rather, it is only in the case of an existent thing that there can be division; for indeed, in the roots *pac* (to cook) and *bhid* (to split), the action resides in the object— the former being softening and the latter being the becoming twofold.

That [action] now resides in the agent, but it is not identical to it; rather, this linguistic usage is based on a distinction in the action coreferential with that [agent], conditioned by the difference between the states of being an object (*karmatva*) and being an agent (*kartṛtva*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of action" (*karmaṇā*): why [is it stated]?

It is so that [the designation of instrument] does not apply to the previously mentioned cases where the action is equal to that of the instrument or the locus, such as in the example "the sword [is the instrument]" (*sādhvasiḥ*), and furthermore—
Let it not be [the case that the suffix *kta* is applied] after verbs whose action resides in the agent, as in:
*gacchati grāmaḥ* ("the village goes") or *ārohati hastī* ("the elephant mounts").

One understands the meaning of the treatise, remembers it, and has faith in that action where a difference produced by the performance of the act is perceived—such as in the case of cooked rice grains or in the case of cut pieces of wood; in those instances, the action resides in the object (*karmasthā kriyā*), and not elsewhere.
For no such distinctness is observed between villages reached and not reached, as one finds between cooked and uncooked rice grains.
The root *kṛ* has the sense of "producing," and production resides in the object;
therefore, one says "a jar will be made" (*kāriṣyate ghaṭaḥ*), and so forth.
If, however, [the object] were the goal of effort (*yatna*), this would not be established,
because effort— like knowledge, desire, and so forth— is located in the agent; by this, the phrase "in the object being subsequently determined" (*anuvyavasyamāne 'rthe*) is explained.
Since there is an absence of the *ya*-affix due to the agent being situated [in the action], when the *śyan* affix is applied and the *o* is elided, the desired form is established;
thus, this *cānaś* affix is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and so forth, but not the *ātmanepada*.
It must be stated as a Vārttika that there is a prohibition for transitive verbs.

It should be stated as a rule (*vārttika*) that "the [agent] touches one another," "he leads the goats to the village," and "he milks" or "he cooks" [the goat]— in these cases, the agent is frequently expressed even when the roots are transitive.
For these [roots], the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur when they function as both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*).
By this [rule], the prohibition applies only to *yaka*;
however, *ciṇ* is desired as an option, while *śabluk* [is not].
The cow yields milk.
The suffix *ciṇ* optionally replaces *cli* after a stem ending in a vowel, when the *ta*-suffix follows in the sense of the object acting as the agent (*karmakartṛ*); for example:
*akāri*, *akṛta*.
He milked. (SK 2769; AS 3-1-63) adohi.
According to the rule *pakṣe ksaḥ lug vā* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), there is optionally elision (*luk*) [of the *ksa* suffix], as in *adugdha*.
The udumbara tree has yielded its fruit; it ripens when conjoined with the root *sṛj* (to emit), or rather, with *yuñj* (to join).
The meaning is that for these two transitive roots, the agent (*kartṛ*) frequently behaves like the object (*karmavat*), and the suffix *śyan* is to be prescribed as an exception to *yaṅ*.
It should be stated (as a Vārttika) that for the root *sṛj*, this occurs only when the agent is motivated by faith (*śraddhā*). Example:
*bhaktaḥ sṛjyate srakjam* ("the devotee creates the garland with devotion").
The meaning is that he accomplishes it through faith;
the religious student (brahmacārī) is joined to yoga.

The meaning is that it should be stated as an option (*vā*) that for roots expressing adornment such as *bhūṣ*, for roots beginning with *kṛ* (the *kirādi* group), and for those ending in the desiderative suffix (*sann*), the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes, as well as the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment, do not occur—provided they are other than when used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). For example:
*alaṃkurute kanyā*.
He has adorned himself;
he has scattered [flowers];
he was scattered upon.
He falls;
he has not fallen;
he is respected.
The *kirīṣtuda* group and others are included within the *ādṛta* class;
[thus] "the mat desires to be made" (*cikīrṣate kaṭaḥ*).

In *acikīrṣiṣṭa*, although the desire (*icchā*) resides in the agent, it is considered here to have an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*) with respect to the action of "doing" (*karoti*).
AS 3.1.64: After this [root], the *ciṇ* substitute is applied to the *liṭ* affix; "the cow was not obstructed."
In the case of the reflexive construction (karmakartṛ), it is simply:
"The cow was blocked by the cowherd.
"The agent shall be like the object;
this is for the purpose of prescribing [the rules]."
However, those who follow the Vṛtti hold that the particle *eva* is indeed redundant;
the meaning is simply that "the ascetic performs austerity," which is to say, he acquires it.
Because of the prohibition of *ciṇ* by the rule *tapo'nutāpe ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.65), there is *sic*; thus [the form] is *atapta*.
What is the purpose of the question "whose was the act of penance"?
A goldsmith heats the gold;
[the suffixes] *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur after roots meaning "to milk" (*duh*), "to praise" (*sun*), or "to honor" (*mā*) when used in the sense of "milking" (*prasnute*). SKsandarbha 2767.
It milks.
The staff bent; it has bent,
it will bend.
In this context, the root *nam* has its causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it;

for there is a Vārttika stating that when the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* applies, there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for roots ending in *hetu-ṇic*, as well as for *śri*, *brū*, and *nam*.
He causes [the staff] to be made;
he caused [it] to be made;
the staff is raised.
The *uda* augment would indeed be applied [after the root *śrī*] when followed by a *ciṇ* suffix, as in the case of the *iṭ* augment,
as in *kāriṣyate*.
He says he will raise it; he told the story;
he spoke.
The followers of Bhāradvāja recite [the following Vārttika]:
"An addition should be made for the roots √śranth, √granth, and √brū when used in the middle voice and when intransitive:
'he shakes his tail' (*puccham udasyati*)."
The cow shakes its tail;
when the causative sense is internalized, one says "he causes the cow to shake its tail."
Furthermore, when there is a desire to express agency,
as in "the cow wags its tail," the form is *udapupucchata*.

Because of the prohibition regarding the causative suffix *ṇic* for the roots *śranth* and *granth*, the forms *śap* (the present indicative marker) and *caṅ* (the reduplication marker of the causative) are included;
since *śranth* and *granth* belong to the *ādhṛṣīya* group, they lack the *ṇic* suffix in one alternative, as in the example:
he strings together a book (*granthaṃ granthati*).
Devadatta ties his girdle; the knot is tied; it was tied.
The root *śranth* forms *aśranthiṣṭa* [in the ātmanepada]; however, in the *krayādi* class, it is different.
The Saindhava horses "tie themselves up," "form knots," and "transform by themselves";
the meaning is that they gallop.

By the rules "veḥ śabdakarmaṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.15) and "akarmakācca" (Pāṇini 1.3.16), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix is applied; thus, when the sense of causation (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) is subsequently abandoned, [the sentence] becomes: "The Saindhava horses exert themselves" (*vikurvate saindhavāḥ*).
They were manifested; they two were manifested; they all were manifested.
They were drawn out; they two were drawn out; they were drawn out.
For these two roots, when used in the sense of the object-as-agent (karmakartṛ), the suffix *yak* is not employed; rather, there is the suffix *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings.
An exception to the middle voice (*ātmanepada*):
*kuṣyati* (he bites) and *kuṣyate* (it is bitten);
*rajyati* (the foot colors itself) and *rajyate* (the cloth colors itself).
But regarding the domain of sacrifice, he has no inclination [to act];
may he desire to protect, may he desire to preserve.
Thus concludes the section on the verbal suffixes (tiṅ) denoting the object and the agent;
now begins the section on the meanings of the primary verbal suffixes (lakāra).
When *smṛti* (recollection) or *bodhinī* (awakening) is the governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *lṛṭ* shall be used for the root in the sense of the past not belonging to the current day;
this is an exception to *laṅ*.

Even in constructions such as "O Kṛṣṇa, do you remember? We shall dwell in Gokula," or "you thus perceive" and "you thus attend," those [roots] can also function in the sense of memory by virtue of the context and other factors.
That which was stated regarding the connection with *yad* does not apply here.
Do you remember, Kṛṣṇa, when we ate in the forest?

The *lṛṭ* (future tense) may optionally be used in the aforementioned sense provided that the meaning of the verbal root is expectant due to a relationship of indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and indicated (*lakṣya*). For example:
*smarasi kṛṣṇa vane vatsyāmaḥ tatra gāścārayiṣyāmaḥ* ("Do you remember, O Kṛṣṇa, how we lived in the forest and tended the cows there?").
Here, "living" (*vāsa*) is the indicator, and "tending the cows" (*cāraṇa*) is the indicated.

In this case, although there is connection with the word *yat*, the rule *yacchabdayoge’pi na yadyadi* (Pāṇini 3.2.112) is superseded by the subsequent rule *parokṣe liṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.115), and thus the *liṭ* suffix is optionally applied. Consequently, [the form] *cakāra* is used.
In the Supreme Person, there is indirectness due to mental distraction and so forth;
indeed, while asleep I prattled much,
and indeed I spoke before Him while intoxicated.
The *liṭ* [perfect tense] should be prescribed for the purpose of absolute concealment (*atyantāpahnava*); [for example:
"Did you dwell among the Kaliṅgas?"—"I did not go to the Kaliṅgas."
When these two [words] are used as upapadas, the *laṅ* suffix shall be employed in place of the *liṅ* suffix.
"He said thus" or "he did thus," or "he constantly said" or "he constantly did."
When the time for asking has arrived and a question is being asked regarding a matter that ought to be asked, the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes occur in place of the scope of the *liṅ*.
Did he come?
Did he go?
But how did he kill Kaṃsa when he was not nearby?
This is an exception to [the suffix] liṭ (Pāṇini 3.2.115).
Yudhiṣṭhira performed a sacrifice.
The *laṭ* suffix shall be used for the past not of today (*bhūtānadyatana*) only when used with *sma*;
thus: *evaṃ sma pitā bravīti*. (SK 2780)
The phrase "not referring to the current day and not being witnessed" (*anadyatanaparokṣa*) is no longer applicable; the suffix *laṭ* shall be used for the past tense (*bhūte*).
"What have you done? Indeed, what shall I do, O sir?
AS 3-2-121: *akārṣīḥ* (have you done?), *kim* (what?),
*na karomi* (I do not do), *nākārṣam* (I did not do).
"I indeed do it; I indeed have done it.
The mention of "not pertaining to the current day" (anadyatana) from Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.111 is carried over by "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkapluti) into this rule.

When used in conjunction with the word *purā*, there is optionally the *luṅ* suffix for the past not pertaining to the current day, and the *laṭ* suffix [is also used], but not when used in conjunction with *smṛ*.
In the past, students lived here according to their previous custom; they have dwelt here.
Did they dwell or did they stay with us? What [is it]?
"He was sacrificing" (yajati sma), with "he will sacrifice" (bhaviṣyati) understood from the context.
As much as one eats before eating.
These two particles indicate certainty.
Why [mention] the two particles?
[For example: "As much as will be given, so much will be eaten."
He will go, having been filled by that which has become the instrument.
The suffix *laṭ* may optionally be used for the future tense when combined with *kadā* or *karhi*, as in: *kadā bhuṅkte* or *kadā bhokṣyate*.
Or the enjoyer.
It will be; it may be; *laḍ* (the present indicative) would be used [in these cases].
Or, [in the sense of "which one?"]: whom (*kam*), which of two (*kataram*), or which of many (*katamam*) do you feed, will you feed, or are you about to feed?
In the sense of desire (*lipsā*), [the suffix] *kim* is used.
Who will go to Pāṭaliputra? (SK 2786; AS 3-3-7)
When the attainment of heaven and so forth is understood through food and the like that is intended to be eaten, the future tense or the *laṭ* (present) may be used:
"He who gives food—whether he has given, will give, or is a giver—goes, will go, or has gone to heaven. (SK 2787)

When the sense of the imperative (loḍ-artha), such as a command (praiṣa) and so forth, is indicated by something, then the suffix *laṭ* may optionally occur in the future tense after a verbal root expressing that sense; for example:
"If Kṛṣṇa eats, you should tend the cows."
The *luṅ* (aorist) and *lṛṭ* (periphrastic future) suffixes are used in the sense of the conditional (*pakṣe*) [when the non-performance of an action is implied].
"Ūrdhvamauhūrtika" means occurring after a muhūrta;

this compound is formed by irregular derivation (nipātana), involving the substitution of the vowel *au* for the final syllable of the second member. When a future action occurring after a muhūrta is indicated, the suffixes *liṅ* (optative) and *laṭ* (present indicative) are optionally used after a verbal root that denotes the sense of the imperative (*loḍ-artha*).
If the preceptor should come after a muhūrta has passed— whether he is arriving now or will arrive later.
Or else, you shall come; meanwhile,
study the Vedic hymns.
*sāmīpya* [is derived from] *samīpa* with the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

From the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123) up to *uṇādayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.1), whatever suffixes are prescribed by means of a particular condition (*upādhi*) may optionally be used in the same way for the past and the future when they are in close proximity to the present; for example:
*kadā āgato 'si?* ("When did you come?
and *ayam āgacchāmi* ("I am coming [now]").
"Where are you going? "I am going. "When will you go? "I am going, or I shall go."
In SK 2790 (AS 3.3.132), the term *vartamānasāmīpya* does not carry over.
In the future tense, there may be verbal suffixes (*pratyaya*) as if they were in the past or present, when expressing a wish (*āśaṃsā*):
"If it rains [in the future]," one says *devaścedavarṣīt*, *varṣati*, or *varṣiṣyati*;
[and] "we shall obtain grain," one says *dhānyamavāpsma*, *vapāmaḥ*, or *vapsyāmaḥ*.
When there is an extension of a general rule, there is no extension of specific rules;
therefore, *laṅ* and *liṭ* are not extended.

AS 3-3-133: When a word synonymous with "quickly" (kṣipra) is used as a subordinate term (upapada), the suffix *lṛṭ* shall be employed in the aforementioned scope [of future time], provided that it refers to rain; for example: "It will rain quickly, soon, or swiftly."
Regarding the statement "we shall sow quickly," the inclusion of the *lṛṅ* (conditional) suffix indicates that it should apply even in the domain of the *luṭ* (periphrastic future), as in:
"tomorrow we shall sow quickly."
When a word expressing a wish (*āśaṃsā*) is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*), the optative (*liṅ*) shall be employed for the future tense, but not for the past.
If the teacher should approach, one should say: "I hope I shall study;
I hope I shall study quickly.
When continuity or proximity of an action is to be understood, the *laṅ* (imperfect) and *luṭ* (periphrastic future) suffixes are not used; for example:
"He ate food as long as he lived" (*yāvajjīvam annam adāt*) or "He will eat food [continuously] as long as he lives" (*yāvajjīvam annaṃ dāsyati*).
Proximity (sāmīpya) is non-intervention by that which is of the same class;
namely, on this full moon day that has passed, one has established the sacred fires and performed the Soma sacrifice.
On this coming new moon day, he will establish the sacred fires and perform the Soma sacrifice.

When expressing a future time with a specified limit (*maryādā*), in reference to the nearer division (*avarasmin pravibhāge*), the suffixes are treated as if they were *anadyatana* (non-current day); for example:
"On that part of the road which is to be traveled as far as Pāṭaliputra, and which is nearer than Kauśāmbī, we shall drink barley-gruel."
In this sūtra (SK 2795), the entire preceding sūtra (AS 3-3-137) is understood to apply by way of anuvṛtti.
This [rule] is for the purpose of prohibiting [study] during the divisions connected with day and night; the separation of the *yoga* (sūtra) is for the sake of what follows:
"In that which is the coming year, during the period prior to Āgrahāyaṇī, we shall apply ourselves to study."
Regarding those that are not days and nights:
we shall study during the final fifteen-day period of this month that is to come.
In the rule AS 3.3.138,
*avarasmin* and the two preceding sūtras are carried over; this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) concerning that which has not otherwise been established.
"In that which is this coming year, after the full-moon day of Āgrahāyaṇī, we shall study;
we will study"—this is used when there is a future action with a conditional cause (*liṅ-nimitta*) and a non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*). It is simply "it will be."
If there had been good rain, then there would have been an abundance of food.
The preceding sūtra is carried over in its entirety.
The analysis is as follows: *vā* and *ā* [are used] after *uta* and *api*.
From the rule *utāpyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.152) up to the preceding rule, the option (*vā*) for the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* when there is a cause for the conditional mood (*liṅ-nimitta*) is governed;
however, the distinction is that the previous rule applies to instances such as *uta* and *api*.
When used in conjunction with these two [words], the present tense (*laṭ*) shall be employed for all three times to express censure.
This [rule] sets aside the *luṅ* and other suffixes due to its higher status;
yet you sometimes abandon your wife and take up a courtesan—this is contemptible.
In the sense of reproach,
the suffix *liṅ* is used for all three tenses, and *laṭ* as well.
How is it that you abandon or do you abandon the Dharma?
Regarding the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) in the three times within this context, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is used eternally for the future, or optionally for the past.
How indeed could the honorable one have disregarded, or even have disregarded, the Dharma?
In the rule "garhāyām" (AS 3.3.144), the word "optionally" (vibhāṣā) does not carry over.
Who—whether "kaḥ," "kataraḥ," or "katamaḥ"—would censure Hari, or will censure him?
The conditional (lṛṅ) is used as before. (SK 2802)
The phrase "in the sense of censure" is no longer applicable;
[it applies here to] impossibility and lack of probability.
*Amarṣaḥ* means intolerance;
[the sense is] "I do not respect nor do I tolerate that you should censure Hari or that you will censure him.
The *lṛṅ* (conditional) is used as before.
The rule beginning with *anavaklṛptyamarṣayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.146) continues up until *garhāyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.150).

The compound *kiṃkila* is an indicator of anger (*krodha*). It is an *upapada* (a subordinate word) for the roots meaning "to be," namely *as*, *bhū*, and *vid*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the application of the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
"I do not believe it, nor do I tolerate it; how indeed will you eat the food of a *śūdra*?
Is it so? Does it exist? Or will you go to a *śūdrī* woman?"—in these cases, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is not used.
An addition [should be made] for *yadā* and *yadā-yadā*. (Vārttika)
This is an exception to the *lṛṭ* (future tense).

When *jātu*, *yad*, *yadā*, or *yadi* are used [with the particle *cet*], [the sense is] "I do not believe" (*nāvakalpayāmi*) or "I do not tolerate" (*na marṣayāmi*) that one such as you would revile Hari; in this case, the *lṛṅ* (conditional) is applied as before.
And whatever you might do, or wherever you might do it, in that very manner [it would be done].
I do not believe it; I do not tolerate it.

The rule regarding *anavaklṛpti* (impossibility) and *amarṣa* (intolerance) is excluded; when used in conjunction with *yacca* or *yattra* to express censure, only the potential (*liṅ*) should be employed—as in:
"If you, O Śūdra, were to officiate at a sacrifice for [someone]," or "Wherever you might do so."
That is unjust.
And that you should officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra, wherever it may be—
this is a marvel! (SK 2808)
When *yat* or *yatra* are used as upapadas, the suffix *lṛṭ* shall be applied to a verbal root when wonder (*citrīkaraṇa*) is implied; for example: "It is a marvel that a blind man should see Kṛṣṇa."
What wonder is there if he were to study at the very beginning?
Is there identity of meaning between these two [words] in the sense of "certainly" (*bāḍham*),
or rather [should one say], "May Hari destroy sin"?
When the two are capable, what need is there for punishment to fall?
It will simply close the door.

From this point onward, in the case of the non-occurrence of an action conditioned by a *liṅ* (potential), the *lṛṅ* (conditional) is invariably used even when referring to the past; this is understood from both the question and the concealment [of the fact].
When one's own intention is being made known, the optative (liṅ) may be used, but not [the particle] *kaccit*; for example:
"I desire that you should eat. (*kāmo me bhuñjīta bhavān*)
"Is it well?
means "Is he living?
In this context, the sense of *alam* is "proficiency" (*prauḍhi*) and "possibility" (*saṃbhāvana*); thus, the word *alam* is transformed into the nominative and the locative cases respectively.

The optative (*liṅ*) should be used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvana*), provided that this possibility is considered sufficient (*alam*). Why is it said "when *alam* is used with a non-established [action]" (*siddhāprayoge*)? For example: "He might split the mountain with his head" (*giriṃ śirasā bhindyāt*).

Why is it specified "when *alam* is used with a non-established [action]"? (Note: The term *siddha* here refers to an action already established as a fact or a certainty; *asiddha* refers to an action not yet established. The rule implies that the optative is used when the possibility is expressed by *alam* in relation to an action that is not yet a certainty.)
Kṛṣṇa is capable of killing the elephant.
The preceding sūtra is carried over [into this one].

When a verbal root expressing the sense of "possibility" (*saṃbhāvana*) is the attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *liṅ* may optionally be used in that expressed sense; however, since the previous rule would have made it obligatory when the word *yat* precedes, this statement is made to allow for the option.
I hope that you will eat, or perhaps you will eat; if not, what do I hope for? I hope that you might eat.
Or it may be that if one should bow to Kṛṣṇa, one would attain happiness.
If one bows to Kṛṣṇa, one will attain happiness;
this is certain and is so desired here.
"Alas, he flees!

In connection with such expressions as "I wish that you eat" (*icchāmi bhuñjīta*) or "May you eat" (*bhuṅktāṃ bhavān*), it should be understood that [the particle *iti*] is used in the sense of expressing a desire (*kāmapravedane*).
Alternatively, it should be stated [as a rule]: "In the sense of expressing a desire."
One does not act here out of desire.
When verbs expressing desire are used as upapadas with a common agent, the suffix *liṅ* is employed; for example:
*bhuñjīyety icchati* ("he desires that one should eat").
In the alternative case, there shall be the optative suffix (liṅ), [otherwise] the present indicative suffix (laṭ).
He should wish; he desires; he might long for.
In the sense of "he desires," the *liṅ* (optative) suffix is used in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*), according to the rule: "The *liṅ* is used in injunction, invitation, etc. (Pāṇini 3.3.161).
One should sacrifice when invited; may you eat here.
In the case of an invitation, one should sit here; in the case of a formal request, one should study.
"Sir, please instruct your son;
in response to this inquiry, shall he study the Veda or logic?"
In the sense of a request,
the optative suffix *loṭ* is used as in "may I obtain food."
An injunction is a command.
Permission is the authorization to act according to one's desire; you should sacrifice,
O Bhava, for those who sacrifice.
The particle *ca* serves to carry over the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*) for the purpose of indicating that the time has arrived (prāptakāla), [according to Pāṇini 3.3.164].
The injunctions and so forth continue; one should sacrifice after a muhūrta has passed, or let those who sacrifice sacrifice, or that which is to be sacrificed should be performed.
Regarding the subject matter of the preceding sūtra, SK 2819, AS 3-3-165.
This is an exception to the optative (liṅ) and the gerundives (kṛtya); one should sacrifice after a muhūrta has passed.
When *sma* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*) in the sense of a request (*adhīṣṭa*), the imperative (*loṭ*) shall be employed; for example:
*tvaṃ sma adhyāpaya*.
When the word *yat* is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), and when [the words] *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā* are present, the potential mood (*liṅ*) shall be employed.
It is the time, the occasion, or the hour that you should eat. (SK 2822,
And you shall carry away the maiden in marriage.
AS 3-3-172: In the sense of capability, the optative (liṅ) as well as the kṛtya suffixes may be used; for example, "you should carry the burden."

Regarding the prohibitive suffix *māṅ* (SKsandarbhaḥ 2219): [in expressions such as] "do not do," "how might it not be," or "may it not come to pass," this is not the suffix *māṅ*, but rather the word *mā*.
When suffixes are prescribed in connection with the meanings of verbal roots at a specific time, they may also occur at other times.
Because the action expressed by the verbal suffix (tiṅ) is primary, the suffixes are applied in accordance with it to those words expressing subordinate actions; thus,
"he saw him dwelling" (*vasan dadarśa*) uses the present tense (*laṭ*) to express the past.
The meaning of "seeing" is that which has as its agent an agent who performed a past residence;
[the phrase] "the son of one who has sacrificed with Soma will be" means that the coming-into-being has as its agent that son who is about to sacrifice with Soma.

When repetition or intensity is to be expressed, the imperative suffix (loṭ) shall be applied after a verbal root; its substitutes hi and sv are also used, serving as exceptions to the personal endings (tiṅ).
Those two, *hi* and *sva*, are respectively designated as *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*, and they are also designated as *tiṅ*.
However, in the domain of *ta* and *dhvam*, *hi* and *sva* may optionally occur; yet the designations of person (*puruṣa*) and number (*ekavacana*) are not extended to these two.
By virtue of the force of its specific rule, *hi* is substituted for the *parasmaipada* suffixes in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) across the entire range of personal endings,
while *sva* is substituted for the *ātmanepada* suffixes in the senses of the object (*karman*), the action (*bhāva*), and the agent (*kartṛ*).
When the conjunction of multiple actions is to be expressed, that which was previously mentioned may optionally [be used].
In the case of the first prescription of the imperative (*loṭ*), the verbal root that serves as the base for that imperative must be employed as the subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*).
When the imperative suffix is prescribed for the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), there should be the subsequent application (anuprayoga) of a verbal root having a general meaning.
From that [root], according to the specific application and so forth, the *laṭ* and other suffixes, as well as *tiP* and others, arise;
from them, there is the manifestation of number, time, and the meaning of the specific person (*puruṣa*).
When there is the repetition of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*), the suffix is doubled to express this.
The meaning of *yāti* is "going" (*yānam*) in the sense of moving repeatedly or excessively, as expressed by "go away, go away" (*yāhi yāhi*).
It refers to a single agent's act of going occurring in the present tense.
The word "iti," however, indicates that the intended meaning (tātparya) lies in a relation of non-difference,
as in "thus he went" or "they go."
you go;
you two go;
you (plural) go.
"Go, go!"— thus you go;
"go, go!"— thus he has gone or will go.
In the domain of the imperative suffix *dhvam*, one studies [repeatedly] saying "study, study"; optionally, one says "you all study, you all study" (*adhīdhvam adhīdhvam*);
but in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), one consumes [both items together], saying "drink the barley-meal, eat the parched grains."
"Eat the food; taste the curd"—thus one causes another to consume; "drink, eat, chew"—thus one causes others to consume;
"eat, taste"—thus one causes you to consume.
In one alternative, the suffixes *hi* and *sva* [occur];
here, there is a non-differentiation relation (*abhedānvaya*) of the specific qualities being conjoined with the general sense of the subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*), as in the example:
"he drinks the barley-gruel" (*saktūn pibati*).
He eats parched grain,
he consumes food, and he tastes curd.

By this, the following is explained: "The powerful one, having waged war with the enemy of Namuci (Indra), performed these acts day and night in heaven: he attacked the city, cut down the Nandana grove, plundered the jewels, and carried off the noble women"—thus [the verse] describes the state of unease (*asvāsthya*) caused by actions such as attacking the city and cutting down the forest, which were performed by a single agent in the remote past (*bhūtānadyatana-parokṣa*). This is the meaning.
Furthermore, the interpretation that the meaning of *caskandeti* and so forth is "repetition" (*punaḥpunya*) is rooted in error;
for [otherwise] the term *kriyāsamabhihāra* would have to be carried over from the second sūtra, and there would be the undesirable consequence of doubling the verb ending in the *loṭ* mood.
The notion held by some that *avaskandeḥ* in the passage beginning with *purīmavaskandeḥ* is the second person singular is merely an error,
because it has been stated here that the designations "person" (*puruṣa*) and "number" (*vacana*) do not apply [to the substitutes for the *l*-suffixes].
Thus ends the section on the meaning of the *l*-suffixes.
Now begins the section on primary suffixes (*kṛdanta*) and gerundives (*kṛtya*).
This governing rule extends up to the end of the third book; therein, a word standing in the locative case is called an *upapada*. A word ending in a *kṛt* suffix is not a finite verb (*atiṅ*).
This is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule), [Aṣṭādhyāyī] 3.1.94.

In this section concerning gender, an apavāda suffix that is dissimilar in form may optionally supersede the corresponding utsarga suffix, with the exception of those prescribed under the heading of feminine gender.
This is the governing rule (adhikāra) for the suffix *ṇvul* prior to [Pāṇini 3.4.67].
When it is established that a *kṛt* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), [the following applies]: Pāṇini 3.4.70.
By this [rule], [the suffixes] should apply only to the action and the object (bhāvakarmaṇoḥ).
(SK 2834; Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.96)
These suffixes are added to a verbal root;
the letters *t* and *r* are for the sake of the accent,
as in *edhitavyam*.
In the sense of "to be kindled by you," the general rule applies regarding the singular number and the neuter gender; thus,
dharma is that which is to be piled up or accumulated by you.
The suffix *ṇic* is optionally applied after the root *vas* [in the sense of the agent],
as in "he dwells" (*vasati*), resulting in *vāstavya*; furthermore, there is an addition of the suffix *kelimara*.
The ripe beans are to be cooked;
the brittle stalks are to be broken.
The suffix [is used] in the sense of the object;
however, the author of the Vṛtti says that this [suffix] is also desired in the sense of the agent-as-object, which contradicts the Bhāṣya on that [sūtra].
There shall be the substitution of *ṇ* for a *n* belonging to a *kṛt*-suffix that follows a vowel which itself follows a cause situated in a prefix; as in *prayāṇīyam*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "a vowel" (*acaḥ*)?
[It is for the sake of] the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding *pramagnaḥ* and *nirviṇṇasya*. (Vārttika)
Since [the condition] of being after a vowel (*acaḥ*) is absent, [the rule] does not apply; therefore, this statement [is made]:
there is *ṇatva* for the subsequent [consonant] and *ṣṭutva* for the preceding one.
Disgusted with the world.
After a prefix (upasarga) that serves as the cause, the *ṇ* may optionally replace the *n* of a suffix (*kṛt*) ending in *na* which follows a root with the causative marker (*ṇi*),
as in *prayāpaṇīyam* or *prayāpanīyam*.
Why is the specific qualification (viśeṣaṇa) prescribed? [It is so that the rule] may apply even when there is no intervention by the letter *y*, as in:
"Look at him being led away" (*prayāpyamāṇaṃ paśya*).
It has been stated that *dur* does not function as a prefix (*upasarga*) when followed by *ṇatva*; thus,
we have *duryānam* and *duryāpanam*.
After a root beginning with *hal* and having *i* as its penultimate letter, when followed by a *kṛt* suffix containing *n*, the substitution of *ṇ* for a following *ac* may optionally take place.
Is *prakopaṇīyam* the same as *prakopanīyam*,
[the suffix] *hal* being [elided]?
Why is it that from a root with *i* as its penultimate letter, the suffix *anīya* is applied to form *prohaṇīya*,
whereas *pravapaṇīya* is not?

If there is a following nasal (anu-m), then [the substitution of *u* for *ū*] applies only to that which is prescribed after a root beginning with a vowel (*ij-ādi*) and ending in a consonant (*hal*), provided it occurs within a *kṛt* suffix.
Why is the suffix *i* prescribed for roots beginning with *ij* and others in the sense of "swinging," while it is not applied to the root *magi* in the sense of "creeping"?
The inclusion of the term *num* in the rule *aṭkupvāṅ-* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) should be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *anusvāra*; the same applies here as well.
Therefore, there is no longing for that here,
but rather it must indeed exist here.
The act of threatening (prombhaṇa) [is expressed by the suffix ṇic], Pāṇini 1.3.68.
For these [roots], there may optionally be *ṇ* or *ṇo* when a *kṛt* suffix follows:
*praṇiṃsitavyam* or *praniṃsitavyam*.
After these [roots], the *ṇ* of a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *na* is not [replaced by *ṇ*].
That which is to be brought forth and that which is to be produced— merit alone is intended here as the object of grasping.
The root *pū* [in the sense of purifying] takes the suffix *ṇic*; by the Vārttika "addition of *ṇi*-derived roots such as *bhā*," the form *prabhāpanīya* is established.

It has been stated that "khśāñah śasya yaḥ" [Pāṇini 8.4.41] applies after the section on *ṇatva*; it should be understood that because the substitution of *ya* is *asiddha*, there is no *ṇatva* due to the intervention of the letter *śa*.
That which is to be made known.
That by which one bathes is "snānīya" (bathing powder);
that to whom a gift is given is "dānīya" (a worthy recipient), such as a Brahmin.
The suffix *yat* shall occur after a verbal root ending in a vowel, provided that *ci* follows.
This non-mention could have been avoided; the analysis of the rule (yogavibhāga) could likewise have been dispensed with.
Because it is easier to recite [the rule] as applying only to the suffixes beginning with -tavya (tavyādi), [it is stated] thus: Pāṇini 6.4.65.
When *pare* follows *āta*,
there shall be *guṇa* as the substitute.
That which ought to be said to those people who are to be reproached is "takya."
The crop is to be gathered;
it is to be carried away.
Since the rule for the suffix *ṇya* applied to "janī" (to be born) serves the purpose of the accent,
the form is established even by that [suffix].

And there is no possibility of the [unwanted] application of *vṛddhi*, because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.5]: "In the case of *jan* and *han*, [the substitution of *iK* does not take place]. Furthermore, it must be stated that for the root *han*, the substitute *vadha* may optionally occur.
The suffix *ṇyat* prescribed for the sense of "to be killed" (*vadhya*) in the [next] section is applied as in *ghātya*.
After a word ending in a labial (pavarga) consonant, having ‘a’ as its penultimate letter, the suffix *yat* shall be applied.
The exception (*apavāda*) [to the rule] ending in *ṇya* is that which is to be obtained (*śapyam*).
Since dissimilarity [of form] is not caused by a suffixal element (anubandha), the suffix *ṇyat* does not apply here;
however, *tavyat* and other such suffixes would certainly apply.
Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.65: The augment *num* is added to the root *labh* when it follows the prefix *āṅ*, provided that a suffix beginning with a vowel (*yādi*) is intended to follow.
Since the vowel *u* is not in the penultimate position in the word *numi*, the suffix *ṇyat* alone applies; thus, "the cow is to be sacrificed" (*ālambhyaḥ gauḥ*).
AS 7.1.66: Why is it stated that *upalambhya* is correct when used in the sense of praise?
That which can be perceived is "perceivable" (upalabhya).
It is possible; it can be endured.
prose is intoxicating.
When preceded by the prefix *āṅ* and when not denoting a person of low status, one may optionally apply the suffix *yañ* to the root *car*;
thus, *ācarya* means a region.
The meaning is "one should go.
In the case of one who is not a guru, is the teacher (ācārya) considered a guru?
This is for the purpose of restriction, so that [the suffix] may not occur after a root with a prefix; thus,
*prayāmyam*.
Because of the usage in the Vārttika, "By [the prefix] *ni* alone, there is *syat*; therefore,
there should not be a reciprocal exchange (*vinimaya*) therein," it follows that there is no logical inconsistency regarding that which is unrestricted.
"Indeed, she is to be restrained by you who possess divine vision," and so forth; this has already been explained, or alternatively, [the term may mean] "one who is skilled in restraint.

According to *Pāṇini* 3.1.101 (*vadernañy upapade vadaḥ sup*), when the negative particle *nañ* is the subordinate word (*upapada*) for the root *vad*, the suffixes *yat* and *kyap* would otherwise be applicable; however, this *nipātana* (irregular formation) is established for both purposes to indicate that it applies only in the sense of censure (*garhā*).
Thus, *avadyam* means "censurable" or "sinful."
What is there to be censured in the name of one's guru?
For that name is not censurable, nor is it unfit for utterance.

"One who desires his own welfare should not utter his own name, nor the name of his guru, nor the name of one who is extremely wretched, nor the names of his eldest child or wife," according to the Smṛti.
"Paṇyā" means "to be traded," that is, "to be bartered"; "pāṇyam" has a different meaning.

The meaning is "worthy of praise. *Anirodha* means absence of obstruction; in that sense, the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *vṛñ*, as in the word *varyā* (a maiden to be chosen) [from *śatena varyā kanyā*].
The suffix *vṛt* is used in the sense of "other" (anyā).
That by which something is carried is a "vahya," such as a cart; what is it that is to be carried? It is the instrument (karaṇa). What is the object to be carried? [It is the patient (karman)].
That which is to be carried (voḍhavya).
The suffix *yat* is applied after the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go"; it is an exception to [the application of] *ṇyati*.
Between an Ārya, a master, or a Vaiśya— of these, which is the Ārya? [Which is] Brahman?
The meaning is "that which is to be attained" (prāptavya).
The meaning is: "if she has reached the time for conception";
*upasarga-gauḥ* means she is fit to be approached by a bull for the purpose of impregnation.
Regarding the phrase "kālyā prajane," does it mean that Kāśī should be approached, in the sense that it must be reached?

After the root *jṛ* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the agent; this is consistent provided that the word ending in *yat* is the qualified term (*viśeṣya*).
"It does not decay, thus it is 'ajarya' (undecaying);
therefore, O noble lady, quickly form an undecaying union with that noble one"—so says Bhaṭṭi.

However, in the passage "The undecaying [union] taught by the deer through old age was bound again for the sake of bodily bondage," the word "saṃgatam" (union), acting as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), must be supplied.
In the sense of "having come together," what [root] is *ajaritā*? It is *kambala*. However, when the agent of the coming together is implied, the suffix *ṇya* alone is used.
The unchanging [is established] by connection.
(Pāṇini 3.1.106)
The word "bhāva" (state/condition) from the subsequent sūtra is drawn back here;

the suffix *kyap* shall be applied after the root *vad* in the sense of state, provided that there is no prefix (*anupasarga*) and a nominal stem (*sup*) is present as an upapada— as in the case of *brahmodyam*.
"Brahmavadyam" means the speaking of Brahman; that is, the speaking of the Veda.
According to some, the suffixes are used in the sense of the object (karman).
But when there is a prefix, only that which ends in the causative suffix *ṇic* is to be mentioned as the subject of the rule and as the object of the exception.
The suffix *kyap* shall be applied [after a verbal root ending in a vowel].
The state of Brahman is "brahmabhūyam"; [the suffix -ya] is indeed to be applied when "su" is the upapada.
It must be explained as being without any prefix (anupasarga).
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.108:

When a word ending in a *sup* suffix is an upapada that is not a prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *kyap* shall be applied after the root *han* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), and the letter *t* shall be substituted for the final letter [of the root]. For example:
*brāhmaṇasya hananam* becomes *brahmahatyā*.
The feminine suffix is applied from the world [of usage],
according to Pāṇini 4.1.109.
The suffix *kyap* shall be applied after these [roots].
(Pāṇini 3.1.109)
The word *itthaḥ* is to be praised;
[the suffix] *śas* is applied after the words *idam* and *hal*.
The word *vṛtyaḥ* [is derived] from the root *vṛ* (meaning "to choose"), specifically from *vṛñ*, and not from *vṛṅ* (meaning "to choose as a bride"). Thus, it means "one who chooses."
The priests are to be chosen, to be honored, and to be gratified.
Furthermore, the citation of *avaśya-stutyaḥ* from the *Kāśikā*— under the rule *śaṃsi-duhi-guhi-bhyo vā*— is intended to refute the application of the suffix *ṇyat* even for another [opponent].
It is to be praised, to be extolled, and to be milked.
To be milked,
secret, and hidden.

The form *praśasya* is established by the force of two rules: Pāṇini 5.3.60 (*praśasyasya śraḥ*) and 3.1.126 (*īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ*). Regarding the other two [forms], their source must be sought;
furthermore, there is an extension of the rule for the root *añj* preceded by *āṅ* when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
The root *añj* is used in the sense of "manifesting," "smearing," and so forth;

by the rule of frequentative application (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *kyap* is added in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), and by the rule *aniditām...* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there is the elision of the nasal (*na*).
Clarified butter (ājya) [is used] according to SK 2859 and AS 3-1-110.
To turn, to be turned, to increase.
But for the roots *klṛp* and *cṛt*, [the form] *kalpyam* is used in the sense of "to be increased."
What is the purpose of the addition of *ta* (the long vowel marker) in the rule concerning *cartvam*?
Why is it not simply *kṛt*?
Since it is stated that the *cur*-class roots are optionally non-ṇic and non-causative, the suffix *ṇyat* occurs in the absence of *ṇic*,
whereas it occurs [only] when *ṇic* is present.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ca*.
In the rule *ād guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), it is better to read *khe yam i ca iti hrasvaḥ* (the short vowel *i* occurs when *khe* and *yam* follow).
Servants are those who perform labor.
The meaning is "they are to be supported";
this is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*), not a technical designation (*saṃjñā*); and [the suffix *yat*] is applied diversely (*bahulam*) after a word ending in the same vowel (*sama*).
Those things to be accumulated and those things to be gathered [are taught] for the sake of conceptual differentiation within the very state of non-conception; this is the purpose of the Vārttika.
In the absence of consciousness, what is it that is called a wife? And how is a wife called a daughter-in-law?
For in this case, by [Pāṇini 3.1.109] *saṃjñāyām samaja-*, the suffix *kyap* ought to apply; however,
it is true that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of "proper name" (*saṃjñā*) serves its purpose in the masculine.

From the root *bhṛ* ending in a long vowel (*bibharti*), either the *ṇyat* suffix (belonging to the *krayādi* class) is applied, or the *kyap* suffix is applied specifically to the root *bharati*; this is according to the paribhāṣā rule: "When a term with a specific marker is mentioned, it does not include a term that lacks that marker."
According to Pāṇini 3.1.113, the suffix *kyap* may optionally be applied after the root *mṛj*, and in its alternative (*pakṣe*), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied.
The suffix *ya* is applied [after a verbal root] to form the word *mṛjya*.

It should be stated as a rule (*vārttika*) that the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs when the suffixes *ghit* or *ṇyat* follow, provided that the root is not one that takes the augment *iṭ* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*);
therefore, it does not occur here.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the roots *garja* and *mṛj*, with the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurring in the case of *mṛj*; thus,
*mārgyaḥ*.
The substitution of *k* for [the palatal *c*] shall take place.
The suffix *u* is applied [to the root *naś*] by virtue of the rule *nyaṅkustācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), which prescribes the suffix *u* after the root *vañc*.
(Kāśikā 2865)
These seven words ending in the suffix *kyap* are irregularly formed (nipātita); [the term] *rājāsuta* means that which is to be produced by the king through the process of pressing (*abhiṣava*).
Alternatively, King Soma, who consists of creepers, is pressed (*sūyate*) or extracted here; the suffix *kyap* is applied in this sense,
and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), resulting in *rājasūya*.
The *rājasūya* begins with the half-verses; the sun moves through the sky.

The suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of the agent by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), whereby the vowel *u* is substituted; alternatively, it is derived from the root *sū*, meaning "to impel," belonging to the *tudādi* class.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *sū* in the sense of "impelling" (*karmaṇi*) with respect to the world; furthermore,
*kyap* is invariably applied after the root *vad* when preceded by the prefix *mṛṣā*, in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).
This [term] is a dependent adjective (*viśeṣya-nighna*) meaning "false";
the qualities of height and beauty are false.
The root *ruc* forms *rucya-*; for the root *gup*, there is the substitution of *k* at the beginning when it is a technical term (*saṃjñā*).
Wealth other than gold and silver is called *kupya*.
Other things are to be hidden;
those that ripen by themselves on cultivated ground are called *kṛṣṭapacyāḥ*, where the term is used in the reflexive sense (karmakartari).
But when the work is pure, one who is beyond affliction does not suffer, even though he is ripened by the furrowed soil. (SK 2866)
After the roots *bhid* and *ujjh*, the suffix *kyap* is applied; furthermore, for the root *ujjh*, there is the substitution of *dh*.
Does the river break its bank? Is it breaking? Does it abandon its water? Is it abandoning? What of the river?
The breaker and the abandoned one.
The suffix *kyap* is prescribed in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*);
[thus], "Puṣya" is that in which objects flourish.
Successes (siddhi) are accomplished in this; [this is the definition of] *siddhi*. (Pāṇini 3.1.117)
From the roots *pū* and *ñij*, the suffix *kyap* is applied;
thus, *vipūya* means *muñja* grass that is to be purified for the purpose of making ropes and the like.
*Vinīyaḥ* means a paste (*kalkaḥ*), that is to say, a specific ground medicinal herb;
or it means sin (*pāpam*).
The meaning is that the plowshare, having been worn down by force, must be drawn [across]; it is a thick piece of wood intended for the purpose of leveling the furrows.
But elsewhere, the contrary should be understood as the object to be trained.
It should be stated that [the rule] applies in the Vedic language (chandas). (Or: it is optional.)
In common usage, however, that which is to be accepted is called *pratigṛhya*, *apigṛhya*, and *pratigrāhya*.
Moreover, it is to be grasped.
A word that is to be elided or to be prefixed; one who lacks self-mastery and is dependent on others.
"Domestic parrots" means those made dependent by being confined in cages and so forth; this refers to the external [practice].
An army belonging to a village means one situated outside the village;
because of the feminine gender used in the designation, it does not apply to the masculine or neuter genders.
*pakṣya* means "belonging to a side" (*pakṣa*), derived with the suffix *yat* because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group;
*āryagṛhya* means "one who is accepted by the noble ones" (*āryaiḥ gṛhyate*).
The meaning is that he relies on that side.
One should perform an act that is aphrodisiac.
In the alternative case,
The suffix *ṇyat* shall be applied after a verbal root ending in an *ṛ*-vowel or a consonant to form a derivative meaning "to be done" (*kārya*), as in the example *varṣyam*.
*patram* means a vehicle.
In the word *yugya*, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *gā-* (to go), and the substitution of *k* for *g* is prescribed by nipātana.

After the root *vas* when preceded by the prefix *ā* and without any other upapada, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) and the locative (*adhikaraṇe*); and when the vowel lengthening has occurred, a short vowel is optionally substituted [for the radical *u*].
The moon and the sun dwell together (*amā saha vasataḥ*) in this [night]; it is *amāvasyā* or *amāvāsyā*.
[This is derived by] adding the suffix *ṇyat* to the roots *ava* and *vas*, according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhalor ṇyat*).
By the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52), there is the substitution of *ku* [for the palatals]; thus, *pākyam*.
Furthermore, it should be stated that the suffix *ṇyat* is optionally applied after the root *sṛj* when preceded by *pāṇau*. (Vārttika).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *kyap* suffix characterized by having a root with a light vowel (*ṛdupadha*). [The suffix *kyap* is applied] after the roots *sṛj* and *vap* when preceded by *sam* and *ava* respectively; for example, "a rope released by the hands" (*pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ*).
Alternatively, [the rule applies] even when preceded by *sam-ava*.
samavasargyā [is formed] by [the addition of the suffix -yaN] after the root *sṛj* with the prefix *sam-*, according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.59.
The substitution of *k* for the *c* and *j* of roots beginning with *kvā* and others does not need to be enjoined;

however, the author of the *Vārttika*, having supplemented the rule *cajoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52) with the condition "in the case of a *niṣṭhā* [suffix] that is not *iṭ*-bearing," rejected the rule *na kvādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.59) and so forth.

Therefore, there is no substitution of *k* for the *ṛ* in roots such as *arji* and *arjip*, because they take the augment *iṭ* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*); however, in the case of roots such as *gruc* and *gluñc*, although they belong to the *kvādi* group, the substitution of *k* for *ṛ* would certainly still occur.
According to the Sūtra system, however, although the opposite result might seem to follow, nevertheless, the authority of the Munis increases in successive order;
this is stated in Sūtra 7.3.60.
The assembly of wanderers is not a mere collection.
These two [words] are these two [specific] substitutes.
That by which one enjoys is "bhuja," meaning the hand;
[the suffix] *ghañ* is applied according to *Pāṇini* 3.3.120 (*halaśca*).
That in which things are turned downward is "nyubja."
Is *upatāpa* [used] in the sense of "affliction" or "disease," while *bhoga* is used in the sense of "hand" or "enjoyment"?
The ocean (samudraḥ) [is derived from] SK 2878, AS 7-3-62.
These two particles [occur] in the context of the sacrificial limb:
there are five *prayāja*s and three *anuyāja*s.
In the context of a sacrifice, what is the *prayāga* and what is the *anuyāga*?
There is no substitution of *k* for *s*.
What is to be deceived when one has gone [to the goal]? What wood is to be bent?
The meaning is "that which has been made crooked.
The substitution of *u* for *ū* and *c* for *k* are irregularly prescribed (*nipātyete*) when the suffix *ka* follows;
thus, *okaḥ* and *śakuntavṛṣalau* [are formed], where the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule governing roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*).
Since [the suffix] ghañ is already established, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of making [the word] end-acute (antodātta).
Kulthood is not something that must necessarily be realized.
AS 7-3-66: In the suffix *ṇya*, the substitution of *k* for *y* does not occur in the word *yājya*.
A specific type of literary work that is to be requested, found pleasing, and proclaimed.
The word *ṛc* is formed with the suffix *ṇyat* (yielding *arcyam*) precisely because of this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), even though it begins with a short vowel (*ṛt*).
The *Kāśikā* states that the suffix *yat* is applied after the roots *tyaj*, *īś*, and *tyāj*.
In this regard, the inclusion of *pūj* should be considered,
since it is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya; for the Bhāṣya states that "there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *tyaj* in the section on *ṇyat*" (Vārttika 2883).
AS 7-3-67: In the case of the expression "word" (śabda), however, it should be stated that [the term] refers to a sentence (vākya).
That which can be employed is "prayojya" (to be employed).
One who can be appointed is an appointee; [the suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of] a servant.

The suffix *ṇyat* is used for other meanings of "to be enjoyed" (*bhogya*); it should be stated that [the suffix] is also applied after the roots *lap* and *dabh* in this context (as a Vārttika): *lāpya*.
Although not listed among the *dāp* roots in the Dhātupāṭha, it must be accepted on the strength of the Vārttika; thus, [the form] *dābhyaḥ* [is derived].
The suffix *ṇyat* shall be applied after a verbal root ending in *u* when the sense of necessity (*avaśya-bhāva*) is to be expressed;
[as in] *lāvyam*.
That which is to be purified (pāvya) [is used in the locative case].
The root *yu* in the sense of mixing is to be conjugated in the sixth class (*suñ*).
That which is to be sacrificed,
that which is to be sown, and that which is to be given.
Shame and remorse.
By Pāṇini 3.1.127, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, and the substitution of *āya* for the root vowel is prescribed;
this refers specifically to a particular type of *dakṣiṇāgni*.

For that [fire] is brought from the *gārhapatya* fire; and because it is not constantly burning, it is "to be brought" (*āneya*), unlike other things such as a jar, or like the *dakṣiṇāgni*, which is brought from the house of a Vaiśya or elsewhere. (SK 2889)
*Saṃmati* is the state of becoming an object of affection; it is the activity of the object, as well as the regard for enjoyments.
*Praṇāyya* means a thief, in the sense of being unworthy of affection;
*praṇāyya* also refers to a pupil.
The meaning is "dispassionate";
the other [type] is to be led.

AS 3.1.129: The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the root *mā* when it means "that by which something is measured" (*mīyate 'nena*), forming the word *pāyya* in the sense of a measuring instrument; furthermore, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the initial sound of the root.

By the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), the suffix *yuk* is applied; it is "well led" (*samyak nīyate*) toward the fire for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), thus it is called *sānnāyya*, a specific type of sacrificial offering (*havir-viśeṣa*).
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied with the substitution of *āy* for *i*, and the lengthening of the vowel in *sam* is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
In this [place], grain and so forth are accumulated; thus *nikāya* means a dwelling.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the initial of the root is irregularly changed to *k* (yielding *niveśa*).
Likewise, that by which fuel is placed (*dhīyate*) is called a *dhāyyā*, a sacrificial verse (*ṛc*).
A sacrifice is called *kuṇḍapāyya* because the Soma is drunk from a vessel (*kuṇḍa*) in it.
That which is accumulated is *saṃcāyya*.
These terms are appropriate for a specific area intended for maintaining the sacred fire; elsewhere, however, they should be understood as "to be surrounded" and "to be tended."
To be carried along; to be moved.
That which is piled up is the *citya* fire; the piling of the fire is *agnicityā*.
According to Pāṇini 3.3.163 (*praiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca*), the gerundive suffixes (*kṛtya*) are used in the sense of command, permission, and the arrival of the proper time.
It must be gone by you; it is to be gone; it is the path of going.

In this context, the rule for the *kṛtya* suffixes is prescribed again so that there may be no sublation by the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix; furthermore, it indicates that after the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), the rule of non-identity of forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply in certain cases.

Consequently, it is established that [this rule] does not apply to the suffixes *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and those having the sense of *khala*. [This is stated in the rule: "The *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* are also used in the sense of fitness (*arha*)" (Pāṇini 3.3.169).

"One worthy of praise" (*stotumarha*) means "praiseworthy" (*stutya*); "the object of praise" (*stutikarma*) refers to the praiser (*stotā*), the agent of the act of praising. The rule for the *kṛtya* suffixes and the agentive suffix *tṛc* is prescribed so that there may be no contradiction with the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
These forms ending in kṛtya suffixes are optionally prescribed as denoting the agent.

In that context, it should be understood that these two suffixes occur after transitive roots in the sense of the object (*karman*), but after intransitive roots in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*);
thus, one who is to become is "bhavya," or that by which one is to become is "bhavya."
"He sings" (gāyati) thus [it is] "to be sung" (geya); this [is] the geya of the Sāmans, or by means of the Sāman—thus [and so forth]. [The suffixes] śaki and liṅ [are used]. (Pāṇini 3.3.172)
The words *voḍhavya*,
*vaśakya*, *voḍhavya*, *vahanīya*, and *vāhya* are used in the sense of "to be carried."

The mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes is made so that there may be no sublation by the optative (*liṅ*). Since the intended meaning can be conveyed by this alone due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the inclusion of "also *kṛtyas*" in the rule regarding commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth would be easily dispensable; furthermore, the mention of *kṛtya* and *tṛc* in the context of fitness (*arha*) [is likewise superfluous].
Thus ends the section on primary suffixes (*kṛdanta*) and gerundives (*kṛtya*);
now begins the section on prior primary suffixes (*pūrvakṛdanta*).
By the rule *dhātoḥ etau staḥ kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), these two [suffixes] occur after a verbal root in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
*yuvoranākau* (Pāṇini 7.1.1): *kārakaḥ*, *kartā*.
One who is worthy to carry is a carrier;
one who performs is an agent.

By the rule *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyo 'ñṇid* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), there is the status of being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅittva*); however, because it is stated that [the suffix] is not *ṅit* when followed by *añ* or *ṇ*, there is no *ṅittva*. Thus: *kuṭitā*.
Koṭaka is one who has conquered. (SKsandarbha 2536) Vijitā.
*hanas-to’ciṇ-ṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.36); *ghātakaḥ*; *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33).
By the rule "dāyakaḥ nodāttopadeśasya" (Pāṇini 7.1.1), there is no vṛddhi [substitution],
resulting in *śamakaḥ*.
The suffix *damaka* is applied after a root ending in a consonant that does not take the augment *iṭ*, while *niyāmaka* is applied after the roots *jan* and *han*. (Pāṇini 3.2.51–52)
*Janaka* means killing or injury; thus,
*vadhaka* is a killer.
By [the rule] *radhijabhor aci* (Pāṇini 7.1.61),
[the forms] *randhakaḥ* and *jambhakaḥ* are derived.
In the *neṭ* (non-causative) and *liṭ* (perfect) tenses, there is no substitution for the root *radh*.
[The forms are] *radhitā* and *raddhā*.
By the rule *masjinaśor num* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.60), the augment *num* is applied, resulting in *maṅktā* and *naṃṣṭā*.
The root *rabh* (to begin) takes the substitution *naś* for its final consonant, except before the suffix *aś* and in the *liṭ* tense;
[thus] *rambhakaḥ*.
One who has attained [it] through gains is a "gainer" (lambhaka).
The suffix *iṭ* is applied because the number 2340 has been obtained; thus,
it is "eṣitā" (sought).
Sought,
accompanied,
and endured.
In the case of the root *daridrāti*, there is elision of the *ā* [before the suffix *tā*]; however, it does not occur before the suffix *ṇvul*.
Let there be only the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113); by its very meaning, [the suffixes] prescribed therein would apply even elsewhere.
And thus, the inclusion of the term *bahula* (in various cases) is for the purpose of showing that the meaning of the suffixes ending in *kṛt* is not fixed;
[as in] *pādahārakaḥ*, meaning "one who is carried by the feet," where the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The prohibition of *iṭ* after the root *kram* when followed by the suffix *kta* should be stated as an optional rule (*vā*) when it occurs in the context of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the active sense (*kartari*). Why [is it specified] "in the active sense" (*kartari*)? [Because the middle voice can also occur in the passive sense.]
One should proceed with the *ātmanepada* endings; what then is the *saṃkramitā*?
The word *viṣaya* is used in the sense of non-difference;
therefore, there is no prohibition for that which is subject to optionality according to the rule *anupasargād vā* (Pāṇini 3.3.48), nor is it to be displaced.
Some maintain that its very fitness (*arhatva*) constitutes its being the object (*viṣayatva*); thus, they argue that even in the form *krānta*,
the mention of the *parasmaipada* in the rule *gam-iṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.58) indicates the absence of the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes.
Thus, it is precisely that which desires to go,
and not that which desires to emerge from the four *vṛt*s.
From a stem ending in a *yaṅ* suffix, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied;
because of the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening,
resulting in *pāpacakaḥ*.
But from a [verbal root] ending in *yaṅ* or *luṅ*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied], as in *pāpācakaḥ*.
(SK 2896; Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.134)
The suffix *lyu* is applied after roots such as *nandi*, the suffix *ṇini* after roots such as *grahi*, and the suffix *ac* after roots such as *pac*. Thus, from *nandayati* comes *nandanaḥ*;
from *janam ardayati* comes *janārdanaḥ*.
Madhusūdana especially causes terror, and thus Lavaṇa is named Vibhīṣaṇa.
In the *nandī* group of words, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*); thus,
[the forms] *grāhī* and *sthāyī*.
The minister is one who possesses objects of sense; the absence of increase [is established] by means of irregular derivation (nipātana).
In this world, even one who possesses the six sense objects may become a conqueror.
The word *paribhavī*, meaning "partial," is derived through the elision of the suffix *vṛddhi*; it belongs to the *pacādi* group, which is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
In the two sūtras *śivaśamariṣṭasya kare* (Pāṇini 5.2.137) and *karmaṇi ghaṭo’ṭhac* (Pāṇini 5.2.35), the suffix *ac* is applied after the roots *kṛ* and *ghaṭ*. Furthermore,
since the elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix is prescribed when *ac* follows, this [application of *ac*] is intended by some to subvert certain exceptions (*bādhaka*).
One who cooks is a *paca*;
one who cries out is a *nadaṭ*;
one who steals is a *coraṭ*.
The river [is named] Devatī and so forth, extending for eight *krośas*.
The goddess Corī is derived from the root *div* (to play/shine).
The suffix *ka* was applicable by the rule *igupadha-* (Pāṇini 3.1.135),
but it is elided because the word is listed among the *nyaṅkvādi* group; furthermore, the suffix *yaṅ* is elided by the rule *yaṅo'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74).
By the rule *na dhātulopa-* (Pāṇini 1.1.4), there is a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; thus,
[the forms] are *cekriyaḥ* and *nenyaḥ*.
The quivering one, the swelling one, the repeatedly cleansing one.
Or rather, it should be stated that there is reduplication of the roots *car*, *cal*, *pat*, and *vad*, and that the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) becomes *ac* when followed by *ā* or *k*.
Due to the force of the lengthening of the augment (*āgama*), the reduplicated syllable is short; [then] *halādiśeṣaḥ* applies, and thus it does not become *carācaraḥ*.
Moving and unmoving,
falling and flying,
speaking and disputing.
By the rule *hanterghatvaṃ ca* (or *ghatvamabhyāsasya uttarasya tu abhyāsācca*), there is the substitution of *gh* for the root *han*; thus,
*ghanāghanaḥ*.

After the root *paṭ*, there is the elision of the suffix *ṇil* and the substitution of *cak* for the root, and optionally the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable; thus, from *paṭ*, one forms *pāṭupaṭaḥ* and,
in the alternative case, *paṭacaḥ*.
Moving,
falling,
speaking.
Or, by the rule "hanaḥ pāṭo rātreḥ kṛti" (Pāṇini 6.3.93), there is optionally the substitution of *mum*.
rātriṃcaraḥ (variant:
rātricaraḥ) means one who wanders at night.
After these [roots],
including *kṣip*, the suffix *ka* shall be applied.
The planet Mercury is thin.
One who knows is "jña";
one who pleases is "priya"; one who scatters is "kira."
By the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), *ṇvul* and *tṛc* are also [possible], as in *kṣepakaḥ* and *kṣeptā*.
What might it be? SK 2898 AS 3-1-136 kaḥ syāt.
By the rule *śyādvyadhā-* (Pāṇini 3.1.141), there is an exception to the suffix *ṇa*; thus,
one who is well-pleased is *suglaḥ*,
and one who is wise is *prajñaḥ*.
That which drinks is called *piba*.
You who smell, you who blow, you who suckle.
Regarding the word *dhayā* (a suckling girl), since it is derived from the root *dheṭ* with the suffix *khaś*, the suffix *ṅīp* would be applicable just as in the case of *stanandhayī*; however,
Haradatta maintains that *ṅīp* is not desired after *khaś* except in those specific instances.
"One who sees" is *paśyaḥ*;
[the suffix] *ghraḥ* is used in the sense of a name, as indicated by the rule: "Not [with the suffix *ghraḥ*] in the case of *vyāghra* and others" (*na vā vyāghrādibhiḥ*).
The substitute *ś* shall occur in place of *s*.
Limpid,
finding,
and sustaining.
The one who brings across,
the one who causes to know,
the one who causes to rise.
The word *cetayati* is derived from the root *cit* with the suffix *ṇic*, meaning "to cause happiness," as it appears in the Sūtra.
Alternatively, by the rule of *asarūpa* (irregular formation), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *sāti*, resulting in *sāt*,
which refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
*Sātvantaḥ* means devotees;
*sah* is used in the sense of endurance (*marṣaṇe*), belonging either to the *curādi* class or as a causative form (*hetumaṇṇyantah*).
Why [is it said] "after a prefix"? [Consider:
*pralipaḥ*.
The suffix *ni* may optionally be applied after the root *lip* [to form *nilimpa*];
*nilimpāḥ* means "gods.
After the root *vid*, the suffix *ni* is optionally applied when forming a proper name, as in *gavādiṣu*.
Govinda [is] the lotus (aravinda).
The substitute *ś* shall take the place of *d* in the root *dad*.
In the case of the root *dhā*, the suffix *ṇa* to be mentioned later applies only when it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasargāt*).
The giver,
the primordial source.
According to Pāṇini 3.1.140, the suffix *ṇa* may optionally occur after roots beginning with *jval* and ending with *kas*, provided they have the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) and so forth.
In the alternative [view], when there is no vowel *ac*,
[the forms] are *jvālaḥ* and *jvalaḥ*.
*Cāla* is *cala*;
this is due to the addition of the suffix *anu*.
Regarding the word *ujjvalaḥ*,
there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*) to the rule for the root *tan* [Pāṇini 3.1.78];
here, neither the restriction "when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) nor the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) applies.
That which extends is "atānaḥ" (SK 2903;

The suffix *ṇa* shall invariably apply after the roots beginning with *śyaiṅ*. Although [the forms] *śyāna* and *avasita* are already established because these roots end in long vowels (*ā*), their separate mention is for the purpose of overriding the application of *ka* when preceded by a prefix; thus, [the form] *avaśyāyaḥ* is obtained.
Coryza and fever.
Dhāyaḥ means a hunter;
sru means to flow.
With the prefixes *ā-* and *sam-*,
the word *āsrāva* becomes *saṃsrāva*.
Transgression, cessation, and withdrawal.
Leprosy, phlegm, and asthma.
The suffix *ṇa* shall be applied [to the word *māsa*].
It is called *dāva* because it "burns" (*dunoti*);
by association with *ni*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied specifically to the root *dunoti*, whereas for the root *davati*, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*.
The word *nāya* means "one who leads"; however, when the prefix *pra-* is added, it becomes *pradava*.
The suffix *praṇaya* [is applied after a word denoting a person] in the sense of "affection" (SK 2905;
Alternatively, this is an optionally fixed rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) regarding the vowel *a* in the [specific] case.
"Therefore, for you, there is a crocodile among aquatic creatures and a planet among the luminaries," so says the Kāśikā.
*Bhava* means God, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*),

and entities (*bhāvāḥ*, i.e., things); however, according to the *Bhāṣya*, it is derived from the root *bhū* belonging to the *curādi* class with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the sense of "attaining."
The state of being (bhāva).
In the sense of an agent, the suffix *ka* would be applied to the root *grah*;
thus, that which "seizes" (*gṛhṇāti*) grain and so forth is a "house" (*gṛha*). By virtue of being located therein (*tātsthya*), the word "house" refers to the wife.
*śilpa* means skill in action; the suffix *ṣvun* is applied after a word denoting that [skill].
From the roots *nṛt*, *khan*, and *rañj* [with the suffix *akan*], one forms *nartakaḥ* (male dancer) and *nartakī* (female dancer).

The suffixes *khan* and *kanī* are applied after the root *as*; furthermore, it should be stated that the elision (*lopa*) of the nasal (*n*) of the root *rañj* optionally occurs before these same suffixes.

According to the Bhāṣya, however, the word *rajaka* (a washerman) is derived from the roots *rañj* and *kṛ*, while *rajakī* (a washerwoman) is derived specifically from the roots *nṛt* and *khan* with the suffix *ṣvun*.
By the rule *rañjeḥ kvun śilpisaṃjñayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.145), the suffix *kvun* is applied; with the feminine suffix *ṭāp*,
it becomes *rajikā*.
But in the sense of connection with a male, [the suffix ṅīṣ is applied] after *rajaka* (a washerman), as in *rajakī*.
(SK 2908; Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.48)
The suffix *thakan* occurs after the root *gai* when denoting an artisan as the agent;
thus, *gāthakaḥ*.
A singer.
The designation *gāyanī* [is applied] because of the presence of the phoneme *ṭi*; Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.45.
The suffix *ṇyuṭ* occurs after the roots *hā* and *hāṅ* when denoting a type of rice (*vrīhi*) or time (*kāla*), provided they function as the agent (*kartṛ*).
Thus, "that which abandons water" is *hāyana*, a type of rice;
"that which abandons [past] states" is *hāyana*, a year.
The root *jihī* means "to go" or "to attain.
(Pāṇini 3.1.149)
By the inclusion of the term *samabhihāra*, excellence of performance (*sādhukāritva*) is indicated; as in the examples *pravakaḥ* and *sarakaḥ*.
A washerman (lavaka).
Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.150.
