The suffix *vuñ* occurs after a verbal root that functions in the sense of an object of a benediction (*āśis*), in the agentive sense; for example:
*jīvatāt*—*jīvakaḥ*; *nandatāt*—*nandakaḥ*.
This utterance is the merit of the one who pronounces the benediction (the *āśīḥ-prayoktṛ*),
such as a father or other relative who offers the blessing (*āśāsituḥ*).

When a word denoting the object (*karman*) is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*), the suffix *aṇ* shall be added to the verbal root; this forms a compound with the subordinate element (*upapadasamāsa*).

In expressions such as "one who makes a pot" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*) resulting in *kumbhakāraḥ*, or "one who looks at the sun" (*ādityaṃ paśyati*), the suffix *ṇa* is not applied because it is not so prescribed [by rule] for these cases; thus, the suffix *ṇa* does not apply after the roots *śīl*, *kāmin*, *bhakṣin*, or *ācārin*.
Or rather, the Vārttika is for the purpose of an exception to the rule [of *aṇ*]:
[the suffix *ṭhak* is used] in the sense of "having the habit of eating meat" (*māṃsaśīla*) or "desiring meat" (*māṃsakāma*).
Those who eat meat may still be of virtuous conduct, as are those who abstain from eating onions and garlic.
How is it that the mountain who bears the Gaṅgā and others, though emaciated by much fasting, remain thus while awaiting their pleasure?
When there is an intention to express the subordinate status (śeṣatva) of the action, [the suffixes] will occur [according to Pāṇini 3.2.2].
The suffix *aṇ* shall apply as an exception to *kā*,
[forming] *svargahvāya*.
A weaver and one who deals in grain.
After a verbal root ending in /ā/ that is not preceded by a prefix, when an object is present as an upapada, the suffix *ka* shall be used instead of *aṇ*;
there is elision (*lopa*) of the final /ā/ of the root.
Why is the word *anupasarge* used [in the rule for the suffix *kha*]? [Because] in *godaḥ* and *pārṣṇitraḥ*, [the suffix applies even though the preceding words are not upasargas].
The suffix *ya* is applied after the word *go* when forming a bahuvrīhi compound; furthermore, the suffix *ḍa* is optionally applied after words ending in a *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel in all cases.
One who overcomes the Brahmins is a *brahmajya*.
Because of the inclusion of the word "sarvatra" (everywhere), by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136), [the suffix -ka is applied], as in *āhvaḥ* and *prahvaḥ*.
In the *Sūtra* 3.2.4 (*supi*),
the rule is divided.
When a word ending in *su* is the upapada, the suffix *ka* shall be applied after a stem ending in long *ā*; for example,
"he drinks from two" is *dvipaḥ*, as in *samasthaḥ*.
Then, from the root *sthā* with the prefix *viṣama-* followed by the locative suffix *su*,
the suffix *ka* would be applied.
Because of the force of the initial effort toward their existence, the rising up of mice is called *ākhottha*.
(SK 29ab)
According to Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.92, *pratiṣṭhatau* means "two lead-bulls" (*praṣṭhau gāvau*),
which signifies that they go at the front.
What is a prastha in relation to the fire?
In the rule *AS* 8.3.97, *sthaḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a word ending in the suffix *kap*,
used in the nominative case with the sense of the genitive.
In place of *stha* following these [prefixes], *ṣa* shall occur;
as in *dviṣṭhaḥ* and *triṣṭhaḥ*.

From this point onward, both [the rules] "in relation to an action" (karmaṇi) and "with a word ending in a case-suffix" (supi) continue to apply; among those, in the case of intransitive verbs (akarmaka), the rule "with a word ending in a case-suffix" (supi) is connected.

When *tuṇḍa* and *śoka* are used as supplementary words (*upapada*) denoting "laziness" and "the act of bringing pleasure" respectively, the suffix *ka* should be applied after these two [roots]; this is to be stated as an optional rule (*vā*).
"One who rubs his belly" (tundaparimṛjaḥ) refers to one who is lazy;
"one who dispels sorrow" (śokāpanudaḥ) is a bringer of happiness.
Alas! Here, he who merely rubs his belly and dispels grief by teaching the worthlessness of saṃsāra is a "dispeller of grief" (*śokāpanoda*).
Regarding this, there is the Vārttika rule: *mūlavibhujādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* ("the addition [of the suffix *ka*] after words such as *mūlavibhuja*").
The word *mūlavibhujaḥ* means "one who breaks roots";
this is a class of words formed according to their etymological structure (*ākṛtigaṇa*),
such as *mahīdhraḥ* ("earth-bearer").
A "swallower" (gila) is so called because the wicked person swallows [the truth].
After the roots *dāru* and *jñā*, when preceded by the prefix *pra* and followed by an object as a subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *ka* shall be applied;
this is an exception to the rule for the suffix *aṇ*.
Because it is stated that "one who gives everything,
one who knows the path, and one who is free from calamity" [are the recipients], when another person exists besides these, why would [the gift] not go to him?
The tradition of the cow (gosaṃpradāya).
The cow-counter (the mind).

When these two roots [gai and śas] are not preceded by a prefix, the suffix *ṭak* shall be applied when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a subordinate word (*upapada*), resulting in *sāmagaḥ* (a singer of Sāmans) and *sāmagī* (a female singer of Sāmans).

But when there is a prefix, it should be stated that [the suffix *ka*] is applied to the root *pā* for the sake of euphonic combination (*sāmasaṃgāya*) in the sense of drinking *surā* and *śīdhu*; thus,
[one who drinks *surā*] is called a *surāpī*.
A Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks *śīdhu* elsewhere is a *kṣīrapā* (milk-drinker),
whereas one who drinks or guards *surā* is a *surāpā*.
An heir who takes a share.
When [the object] is not being lifted (*anudyamane*), why is the bearer of the burden (*bhārahāra*) [not included]?
There is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating that the root *grah* [is used with the genitive] in the case of *śakti*, *lāṅgala*, *aṅkuśa*, *tomara*, *yaṣṭi*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭī*, and *dhanus*.
The apprehension of capacity,
like the grasping of a plow,
occurs when the meaning is to be maintained by the rule.
Regarding "grasping the thread" (*sūtragrāha*): one who merely takes up the thread but does not maintain it is called a "grasper of the thread" (*sūtragrāha*).
A sūtra for the purpose of lifting;
the prince is clad in armor.
One whose habit is to gather flowers is called "puṣpāharaḥ" (a flower-gatherer).
What is the purpose of [the suffix] in the sense of habitual action?
For example: *bhārahāraḥ* (a bearer of a burden).
The suffix *ac* shall be applied after the root *arh*, when a word denoting the object (*karman*) is used as an upapada; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.
A Brāhmaṇī woman worthy of worship (SK 2927; AS 3.2.13).
It should be stated that [the elision of the case-ending] occurs after the words *hastin* and *sūcaka*.
[In the example] "he delights on a pillar" (*stambe ramate*), the word *stamberama* means "an elephant";
here, there is an elision of the *ṅi* case-ending either by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti* (Pāṇini 6.3.14) or by the rule *halantāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.9).
A backbiter is a slanderer.
Śambhava and Śaṃvada;
furthermore, the mention of the verbal root (dhātu) is for the purpose of ensuring the application [of the rule] even in cases where there would otherwise be an obstruction.
Let there not be the suffix *ṭa* after the root *kṛ* when [the agent] is the cause (*hetu*) or other such factors; for example,
"a female wandering ascetic named Śaṅkarā who is habitually inclined toward that" (SK 2929).
"He who sleeps in the sky is *khaśayaḥ*";
there is an addition [to the rule] regarding words such as *pārśva* and others (Vārttika).
One who sleeps on his sides is a *pārśvaśaya*; one who sleeps on his back is a *pṛṣṭhaśaya*;
one who sleeps on his belly is an *udaraśaya*.
When the agents are lying on their backs and so forth, [the compounds are] *uttānaśayaḥ* (lying on one's back) and *avamūrdhaśayaḥ* (lying head-downwards).
"One whose head is bent down" is *avamūrdhā*, meaning he lies with his face turned downward;
[the suffix] *ḍa* is applied after "mountain" (*giri*) in Vedic usage.
He sleeps on the mountain, thus he is Giriśa; how then did that fair-haired woman attend upon Giriśa every day?
In the analysis of the compound as "one who has a mountain" (*giri asyāsti*), the suffix *cha* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *loman*.
When a word denoting a location (*adhikaraṇa*) is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*).
The male wanderer of Kuru and the female wanderer of Kuru.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in *carati* when preceded by *bhikṣā* or *senā*,] as in *bhikṣācaraḥ* ("one who goes for alms") and *senācaraḥ* ("one who moves within an army").
The word "ādāya" is a gerund (lyap-anta);
how then [is it used] in the expression "ādāyacaraḥ," as in "having seen his companion standing there"?
Because of the reading "caraṭ" in the *pacādi* group [of verbal roots], according to Pāṇini 3.2.18.
*Purassaraḥ* means "going in front" (*agrataḥsaraḥ*); one who goes at the front (*agram*), with the front (*agreṇa*), or toward the front (*agre*) is called *agresaraḥ*.
In the rule *sūtrāgre*, the form ending in *-e* (edantatva) is also treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
If so, how is it that [the word] *yūtham* appears in the phrase *tadagrasaragarvitakṛṣṇasāram*?
Haradatta explains this by means of the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*).
When the word *pūrva*, denoting an agent, is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṣṭan* is applied after the root *sṛ*.
In *pūrvasaraḥ*, [the suffix *kvin* is applied] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as in "he moves forward"; whereas in *pūrvasāraḥ*, it means "one who moves toward a region that is to the east."
When these meanings are to be expressed, the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *kṛ*.
Therefore, by the rule *kṛkami* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), the *s* becomes *ṣ*; thus,
the one who performs the *śrāddha* possesses the knowledge that brings glory.
One who carries out what is said.
In these cases, according to Divākara, the suffix *ṭa* occurs after the root *kṛ*, even when there is no cause (*ahetu*) or other such conditions, as in *vibhākara*.
*niśākaraḥ* and *bhāskaraḥ* [are formed] by the addition of the suffix *sa-* due to their inclusion in the *kaskādi* group.
*Bahukaraḥ*: the word *bahu* has the sense of "extensiveness" (*vaipulyārtha*); it is mentioned separately from "number" (*saṃkhyā*). The words *lipi* and *libi* are synonyms.
Number: that which effects one, that which effects two.
Because it belongs to the *kaskādi* group, *ahaskaraḥ* takes the *ṣatva* substitution according to Pāṇini 8.3.48 (*nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya*),
as does *dhanuṣkaraḥ*.
The Vārttika states: "In the sense of 'many,' the suffix *ac* is prescribed after the root *kṛ* in the case of *aruṣkara*, *kiṃyattad*."
Servants do whatever they are commanded to do.

Having set aside the *ṭāp* suffix [prescribed] for words beginning with *hetu*, the *ac* suffix applies by virtue of its higher status; and in the sense of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the *ṅīṣ* suffix is applied, as in *kiṅkarī*.
When the word *karman* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *kṛ*.
A *karmakara* is a hired laborer; a *karmakāra* is another [kind of worker].
In these cases, the suffix *ṭa* prescribed after the root *kṛ* is prohibited, even though it would otherwise have applied by virtue of being among [the categories] beginning with "hetu" (cause).
"The author of the word," and so forth (SK 2938;
It should be stated that [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the words *vrīhi* and *vatsa*:
*stambakariḥ* means "rice," and *śakṛtkariḥ* means "calf."
In the case of rice and goats, what is the "stump-maker" or the "dung-maker"?
When *dṛti* or *nātha* are the upapadas, the suffix *in* shall be applied to the root *hṛ* (to take away) when the agent is an animal.
One who takes away a leather water-bag is a *dṛtihari*;
one who takes away the nose-rope of a beast is a *nāthahari*.
Why [is this mentioned] in the context of "beast"?
The destroyer of the snare and the destroyer of the protector;

*phalegrahiḥ* (the fruit-bearing tree) [is derived from the sense] "it takes fruits. The substitution of the vowel *e* for the final syllable of the upapada (*phala*) and the suffix *in* after the root *grah* are irregularly prescribed (nipātana).
One who nourishes oneself is called *ātmambhari*; here,
the augment *mum* is added to *ātman*, and the suffix *in* is applied to the root *bhṛ*.
The author of the *Cāndra* grammar read "ātmodara-kukṣiṣu," while Murāri stated, "the cakora birds have bellies filled with the *karambha*-like moonlight."
After the root *ej* (to move) ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *khaś* shall be applied.

The augment *mum* is added to the end of *aruṣa*, *dviṣat*, and words ending in a consonant (*ajanta*), when followed by a word ending in *khid* as the second member of a compound, but not when the preceding word is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
Because it has the *śit* designation, there is the substitution of *śap* and so forth.
[The word] *janamejaya* means "one who causes people to tremble.

Regarding the rule *vāta-śunī-tila-śardheṣu ajadheṭ-tuda-jahātibhyaḥ khaś upasaṃkhyānam*, this is an addition to the sūtra. [That is, the suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots √aj, √dheṭ, √tud, and √hā when preceded by the words *vāta*, *śunī*, *tila*, and *śardha*, respectively.]
The deer were born from the wind.
When the word *khidanta* follows, there shall be a short vowel for the first member of the compound, and then the suffix *mum*; thus,
*śunindhayaḥ*.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *tilantudaḥ* means "one who crushes sesame seeds," and *śardho'pānaśabdaḥ* means "one who abandons the sound of flatulence"; thus, [the term] refers to one who abandons that [sound].
The root *jahāti* includes the causative sense within itself.
Regarding this, the Vārttika states:
"It should be stated that [the suffix *kyac* is applied] after the root *dhayati* when preceded by *stana*, and after *dhamati* when preceded by *nāsikā*.
Thus, one who drinks from the breast is called *stanandhayaḥ*.
Because the root *dheṭ* has the marker *ṭi*, [the forms] *stanandhayī*,
*nāsikandhamaḥ*,
and *nāsikandhayaḥ* are derived.
AS 3.2.30: When these two words are used as upapadas, the suffix *khaś* shall be applied after the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ* when they have an object.
The correspondence of numbers is not intended here for "the bellower" (nāḍindhama) and "the sucker" (nāḍindhaya).
The terms *muṣṭindhama* and *muṣṭindhaya* [are valid];
there is an extension of the rule to include *ghaṭī*, *khārī*, and *kharī*.
"Ghaṭindhamaḥ," "ghaṭindhayaḥ," and so forth;
a *khārī* is a specific measure of capacity.
*kharī* means "female donkey" (gardabhī).
The suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *ruj* and *vah* when preceded by the prefix *ut*, provided that *kūla* (bank) is the object (*karman*) in composition; thus,
one who breaks the bank is called *kūlamudrujaḥ*, and one who carries away the bank is called *kūlamudvahaḥ*.
"vahaḥ skandhaḥ taṃ leḍhi" means "a cow that licks the shoulder (of its calf)."
Because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap*;
because *khaś* is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution:
the wind is "cloud-licking" (*abhraṃliha*).
A cooking pot that cooks a *prastha* [of grain].
A frying pan is called *khārimpaca*.
The term *mitampacā* refers to a Brahmin woman; *nakhampacā* refers to barley-gruel (*yavāgū*);
here, the root *pac* denotes "to heat."
vidhuntudaḥ (the devourer of the moon) [is derived from] SK 2950 AS 3-2-35.
When *mum* is applied, there is the elision of a final conjunct;
[as in] *aruntudaḥ*. (SK 2951)
*asūryam* is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) because the negative particle *nañ* is connected with the verb *dṛśi* ("to see").
Those who do not see the sun are "sun-blind," such as the wives of kings;
the sun is "scorching the forehead.
These [forms] are derived as irregularities (nipātana).
When *ugram* is used as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) as an accompanying word (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *dṛś*.

"Ugrampaśya" means one who sees the fierce. "Iramada" refers to the light of the clouds; it is called thus because it rejoices—that is, blazes—by means of *ira*, which is water, since its fuel consists of water.
[The suffix] *śyan* is applied here by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
The term *pāṇidhama* refers to a path where hands are blown upon;
the meaning is that it is shrouded in darkness and the like,
for in such a place, hands are indeed blown [upon the ground] to drive away snakes and other creatures.
One who speaks pleasantly (SK 2953; AS 3.2.38).
The suffix *vaś* should be stated [after the root] *gam* when followed by the word *su*,
for the purpose of excluding its status as a technical term (*saṃjñā*).
The word *mitaṅgama* means "elephant," and *vihāyas* means "bird"; it should be stated that the suffix *khac* is optionally treated as having an indicatory letter *ḍ*.
A bird (literally: one who moves through the air), a winged creature, a serpent (literally: one who moves on its belly).
A serpent (bhujaṅgaḥ) [is so called] because it moves by bending its body (bhujaṃ gacchati).
The suffix *khac* occurs after [the verbal root] *syā* (to lie down), [provided it is preceded by a prefix].
Before the causative suffix *ṇiC* ending in *kh* or *p*, there shall be shortening of the penultimate vowel; thus,
from "he intensely torments his enemy" (*dviṣantam param vā tāpayati*), we derive *dviṣantapaḥ* and *parantapaḥ*.
Because of the inclusion of the forms *ghaṭa* and *ghaṭī*, the maxim regarding gender-distinction (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is non-eternal; therefore, in this case,
there is no [application of the rule] in *dviṣatītāpaḥ* (one who torments an enemy woman).
When the word *vāk* is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*) for the root *yam*, the suffix *khac* shall be applied if a religious observance (*vrata*) is to be understood.
The state of having the suffix *am* at the end of the words *vāk* and *puraḥ* is established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
One who restrains speech is one observing the vow of silence (*maunavratin*);
or, "one who restrains speech" (*vāgyāma*) refers to restraining speech due to incapacity or other such reasons within the context of a religious observance (*vrata*).
He who shatters the city is Purandara.
The inclusion of the term *sa* in *sarvasahaḥ* is for the sake of excluding [other] meanings;
and according to the Kāśikā, [the rule applies] to *bhaga* when it means "wife."
They say this [term] is derived from the frequentative form (*bāhulaka*):
it is called *bhagaṇḍara* because it tears open the *bhaga*.
AS 3-2-42: *sarvaṃkaṣaḥ khalaḥ*,
*kūlaṃkaṣā nadī*.
The wind that scrapes the clouds;
the whirlwind that scrapes the peaks.

AS 3-2-43: [The suffix *kha* is applied after a verbal root] when preceded by *megha*, *bhaya*, etc., to form [the agentive nouns] *meghaṅkaraḥ* ("cloud-producer") and *bhayaṃkaraḥ* ("fear-inspiring").
By the word "bhaya," there is an elision of what follows it (tadanta-vidhi), as in the example *abhayaṃkaraḥ*.
AS 3-2-44: After the verb *kṛ*, the suffix *aṇ* shall apply for these [words listed in the preceding sūtra], and *khac* as well.
He who brings security, he who creates well-being, he who brings what is dear.
He who does what is pleasing,
he who brings about joy,
he who performs what is delightful.
Since it could have been stated simply as "or" (veti), the inclusion of the term "aṇ" is to prevent [the suffix] *ṭa* from applying in cases such as *hetu*.
How then [is the form] *alpārambhāḥ kṣemakarāḥ* derived?
It is derived by adding the suffix *pacādyac* when there is a desire to express the object (*karman*) as a residual factor (*śeṣatva*).
When the word *āśita* is used as an upapada, the suffix *khac* is applied after the root *bhū*.
One becomes satiated by means of this; thus it is *āśitambhava*, such as boiled rice.
The state of becoming satiated is *āśitambhava*.
That which bears the universe is *viśvambhara*;
[the feminine form is] *viśvaṃbharā*.

The term *rathaṃtara* as a *sāman* is merely an etymological derivation based on "crossing by means of a chariot" (*rathena tarati*), yet it does not follow the literal meaning of its constituent parts; it is like a maiden choosing her own husband (*patiṃvarā*).
Śatruñjaya is the elephant,
Yugandhara is the mountain, and he is the subduer of enemies.
It has been stated that *śatruṃtapaḥ*, *ariṃdamaḥ*,
and *damiḥ* are transitive when used with the suffix *śamanī*.
According to another opinion, however, the root *dam* here has the causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*) implied within it (Pāṇini 3.2.47).
The word *sutaṅgama* [is derived with the suffix *aṇ*] according to Pāṇini 3.2.48.
The word "saṃjñāyām" (in the sense of a name) is understood here; the suffix *ḍa* shall be applied after the root *gam* in these cases,
and by virtue of the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is elision of the final vowel even though it does not belong to a nominal stem (*abha*).

"One who goes to the end" (*antaṃ gacchati*) is called "one who has reached the end" (*antaga*); [this is an example of] the addition of the suffix *ap* in all cases (according to the Vārttika), as in "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*).
It is called a *pannaga* because it goes (*gacchati*) by means of what has fallen (*patitam*), that is, by means of its belly (*pannam*).
The word *pannam* is the past passive participle (*ktānta*) of the root *pad*, used as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), and there is an elision (*lopa*) of the syllable *ura-* [from *uraga*].
It is called *uraga* because it moves by means of its chest (*urasā gacchati*); according to the rule *suduror adhikaraṇe*, it is called *suga* because one moves easily (*sukhena gacchati*) therein.
It should be stated that *durga* is also seen elsewhere, as in *grāmaga*.
And the substitution of *vihā* for *vihāyas* should be stated [as an option]:
*vihaga*. (SK 2966)

AS 3-2-49: [The suffix *khan* is applied after the root *han* when preceded by *śatru*, provided that the sense is a benediction. Why is "in the sense of a benediction" (*āśiṣi*) stated? [To exclude forms such as] *śatruhaḥ*.
*Śatrughātaḥ*;
"and *ṭaḥ* [is added] after *ā-han*, when *dāru* is the *upapada*, provided it is a name (*saṃjñāyām*).

The meaning is that when the word *dāru* is the *upapada*, the suffix *ṭak* is to be prescribed after the root *han* preceded by *āṅ*, and the letter *ṭ* is the substitute for the final [letter of the root].
The woodpecker is either called *cāru* or *cārvāghāṭa*.

The meaning is that [the suffix *ghañ*] is optionally prescribed after the root *han* when preceded by *sam* and used in the sense of the object (*karman*), or when it occurs in the *upadeśa* (original grammatical instruction). Thus,
one who destroys the castes is called a *varṇasaṅghāṭa*.
A collection of words, a collection of syllables,
and a collection of others.
After the root *han* preceded by the prefix *apa*, the suffix *ḍa* shall be applied.
This son, who removes afflictions like the sun that dispels darkness, is for the sake of fulfilling one's aspirations.
SK 2968 AS 3-2-51 kumāraghātī (one who kills a child)
The form *śīrṣa-* is substituted for *śiras-* [in the compound],
as in *śīrṣaghātī*.
The suffix *iṣṭak* shall be applied after the root *han*, when the agent possesses a characteristic [mark],
as in *jāyāghna* ("one who kills his wife").
A woman who destroys [her husband's] anger.
A mole on the forehead kills the wife;
a line on the hand kills the husband; clarified butter cures bile.
Regarding the term "non-human" (*amanuṣya*):
is it a rat-killing Śūdra,
or rather Balabhadra, the slayer of Pralamba?
The word *śatrughna* ("enemy-destroyer") and others are established by virtue of belonging to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*.
However, in the case of *coraghāta*, *nagaraghāta*, and *hastī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by virtue of the rule of "generality" (*bāhulaka*).
The suffix *han* shall be used when the sense of capability is to be expressed; this [rule] is for the purpose of denoting a human agent, as in the case of *hastighnaḥ* ("an elephant-killer").
The thief who strikes the door-panel; "kavāṭa" is an alternative reading for "kapāṭa. (SK 2972)
AS 3-2-55: When *pāṇi* and *tāḍa* are used as upapadas, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied to the root *han*, with the elision of the *ṭi* portion and the substitution of *gh* for *h*; thus, *pāṇighaḥ*.
Is "tāḍagha" used for an artisan,
as in "pāṇighāta"?
The addition of *tāḍaghātaḥ* and *rājaghaḥ* should be stated [as exceptions].
One who kills a king is a *rājagha*.

In these cases, when words having the sense of *cvy-artha* (intensive/transformative) that do not end in *cvi* are used as objects (*karman*) as upapadas, the suffix *khyun* shall be applied after the root *kṛ*.
That by which one makes the wealthy wealthy is "wealth-making" (*āḍhyakaraṇa*); why not [apply it] to *acvau*, as in "that by which they make [them] wealthy" (*āḍhyīkurvanti*)?
By the force of the prohibition, the suffix *lyuṭ* is also excluded here according to the *Kāśikā*; however,
in the opinion of the *Bhāṣya*, *lyuṭ* would indeed occur, as [the exclusion] is for the sake of subsequent rules such as *acvau*.

After the root *bhū* (to become), these two suffixes [kyaP and kyaṅ] occur when it is preceded by words such as *āḍhya*, provided they have the sense of the suffix *cvī* and do not themselves end in *cvī*.
"One who was not wealthy becomes wealthy" is expressed by the terms *āḍhyambhaviṣṇu* and *āḍhyambhāvukaḥ*.
[The suffix *kvin* is applied after the root *spṛś* when it does not mean "water. (Pāṇini 3.2.58)
The phrase "touching the ghee during the ritual" is excluded;
rather, it is one who touches with the mantra that is called "mantra-touching."
The [roots] *ṛtvid*, *gadhṛc*, *srat*, *gig*, *guṣṇig*, *añcu*, *yuj*, and *kruñc* [take the suffix *kvip*];
this has been explained.
In the case of words beginning with *tyad* (demonstrative pronouns), the root *dṛś* takes the suffix *kañ* when it does not mean "seeing" (*anālocane*).
It should be stated that [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the words *samāna* and *anya*; thus, from *sadṛś*, we have *sadṛśaḥ*.
Something entirely different,
or even something else, should be expressed.
Such-like, similar, different-like.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after these [roots], whether a prefix (*upasarga*) is present or absent, when a nominal stem (*sup*) is present as an upapada.
The celestial secret doctrine,
the progenitor of the cosmic egg.
The mother hates her friend; she is a hater.
A betrayer of friends, a betrayer of the earth, a betrayer of cows.
O you who are yoked with horses, you who are well-yoked, drink!
In the case of *vedavit*, *nividitya*, and so forth,
it should be stated that the suffix *ṇa* optionally applies after the roots *nī* preceded by *agra* and *agrama*.
A leader, a village headman.
When *sup* (a nominal suffix) or a prefix (*upasarga*) is present as an upapada, the suffix *ṇvi* shall be applied after the root *bhaj*;
[the resulting form is] *aṃśabhāk*.
The suffix *prabhāk* [is applied after a word ending in the genitive case] when expressing the meaning "he shines forth" (SK 2977;
A *viṭ* is one who eats raw food; from that raw grain comes [the name].
In the absence of food, how can there be an eater of food?
In the rule *aderviṭ* (AS 3.2.69), although [the substitution of *viṭ*] is already established by the preceding rule, this statement is for the purpose of preventing [the application of] *aṇ*.
*Kravyād* means "one who eats raw meat.
How then [is it explained] as *kravyāda*, *asrapa*, and *āśara*?
[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied when the word for cooked meat (*pakvamāṃsa*) occurs as a governing term (*upapada*).
The substitution of *kravyād* for *upapada* occurs by virtue of its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular formations]. (SK 2979; Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.109)
kāmadughā (the cow of plenty) SK 2980 AS 3-2-75
The phrase "in the Vedic language" (chandasī) is no longer applicable;
the suffixes -manin, -kvanip, -vanip, and -vic shall be added to verbal roots (dhātu).
After a root beginning with *vaś* and others, when followed by a suffix marked with *kṛt*, the augment *iṭ* shall not be applied. (The exception is for the root *śṝ*.)
Suśarman, who travels at dawn.
For a nasalized vowel, *āt* shall be substituted; thus, from *vijāyate*, [we derive] *vijāvā*.
O you who protect us from distress.
Roṭ reṭ sugaṇ!
This also is observed. (SK 2983; AS 3-2-76)
The rule *satsūdviṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.61) is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very principle; as in the examples *ukhāsrat* and *parṇadhvat*.
The suffix *vāh* is substituted for the root *bhṛ* when preceded by *pra*.
(Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.20)
The substitution of *ṇ* shall occur for the *n* at the end of a word that is not part of the root *ani*, provided it follows a cause situated in a prefix;
[and] in *he prāṇ* and *śāsaḥ*, there is the substitution of *i* by rule 2486.
*Mitraśīḥ* [is derived from] *mitrāṇi śāsti*;
*āśāsaḥ* [is derived from] *āśāsānaḥ*. In what case is *itvam* (the substitution of *i*) to be stated? [In the case of] *āśīḥ*, where *itvam* and *utvam* [apply].
Speech is the city.
In these [words], there shall be a short vowel for the root *chad*; thus, *tanucchad*.

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *anunāsikasya kv-i-* (Pāṇini 6.4.15), and the substitution of *na* for *m* at the end of a verbal root (*mo no dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 8.2.64) results in *pratān*.
By the rule *praśān cchvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), *ūṭh* is substituted [for the vowel of the root], resulting in *akṣadyūḥ*.
By the rule *jvaratvara-* (Pāṇini 6.4.20), the substitution of *ūṭh* occurs, resulting in *jūḥ*, *jūrau*.
Jūraḥ, tūḥ, srūḥ.
The vowel *ū* is the "growth" (*vṛddhi*); it protects people, thus it is *janauḥ*.
The people have perished;
the people have been destroyed.
muvaḥ, muvaḥ, sumūḥ.
The *suṃ* and *vuṃ* [suffixes] cause the elision of the *r* following a long vowel.
mūrchā, mūḥ, murau, muraḥ
The word *dhurvī*, as well as *dhūḥ*,
[is formed with the suffix *kvip*] according to Pāṇini 6.4.40.
It should be stated as a Vārttika: "The elision of the nasal [of the roots] *aṅg* and those beginning with *gam* occurs when they are members of a verbal complex (*aṅga*)."
Being purified and restrained, press [the soma].
It should be stated that the suffix *ūṅ* is added after the roots beginning with *gam*, and there is also elision [of the final consonant]; thus,
*agregūḥ*.
The word *agrebhrūḥ* [is formed by the elision of the middle member] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.77.
And [the suffix] *kvip* occurs after the root *śam*, as in *śaṃsthaḥ* and *śaṃsthāḥ*.
The sūtra (Pāṇini 3.2.78) is intended to override the *ac* suffix [prescribed] by the rule "śami dhātoḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.15).

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root when a *sup*-ending word meaning "non-birth" (i.e., not denoting an action) follows, provided that the quality of habitual practice (*tācchīlya*) is to be expressed; for example:
*uṣṇabhojī* ("one who habitually eats hot food") and *śītabhojī* ("one who habitually eats cold food").
In the case of one who has not been born [into that state], what is the agent of addressing the Brahmins?
What is it in the sense of habitual action?
Sometimes he eats hot food here;

having explained that the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a *sup* (nominal suffix) when it is not preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), the author of the *Vṛtti* cited the rule "there is an addition [to the rule] for *ut*, *prati*, and *āṅ* before the root *sṛ*" (*utpratibhyām āṅi sarteḥ upasaṃkhyānam*),
and Haradatta, Mādhava, and others have followed that very same view.
And that [interpretation] should be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya; moreover, the suffix *ṇini* is well-established even after a prefix, as in the case of *upajīvin*.
"In such passages as 'The retinue of followers falls downward when the light spreads out,' [it is shown that] 'sovereigns must not be deceived by their dependents.'"
The two Vārttikas— "the addition of *sādhukārī*" and "*brahmaṇi vadaḥ*"— are for the purpose of excluding the sense of habitual action (*ātācchīlya*).
One who performs good deeds, a speaker of Brahman.
AS 3-2-79: The suffix *ṇini* occurs when the agent expressed by the base word is the object of comparison for the agent expressed by the meaning of the suffix.
"He cries out like a camel" is *uṣṭrakrośī*; "one who caws like a crow" is *dhvāṅkṣarāvī*.
This sūtra is for the purpose of expressing a lack of habitual behavior (*atācchīlya*) and for the purpose of expressing a genus (*jāti*).
In the sense of the agent (*kartari*),
as in "he eats the beans like cakes" (*apūpān iva māṣān bhakṣayati*),
why is the word *upamāne* used?
The camel cries out.
The suffix *ṇini* occurs [after a verb] when "sthaṇḍila" is the object, as in *sthaṇḍilaśāyī*. (SK 2991)

AS 3.2.81: When repetition is to be indicated, the suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root when a *sup*-ending word is present as an upapada; for example, "the Uśīnaras are drinkers of milk" (*kṣīrapāyiṇa uśīnarāḥ*).
After the root *man*, when followed by a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*), the suffix *ṇini* shall be applied.
One who considers himself handsome.

The suffix *khaś* (which becomes *man*) occurs after the verb *man* when it means "to consider oneself" (*svakarmake manane vartamānāt*), provided that a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) is present; optionally, the suffix *ṇini* may also occur.
One who considers himself a scholar is called *paṇḍitamanyaḥ* or *paṇḍitamānī*.
Regarding the rule *khity anavyayasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.66): what is the purpose of the condition *anavyayasya* ("not being an indeclinable")? [The example is] *kālimanyā*.
The suffix *manya* is applied after a word denoting time when used with the sense of "day.
(Pāṇini 3.2.11)

The suffix *am* is applied after a monosyllabic stem ending in a consonant (other than *m*), and when followed by a word beginning with *khid*, the *au* of the nominative-accusative dual endings (*au*, *am*, *śas*) becomes *am*. Example:
*gāṃmanyaḥ*.
In the case of the suffixes *vām* and *śas*,
[the form] is *striyammanyaḥ* or *strīṃmanyaḥ*.
One who considers himself a man, one who considers himself a hero.
One considers oneself to be "Śrī" (prosperity) and the family to be "Śrīmat" (prosperous);
according to the statement of the Commentator, there is shortening of the vowel for the word *śrī* and the absence of the suffixes *mum* and *am*.
AS 3.2.84: This is a governing rule (adhikāra); [the suffix] *laṭ* is used for the present tense (*vartamāna*).
Thus, up to [the point where] SK 2996 and AS 3.2.85 [apply].

When a word denoting an instrument (*karaṇa*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) in the sense of the past action, in the active voice (*kartari*). For example:
one who has sacrificed with Soma is a *somayājī*; one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma is an *agniṣṭomayājī*.
One who kills his paternal uncle.
The term *karmaṇi* (in the sense of the object) is governed [by this rule] up to *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19), as established by *SK 2998* and *AS 3.2.87*.
When these verbal roots are used as upapadas, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *han* (*to kill*) in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta*):
*brahmahā* (a killer of a Brahmin), *bhrūṇahā* (a killer of an embryo).
Since the form *vṛtrahā* is already established by the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76), this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

According to the *Kāśikā*, there are four types of restriction here: [the suffix *kvip* is applied] only after the root *han* when it refers to the Brahmanas and others, only in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta*), and only with the suffix *kvip*.
The Bhāṣya states that regarding *brahmā* and the others, there is a twofold restriction: namely, [the suffix] *kvip* alone [is used].
The *Kāśikā* states that after the root *kṛ*, the suffix *kvip* occurs in connection with objects such as *sukṛta* and others; here, the restriction is threefold.
A performer of actions, a doer of evil, and a creator of mantras.

By the rule that the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *puṇya*, one forms *puṇyakṛt* ("one who has performed merit"). By the rule that the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *mantra*, one forms *mantrādhyāya* ("one who has studied the mantras") from the expression "he has studied the mantras" (*mantram adhītavān*).

In this context, because of the restriction that the suffix *kvip* occurs only when the action has already been completed (*bhūte eva*), the suffix *kvip* does not apply when one intends to say "he performs a mantra" or "he will perform a mantra.

However, because there is no such restriction that [the suffix *kvip*] applies only when words beginning with *sva-* are present as upapadas, the suffix *kvip* does occur even when another word is present as an upapada.
The author of the treatise and the author of the commentary. (SK 3000)
Regarding *somasut*, the *Kāśikā* states that there is a fourfold rule (*niyama*) here.
The same applies to the subsequent sūtra as well (SK 3001, AS 3.2.91).
Agnicit SK 3002 AS 3-2-92: [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the word *agni* when it is followed by the word *cit*, provided that the resulting compound denotes a proper name.]

When *karman* is the upapada, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ci* (to pile) when it denotes the specific location that serves as the receptacle for the fire (*agni*), provided it is used as a name;
for example, "piled like a hawk" is *śyenacit*.

When a word denoting the object (*karman*) is present as a governing term (*upapada*), the suffix *ini* shall be applied after the root *krī* preceded by the prefix *vi*; [Vārttika: the mention of "contemptible" (*kutsita*) must be supplied.
A seller of Soma and a seller of clarified butter.

[The suffix *kvin* is applied] after a verbal root meaning "to have seen" when used in the sense of an object, provided it denotes the past; for example, *pāradṛśvā*, meaning "one who has seen the further shore."
The suffix *kvanip* shall be applied [after verbal roots] in the sense of "one who performs that action habitually."
The root *yudh* has the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied; thus,
"one who has caused the king to fight" is expressed as *rājayudhvā* or *rājakṛtvā*.
The word "karmaṇi" (in the objective case) is discontinued.
Having fought together and having acted together.
AS 3-2-97: *sarasijam* (a lotus) and *mandurajaḥ* (born in a stable).
The short vowel [is substituted] for *ṅī* and *āp*— by Sūtra 3.2.98 (Pāṇini), which corresponds to SK 3008 and AS 3-2-98.
When a word other than a genus-term (*jātiśabda*) ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ḍa* shall be applied to the root *jan* (to be born); for example:
*saṃskārajaḥ* (born of refinement) and *adṛṣṭajaḥ* (born of the unseen).
The word *prajā* may mean either progeny or people.
After the root *jan* preceded by *anu*, the suffix *ḍa* shall be applied when a word in the objective case (*karman*) is used as an upapada.
The term *pumanujā* is formed by applying [the suffix *aṇ*] after the word *pumāṃs*, meaning "born from a man" (*pumanurudhya jātā*).
The suffix *ḍa* (which becomes *a*) may also be applied after the root *jan* when preceded by other upapadas; for example:
*aja* ("unborn") and *dvija* ("twice-born").
The word "also" (*api*) in the term *brāhmaṇaja* is intended to indicate deviation from all limiting conditions (*upādhi*);
by this, [the suffix occurs] even after other verbal roots (*dhātu*), and in some cases, even with different grammatical relations (*kāraka*).
A moat dug all around.
These two [suffixes] are designated as *niṣṭhā*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.102)

According to the rule "The *niṣṭhā* suffixes shall follow a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting an accomplished action; in that case, they occur only after those two [roots]" (Pāṇini 3.2.102), the suffix *kta* is used for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). According to the rule "The *kṛt* suffixes occur in the sense of the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the suffix *ktavat* is used in the sense of the agent.
In both cases, the letter *u* is elided.
I have bathed;
Viṣṇu has been praised by you;
Viṣṇu has created the universe.

A long vowel occurs for the root *kṣi* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) when it is used in senses other than those denoted by the affix *ṇyat*, namely, in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
After the root *kṣi* preceded by a long vowel, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix shall be replaced by *n*.
I have destroyed desire for both existence and action; it has been exhausted by me, O glorious one. (Pāṇini 7.2.5)
He has resorted; he has taken refuge.
The word *bhūtavān* is derived from the root *kṣu*;
alternatively, it should be stated that the substitution of *ūrṇu* occurs [for *kṣu*].
Therefore, because it consists of a single syllable, there is no substitution of *iṭ* for the roots *ūrṇu* and *nu*.
Surrounded (vṛtaḥ) [is used] when [the agent is] not present (SK 3016;
After the letters *r* and *d*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix becomes *n*; furthermore,
by virtue of that *niṣṭhā*, the *d* of the preceding verbal root and [the *d* of] *śṝ* [also become *n*].
In the word *ṛta*,
the substitution of *ṇ* occurs when followed by *r*.

Because *śīrṇa* is external (*bahiraṅga*), it is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purpose of the *vṛddhi* substitution; therefore, the offspring of one who has performed [the action] is not *kārtiḥ*.
Divided and cut.
AS 8.2.43: After a root ending in *r*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes becomes *n*, as in *drāṇaḥ*.
Styāna (stiffness), glāna (sickness), mlāna (dejection).
After the twenty-one roots beginning with *lūñ*, [the suffix *niṣṭhā*] is applied as previously stated.
The sine of the arc is the jyā-grahijyā— [Sanskrit Text 2412].
The root *du* (meaning "to go") becomes *jī* and its vowel is lengthened [to form *jīna*]; alternatively,
from the root *du* (meaning "to go"), [the past passive participle] is *dūna*.
The root *ṭudu*, meaning "to afflict," is not included here because it possesses an *anubandha* (indicatory letter); thus Māgha uses the forms *mṛdutayā* and *dutayā*. It has been omitted.
Upon the destruction of the *pūpa*,
the barley grains (*yava*) are destroyed; this is the meaning.
The other [form] is *pūta*, derived from the root *sī* when it has "swallowing" as its object and "agent" as its subject; thus,
the "swallowed morsel" (*sinaḥ grāsaḥ*).
Why is it called "the devouring"? Why is the sow [described] as having both karma and agent? Why is it called "by the noose"? Why is it "karma-agent"?
The morsel was eaten by Devadatta.
The root *bhujo* (to bend) becomes *bhugna*, and the root *ṭuośvi* (to swell).
*Ucchūnaḥ* means abandoned; *ohāk* means to abandon.
(ga) It has been stated that [roots] beginning with *svad* are marked with the *iṭ* indicatory vowel; thus,
*sūna* becomes *sūnavat*.
*dūnaḥ* means "pained" or "distressed"; it is derived from the root *du*, with the suffix *kta*.
The form *dūnavān* is also possible.
The root *ḍīṅ* (to fly) does not take the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *ktvā* because it belongs to the class of roots beginning with *mṛj*.
Flown up.
When the meaning is "solidification" (*mūrti*) or "hardness" (*kāṭhinya*) of a liquid, there shall be *saṃprasāraṇa* of the root *śyaiṅ* before the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.47)
By the rule *śyaiṅo niṣṭhāyāṃ ta-sya naḥ syād asparśe 'rthe halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.25), there is lengthening [of the vowel],
resulting in *śīnaṃ ghṛtam* (solidified ghee).
If there is no touch, how can water be cold?
What is the relationship between fluidity and the nature of touch?
"Saṃśyāna" means a scorpion that has contracted due to cold; such is the meaning.
AS 6.1.25: There is vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) of the root √śyai when preceded by *prati* before the suffix *niṣṭhā*;
[thus] *pratiśīnaḥ*.
In the case of the suffix *śyan*, there may optionally be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
Abhiśyāna is clarified butter;
abhiśīna is dew; avaśyāna is frost; avaśīna is a scorpion.
This is a fixed option; therefore, there is no necessity here.
In the case of the root *añc*, when used with the sense of "departure" (*apādāna*), the *t* of the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is replaced by *n*.
For that [root] for which the substitution of *iṭ* is optionally prescribed in some instances, the augment *iṇ* shall not occur after the *niṣṭhā* suffixes.
Regarding the rule *udito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56), although there is an option for the augment *iṭ* after a root marked with *u*, here [in *samaknaḥ*] it is not applied because the suffix is *ktvā*.
Why is "when there is no *apādāna*" specified?
When water has been drawn from a well (*udaktam udakam kūpāt*),
although *ṣatva* would otherwise apply by the rule *vraśca-* etc.,
it must be stated that the substitution for the *niṣṭhā* suffix is established (*siddha*) with respect to the rules concerning *ṣatva*, accent, suffixes, and the addition of *iṭ*.
One who has cut;
one who has caused to be cut.
AS 8.3.75: When the retroflex substitution [of *ṣ*] would have been obtained by the preceding rule, its absence is prescribed as a nipātana; thus, *pariskandaḥ*.
Regarding the word *prācyā*: is it *pariṣkandaḥ* or *pariskandaḥ*?
Regarding the option provided by *pareśca* (Pāṇini 8.3.39),
since the substitution of *ṣ* would have been required by *stambheḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.67),
[the rule] SK 3027 [applies].
In this case, by AS 8.3.114, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur.
After the root *div*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (kta) becomes *na* when it does not denote the desire for victory;
[e.g.,] *dyūnaḥ*.
But in the case of a desire for victory, there is gambling. (SK 3029, AS 8.2.50)
The word *avāte* is a compound split (*cheda*).

There is the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *vā-* preceded by the prefix *ni-*, provided that *vāta-* (wind) is not the agent; thus, fire and the sage are "not extinguished" (*anirvāṇaḥ*).
But when there is wind, the wind is extinguished.
It is dried up simply because it has reached its end.
AS 8-2-52: *pakvaḥ* (cooked/matured) SK 3032.
*kṣāmaḥ* (SK 3033) means "wasted" or "emaciated."
Before the suffix niṣṭhā, there shall be vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) of the root √styai.
According to Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.54,
the *t* of a *niṣṭhā* suffix may optionally become *m*; thus,
*prastīmaḥ*.
Is that which has become solid (prastīta) [the same as] that which was previously coagulated (styāna)?
The suffix *ñi* is applied after the root *phal*.
In the word *phulla*, the substitution of *l* for *ṣ* is prescribed by nipātana; this nipātana is also intended to apply to a portion of the suffix *ktavatu*.

In words such as *phulla* and *kṣība*, however, there is the elision of the suffix *t* belonging to the *kta* affix itself; furthermore, due to that [elision] being treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the absence of the augment *iṭ* which would otherwise have applied is also prescribed by nipātana.
*Kṣība* means intoxicated; *matta* means drunk; *kṛśa* means emaciated; *tanu* means thin; *ullāgha* means free from disease or healthy.
Why [is it said] "not preceded by a prefix" (anupasargāt)? [This refers to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.16.]
The augment *iṭ* shall not be applied after the affix *niṣṭhā* when it follows a verbal root ending in a consonant.
(Pāṇini 7.2.48)
The suffix *ut* is applied after the roots *car*, *phal*, and *upat*; for example, *praphultaḥ* (from *phal*) and *prakṣīvitaḥ* (from *kṣīv*), when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*.
How then is it that the lodhra tree on the mountain peak, though withered and parched, is in full bloom?
The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *phulla* in the sense of "blooming" according to the rule for *pacādyac*;
however, that rule is intended to exclude forms such as *phulta*, and thus there is a supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding the forms *utphulla* and *saṃphulla*.
After these [roots], the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is optionally changed to *n*.
The root *nū* in the sense of "shaking" (*vidavicāraṇe*) is understood specifically as belonging to the *raudhādika* class, because of its association with the subsequent root *und*.
Known, found, may you know; understood.
The suffix *vinna* is applied after the roots *vid* and *und*.

AS 7.2.14: After the root *śvi* and after roots marked with the indicatory vowel *ī*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*) does not take the augment *iṭ*; thus [from *śvi*] we have *śūna*.
The supreme protector, the savior, the one who has saved.
The one who smells,
that which is smelled,
and the one who is ashamed.
hrītaḥ (the suffix *kta* is applied after the root *hrī*) 3040;
Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.57.
The *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *t*) does not apply to the suffix *niṣṭhā* after these [roots]:
*dhyātaḥ*, *khyātaḥ*.
By Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.71 (*pūrtah rāllopaḥ*), there is the elision of the suffix *ra* after the root *pṛ*, resulting in *pūrtaḥ*; similarly,
*mūrtaḥ*.
After the word *mattaḥ* [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied].
This is a particle used after a word ending in the past passive participle suffix *niṣṭhā*; it is employed when the object of enjoyment is already known,
as in "vittaṃ dhanaṃ" (wealth is acquired) or "vittaḥ puruṣaḥ" (a man is known).

Regarding these two, why is there no optionality (*vibhāṣā*) [of *iṭ*] in the case of the suffix *kvasu*, as prescribed by the rule *gama-hana-...* (Pāṇini 7.2.68), such that *iṭ* would not be applied here?
That which is different is distinct.
In the context of transactions involving debtors, the substitution of *na* for the *ta* of the root *ṛdh* is prescribed when the suffix *kta* follows.
The other is *ṛta*.
Sphītaḥ (is formed by the suffix *kta* after the root *sphāy*) [Pāṇini 8.2.57].

The augment *iṭ* shall be applied to the *niṣṭhā* suffix after the root *kuṣ*, since the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "for that which is optional" (*yasya vibhāṣā*) would otherwise apply; this is a restatement of the rule [to establish it]. Thus: *niṣkuṣitaḥ*.
According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.52, the augment *iṭ* must invariably be added to the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* after these two [roots].
Having stayed there,
he became hungry.
After the root *añc* meaning "to honor," the augment *iṭ* shall be applied before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*;
[thus] *añcitaḥ*.
But when *gati* follows, [the augment] *kt* is applied.
(Pāṇini 7.2.54)
After the root *lubh*, the augment *iṭ* is always applied in the *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* suffixes, except when it means "longing"; thus,
*lubhitaḥ* is used for longing, whereas *lubdhaḥ* is used otherwise.
The augment *iṭ* may optionally be inserted [before the suffix *liṭ*].
The root *kliś* is used in the sense of "afflicting" (*upatāpa*) and "constant torment" (*nitya-prāpta*), while *kliś* is used in the sense of "oppressing" (*vibādhana*).

Although an option was already established for the suffix *ktvā*, there arose a prohibition regarding the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*); therefore, this [rule] provides an option for that case as well.
That which is afflicted is the afflicted [mind].
After the root *pū*, the augment *iṭ* may optionally be applied before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*.

According to Pāṇini 1.2.22 (*pūṅaḥ ktvā niṣṭhā ca seṭ kin na syāt*), the suffixes *ktvā* and the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) following the root *pū* (to purify) should not be marked with the *k* it-marker when they are followed by the augment *iṭ*; thus,
[the form] is *pavitaḥ*.

The mention of *ktvā* in the rule *pūtaḥ ktvā* (Pāṇini 7.2.54) is for the sake of what follows; for in the rule *nopadhāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.56), it is *ktvā* alone that is connected [with the preceding term].
Why should not the suffix *kta* (niṣṭhā) with the augment *iṭ* be prohibited after these [roots]?
The mention of "śayitaḥ" (the past participle) implies "śayitavān" (the active past participle); this specific instruction is intended to exclude the application of the *yaṅ* (intensive) suffix.
The *niṣṭhā* suffix should be stated [to be used] after the root *śī* (*śeśyitaḥ*, *śeśyitavān*) when expressing the inception of an action (*ādikarman*). (Or: it is optional.)

The suffix *kta* used in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarma*) occurs in the agentive sense; and by the word "also" (*ca*), it also occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).
In the sense of an abstract state (bhāva) and in the case of an initial action (ādikarman), the augment *iṭ* may optionally be applied to the *niṣṭhā* suffixes at the beginning [of the formation].
"Caitra has perspired" (*prasveditaścaitraḥ*); here, the root *ñiṣvid* belonging to the *bhvādi* class is understood in the sense of "to sweat."
Because of its association with the two [roots], however, from the root *svid* (to sweat) one forms only *svidita*, whereas from *ñimidā* [one forms *nimidita*].
The root *ñikṣvidā* belongs to both the *divādi* and *bhvādi* classes; it is conjugated as *prameditaḥ*.
He has smelled; he has sniffed; he has smelled repeatedly.
He was assailed; he assailed; that which was assailed by him.
What is the purpose of this?
[It is] because he has perspired, and by that [perspiration], and so forth.
In the case of *seṇi*, the suffix *-niṣṭhā* should not be elided.
Was he patient?
Did he exercise patience?
Regarding forbearance, what [is there]?
"Apamṛṣita" means a statement that is unclear; such is the meaning.

Why should the rule "the *niṣṭhā* suffixes following a root with *u* as an upadhā take the *kta* suffix optionally in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) or the beginning of the action (*ādikarman*)" not also apply here, as in *dyutitam*?
It was illuminated, gladdened,
and rejoiced in by the virtuous one.
Radiant, illuminated, and joyful.
Why [is it said] "pramoditaḥ sādhuḥ" from a root with *u* as the penultimate letter? [Answer:
It is "viditam."
"Is it 'bhāva' and so forth? Is it a kārṣāpaṇa that you desire?
"What is that, Seṭ?"
The term *kruṣṭa* is desired [to be applied] only after verbal roots that take the suffix *śvi*, but not here.
The word *gudhitam* is derived from the root *guh*.
There is elision of the suffix *ni* in the forms *bhāvitaḥ* and *bhāvitavān*.
By the rule *śvīditaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.14), the augment *iṭ* is not applied; there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), resulting in *śūnaḥ*.
Dīptaḥ is guhū; gūḍhaḥ is vanu; vataḥ.
*Tanu*:

From that [root], by the rule *pateḥ sani veṭ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.52), the absence of *iṭ* would have been expected; however, since it is established by the rule *dvitīyā-śrita-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.48) due to its having *veṭ*, or alternatively because it is known to be non-universal (*anitya*) due to the *īdit* designation of roots such as *kṛntati*, [the form] *dhāvitam ibharājadhiyā* and so forth is justified.
In the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), because of the word *ekācaḥ* [in the subsequent rule],
[the substitution] occurs for *daridrataḥ* (SK 3058).

Eight roots beginning with *kṣubh* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) as aniṭ (without the augment *iṭ*) when they denote specific objects such as *mantha* and others; *mantha* refers to parched grain mixed with a liquid substance, as well as the churning stick.
If the churning-stick is agitated, the internal mind becomes darkness, that is, delusion.
"Lagna" means attached;
"niṣṭhānatva" is also [a form] due to irregular derivation (nipātana);
"mliṣṭa" means indistinct, while "vispaṣṭa" means clear.
In the words *viribdha* and *svara*, as well as in *mleccha* and *rebhṛ*, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel is also prescribed by nipātana;
*phāṇṭa* refers to a specific kind of decoction that is prepared without effort.
Mādhava, however, states in his Vedabhāṣya that a substance which has reached a state prior to the condition of fresh butter (*navanīta*) is called *phāṇṭa*;
[he uses] *bāḍham* in the sense of "intensely," whereas elsewhere it means "agitated."
The king was agitated; thus, because the rules of grammar are not universally binding,
"svanita" is used in the sense of "dhvanita" (resounded).
Lagita, mlecchita, and virebhita.
The molasses has been removed.
These two [roots] remain without the augment *iṭ* only when used with the suffix *niṣṭhā* in the sense of "boldness" (*avinate*); for example, *dhṛṣṭaḥ*.
*viśastaḥ* means "slaughtered," while *viśasitaḥ* means "violated elsewhere."
However, the root *dhṛṣ* does not exist in the sense of "impudence" (*vaiyātya*) when used in the sense of an action in progress (*bhāva*) or a beginning of an action (*ādikarman*);

for this very reason, the Vṛtti states that this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Haradatta maintains that the result of *dhṛṣ* being classified as having an indicatory letter *ā* (*ādittva*) should be considered.
Mādhava, however, states that there is an option regarding the states of "being" (bhāva) and "action" (karma) when there is no lack of boldness:
*dhṛṣṭam* and *dharṣitam*.
He has been assailed;
he has been overcome.
When [the object] is large or strong, the suffix is not applied; [the roots] *dṛh* and *dṛhi* mean "to grow strong."
There is the absence of the augment *iṭ* for that which has been prescribed; there is the substitution of *ḍha* for that [consonant], the elision of *ha*,
and the elision of the nasal (*n*) following an *it*-marked root.
Dṛhita means "strengthened," while another [form] is dṛṃhita. (SK 3061)
AS 7.2.21: *vṛha* and *vṛhi*, meaning "to grow," are irregular formations (nipātana) as previously [stated].
One is augmented,
while the other is fully nourished.
AS 7.2.22: After the root *kaṣ*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* shall not take the augment *iṭ* in these two meanings: *kaṣṭam* means suffering and its cause.
Painful is distress, painful is hardship, painful is delusion, and painful is the scripture.
The meaning is that it is difficult to fathom; the rest has been explained. (SK 3063)
The root *ghuṣ* shall not take the augment *iṭ* before the suffix of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*);
for example, *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope has been sounded").
Regarding "aviśabdane" (in the absence of making a sound): what is meant by "ghuṣitaṃ vākyam" (a proclaimed statement)?
It means a statement whose intended meaning has been made manifest by sound.
After this [root *pū*] and after roots beginning with *arda*, the augment *iṭ* shall not occur before the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*).
sam-arṇaḥ, ni-arṇaḥ, vi-arṇaḥ.
Another is afflicted.
"Nearby" means neither too far nor too close; it is something that is not excessively crowded.

Pāṇini 7.2.26: After a root ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* and the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṇi* when the word ending in *kta* denotes the act of learning.
The meter was mastered— that is to say, accomplished and studied— by the student.
But elsewhere, they exist as a rope.
When the suffix *kta* follows the roots *śrā* and *śrapayati*, the substitution of *śṛ* is prescribed; thus, when milk or sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is cooked,
it is called *śṛtam* (cooked milk).
The meaning is that it has become soft by itself or is cooked;
however, anything other than milk or clarified butter is called *śrāṇa* or *śrapita*.
These [roots], when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, are optionally prescribed as having the forms ending in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) suffix.
Tamed, pacified, and fulfilled.
Enslaved, watched over, and concealed.
Made known; informed.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ* after these [roots]:
*ruṣitaḥ* or *ruṣṭaḥ*.
Endless, immeasurable, and swift.
The fruit of this [action] is swift when undertaken with zeal, but it is meager when merely proclaimed.
Resounding, filled with noise, and echoing.
In the case of the root *hṛṣ* followed by the suffix *niṣṭhā*, the augment *iṭ* may optionally be applied when the word refers to body hair (*loman*).
The root *hṛṣ* [is used] in the sense of being thrilled, having the hair standing on end, and in the sense of being astonished or struck by resistance; thus,
*hṛṣita* refers to one who is friendly (*maitra*).
The meaning is "astonished" or "struck"; however, elsewhere [the root] *hṛṣ* is used in the sense of "falsehood."
The augment *iṭ* is not applied after [roots] ending in *u* when the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows;
however, it is applied after the root *hṛṣ* in the sense of satisfaction.
This is a nipāta (irregular form) derived from the root *cāy*, or it is [the form] *apacitaḥ*.
Honored (apacāyitaḥ) [is formed by the suffix -ta after the root *apaci* according to Pāṇini 6.1.28].

Or it may be that this is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) regarding the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*); therefore, [the suffix *ktvā*] is obligatory when used with one's own body part (*svāṅga*).
The word *pīna* means "happiness" when it occurs elsewhere;
however, *pyānaḥ*, *pīnaḥ*, and *svedaḥ* do not [apply] when the word is accompanied by a prefix (*upasarga*). Alternatively, [the rule does not apply].
The suffix *syat* (i.e., *ya*) is indeed applied after the root *āp* preceded by *āṅ* when followed by *andhu* or *ūdhas*; thus,
[the form] is *āpīna-andhuḥ*.
The word *āpīna* is used for the udder [of a cow].
One who is prostrate should be short.
For these [roots], the vowel *i* shall be the final substitute when followed by an affix beginning with *t* that has a *k*-sign;
this is an exception to the rules for *ī*-substitution and the substitution of *ad*.
Ditaḥ sitaḥ mā māṅ meṅ.
Standing at a measured distance.
AS 7-4-41: For *śita*,
[the substitute] *śāta* [is applied].

The forms *chitaḥ* and *chātaḥ* [are established] because of the optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣātva*) [of the rule]; however, in the domain of religious observances (*vrata*), the substitution of *śya-* [for *chā-*, as in *śyena*] is obligatory.
"Saṃśita-vrata" means that the vow has been perfectly accomplished; thus,
he is a "saṃśita-brāhmaṇa."
The meaning is: one who exerts effort regarding the subject of religious observances (vrata).
When a suffix beginning with *t* follows a kit suffix, that which has been stated is placed [before it].
For the root *dā*, which bears the designation *ghu*, the substitute *dath* shall occur before an affix beginning with *t*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "before *t*" (*tādau*)?
What is the point of giving a cart to a cow?

This substitute is either *dā* or *tām*; thus, in cases such as *vidattam*, there is no possibility of the application of the rule *dasti* (Pāṇini 6.1.162), which prescribes lengthening for a preceding preposition before the root *dā* when followed by a *t*-initial suffix,
because that rule is specifically prescribed for a *t*-initial [suffix].
Whether it be *dānta* or *dhānta*,
one should not suspect the substitution of *d* for *dh*— as prescribed by the rule *na ca dāntatve niṣṭhānatvaṃ dhāntatve jhaṣastathoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.41)—
because that would contradict the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.
After a prefix ending in *a*, the substitute *ghu* (i.e., *dā*) shall take the designation *ra* when followed by an affix beginning with *t* that has the marker *k*.
The state of being offered and the state of being portioned out.
In the sense of the initial action (*ādikarman*), the forms *avadatta*, *vidatta*,
and *pradatta* are prescribed; furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*), the forms *sudatta*, *avudatta*, and *nidatta* are also intended according to their respective applications.

A long vowel shall be substituted for the final vowel of a preposition ending in *i* or *u*, when it is followed by a subsequent member of a compound beginning with a *t* that has undergone substitution [for the root *dā*].
By the rule *kharica* (Pāṇini 8.4.55), the substitution of *car* is established by virtue of its dependence [on the preceding rule]; thus, the *sūtra* is considered as having been recited (*nīttam*).
By the rule *ghumāsthā...* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), there is the substitution of *i* [for the vowel]; thus, from the root *dhēṭ*, we have *dhītam*.
In the word *gītam*, the substitution of *ā* for *i* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.44 (*pītam janasana*), resulting in *gātum*. (Source: *Sārasvataprakriyā-sandarbha* 2504).
What is born, what is pleasant, and what is eaten.
In the rule *lyapi*, the locative case ending has been elided (*luptasaptamīkam*).
The root *ad* becomes *jagdhi* when followed by the suffix *lyap* or a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*;
the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation, and the change to *dh* occurs [by rule].
*jharo jhari* (Pāṇini 8.4.65); *jagdhaḥ* is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*) and also in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). (Vārttika 3053).
"He made the mat" (*prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ saḥ*) and "the mat was made by him" (*prakṛtaḥ kaṭas tena*);

in these instances, there is lengthening of the vowel according to *Pāṇini 6.4.60*: "In the case of a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), [the vowel of the root] is long, except when it has the sense of the agent (*aṇyadarthe*)."
By the rule "kṣiyo dīrghāt" (Pāṇini 8.2.46), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*; thus, he is *prakṣīṇaḥ*.
In the case of the root *kṣi*, there may optionally be a long vowel before the *niṣṭhā* suffix when expressing either abuse or dejection;
for example, "may you become one whose life is exhausted" (*kṣīṇāyur bhava*).
Either his lifespan is exhausted, or this poor man has perished, or he has been destroyed.
When these two [words] are used, the *s* of the root *snāti* becomes *ṣ* when skillfulness is implied.
One who is proficient in the scriptures is "nadīṣṇaḥ," as in the expression "he bathes in the river" (niṣṇātaḥ śāstreṣu nadyāṃ snātīti nadīṣṇaḥ).
By the rule *supi* (Pāṇini 5.4.111), the suffix *ka* is applied [by the rule] *AS 8-3-90*.
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs after the prefix *prati* when it precedes the root *snā*; thus, *pratiṣṇātam* means "a purified thread."
Except when it has been washed.
There is one named Kapiṣṭhala, whose son is Kāpiṣṭhali; as for the lineage name (gotra), is it "Kapisthala," meaning the place (sthala) of the monkeys (kapīnām)?
In these cases, the *s* of the word *sthalasya* shall become *ṣ*.
Viṣṭhala, Kuṣṭhala, Śamiṣṭhala.
*pariṣṭhalam* (SK 3086; AS 3.4.72)
The suffix *kta* occurs after these roots in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), as well as in the senses of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); for example:
*gaṅgāṃ gataḥ* (gone to the Ganges) and *gaṅgāṃ prāptaḥ* (arrived at the Ganges).
He is sick;
he is Hari embraced by Lakṣmī,
reclining upon Śeṣa.
Residing in Vaikuṇṭha,
he worshipped Śiva and observed a fast on the day of Hari.
Born after Rāma, mounted upon Garuḍa,
he has outlived the entire universe.
"By whom the Gaṅgā was brought to the side," and so forth (SK 3087;

The suffix *kta* may be used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with these [verbs], provided that the state of being fixed (*dhrauvya*) or stability is not already established by other means; for example:
"This is the dwelling place of Mukunda," or "This has become the abode of the Lord of Ramā."
Desiring to see him, the gopīs said, "This has been eaten by Ananta";
for since the root *ās* is intransitive, the form *āsitaḥ* denotes either the agent or the action itself, as in:
"Mukunda has sat."
This was eaten by him; [this is] from roots meaning "to go" used with the suffix *āsa* in the sense of the agent or the object, followed by the suffix *ana*.

In the expression *kathaṃ bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ* ("How were the Brahmins fed?"), the word *bhuktāḥ* means "they have eaten"; here, the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) under the governing rule *vartamāne*.
The verbal root √kṣvidā (to sneeze) with the suffix ñi.
The root √indh (to kindle) becomes *iddha* when followed by the suffix *kta*.
The desire for knowledge.
Because of the separate mention of "of the Buddha," the meaning is that it is approved by kings— that is, desired by them.
The Buddha was known and honored.
The particle *ca* (and) following *arcitaḥ* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned,
such as *śīlitaḥ*, *rakṣitaḥ*, *kṣāntaḥ*, *ākṛṣṭaḥ*, *juṣṭaḥ*, and so forth.
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.114:
The suffix *kta* occurs after a verbal root to denote a neuter state (*bhāva*) when the time is unspecified.
spoken, slept,
laughed.
The suffixes *caṅ* and *vanip* are applied after the roots *su* (to press) and *yaj* (to sacrifice) when used in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta*).
Having heard and having heard again, the sacrificer.
The two performers of sacrifice (yajvānau) [are formed by the suffix -vanip according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.104].
"Beings," indeed, [are] the two growing old as they grow old.
By the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is also [formed]: *jīrṇaḥ* and *jīrṇavān*.

In this matter, according to the opinion of the three Munis, since the *liṭ* (perfect tense) is prescribed for the Vedic language (*chandas*) in the sense of a general past time (*bhūtasāmānya*), the suffixes *kvasu* and *kānac* which are ordained for it are also Vedic; however, poets employ them extensively, as in the example:
"him who stood there on the outskirts of the city" (*taṃ tasthivāṃsaṃ nagaropakaṇṭhe*).
"For you who have attained all blessings," and so forth (SK 3096;

The augment *iṭ* is added after the suffix *vasu* following monosyllabic roots ending in /ā/ that have undergone reduplication, as well as after the root *ghas*, but not after other monosyllabic roots beginning with a vowel.
Having brought hither, having bestowed.
Having eaten of these, what has he become?

After the words *sad* and others, when expressing a general past action in the common language (*bhāṣā*), the suffix *liṭ* may optionally be used; and for that [suffix], the suffix *kvasu* is always substituted.
Steadfast in his posture,
he sat down facing her as she was seated,
while listening to the people who had gathered there.
These are treated as irregular formations (nipātana).

After the root *i* preceded by *upa*, even in the secular language (*bhāṣā*), the *liṭ* suffix may optionally be used to denote mere past time; however, for that [root], the *kvasu* suffix is compulsory, with the augment *iṭ*:
*upeyivān*.
Having approached her own supreme form,
she approached [him] with the desire to speak what was intended.
The forms *īyivān* and *samīyivān* are derived from the root *aś* (to eat) preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, with the suffix *kvasu* and the absence of the augment *iṭ*.
In the verse "dhṛtajayadhṛteranāśuṣaḥ," Bhāravi uses the suffix *kānac* after the prefix *anu* with the root *vac* in the sense of the agent; thus,
one who has performed the recitation (*anuvacana*) of the Veda is called *anūcāna*.
After these [roots], the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs before the suffixes *vas* and *u*.
one who has gone, one who has gone, one who has slain.
Having gone,
having sought to know,
having known.
The forms *viviśivān* and *viviśvān* are included because of their association with the root *viś*, [which is] understood as the root *vid*.
By the rule "vettestu vidvān neḍvaśi kṛti" (Pāṇini 7.1.36), there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*; and [the same applies] to the root *dṛś* (according to the Vārttika).
One who has seen;
having seen.
The meaning of [the rule] "when there is coreferentiality with that which does not end in the first case" (AS 2-2-124) is that [the suffixes] śaP and so forth [are applied].
See Caitra cooking.

The augment *mum* shall be added to the stem when *āna* follows; while the rule for the present tense (*laṭ*) continues to apply, the repeated mention of *laṭ* here is for the purpose of prescribing an additional application.

Therefore, it should be stated (as a *vārttika*) that even when there is coreferentiality with a word in the nominative case, the suffix *san* occurs in certain instances, as in "he is a Brāhmaṇa" (*san brāhmaṇaḥ*) used in the sense of insulting (*māḍhyākrośe*).
"One should not live who lives even while consumed by the pain of others' contempt"—

this being the case according to Pāṇini 3.3.175 (*māṅi luṅ*), the absence of the augment *aṭ* (the *luṅ* suffix) occurs here by virtue of the force of this specific statement, as per Pāṇini 6.4.74 (*na māṅyoge*).
*he pacan*,
*he pacamāna* (vocative singular masculine of the present active and middle participles).
After a verbal root expressing an action that indicates another action, and when used in the sense of a cause, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are applied in place of *laṭ*.
The Yavanas eat while lying down; one who acquires wealth dwells [in peace],
and by seeing Hari, one is liberated.
The cause, the fruit, the instrument,
and the action— the Soma being drunk.
After the root *ās*, the substitute *ī* shall take the place of the subsequent suffix *an*.
"Of that which follows, [the substitute takes the place of] the first. (Pāṇini 1.1.54) "Sitting.
After the root *vid*, the suffix *śatṛ* may optionally be replaced by *vasu*; thus,
[we have] *vidan*.
The wise man and the wise woman.
AS 3-2-127: Those two, namely the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, are designated as *sat*.
This is a rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*);

therefore, when there is coreferentiality with a word other than the nominative, the suffix and the subsequent member [of a compound] are used invariably in the sense of addressing, as well as in the senses of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and cause (*hetu*).
Behold the one who will act, the one who is about to act, the offspring of the one who will act, the one for whom action will be performed, and devotion toward the one who is acting.
In some cases, the verb *vasati* (he dwells) is used even when it is not in grammatical apposition with the first [future] suffix, provided that he intends to act or intends to acquire [the object].
*kariṣyan* (the form *kariṣyan*) is [derived] from *kariṣyati* ("he will do") by [Pāṇini's rule] SK 3108 = AS 3.2.128.
In the present, the Pavamāna is the sacrificer.
When these [meanings] are to be expressed, the suffix *ānaś* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
Enjoying his pleasures, wearing his armor, and slaying his enemies.
By these two [roots], the suffix *śatṛ* occurs when the agent is not acting with difficulty.
What is there for one who studies and retains [the teachings] without difficulty?
He studies and retains [the text] with difficulty.
One who hates is an enemy. (AS 3.2.131;
All who press [the Soma] are sacrificers; all are performers of a sacrificial session (sattrin).
The word *arhat* [is formed with the suffix *kan*] according to Pāṇini 3.2.133 and Śakaṭāyana 3114.

The suffixes to be described hereafter, up to and including *kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.76), are to be understood as denoting the agent who is habitually engaged in an action (*tacchīla*), possesses its nature (*taddharma*), or performs it skillfully (*tatsādhukārī*).
The agent [is expressed] by the accusative case when used with "mats" (to weave), as in "the weaver of mats."

*nirākariṣṇuḥ*.

One who is prone to madness,
radiant,
and shameless.

The suffix *iṣṇu* is applied after a verbal root denoting motion.
Climbing plants that lead to fulfillment.
Since the rule applies only to Vedic usage (*chandasi*),
how then can it be said that "the Vaiṣṇava [weapon] is not capable of prevailing against the Lord of the World"?
Poets are unrestrained;
the letter *ca* has the sense of an unmentioned inclusion (*anuktasamuccayārtha*);
"resplendent" (*bhrājiṣṇu*) is the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Thus it is perishable;
this is not seen in the Bhāṣya. (SK 3119)

Therefore, by that [rule],
there is the substitution of *ī* for *sthā*;
because it is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa*.
Victorious,
stable,
and wonderful.
In the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), because of the inclusion of the letter *ga* [from the preceding rule], there is no *iṭ* augment; thus, *bhūṣṇuḥ*.
There is an addition to the Vedic rules regarding the root *daṃś* (Vārttika).
Fanged animals [are denoted by the suffix -aṇ].
Trembling, greedy, bold.

From the intensive (yaṅanta) form of the root *yā*, the suffix *varac* is added; there is elision (*lopa*) of the *a*. When the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if the substitute were the original) is about to apply by the rule "that which has an *ac* [vowel] is like the original when something follows," it is stated that when the final element of a word or operations such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*) are to be performed, a substitute for an *ac* caused by a subsequent factor is not *sthānivat*. This is because the *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited with respect to the elision of *y* (by the rule "there is elision of *y* and *v*"). Thus, the elision of *y* occurs by the rule "there is elision of *y* and *v*."

Relying on the status of the substitute as being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), when the elision of the long vowel *ā* would otherwise apply, that which is elided by *vṛddhi* is not treated as a substitute; thus, [the form] *yāyāvaraḥ* is established.
