After the word *antar*, the *ṇ* replaces the *n* of the root *han*;
[thus] *antarhaṇanam*.
But in the case of a place, it is a place that causes disappearance; thus, by the rule "of what does not begin with 'at'," they disappear within.
Why is there a *tapara* [long vowel] marker? [To indicate:
"the vowels *a*, *i*, and *u* are included within [the scope of the rule].
The suffix *ṇa* is added after the word *ayana*, provided it follows [the word] *śabda*; thus, *antarayaṇam*.
"An improper place" means a place that is obstructed by a vehicle.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.118;
Siddhāntakaumudī 3297; Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.96.
For the root *chād* (to cover), when preceded by two or more prefixes and lacking an upasarga, there shall be a short vowel before the suffix *ghañ*;
[thus] that by which the teeth are covered is *dantacchadaḥ* (lip); that in which they act is *ākaraḥ* (mine/source).
Words ending in *gh* are formed as irregularly prescribed (*nipātyante*) [by this rule].
The suffix *ghañ* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 3.3.18, *halaś ca*), which is about to be mentioned, is superseded [by this rule].
Thus, *gocaraḥ* is a place where cows (*gāvaḥ*) graze;
*sañcaraḥ* is a path by which they move about (*sañcaranti*).
That by which one carries is a *vaha*; a shoulder (*skandha*),
a cow-pen (*vraja*), and a palm-leaf fan (*tālavṛnta*) are also [called] *vyaja*.
By virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the substitution of *v* for *vi*; thus,
*āpaṇaḥ* means a marketplace (*paṇyasthāna*), and *nigamaḥ*— derived from the sense "they enter by this"— means the Veda (*chandas*).
Cātkaṣa is a touchstone.
*Avatāraḥ* refers to the descent of a well and the like; *avastāraḥ* refers to a curtain.
After a stem ending in a consonant (hal), the suffix ghañ shall occur.
It is called *rāma* because yogins delight (*ramante*) in it;
it is called *apāmārga* because by means of it, diseases and other afflictions are wiped away (*apamṛjyate*).
The wrong path is to be abandoned.

*Adhyāya*: [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] in the sense of "that in which one studies. The etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: "by means of this, they go forth, rise up, or withdraw. [This is an example of] the supplementary rule: "There is the inclusion of *ava-hṛ*, *ā-dhṛ*, and *ā-vā* [in the scope of the suffix *ghañ*]."
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *añc-* preceded by the prefix *ut*, but not when it means "water."
A *ghṛtodan* is a leather vessel [so called] because ghee (*ghṛta*) is poured out (*udacyate*) or drawn up (*uddhriyate*) in it; in the absence of water, how could there be a "water-drawing vessel"?
That by which fish and other creatures are brought in is called an *ānāya* (a net).
What is meant by "the net"?
It is that which brings [them] forth.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ca*, except for the root *ā-khan*.
The mention of *ākhyāna* (narrative) is for the purpose of making it known that this [term] applies even to other cases;
by this, [expressions such as] *bhagaḥ padam* and so forth are included.
The words *khan*, *ṛda*, *reka*, and *eka* are to be stated [as having the suffix *va*];
[the resulting forms are] *ākhaḥ* and *ākharah*.
Ākhanika and ākhanikavaka are terms for a digger.
The rule "in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa) and the locus (adhikaraṇa)" is no longer applicable.

When these words— *duḥkha*, *sukha*, and *artha*— are used as upapadas, the suffix *khal* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), provided there is difficulty (*kṛcchra*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.126.
The mat was difficult for you to make; it was not done with hardship, but was easy to perform.
It should be stated that *ātva* does not apply after the roots *nimīli* and *khala*; thus,
there is slight closing (*īṣannimayaḥ*).
Immeasurable,
well-dissolved,
and beyond measure.
Delusion and dissolution.
The augment *num* shall be applied to the root *labh* only after a prefix; for example, *īṣatpralambhaḥ*.
Difficult to deceive, easy to deceive, and subject to reproach.
What is the benefit of [specifying] "after a prefix" (upasargāt)?

The augment *num* shall not be applied after the prefixes *su-* and *dur-* when they are devoid of other prefixes, before the verbal roots *labh-* followed by the suffixes *khal* or *ghañ*; for example, *sulabham*.
What is difficult to obtain through the two alone? It is easily obtained.
How, then, can that which is extremely difficult to obtain be "extremely easy to obtain"?
This will be the case when the two words *ati* are used as *karmapravacanīya*s.

When *kartṛ* (agent) or *karman* (object) are used as co-occurring words (*upapada*), or when words such as *īṣat* (slightly) and others are used, the suffix *khal* shall be applied after the roots *bhū* and *kṛ*.

It should be stated that the correspondence [of the suffixes] by number is not intended for the agent and the object when they are employed without intervention from the verbal root; however, in the case of *īṣat* and so forth, [the correspondence applies] before the agent and the object, as these express the sense of *cvi*.
Having cast off poverty, one experiences suffering through wealth; the state of being "poorly wealthy" is better than the state of being "slightly wealthy."
Svāḍhyambhavaḥ means "one who becomes somewhat wealthy";
āḍhyaṅkaraḥ means "one who makes wealthy"; durāḍhyaṅkaraḥ means "one who makes very wealthy."
The suffix *svāḍhyaṅkaraḥ* is used in the sense of *cvy-artha*; for example: "Is he made wealthy by means of wealth? (*kim āḍhyena subhūyate*).
The suffix *khal* expresses censure (*apavāda*).
The Soma was easy for you to drink, though it was difficult to drink; now it is easy to drink.
In the vernacular language, the suffix *yuc* should optionally be stated after the roots *śās*, *yudh*, *dṛś*, *dhṛṣ*, and *mṛṣ*: thus,
*duḥśāsanaḥ*, *duryodhanaḥ*, and so forth.
The *ṇ* of *nasya* becomes *na*.
The drinking of ghee is the drinking of poison; what is the use?
Is it from the end of a word that [the rule] *nirṇayaḥ* applies? [Does it apply to] *puṣṇāti*?
Since this is a locative compound (saptamīsamāsa) based on the principle that "the end within a word is [treated as] the end of a word," there is no *visarga* in the form *susarpiṣkeṇa*.
That which must necessarily be done.
The suffix *dāyin* is applied after a word ending in *śata* to denote the person who gives that [hundred].
By the rule "āvaśyakādhamarṇyayoḥ" [Pāṇini 3.3.170], [the suffix ṇini is applied] precisely in the sense of necessity and debt:
Hari must necessarily be served;
a hundred must be paid.
After a verbal root, the suffixes *ktic* and *kta* may be applied in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*) when it forms a proper name (*sañjñā*).
By the rule *titutra-SKsandarbhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.9), the augment *iṭ* does not occur; thus, the forms are *bhavatāt* and *bhūtiḥ*.
For roots that do not take the augment *iṭ*, such as *vanati* and *tanoti*, there is neither lengthening nor elision of the nasal when *ktic* follows.
Yantiḥ, rantiḥ, vantiḥ.
The thread [of the loom] (tantuḥ) [is the cause of the cloth],
according to Sūtra 6.4.45 of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*.

From the root *san*, when the suffix *ktic* is applied, there may optionally be the substitution of *ā* for the radical vowel, and there may also be its elision; thus, the forms *sanutāt* and *sātiḥ* are derived.
The gods are existence and peace; may they grant him [the state of] being given by the gods (Devadatta).
When *alam* and *khalu* are used as accompanying words (*upapada*) in the sense of "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) and "purpose" (*artha*), the suffix *ktvā* shall be employed.
The mention of "prācām" (of the Eastern grammarians) is for the sake of honor;

because of the restrictive rule "amaivāvyayena" (Pāṇini 2.2.20), there is no compound with an upapada [in this case]. [The substitution of] "da" for "dha" occurs by the rule "do daddhoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.46).
Having indeed given [the gift],
having drunk [the draught]— *ghumāsthā*— truly.
In the presence of *alam* and *khalu*,
[the suffix *ktvā* is used];
in the presence of *kim* used as a prohibitive, [the suffix *māṅ* is used].
The Ornament (alaṃkāraḥ) [is defined] in Sūtra 3317 and Āhnika 3.4.19.
In the sense of reciprocal action (vyatīhāra), the suffix *ktvā* may be used after the root *mā*;
this rule is intended to apply even when there is no sequence of time (apūrvakāla).
In the case of the suffix *lyap*, the vowel *i* optionally replaces the final *e* of the root *meṅ*;
as in *apamitya yācate*.
Having caused [the water] to be carried away by means of the northern drawing-in and so forth, even though it was already present,
he causes it to be removed after having requested it.
When connection (yoga) is to be understood between what precedes and what follows, or between what follows and what precedes, the suffix *ktvā* shall be applied to the verbal root.
Without reaching the river, the mountain [is joined by it];
here, "contact with another river" refers to the river situated after having passed over the mountain.
In this case, there is a conjunction with the mountain on the opposite bank of the river.
The suffix *ktvā* occurs after a verbal root denoting an action that precedes in time, provided both roots have the same agent; furthermore,
*ktvā* is an indeclinable *kṛt* suffix used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), as in "having eaten,
he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*).
The dual number is not essential;
having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he goes— here, by *anudātta-SK-sandarbhah* 2428, there is elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*).
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, he praises him;
by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), there is an obligatory absence of *iṭ*, and by prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), [the form] is *svaritvā*.
Having given birth and having shaken off [impurities],
According to AS 6.4.31, there shall be no elision of the *n* of these two [roots] when followed by the suffix *ktvā*, as in *skantvā*.
Due to the quality of having *ū* as an *it*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied:
*syitvā* or *syanditvā*.
Why should the suffix *ktvā* not be *seṭ*? (SK 3322; AS 1.2.18)
Having lain down,
what did he do?
After these [roots], the suffix *ktvā* is marked with the *k*-sign when followed by the augment *iṭ*.
According to the rule *mṛḍitvā kliśaḥ ktvā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56), there is optionally the augment *iṭ*, resulting in *kliśitvā*.
Having arisen and having remained in a defiled state.
By the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahisvapipracchaḥ saṃśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.8), the suffix *kit* applies; thus: *ruditvā*, *viditvā*.
Having stolen and taken [it].
A *ktvā* suffix that has an *iṭ* augment may optionally be treated as having the *kit* designation;
for example, *śrathitvā*.
having bound, having concealed, having interwoven.
Why [is it specified] "not having a penultimate vowel"? [Examples:
*kothitvā*, *rephitvā*.
A *ktvā* suffix following a verbal root that has a *seṭ* augment may optionally be treated as having the *kit* designation.
Having spoken falsely, having deceived, and having plucked out.
Having plucked out, having pained, having suffered.
After these [roots], the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ*.
Having thirsted, having thirsted, having endured.
Having endured, having emaciated, having become lean.
Alternatively, by rule Pāṇini 1.2.26 (ralo vyupadhāt...), the suffix *kit* is optionally applied,
resulting in *dyutitvā* or *dyotitvā*.
Having written and having caused to be written,
what is the use of jewels?
Having served [the teacher] and having lived apart from the acquisitions.
Why [is it said] "after *halādi*" and "provided it is *seṭ*"? Why [the suffix *ktvā*]? Why [the suffix *iṭ*]? Why [the suffix *kim*]?
Having eaten, [he] dwelt for the hunger of the residence. SKsandarbhaḥ 3046.
Having stayed.
In the sense of worshiping, the suffix *iṭ* is invariably applied after the root *añc* following the reduplication *kṣudhitvā* and *kṣodhitvā*. (Pāṇini 7.2.59)
But [the suffix] *ktvā* is also applied after the roots *añc* and *gam*.
The augment *iṭ* is applied [after the root *lubh*] in the sense of "not deluding," according to the rule: *lubhitvā lobhitvā lubho'vimohane* (Pāṇini 7.2.54).
But having taken [the suffix] *vimohana* by means of *lub*,
[Pāṇini’s rule] SK 3327 = AS 7.2.55 applies.
After these two, the suffix *ktvā* shall take the augment *iṭ*:
*jarītvā*,
*jaritvā*.
After the verbal root *vraśc*, [the suffix *ktvā* takes the substitute *lyap*].
The suffix *ktvā* following a root ending in a vowel optionally takes the augment *iṭ*,
as in *śamitvā*; furthermore, by the rule *anunāsikasya kvi*, there is lengthening of the vowel when followed by the suffix *kvip*.
Having consoled,
having gambled, having played at dice.
When *ktvā* follows, a long vowel may optionally replace the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) before a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant.
Having stepped again and again upon the palatal sound, what?
Having stepped forward,
[the suffix] *iṭ* is optionally applied by Pāṇini 7.2.50;
having purified.
Having purified.
The elision of the nasal (ṇ) and of *na* may optionally occur before the suffix *ktvā*; thus,
*bhaktvā* or *bhaṅktvā*.
By the rule *rañjeś ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.61), which states that the augment *num* is added after the roots *rañj* and *masj*, the augment *num* is applied.
In its place, there is elision: *naṣṭvā*,
*naṃṣṭvā*.

By the rule *radhādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.45), the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied; in the alternative where it is not applied, it should be stated that [the substitution of *naś* for *naś*] occurs before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant (*vā*).
Having anointed here, one should not speak or wear a turban.
In the alternative case,
by [Pāṇini 6.1.15] *janasana-khan-ām sañ-jhaloḥ*, there is the substitution of ā for the vowel.
Having [the roots] *khā* and *khan*,
by [the rule] *dyatisyati-SKsandarbhaḥ 3074*, there is the augment *iṭ*.
having spoken,
having smiled,
having measured; or, having gone.
From the root *sthā*, *dadhāti*, and *hi*, [the suffix] *hit* is applied. *Hitvā*.
having abandoned (SK 3331 AS 7-4-43)
The root *hāṅ* (to abandon) becomes *hātvā*, while for the root *ad* (to eat), it becomes *jagdhiḥ*. (SKsandarbhaḥ 3080)
Having eaten (SK 3332;
In a compound where the first member is an indeclinable (avyaya), provided it is not the negative particle *nañ*, there shall be the substitution of *lyap* for the suffix *ktvā*;
as in *prakṛtya*.
What else could it be?
Since there is no negation here by relying on exclusion (*paryudāsa*), [it must be understood as absolute negation].
Having made it supreme, [the suffix *ka* is applied]. (Pāṇini 5.4.33)
When the substitution of *ṣ* and the augment *tuk* are to be applied, the rule governing the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) should be considered as not having taken effect; thus,
in the example *ko 'sicat*,
the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur here.
Having studied [the Veda],
after death, there is the *tuk* augment according to Pāṇini 6.1.71 (*adhītya pretya hrasvasya*).
For roots taught with an anudātta vowel, such as *van* and *tan*, there may optionally be the elision of the nasal before the suffix *lyap*.

This is a rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, for roots ending in *m* that are optionally aniṭ, and for those ending in *n* that are invariably aniṭ, as well as for roots beginning with *v*, the augment *iṭ* is added invariably.
having approached, having bowed down,
having prostrated;
Having struck down, having made them heedless,
having caused them to fall.
Having spread out [this rule],
the *lyap* suffix, being external (*bahiraṅga*), subverts even internal (*antaraṅga*) grammatical operations— this is the "eating" (the result) of this [maxim]. (SK Sandarbha 3080)

Because of the mention of the *lyap* suffix in the rule for the formation of gerunds (*jagdhi-vidhi*), the operations of *hitva*, *dattva*, *āttva*, *etva*, *dīrghatva*, *śū*, and *ṭiṭ* do not occur when *lyap* follows.
Having arranged,
having placed,
having dug out.
having set out, having departed,
having taken leave.
Having played at dice and having recited [the scriptures].
AS 6.4.69: When *lyap* follows, the substitution of *ī* occurs for the vowels of roots belonging to the *ghu*, *mā*, and *sthā* groups, but not for *dheṭ*.
Having established,
having measured,
having sung forth.
Having drunk,
having abandoned,
having flowed forth.
By the rule *mīnāti-minoti-śāsty-ātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.1.50), there is the substitution of *ā*;
having measured (*pramāya*) and having inferred (*nimāya*).
The *vibhāṣā* [explains] that it is derived from the root *lī*,
meaning "to dissolve" (*vilāya*).
Having dissolved it, [there is] disappearance; having drawn it up.
Having reflected upon this (SK 33),
[it is stated] in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (AS 6.4.56):
The substitution of *ay* for the suffix *ṇi* occurs after a light-pūrva (light-initial) root when *lyap* follows; as in *vigaṇayya* and *praṇamayya*.
Having pierced it through from the front with ease, what should be considered next?
In the case of the suffix *lyap*, the substitution of *ay* for the root *āp* may optionally take place after the causative suffix *ṇi*.
having caused to reach and having reached;
AS 6.4.59: There shall be lengthening of the vowel of the root *kṣi* when the suffix *lyap* follows;
as in *prakṣīya*.
In the case of the root *veñ*, there shall be no *samprasāraṇa* substitution when the suffix *lyap* follows.
Having caused to go forth;
To the one who has grown strong, [the suffix *yat* is applied].
Having put on [the upper garment].

The semivowel *i* of *pari* may undergo *samprasāraṇa* even when followed by *lyap*, because it is subsequent [to the rule for *tuka*] and thus prevails over it; consequently, by Pāṇini 6.4.157 (*thali ca seṭi*), the long vowel is applied,
resulting in *parivīya*.
Having wrapped himself up, how can he sleep with his mouth open?
Having closed his eyes, how can he laugh?
Because sleep and laughter continue even after the moments of opening and closing [the eyes], it will be [understood] with the intention of referring to those parts [of the action].
When repetition is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇamul* shall be used in the same cases as *ktvā*, and there is reduplication;
for example: *smāraṃ smāraṃ namati śivam* ("remembering again and again, he bows to Śiva").
Remembering again and again,
drinking again and again, eating again and again.
By the rule *śrāvaṃ śrāvaṃ ciṇṇamuloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.12), there is optionally a lengthening of the vowel before a *ṇamul* suffix when it follows a causative (*ṇi*) suffix; thus,
*gamaṃ gamam*.
According to Pāṇini 7.1.64 (*gāmaṃ gāmam vibhāṣā ciṇṇamuloḥ*), there is optionally the augment *num* after the root *labh*,
as in *lambhaṃ lambham*.
According to the established option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the augment *num* is always applied after [the word] *lābha* when it is preceded by another [word],
as in *pralambhaṃ pralambham*.
By the rule *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu* (Pāṇini 7.3.85), there is *guṇa*;
thus, *jāgaram*. The same applies to the causative (*ṇyanta*) as well.

When the word *yat* is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), that [suffix] which is otherwise obtained for denoting a prior time is not applied if the sentence— consisting of two actions, one prior and one subsequent— does not require another [sentence] to complete its sense.
Since he eats and then recites,
why are the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* not used here when there is no mutual expectancy?
When one goes after having eaten, and then studies, [the suffix -yaṅ is applied].
The term "repetition" (ābhīkṣṇe) does not carry over;
when these words are used as upapadas, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are optionally employed for two actions having the same agent when referring to the prior action, as in:
*agre-bhojam vrajati* ("he goes while eating first").
Having first eaten the foremost meal, having first eaten the first meal.
Having first eaten the food, the suffixes *laṭ* and so forth are used in the sense of the past tense (*pūrva*).
He eats first and then goes;
however, in the case of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), by the rule of prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the [repetitive] suffix is always applied:
*agre bhojaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* ("he goes eating and eating").
Having eaten and eaten.

When a verbal root meaning "to call out" (ākrośa) has a direct object (*karman*) as its upapada, and the sense of "calling out" is implied, the word *cauraṅkāram* is used; here the root *kṛ* signifies "uttering."
The meaning is: having uttered the word "thief" (cora).

The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after the root *kṛ* when it refers to pleasant things (*svādu*), provided that both actions have a single agent and the action denoted by the *ṇamul*-ending precedes the other in time; furthermore, the final vowel of the preceding word is prescribed to be replaced by *m*. For example:
*asvāduṃ svāduṃ kṛtvā bhuṅkte* (having made it tasty, he eats) becomes *svāduṅkāraṃ bhuṅkte*; likewise, *sampannaṅkāram*.
In the word *lavaṇaṅkāram*, the two forms *sampanna-lavaṇa* and *lavaṇa-śabda* are synonyms for "sweetness";
or, by the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the suffix *ktvā* may also be used.
Having made it sweet, he eats.

In these cases, the suffix *ṇamul* shall be applied after the root *kṛ*. "Established non-employment" (*siddha-aprayoga*) means that the root *kṛ* is unfit for employment because it is redundant; that is to say, it is superfluous. For example:
*anyathākāram*.
He eats in this manner, in that manner, and in such a manner.
The meaning is "he eats in this manner"; why [is the term] *siddha* used? [For example:
"having turned his head otherwise, he eats."
[The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *kṛ*, provided that the action has been accomplished and there is no usage [of the verb].
In response out of malice: "I shall eat according to my desire; I shall eat however I wish; what is this of yours to you?
When a verbal root meaning "action" (karman) is used as an upapada, the suffix ṇamul shall be employed; for example:
*kanyādarśaṃ varayati* ("he asks for the hand of the girl upon seeing her").
The meaning is "all the girls.
The phrase "he feeds the Brāhmaṇas according to the Veda" means that he feeds every single Brāhmaṇa whom he knows, obtains, or considers.
He eats as much as he finds in the Veda.
The meaning is "as much as can be obtained"; for example: "he studies as long as he lives" (yāvajjīvam adhīte).
Only when [the action] is an object [is it expressed in the accusative],
as in "he spreads a leather mat."
He eats until his belly is full.

When *pūri* (to fill) has a verbal noun (*karmopapada*) as its object, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied and the vowel *ū* may optionally be elided, provided that the total amount of rain is understood from the whole expression; for example:
*goṣpadapūraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* or *goṣpadapraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("the god rained enough to fill a cow's footprint").
Regarding the word "asya" (of this), why [is it mentioned]?
So that it does not apply to a derivative such as *mūṣikābilapra*.
Pāṇini 3.4.33: When words meaning "clothing" are used as objects, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied to the root *knū* (to moisten) to express the measure of rain.
The god rained so as to wet the robe, to wet the garment,
to wet the clothing.
He will state that in the case of *kaṣ* and other roots, there must be an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*) even when the object is present.
In this context, the term "prior time" (pūrvakāla) is not connected [to the following],
as in the expressions *nimūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati* and *samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati*.
The meaning is that it "grazes" (destroys) both rootless and rooted [objects].
Even for a single verbal root-meaning, there is a distinction due to its connection with qualifiers such as "rootless" and so forth;
thus, by way of the relationship between the general and the particular, there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified.
In these actions, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *piṣ*.
*Śuṣkapeṣam* means he grinds dryly; that is, he grinds it dry, as in *cūrṇapeṣam*.
With a rough grinding.
Thus, regarding actions,

In the Vedic domain, when *su* or a prefix (*upasarga*) is the upapada, the three suffixes beginning with *manin* may be added to verbal roots ending in long *ā*; furthermore, by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *vic* is also included.
Sudāmā,
Sudhīvā, Supīvā.
The bountiful giver,
the drinker of ghee,
the all-pervading one.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *pā* (to drink) when preceded by the words *brahma*, *bhrūṇa*, and *vṛtra*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.87)
AS 3-2-88: Even when there is another subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *kvip* may optionally be applied frequently after the root *han*; for example, *mātṛhā*.
The *liṭ* [affix] is used for the past tense in general in Vedic literature (*chandasi*), as in the case of "pitṛhā" (the killer of a father).— *Sārasvatī Kaṇṭhābharaṇa* 3093.
I have stretched across heaven and earth; [the form] *ātatāna* is derived from the root *tan* with the suffix *kānac* (or *kvasu*) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the suffixes *kānac* and *kvasu* optionally take the place of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) marker;
[as in] *cakrāṇā vṛṣṇi*.
O Agni, whoever is ungenerous toward us and seeks to do us harm... [yo no agne ararivā~ aghāyuḥ].

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *iṣṇuc* may be added to a verbal root ending in the causative marker *ṇi*, in the sense of "one who habitually performs that action" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; as in: "the plants are those that cause one to cross over" (*vīrudhaḥ pārayiṣṇavaḥ*).
And from this [root] *bhu* alone, as before, [the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied] to form *bhaviṣṇuḥ*.
In the Vedic language, there is an addition [to the rule] regarding the suffix *kyac* when expressing the desire of another;
[thus], by the rule *kyācchandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.170), the suffix *u* may occur after a word ending in *kyac*.
In the section concerning *aghāyu*, the forms *javas* and *java* should be stated as Vedic alternatives;
for example, "in speed" (*jave*) and "with which [steeds] the youths" (*yābhir yūnaḥ*).
May there be speed in my thighs at the impulse of the god Savitṛ. (At the impulse of the god Savitṛ.
AS 3-3-96: After the group of words beginning with *vṛṣan*, the suffix *ktin* occurs, and it is acute-accented; [as in] *vṛṣṭim divaḥ* ("the rain from heaven").
For the sake of bliss,
cook the cooked offerings;
this is your newest prayer.
Prosperity, abundance— O Agni, come for the feast! (Agni, come for the feast!)
May we be free from fear at night. (rātau syāmo bhayāsaḥ) SK 3421 AS 3-3-129.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *yuc* may be added after verbal roots meaning "to go" when words such as *īṣat* are used as upapadas; this is an exception to [the rule for] *khal*. For example:
*sūpasadano 'gniḥ* ("the fire is easy to approach").
Pāṇini 3.3.130:
After verbal roots other than those meaning "motion," the suffix *yuc* may also be applied in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
You made the cow easy to find for the priest.
When there is a connection between the meanings of verbal roots across all tenses, these suffixes may optionally occur according to their respective rules; for example:
*devo devebhirāgamat* ("the god came with the gods").
The *luṅ* [aorist] is used in the sense of the *loṭ* [imperative]:
"I have offered this salutation to them" (*idaṃ tebhya akaraṃ namaḥ*).
The *laṅ* [imperfect] [is also used in this sense].
"Today this sacrificer has chosen Agni as the Hotṛ priest; today someone has died. (Today someone has died.)
The meaning is "he dies today" (SK 3424; AS 3.4.7).
In the Vedic language, the suffix *leṭ* occurs after a verbal root in the sense of an injunction and in the sense of the relation between cause and effect, etc.; Pāṇini 3.4.7.
In the *leṭ* mood, the *i* of the *tiṅ* suffixes may optionally be elided when followed by parasmaipada endings.
In the case of the *leṭ* suffix, the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ* are added; both of these are marked with the *p* indicator.
It should be explained extensively (or):
"May he prolong our lives" (*pra na āyūṃṣi tāriṣat*).
He makes it well-adorned, for he shall enjoy it; he has impelled [it] for the one who desires to see,
provided there is the absence of the *sip* and *lopa*.
The lightning shall fall;
he shall become dear to Sūrya, dear to Agni.
There may optionally be elision of the *s* of the first person plural ending (*leṭ*) [before the suffix *vā*],
as in *karavāva*.
We shall cause [the substitution] of *re* for *et* to be performed;
AS 3.4.95: In the *leṭ* mood, the vowel *ā* is replaced by *ai*.
Example: *sutebhiḥ suprayasā mādayaite* (with the pressed juices and excellent food, may you two rejoice).
The substitution of *ai* for the form *ātām* occurs by virtue of the rule's specific injunction;
otherwise, the rule would have simply prescribed *aiṭ*.
Whoever sacrifices, whoever causes to sacrifice (whoever sacrifices, whoever causes to sacrifice).
In the case of the *leṭ* [Vedic subjunctive] ending *ekār*, by the rule *aisādvā āta ai* (Pāṇini 3.4.93), except for its specific scope,
the *grahas* (sacrificial vessels) are seized with the formula *paśūnām īśe*.
Elsewhere, how may they two be exhilarated by the excellent offering? (suprayasā mādayete) SK 3431
The *leṭ* suffix shall be used in cases of a wager and in expressions of doubt; for example:
"I alone am the lord of cattle."
"nejjihmā yantau narakaṃ patāma" (nejjihmā yantau narakaṃ patāma); [the substitution of] *śnā* for *hal* [before] *jha* is replaced by *śānac*. (Pāṇini 3.1.83). SK Sandarbha 2557;

By virtue of the word "api" [in the preceding rule], there is the substitution of *bh* for *h* in the case of the roots *hṛ* and *grah* when followed by the suffix *śānac*, according to the Vedic usage. (Vārttika)
"Seize the honey with your tongue;
bind it, O divine Savitṛ"— in this [mantra], there is no elision of the *n* in the word *badhāna*.
I take hold of you; he has brought [you] with honey.
AS 3.1.85: In the Vedic language, there is frequently an interchange of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*); for example: *āṇḍā śuṣṇasya bhedati*.
In the case of *bhinatti*,
it is obtained as *jarasā mriyate patiḥ* (the husband dies from old age), whereas in the case of *mriyate*, it is obtained as *jarasā mriyate patiḥ*.
May Indra lead you with wealth;
*neṣatu* is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *nī*, with two suffixes, *śap* and *sip*. With Indra as our ally, may we overcome Vṛtra.
The meaning is "let us cross";
here, the suffix *liṅ* is used for the optative (*vidhi*) and other moods of the root *tṛ*, and there are three affixes: *u*, *śap*, and *sip*.

The author of the grammar intends a transposition (vyatyaya) of the following: case endings (sup), verbal suffixes (tiṅ), voice (upagraha), gender (liṅga), number (nara), tense (kāla), suffixes beginning with ha or la (halac), accent (svara), the agent (kartṛ), and the yaṅ affix; and that [transposition] is also established by means of the principle of diversity (bāhulaka).

Regarding "on the yoke-pole of the sacrificial fee" (*dhuri dakṣiṇāyāḥ*), where one would expect "of the southern [pole]" (*dakṣiṇasyām*), there is the verse: "Those who carve the *caṣāla* for the horse-sacrifice pillar" (*caṣālaṃ ye aśvayūpāya takṣati*).
Where *takṣanti* would otherwise be expected, there is the substitution of the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings; [as in the case of] one who desires a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
Where "icchatī" (he desires) would otherwise be expected, another wave [of meaning] arises as "pratīpam" (in opposition);
where "yudhyate" (he fights) would otherwise be expected, [another arises].
"They sit as if satiated with honey" (*madhostṛptā ivāsate*); where *madhunaḥ* was expected,
the word *naraḥ* means "man."
"Then may he be separated from his ten heroic sons"—
the form *viyūyāt* is used where *viyūyīta* was expected; here the suffix denotes time (*kāla*).
By one who is about to establish the sacred fires tomorrow, [it is said]:
"He milked the cows of darkness" (in the domain of the *luṅ* tense, the *lṛṭ* is used).
In the case where *adhukṣat* is expected,
[the reading is] *mitra vayaṃ ca sūrayaḥ*; and in the case where *mitrā vayam* is expected, [the reading is likewise].
The reversal of vowels will be explained later;
the word *kartṛ* (agent) refers here to the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) in general,
and thus there is a reversal of the primary suffixes (*kṛt*) and secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) that express it.
Regarding the word *annādya* in the sense of "food," there is a specific rule concerning the absence of an avagraha.
Starting from the word *yaṅ* up to the rule *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.4.104), there is a pratyāhāra formed by the letter *ṅ*;
the transposition (*vyatyaya*) of these, such as in the case of *bheda-ti*, has already been stated.

In the Vedic language, when the suffix *liṅ* of the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) follows, the substitute *aṅ* is applied to the verbal root; furthermore, for the root *vac*, the substitute *um* is applied.
Let us speak a mantra to Agni;
may I behold my father and my mother.
In the case of the suffix *aṅ*, however, there would be *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *ṛdṛśo'ṅi* (Pāṇini 7.4.16).

In the section on verbal roots (*dhātu*), it has been stated that a suffix (*pratyaya*) may bear both the designation *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka*. Thus, in the example *vardhantu tvā suṣṭutayaḥ* ("May the excellent praises increase thee"), the meaning is "may they cause thee to grow."
Because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, there is the elision of the *ṇi* affix;
[in the case of] *viśṛṇvire*,
because it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, there is the *śnu* affix and the substitution of *śṛ*.
By the rule *huśnuvoḥ...* (Pāṇini 6.4.87), *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs;

by the rule *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.171), the suffixes *kikin* occur after roots ending in long *ā*, roots ending in *ṛ*-vowels, and the root *gam*, and these two suffixes function like the *liṭ* (perfect) suffixes.
Bearing the thunderbolt,
drinking the Soma, bestowing the cows.
The youth who has gone forth,
the slayer of Vṛtra, the enemy;
he has been born.

Since the status of being like the *liṭ* (perfect tense) suffix would have already established this, the *kittva* (the property of having a *k* as an it-marker) is for the purpose of subverting the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by *ṛcchatyṝtām...* (Pāṇini 7.4.11).
Furthermore, the *utva* (substitution of *u*) is applied by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.4.78), resulting in the form *taturiḥ*.
The suffix *jaguri* occurs after [the root] *skand*,
according to Pāṇini 3.4.9.
May he speak of wealth to us.
Grant those [autumns] for us in the left-hand quiver, that we may live through many autumns.
Because it is a future participle (*asennit*), it has the acute accent on the first syllable;
[the suffix] *kse* is used in the sense of an injunction (*preṣe*).
Like a bull for the sake of the beauty of the cows, for the sake of glory.
In *adhyain* and *jaṭharaṃ pṛṇadhyai*,
the first syllable of the second member (*pakṣa*) is udātta.
To be praised at every moment, to be invoked at every moment.
In this case,
the *nitsvara* accent is established for the purpose of rejoicing together with the gift of wealth.
To drink for Vāyu, for you to drink.
The two must be given for the sake of procreation and for the sake of giving birth.
To be performed by means of austerity.
AS 3-4-10: These are prescribed as irregular forms (nipātana) in the sense of the infinitive suffix -tum;
the meaning is "to go," "to obstruct," and "to be free from pain."
"To see" means "to become famous."
When the word *śaknoti* ("is able") is used as a governing term (*upapada*) in the sense of "being able to," these two suffixes [the infinitive suffix *tumun* and the gerundive suffix *kṛtya*] occur.
He was unable to divide,
he was unable to tear apart; the meaning is that he could not separate or dismember.
The Lord is capable of moving about. (SK 3440; AS 3.4.13)
The Lord is capable of scratching; that is to say, of wandering about or scratching.
One should not speak barbarously while bathing.
Deserving to be seen,
he is one whose deeds are manifold and manifest.
AS 3-4-15: "One should not look down upon [it] by means of an enemy" (ripuṇā nāvacakṣe); the meaning is that it must not be viewed [with hostility].
They sit down until the conclusion [of the rite].
The meaning is that they sink until completion; [this refers to] one who rises up or one who causes decline.
"We shall come into being from desire and from the vital breath," so says the Śruti.
AS 3-4-17: *bhāvalakṣaṇe* ity eva;
*purā krūrasya visṛpo virapśin* (O mighty one, before the onset of the cruel).
"Before piercing the collarbones"—
this is the third chapter. SK 3445.
The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after the word *rātri* in the Vedic language when it does not denote a cow;
[as in] "The night, approaching, has shone forth" (*rātrī vyakhyad āyatī*).
In common usage, however, by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.45), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, and the word is oxytone.
In the Vedic domain, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is obligatorily applied after words such as *bahu*;
for instance, *bahvīṣu hi tvā*.
The inclusion of the word "obligatorily" (*nitya*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied [after a stem ending in *a*].
In the sūtra "vibhvī prabhvī viprasaṃbhyo ḍuḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.89), the form ending in the suffix *ḍu* is cited as it appears in the rule.

Because of the recurrence of the word "uta," the substitution of *uvaṅ* is based on a Vedic rule; furthermore, according to the Vārttika, the suffix *liṭ* is optionally applied after the word *mudgala* in the Vedic language.
Because of the *li*-characteristic of the suffix *ṅīṣ*, there is the augment *mānuk* and the accent of the *li*-suffix;
thus [we have] *rathīrabhūnmudgalānī*.
In rule Pāṇini 4.1.59, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not otherwise apply because the word ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), it is here prescribed.
Dīrghajihvī was indeed the daughter of Asura; she was the sacrificial ground of the gods.
The word *uṅ* should be [the suffix] for *kadrū*, *kamaṇḍalu*,
and [words ending in] *-guggulu*, *-madhu*, *-jatu*, and *-patayālu*; thus it should be stated as an alternative (*vā*).
Guggulu, Madhu, and Jatū.
The suffix *tyap* is applied after the word *patayālu*;
furthermore, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of this rule for the word *āviṣṭya* in Vedic usage.
He grows when entered [by the breath]. (āviṣṭyo vardhate) SK 3450 AS 4-3-19
The suffix *aṣṭaka* is an exception (*apavāda*) for [the suffix] *varṣābhyaḥ*;
there is a difference in accent:
*vārṣikam*.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffix *ṭhañ* shall occur [after the word "chandasa"].
The spring season (vāsantika) [is derived from vasantā], Pāṇini 4.3.21.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied] to form *haimantika*;
the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after [words such as] *śaunaka* and others in the sense of "proclaimed" (*prokta*) according to the Veda (*chandas*); it is an exception to the suffixes *cha* and *aṇ*.
Those who study what was proclaimed by Śaunaka are called *śaunakinaḥ*.
Are the Vājasaneyins [the followers] of the *Śaunakīya-śikṣā* regarding the Vedic meters?
The suffix *mayaṭ* may be used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).
He for whom the sacrificial grass is made of reeds and the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood.
A sling made of muñja grass that has undergone the change to *u* (i.e., contains the vowel *u*) [is used].
A leather thong is a product of hide; a rope made of it is called *vārdhrī*.
A sacrificial post (*yūpa*) made of *bilva* wood is that which belongs to the assembly hall (*sabhā*).
A youth who is fit for the assembly.
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.4.110:
The suffix *yat* is applied after a word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*) in the sense of "being there" (*bhava*).
And for *meghya* and *vidyutya*—
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) such as *aṇ* and others, as well as those beginning with *gha*, according to their respective rules;
that these [suffixes] also occur in the alternative case.
Since all rules are optional in the Vedic language (chandas),
it is as follows: for example,
there is a mountain named Muñjavat.
In that context, "bhava" refers to the consumption of *mauñjavat* soma, as in "the consumption of *mauñjavat* soma.
This heading concerning the meters (*chandas*) applies up to the completion of the fourth [chapter].
"Then Pāthya, the bull... (RV 8.91.2).
May he who dwells in the river accept my songs; may he who dwells in the water be one who accepts the water-offering.
He who dwells in the river is the river-dweller; he who dwells in the water is the water-dweller.
In the sense of "becoming" (bhāve), [the suffix *ghañ* is applied].
Hail to the Vaiśantī waters!
Hail to the Haimavatī waters!
According to Pāṇini 4.4.113, the suffix *yat* is optionally used; however, there is a difference in accentuation between [the forms ending in] *ḍyaṅ* and *ḍyaya*.
That which exists in a stream is *srotya* or *srotasya*.
*anubhrātā* means "a brother from the same womb"; *anusakhā* means "one belonging to the same herd."
"He who has struck us from afar or even one who has struck us close by"—
the word *nuti* (striking) is derived from the root *nṛt* with the suffix *kta* used in the neuter sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

The three compounds beginning with *sagarbha* are also *karmadhārayas*; by the rule *samānasya chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.3.84), *sa-* is substituted for *samāna-*, and from that, the suffix *yañ* is added in the sense of "originating therein" (*bhavārtha*).
Because there is an exception (apavāda).
In the context of existence, even that which is [found] in the *pakṣa*:
"Bring hither for us the bull among you in the *tugryā* [battles]. (ā vaḥ śamaṃ vṛṣabhaṃ tugryāsu).
Thus say the Bahvṛcas;
in another recension, [it says] "among the Tugriyas," and the commentary states that the word *tugra* refers to those who possess wealth, space, and excellent sacrifices.
That which exists at the beginning is "agrya."
Foremost; the foremost.
[The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *agra*] when preceded by *ca*, etc.;
that which exists at the front (*agre*) is *agrya*.
foremost,
preeminent; the very first.
The ocean-born waters [protect] the wise one,
like the thundering cloud.
The sounds [are produced].

By the rule *prāg-hita-ād-yat* (Pāṇini 5.1.1), the suffix *yat* is applied [to form *barhiṣya*] in the sense of "deposited on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣyeṣu nidhiṣu*) which are "beloved" (*priyeṣu*). (Barhiṣyeṣu nidhiṣu priyeṣu) [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.4.6.6].
The office of messenger belongs to Bhārgava Aṃśa.
O Agni, that body of yours which belongs to the Rākṣasas.
When *yat* is used in the sense of praise, it occurs [after the word *praśasta*]. (Pāṇini 5.1.122)
The praise of Revatī and the others is the Revatya, the Jāgata, and the Haviṣya.
All that belongs to the Asuras has been taken away by the gods.
The demoniacal illusion (āsurī māyā) [is the subject] of Sūtra 4.4.124.
The bricks for which the mantra used for placing them contains the word *varcas* are called *varcasyāḥ*. (Śulba-sūtra 3471; Āpastamba-śulba-sūtra 4.4.125)
The seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā).
*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 3.4.7.2;
*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 4.4.126.
He places the Āśvinī verses.
The entire sūtra *tadvānāsām* applies here.
By repeating the word *mātuḥ* so that it ends in the ablative case (*matuḥ*), it should be understood as follows:

after the word *mūrdhan* which possesses the suffix *matup*, there shall be the suffix *matup*, and there shall be the elision (*luk*) of the first *matup*. Thus, the usage is seen in the rule: "He places the bricks called *mūrdhanvatī*, which are to be laid down with mantras containing the word 'head' (*vayas-'), like the word *vayaḥ*."
*nabhas* (the sky) and *abhra* (cloud).
Because it exists in this [month], it is the month Nabhasya; it is the body of vital energy (ojas).
*mādhavaḥ* and *madhavyaḥ*.
In the sense of "strength," the word *ojas* takes the suffix *amahan*.
Or [the suffix *kha* is applied] after a word ending in *ojas*, when it denotes the recipient (*ojasīnam*).
According to their respective order, "veśa" (entrance) is not accepted; rather, that very "bala" (strength) is "bhaga" (fortune),
thus [the term] is "veśobhagya."
Possessing a share of the dwelling,
possessing a share of glory, possessing a share of fame.
The separation of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of subsequent rules and for the sake of setting aside the [specific] order.
By deep and ancient paths.
Those paths of yours, O Savitṛ, which are ancient—
To whom this oblation belongs. (To whom this apyam oblation belongs.
"Thousandfold like the waves of the waters"— the meaning is that they are equal to a thousand.
After the word *sahasra*, the suffix *gha* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
Thus, "one who possesses a thousand" is *sahasriyaḥ*.
A Brahmin is gentle.
The meaning is "worthy of sacrifice" (yajñārha).
From the word *soma*, that which occurs in the sense of *mayaṭ* is *somyam madhu* (sweetness of Soma),
meaning "consisting of Soma."
From the word *madhu*, the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of *mayaṭ*.
*Madhavyaḥ* means consisting of honey (*madhumaya*). (SK 3486)
By the rule *cānmayaḍarthe yat* (Pāṇini 5.4.25), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of *mayaṭ*; thus,
*vasavyaḥ*.
There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the word *chandas* when it refers to a collection of syllables (*akṣarasamūha*).
The meaning is that the suffix *yaT* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after the word *chandas* when it denotes such a collection of syllables.

"Āśrāvaya" consists of four syllables; "astu śrauṣaṭ" consists of four syllables; "yaj" consists of two syllables; "ye yajāmahe" consists of five syllables; and the *vaṣaṭ*-call consists of two syllables. This, indeed, is the seventeen-syllable *chāndasya*.
In its own sense (svārthe) [the suffix is applied]. (Pāṇini 5.4.15)
Hail to the Nakṣatriyas! (Hail to the Nakṣatriyas!
May Savitṛ impel for us our own welfare; may Savitṛ impel for us complete well-being,
turning toward the gods with a rightward turn, being gracious.
That which performs [an action] is called a *kara*.
The suffix *ac* is added after roots beginning with *pac*;
thus, "that which makes auspicious" is *śivatāti*.
With those [powers] by which you two become sources of peace for the giver (*dadāduṣe*).
And also for safety from harm.

The suffix *tāti* occurs after words such as *śiva* to denote a state (*bhāva*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*); for example, the state of being auspicious is *śivatāti*, and the state of being peaceful is *śantāti*.
The state of being free from misfortune (ariṣṭatāti).

Its measure is this: [it is called] a *varga* and there are seven *sāptas*; he created the seven *sāptas*. [The suffix] *ḍini* is prescribed after the word *sapta* in the Vedic language in the sense of "its measure is this" (*tadasya parimāṇam*). [Thus: *sapta-sāptin*. He created the seven groups of seven.
It should be stated that half-months consist of fifteen [days], months consist of thirty [days], and [the year consists of] twenty [months].
The suffix *vatup* is optionally prescribed after words ending in *viṃśati*, after *aṅgiras*,
and after the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when expressing similarity;
thus [we have] *tvāvataḥ* and *purūvaso*.
But there is no other like you who [accepts] the sacrifice of a sage such as I.
From a nominal stem alone, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "that which is fit for it" or "that which is capable of it," as in *sādanyam* and *vidarthyam*.
[The suffix *kṛt*] is used in the sense of "accomplished" (*nirvṛtta*) and so forth.
The suffix *idvatsara* is applied [to denote a year] according to Pāṇini 5.1.92.
Transparent, lasting a year,
pertaining to a year.
Annual; belonging to the year.
From the word *ṛtu*, in the sense of "that has been obtained by him," the suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is applied; thus, *ṛtviyaḥ* means "one who has obtained his share at the proper season."
The suffix *vati* occurs in its own sense after a word denoting an instrument (*sādhana*) that is qualified by the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
"From the high places and the low places" means from those that have gone upward and those that have gone downward; this is the meaning.
AS 5.2.50: After a word ending in *n* that is not a numeral, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is replaced by *thaṭ*, and the augment *maṭ* is added; for example, *pañcatham*.
The fifth [sūtra] in the Veda is: "paripanthin and pariparin [are used] in the sense of one who lies in wait"; *paryavasthātā* means an enemy (*śatru*).
May they not find you as an obstacle; may they not find you as those who block your path.

The suffix *vini* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) within the section on Vedic terminology (*chandasi vinprakarane*). It should be stated as a supplementary rule (*vārttika*) that there is lengthening of the vowel in *aṣṭrā*, *mekhalā*, *dvaya*, *ubhaya*, *rujā*, and *hṛdaya*.
Thus, the long [hymn] for the most bountiful one who protects both sides;
auspiciously he moved about with the goad.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffixes *īvan* and *īp* should also be mentioned;
[as in] *rathīr abhūt*.
This bride is most auspicious;
we pray for wealth.
In the rule AS 5.3.20,
the forms *idam* and *etad* occur respectively [in place of *idam* and *etad*]:
"For now indeed is your praise" (*idā hi va upastutim*).
In that case,
[the rule] is Sāṃkhyakārikā 35 and *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 5.3.26.
What would be the point? What kind of talk is this? Why do you not ask about the village?

Two indeclinables are substituted for *avara* in the sense of *astāti*.

He who is ill-disposed toward us for his own sake,

In a bahuvrīhi compound, the word *datṛ* shall be substituted for *danta*; for example, *ubhayatodan* "one who has teeth on both jaws" [accepts].
The suffix *kap* is not added to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ṛ*.
He whose mother is slain is "one whose mother is slain" (hatamātṛ).
The *tudīdi* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*):
*prabhara*, *tūtujānaḥ*,
*sūrye māmahānam*.

There shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *hvṛ* root;

Regarding the word *ṛc* in the Veda:
it should be stated that when the word *ṛc* follows, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel *i* in *tri*, and the elision of the initial sound of the subsequent member;
thus [we have] *tṛcaṃ sūktam*.
In the Vedic language,
[the substitution of] *tryṛca* for *rayermatī* occurs diversely.
Possessing wealth, possessing riches, the increaser of prosperity.

In the case of *liṭ* with the suffix *us*, the forms are *nyaṃnyaṃ cikyuh* and *nicikyur anyam*. (The repetition *nyaṃnyaṃ* and *nicikyur* are included for clarity. This is the form in *liṭ* with the suffix *us*.
Because the term "frequently" (*bahula*) is understood to carry over here, [the rule does not apply] in this case:
*agnim jyotir nicāyya* (having perceived Agni as light).
These are irregularly formed (nipātita) in the Veda:
"O Indra and Viṣṇu, when we two contended" (indraśca viṣṇo yadapaspṛdheyām).
In the *laṅ* tense of the root *spṛdh*: *aspardhetām*; they sang praises to the Sun (*arkam ānṛcuḥ*); they bestowed riches (*vasūni ānṛhuḥ*).
And for the root *arc*, when followed by the affix *us* in the *liṭ* tense,
[the form] is *cicyuṣe*; for the root *cyu*, when followed by *thās* in the *liṭ* tense, [the form is *cicyuṣe*].

Those Soma-draughts, O Indra, which one has abandoned— [the root] *tyaj* with the suffix *naḷ*, [meaning] they have been left behind; those Soma-draughts of yours, O Indra, have been prepared (*śrātāḥ*).
Our cups are supported;
they yield the mixed milk when the cooking is complete.
In the form *madhyata āśīrtaḥ*, the root *śrī* [is used] with the suffix *kvip* and the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) suffix [respectively]. (SK 3513)
In the sense of dejection, the root *khid* may optionally take the prefix *ā*.
"Cikhāda" means "he chewed.
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.60: For the word *śiras*, the substitute *śīrṣan* shall occur [in the nominative singular];
[as in] *śīrṣṇaḥ śīrṣṇo jagataḥ*.
After a long vowel, before the suffix *jas* and before *ic*, there may optionally be a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one.
The boar-like Vārāhī and the two Vārāhyas are praised by the human tribes.

As in "sūrmaṃ suṣirāmiva" (sū̱rma̭ṃ suṣi̱rāmi̭va), there is also the formation of the single substitute by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), or [as in] *ijyamānaḥ*.
being sacrificed (yajyamānaḥ) [is formed by the suffix śānac according to Pāṇini 3.2.126] SK 3516,
There shall be an elision:

Regarding those various [forms] of *piṇḍānām*, it should be stated that the substitution of *eman* occurs in the Veda; for example,

*Bhayya* means "one who fears this"; *pravayyā* is a feminine-only irregular formation (*nipātana*) from the root *vī*,
whereas elsewhere it is *praveyā*.
What difference is there in the Veda that ought to be understood?
The addition of *hradayya* is prescribed (as an alternative).
Water existing in a lake is called *hradayyā āpaḥ*; in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of "being in."
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.115:

An *eṅ* (the vowels *e* and *o*) situated in the middle of a quarter of a Vedic verse remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by *ati*, provided that the *a* of *ati* is not followed by *va* or *ya*.
Approaching the sacrifice,
O well-born one, rich in horses and gifts— what is within the foot?
They sing praises to these; what did they say to those who were behind the sheep?
In these [words], even when followed by *vy*, *apa*, or *ati*, the *eṅ* vowels remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*).
May the Vasus protect us from reproach; may the auspicious ones not step upon us.
May those who are without vows [be kept away];
this amulet with a hundred streams—
may they protect us.

In the case of *kuśikāso avasyavaḥ* (*kuśikāso avasyavaḥ*), although the *bahvṛcas* [the Ṛgvedins] maintain that there is no sandhi here, and thus the form *rathatūḥ* occurs and this [word] has arrived [in its uncombined state], and likewise in *te aruṇebhiḥ* and so forth, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) is not performed; nevertheless, it should be resolved by the principle of *bāhulaka* (diversity/exception).
However, in the *Prātiśākhya*, this matter is indeed expressly stated as a rule.
In the Yajurveda, the word *uras*, ending in the vowel *e* (eṅ), remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) before the particle *ati*.
"Uro antarikṣam" (Wide is the intermediate space);
because there is no metrical foot in the *yajus*, the statement "without a foot" is made for the sake of indicating the meaning of a foot.
In the *yajus*, the word *āpaḥ* retains its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by *asmān mātaraḥ*, as in *āpo asmān mātaraḥ*.
May Agni, enjoying the clarified butter,
[enjoy] the stalks of the bull upon the highest firmament.
In the case of *ambe*, *ambāle*, and *ambike*,
the short vowel [prescribed] by the rule *ambārtha-* (Pāṇini 7.3.107) does not apply because of this very statement.

In the word *aṅga*, when there is *eṅ* (e or o) at the beginning of a syllable followed by *akāra* (a), that *eṅ* which precedes it remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) before *ati* in the Yajurveda;
as in *prāṇo aṅge-aṅge adīdhyat*.
In the Yajurveda, when followed by an unaccented *at* that is itself followed by a guttural (*kavarga*) or the letter *dh*, the *eṅ* vowels remain in their original form.
This is that Agni; this is that sacrifice.
What [is the result] when [the word] is unaccented?
Furthermore, in the word *agre* when followed by *rudra*, the initial syllable is udātta; [this applies] when *kruddha* follows? What is the point?
This refers to one who maintains the sacred fire (agnimān).

In the Yajurveda, when followed by the word *avapathāḥ* beginning with the vowel *a* and having an unaccented (*anudātta*) initial syllable, the *eṅ* diphthongs [of the preceding word] remain in their original form (*prakṛti*). For example:
*trīruṃdrebhyo avapathāḥ* (*trīru̱ṃdrebhyo̭ avapathāḥ*).
Here, the unaccented status is established by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), which prescribes the unaccented nature of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) following another finite verb in the *laṅ* tense.
In the case of *anudātta* (unaccented),
as in *yad rudrebhyo 'vapathāḥ*,
there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent) due to the rule *nipātair yadyadi-* (Pāṇini 8.1.30).
When the vowel *aci* follows the prefix *āṅ*, it becomes nasalized, and that [nasalized vowel] retains its original form (*prakṛtyā*).

In the Vedic language, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) should be stated for *abhra-āṃ*, *apaḥ*, *gabhīra-āṃ*, and *ugraputre*, as well as for [words] beginning with *īṣā-akṣa*. (Or: it should be stated that these remain in their original form in the Veda.)
The axle-pole is golden;
this bowstring is Pūṣan— may he protect us!
In the case of the suffix *sya*, there shall be elision (*lopa*) of the *su* [case-ending] before a consonant (*hal*).
This is his light. (This is his light.
The augment *suṭ* is added to the word *candra* when it follows a short vowel as a final member of a compound, as in the mantra:
*hariścandro marudgaṇaḥ* (*hari̭ścandro ma̱rudga̭ṇaḥ*) and *suścandra dasma* (*suśca̭ndra dasma*).
In a *dvandva* compound, [the word] is an irregular formation (*nipāta*).
May the father and the mother come to me; may they both come to me without fail. May the mother and the father never indeed neglect my sacrifice.

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), for the word *samāna*, the substitute *sa* occurs when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is not *mūrdhan* or its synonyms, provided it does not begin with a vowel or a guttural nasal; however, in the feminine gender, this substitution occurs diversely (*bahulam*). For example: *sagarbhyaḥ*. In the Veda, [the forms] from *amūrdhan* onwards, including the final syllables (*udarka*), [are subject to these rules].
The region between the two worlds is for all the gods;
both Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī—
lead them toward the gods, O seekers of the divine.
kadrīcī (kadrīcī) SK 3529 AS 6-3-96
The substitute *sadha* should take the place of *saha*; and [the word] *indra* [is used] in this context of *sadhamāda* (*indram cāsmin sadhamāde*),
as is *soma* in *sadhastha* (*somam sadhastham*).
In the case of the word *pathin* as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitute *kava* is applied for the word *ku*, and there is also the substitution of *kā*.
A bad path, a wrong path, a wicked path.
In the case of the root *sah* with the suffix *ktvā*, the first two [forms] and the third [form] ending in *tṛn* are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*).
"Marudbhirugraḥ pṛtanāsu sāhlā"—
in the Prātiśākhya, it is prescribed that for a *ḍa* situated between vowels, there is *ḷ*, and for a *ḍha*, there is *hlā*; thus [it becomes] *āhahlī*.
When it reaches the middle between these two vowels, that *ḍa*-sound becomes *ḷ*; that very same sound, being the *ḍha*-sound, attains the state of *hlā* when joined with a sibilant (*ūṣman*).
The substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan* occurs when it is followed by a subsequent member of a compound;
[as in] *aṣṭāpadī* (*aṣṭāpa̱dī*).
In a mantra, there shall be a long vowel in the words *aśvāvatīm* and *somāvatīm*.
Possessing power, most intoxicating,
[consecrated] by Viśvakarman, accompanied by all the gods.
A long vowel shall be substituted [for the final vowel] before the word *mātrā*, when it follows *yad* or words ending in *oṣadhī*.
He places [it] in the plants. (He places [it] in the plants.

we quickly beg for wealth in cattle;
bring hither Jātavedas!
The word *taṅ* includes the substitution of *th* when it has the marker *ṅ*; therefore, in this case,

here are your blessings, where you have brought us prosperity.
Protecting widely.
In the *ṛc*, [the vowel] is long; thus,
in *abhīṣuṇaḥ sakhīnām* (*abhīṣuṇaḥ sakhīnām*),
the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.107] *suñaḥ*.
And [the substitution of] *ṇ* occurs for *na*, according to Pāṇini 6.3.135 (*naśca dhātusthoruṣabhyaḥ*).

Regarding *ṛbhukṣāṇam* and *ṛbhukṣaṇam*: what is [the form] in the Vedic usage (*nigama*)?

The elision of the suffix *ṇi* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) before the third person plural ending *tṛc* when it begins with *iṭ*, as in [the mantra]:
"He who is our father, our progenitor" (*yo naḥ pitā janitā*).
The meaning is "having pacified," according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.54.
the word *lyapi* is understood by way of anuvṛtti.
The substitution of *vi* for *vi-yū* and *vi-plū* occurs before the affixes beginning with *āṬ* (i.e., the kṛt suffixes marked with the indicatory letter *ā*) and so forth. (Pāṇini 6.1.44)
The meaning is "of those [stems] which do not begin with 'a' or 'ā'," as stated in Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.73.
The substitution of *aṭ* for *āṭ* does not occur when there is conjunction with the prohibitive particle *māṅ*. (Pāṇini 6.4.74)
The augment *aṭ* and the substitute *āṭ* do not occur [before the first syllable of a verbal root]; however, they do occur even when there is conjunction with the particle *māṅ*.
You have been born fierce for victorious power;
let them not sow other men’s seeds in your field.

AS 6.4.76: *prathamaṃ dadhra āpaḥ*— the elision of the *ā* [of *āpaḥ*] occurs because the substitution of *rebhāva* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) by virtue of its being an *abhīya* (intermediate) operation.

In this context, once the augment *iṭ* has been applied to the word *re*, the substitution of *rebhāva* occurs again; for that purpose, the dual ending is specified in the rule as *irayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.86).
In the case of *bhū* and *sudhī*, there is *yaṇ*; and in the case of *vanas*, there is *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.
Is it "vibhya" (from fear) or "vibhuvaṃ" (pervasive)? [The reading is] "vaneṣu cittaṃ vibhya."
"O wise one, O new one, O Agni"—
or rather, in Vedic usage, there is frequently the substitution of *sudhiyaḥ* for *tanū* and other words.
May we nourish our bodies; or may we nourish the body of Tryambaka.
The word *triyambakam* [is formed by the suffix *ṭaC*] according to Pāṇini Sūtra 4.2.24 (SK 1078),
as well as Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.99 (AS 6-4-99).
In these two cases, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) before a suffix beginning with *k* or *ṅ*; thus the poets have expanded [the Veda] (*vitatnire kavayaḥ*),
and we have flown like birds (*śakunā iva paptima*).

For the root *hṛdhi*, there shall be *syāt* [in place of *hi*],
as in *rārandhi* (*rārandhi*).

*yuyodhi jātavedaḥ*: [the root] *yu* takes the substitution of *śap*-luk (elision of the *śap* suffix),

By oneself among the gods. (tmanā deveṣu) SK 3555 AS 6-4-162
In place of *ṛtaḥ* in the word *ṛju*, *raḥ* may optionally occur before the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*,
and *īyasun*; [thus] *tvaṃ rajiṣṭham anuneṣu* (or *tvaṃ rajiṣṭham anuneṣu*) or *ṛjiṣṭham*.
That which occurs during the season is *ṛtvyam*. (SK 3556; AS 6-3-175)

The word *vāstvyam* and *vāstvam* mean "pertaining to a site" (*vāstu*). In the case of the word *madhu*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed for the feminine; thus [we have] *mādhvīr naḥ santvoṣadhīḥ* ("may the plants be sweet for us").
The elision of the letter *ma* of the suffix *mayaṭ*, which is prescribed after the word *hiraṇya*, is irregularly formed [as *hiraṇyaya*], as in:
*hiraṇyayena savitā rathena* (with a golden chariot, O Savitṛ).
AS 7.1.8: *śīṅo ruṭ*— the augment *ruṭ* shall be applied after the root *śī*.

In the alternative view [of the rule] *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.1.41), there is elision of the suffix *ta*; thus, *dhenavo duhre*. In the absence of such elision: [the form remains as *dhenavas tuduhre*].
They milked the clarified butter; I have seen his [rays] from here. (By the rule *ato bhisa ais*, *bhis* becomes *ais*).
Agni with the gods, Agni with the gods.
In place of the dual suffixes *au* and *śas*, the substitute *ad* is applied after a neuter stem ending in *a*.
However, this does not apply after the singular suffixes *su* (nominative) and *am* (accusative).
In the Vedic language, what is the word for "other" than *vārtraghna*,
and what is the word for "other" than *kāṣṭha*?
In a compound that does not have *nañ* as its first member, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. (Pāṇini 7.1.37–38)
Having caused the sacrificer to put on [the garment],
In the phrase *ṛjavaḥ santu panthāḥ*, where *panthānaḥ* is expected, [the form *panthāḥ* occurs]; and in *suḥ parame vyoman*,
where *vyomani* is expected, there is elision (*luk*) of the dative case ending (*ṅe*).
In *dhītī matī suṣṭutī*,
when *dhītyā matyā suṣṭutyā* is reached, there is the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). [And] *yā surathā rathītamo bhā devā divispṛśā*.
When [the rule] beginning with "O Aśvins, you two who possess a good chariot, who touch the sky" would otherwise apply, [the rule] "until the word *brahmaṇam*" applies instead.
When *natam* was expected, it becomes *āt*;
when *yā deva vidma tā tvā* was expected, it becomes *yā de̱va vi̱dma tā tvā̭*; when *yam* was expected, it becomes *na yuṣme vājabandhavaḥ*.
"O Indra and Bṛhaspati, [grant] for us..."—
where "for us" (*asmabhyam*) was expected, it is [expressed] as *śe uruyā*.
With boldness, through the wide and bold one— referring to that which is at the navel of the earth.
When it was concluded that [the suffix] *ḍā* is not applicable, it is stated that *anuṣṭhyā* is used;
*anuṣṭhāna* means "establishment" (*vyavasthā*) and possesses the sense of "arrangement" (*aṅga*).
After the prefix *āṅ*, [the suffix] *ḍyā* is used;
where *sādhu-yā* would otherwise be obtained, it becomes *sādhu-yā*.
Thus, it is *sādhu-yā*. When [the sense of] "requesting" (*yāc*) is intended, [it is *sādhu-yā*].

Regarding the rule "one should sacrifice in spring" (*vasantā yajeta vasante*), which is already established, there is an addition to the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.12] stating that the suffixes *āl*, *īyaṅ*, *īyāṅ*, *īkār*, and others should also be included.
In place of *urviyā*,
*dārviyā*,
and *uruṇā*, the forms *dāruṇā* and *iyā* are obtained respectively.
Regarding *sukṣetriyā*, it is derived from *sukṣetriṇā* with the suffix *ḍiyāc*;
[he is like] one who [revives] a dried-up leather bag lying in a lake.

The *āgama* [is applied] three times before the villages;

This applies specifically at the end of a question, in expressions of respect, during deliberation, in a formal greeting, and at the end of a sacrificial verse;
however, [the substitution of *i* or *u*] occurs only at the end of a question.
The sacred tradition, the three eastern villages,

"One should not say 'hotavya' three times in response to a greeting; rather, one should say:

At the end of the *yājyā*, [one says] "may we worship with hymns, O Agni.

Let it not be that [the rule] "you are doing good, O cow" applies here; what is the purpose of the condition "not being a pragṛhya"?
When *śobhane* and *māne* are addressed, this protracted modification (*pluta-vikāra*) should be stated [as an option] in the Vedic language (*chandas*); for example:
*agna 3 i patnī vaḥ*.
In the *saṃhitā* state, when followed by a vowel, the short vowels *i* and *u* become *ya* and *va* respectively.
O Agni, roar! Roar! O Agni, roar toward Indra!
O Waters,
what [is it] in Agni? O Varuṇas, [what is it] in the fire?
"In the *saṃhitā*, [is it] 'kim agna 3 i indraḥ' in the *saṃhitā*?"— this is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending to the end of the chapter.
This undertaking is for the purpose of setting aside the rule regarding the lengthening of a vowel before a homorganic consonant (*savarṇadīrghatva*) and the rule of Śākalya; or alternatively,

because *y* and *v* are not established [as having their own accent], it is for the purpose of superseding the rule "the circumflex (*svarita*) replaces the *yaṇ* of an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel followed by an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel" (Pāṇini 8.2.4).

By the paribhāṣā rule *alo’ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52], [the substitution applies] to the final letter: in the case of *nakāra* (the letter *n*),
as in *indra marutva iha pāhi somam* (*indra̭ marutva i̱ha pā̭hi soma̭m*) and *harivo medinaṃ tvā* (*harivo me̱dina̭ṃ tvā*).

These forms ending in *kvasu* are treated as irregular (*nipātita*):

In the case of *kvan* and *kvaniP*, there is the inclusion of both the general form and the specific marker; however, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding markers does not apply here, because no marker is specified in this instance.

After a long vowel, the *ru* (visarga) may optionally replace the letter *n*, provided that both [the preceding vowel and the following consonant] are not part of a verbal root (*na-aṭau*) and stand within the same foot (*eka-pāda-sthau*).
"Towards the gods with a good thought;

When *ru* follows, the nasalized substitute (*anunāsika*) necessarily takes the place of the preceding *a*; thus, *mahāṃ indraḥ* (as in *ma̱hā~ indra̭ḥ*). However, the Taittirīyas read it as *anusvāra*.

When *pati*, *putra*, and so forth follow.

Regarding "anāsevana" (non-cultivation), what does it "heat"?

According to Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.103 (pādamadhyasthasya sasya mūrdhanyaḥ syāttakārādiṣveṣu pare�ṣu): when these [sounds] beginning with *t* follow, the *s* situated in the middle of a verse-quarter (*pāda*) becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*).

"Agni fashioned you first with his flames;

Of that which is praised by men (nṛbhiṣṭuta).

The *s* following a cause (*nimitta*) situated in the preceding word becomes optionally *ṣ*,

further us with your aids.

Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.158.

This is a general rule concerning the application of accents: in whatever word a specific udātta or svarita accent is prescribed, with the exception of that single vowel, the remainder of that word shall consist of anudātta vowels;
as in *gopāyataṃ naḥ* (*gopāyataṃ naḥ*).

In this case, by the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), [the bases ending in *san*, etc. are treated as verbal roots (*dhātu*). Consequently, by the accent of the root, the vowel *ā* of *yak* becomes acute (*udātta*), while the remainder is grave (*anudātta*). It should be stated as a Vārttika that "the accent assigned later is stronger, except in the case of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). Therefore, in the example cited, both the root-accent of *gup* and the suffix-accent of *āya* are not retained.
In the phrase *yajñaṃ yajñam abhivṛdhe gṛṇītaḥ*,
why is it that even though the accent of the suffix *śnā* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 6.1.186], it is not retained here, but rather that of the suffix *tas* itself?
When an udātta vowel is elided after an anudātta vowel, that [anudātta] shall become udātta.
In the word *devīṃ vācam*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is udātta according to SK 3652.
When the suffix *añc* follows with its initial vowel elided, the preceding [syllable] shall be udātta;
this is an exception to the rule regarding the accent of the substitution for an udātta vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*).
"Lead her toward the gods, O seekers of the gods"—
it should be stated that [the suffix] *at* is not added here; as in *dādhīcaḥ*.

AS 6.1.198: An *āmantrita* (vocative) beginning with a vowel shall have its first syllable acute-accented.
For example: *agna indra varuṇa mitra devāḥ*.
In the case of a vocative (āmantrita) standing at the beginning of a line (apādādi), following a word ending in a pause (padāt), the entire form shall be anudātta (unaccented).
This eighth [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the previously mentioned sixth [rule].
[In the mantra] "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati," why is there no [elision of the *m*] at the beginning of the word?

The vocative *śutudri* in *śutudri stomam* is treated as if it were non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) when followed by another vocative, such as *agne* or *indra*. *Sanskrit Text*: *śutudri stomam* (vocative), *agne*, *indra*. *English Translation*:
"O Śutudrī, [accept] the hymn!"—here the vocative *śutudri* is treated as if it were not present for the purposes of sandhi with the subsequent vocatives *agne* and *indra*.
In this case, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for Indra and the others because, due to the non-existence of what precedes them, they lack the status of being "after a word" (*padāt paratva*).

According to the rule *amantrite samānādhikaraṇe sāmānyavacanam* (Pāṇini 8.1.73), when a vocative in grammatical apposition follows, the preceding substantive is treated as if it were non-existent. Thus, in the case of a subsequent vocative in apposition, the preceding qualifier is not considered present.
"O Agni, the radiant!
O Agni, the protector!"— why is this stated in general terms?
Let there be no [confusion] regarding the synonyms:
"O inviolable goddess Sarasvatī" (aghnye devi sarasvati).
Regarding Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.74, the author of the Bhāṣya supplied the word *bahuvacanam* and applied the term *sāmānyavacanam* from the preceding rule.
When a vocative follows a qualifying word, the preceding plural form may optionally be treated as if it were non-existent;
for example: *dvevīḥ palurvīruru naḥ kṛṇota* (*dvevī̭ḥ palurvīru̱ru na̭ḥ kṛṇota*).
Here, *ṣaḍ* is the qualifier of the goddesses (*devīnām*).
The gods are the refuge here; for the second [word], the elision of the *nighāta* accent is optional.
A word ending in a case-suffix is treated like the member of a compound when a subsequent vocative follows, for the purpose of applying the accent;
as in *dravaspāṇī śubhaspatī* (*dravaspāṇī̱ śubha̭spatī*).

In the word *śubha*, derived from the root *śubh* with the suffix *kvip*, which ends in the genitive case, there occurs the sixth-type (*ṣāṣṭhika*) acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative due to its entry into another's body;
nor should the eighth-type (*āṣṭamika*) elision (*nighāta*) be suspected,
because the preceding vocative is non-existent [in this context], as it constitutes the beginning of a *pāda*.
"O Daughter of Heaven, that mortal nourishment which is yours..."—
here, the eighth syllable of the word *divaḥ* receives the *nighāta* accent because it is followed by *paraśunā*.

The meaning is that a restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made regarding the statement "the sixth case [ending] and the word denoting the agent (*kāraka*) related to the vocative (*āmantrita*)," namely, that it refers to that which is the agent in relation to what ends in the sixth case or the vocative.
Therefore, in this case, it is not [so].

For indeclinables, there is no [requirement for] pronunciation or study; however,
