The suffix *kha* is applied after a verbal root denoting study when preceded by the prefixes *upa*, *abhi*, or *adhi*.
In the place of an acute (udātta) vowel and in the place of a circumflex (svarita) vowel, wherever there is a semi-vowel (yaṇ), the following grave (anudātta) vowel shall become circumflex (svarita),
because [the rule] "abhyabhi" applies to the circumflex semi-vowel.
Because the *khalapvi* accentuation of this *svarita* is *asiddha* (non-existent) by virtue of belonging to the third *pāda*, the *nighāta* (suppression) of the remaining syllables does not occur.
AS 8.2.5: A single substitute (ekādeśa) for [a vowel] together with an acute (udātta) [vowel] shall be acute; as in *vo’śvāḥ*.
Where indeed do you bring the lower one? (Where indeed do you bring the lower one?

When an unaccented vowel at the beginning of a word follows an accented vowel, the resulting single substitute may optionally be circumflex (*svarita*); alternatively, by the preceding rule, it may be acute (*udātta*). For example:
*vī̭daṃ jyotirhṛdaye* (vī̭daṃ jyotirhṛdaye).
The verse regarding this is: *asya śloko divīyate*.

Due to the rule of optional application (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the initial *i* is either circumflex (*svarita*) or acute (*udātta*). When the long vowel is substituted, it is acute; otherwise, it is circumflex.
Furthermore, by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), when the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* occurs, [the result] is indeed *svarita*:
*te'vadanam* (*te'vadanam*), *so 3 yamāgāt* (*so̱ 3̱̭ yamāgā̭t*).
And it is stated in the Prātiśākhya: "In the case of the coalescence of two *i*-sounds, and in the cases of *kṣaipra* and *abhinihata* [svaritas]," (SK 3660).
AS 8.4.66: A non-udātta vowel following an udātta vowel shall become svarita;
as in *agnim īḷe* (*a̱gnimī̭ḻe*).
Because this [rule] is also unestablished, there is no suppression of the remainder; thus: *tam īśānāsaḥ*.
AS 8.4.67: An unaccented vowel followed by an acute (udātta) or a circumflex (svarita) accent would not itself become circumflex;
however, according to the opinion of Gārgya, it would indeed become so.
Those who have mounted you—where are your horses? Where are your reins?
AS 1.2.33: In addressing someone from a distance, the sentence shall be in monotone; this is an exception to the rule of three accents (traisvarya).
Come, young man!
In the performance of a sacrifice, the mantra should be recited in a single tone (*ekaśruti*), with the exception of *japa* and similar practices; for example:
"Agni is the head of heaven, the summit of heaven" (*agnirmūrdhā divaḥ kakut*).
Regarding "yajña": does this mean that at the time of recitation, there must be the threefold accent (*traisvarya*)?
Regarding "ajapa": what is meant by this?
"O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations. The *japa* is a practice performed in a whisper,
like that of one submerged in water.
The *nyūṅkha* consists of sixteen *o*-sounds; these are what are designated as *sāman* in the songs.
AS 1.2.35: In the ritual of sacrifice, the word *vauṣaṭ* may be pronounced loudly, or in the middle tone, or with a single accent (monotone).
In the Vedic language (chandas), there may optionally be monotone (ekaśruti); this is a restricted option (vyavasthitavibhāṣā).
In the *Saṃhitā*, there is the threefold accent (*traisvarya*);
in the *Brāhmaṇa*, there is monotone (*ekaśruti*) for the followers of the Rigveda (*Bahvṛca*),
and for others as well, the arrangement is according to their respective traditions.

In the *nigada* called *subrahmaṇyā* during the sacrificial ritual (*yajñakarman*), the monotonous accent (*ekaśruti*) which would otherwise apply by the rules *vibhāṣā chandasi* (Pāṇini 1.2.37) and *chandasi* (Pāṇini 1.2.35) shall not occur; instead, the circumflex (*svarita*) and the acute (*udātta*) accents shall be used.
Regarding *subrahmaṇya-oṃ*:

it might be argued that since [the term] is derived from *subrahmaṇi-sādhuh* (meaning "one who is proficient in the Subrahmaṇī"), and since the result would already be established by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), the further prescription of an acute accent (*udātta*) here is redundant. However, this objection should not be raised.

There, because of the recurrence of the term "anudātta" (unaccented), the end of the word "asau" (that one) [is optionally] acute; in that very recitation, the end of the nominative singular form shall be acute.
In the case of *gārgyaḥ* performing a sacrifice,
the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) which would have applied by virtue of the suffix *ñit* is superseded by this [rule];
for *amuṣya*, the final syllable is [acute] (or, according to another view, the penultimate).
In a word ending in *syat*, the penultimate syllable and the final syllable are optionally acute;
according to Gārgya, both [the penultimate and the final] are acute when the suffix is *ina*: *pitā yajate*.
Alternatively, in the case of a name, the penultimate syllable of that name may be acute; for example:
*devadattasya pitā yajate*.
In these two [cases], within the *Subrahmaṇyā* formula, the circumflex (*svarita*) vowel shall become unaccented (*anudātta*).

That which follows an unaccented vowel and is preceded by an acute or a circumflex vowel shall have a more acute accent (*udāttatara*). For example:
*sarasvati śutudri*.

The mention of *ubhau* [in Pāṇini’s rule] is for the purpose of setting aside the rule that "a word [consisting of] more than one syllable is unaccented except for one. (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 6.1.122; Paribhāṣenduśekhara Phiṭ-sūtra 84).
AS 10-4-84 is clear; SK phi85.

The meaning is that when the suffix *cita* follows, the final syllable of the entire combination of base and suffix is to be stated as having the acute accent (*udātta*) for the sake of clarity; as in:

AS 6.1.164 states that the final syllable of a taddhita suffix added to a word denoting a collection (cita) is acute; since this was already established by the preceding rule, this [present rule] is for the purpose of overriding the accent of the *ñi* suffix.
The Kauñjāyanas (SK 3712, AS 6.1.165).

The final syllable is udātta;

In that regard, when a monosyllabic word is followed by a third-person case ending (*vibhakti*) or one beginning with the third person that is accented, as in *vācā virūpaḥ* (*vā̱cā vi̭rūpaḥ*), what is the case?
In the case of *rājñaḥ* and so forth, let it not apply even when [the suffix] follows the word *rājan*, which consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*),

Why [specify] "consisting of a single vowel"?
While you, O King, were performing the rites, did he not see speech from the third [day] onwards? No, he did not see speech.

Except in the case of a compound prescribed under the heading of "nitya" (invariable), when the final member of the compound is a monosyllabic word that is oxytone, the case-ending beginning with the third case (instrumental) following it may optionally be udātta; for example, *paramavācā*.
A case ending following the root *añc* is udātta.
In the case of *indro dadhīcaś ca*, the rule *pūrvapadāntodāttatvam* (the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member) would apply;

however, while the term *tṛtīyādiḥ* (beginning with the third [case-ending]) is still in force, the inclusion of the phrase *asarvanāmasthāna* (not being a sarvanāmasthāna suffix) is for the purpose of including the accusative plural suffix *śas*.
The two arms of the western [direction]. (The two arms of the western [direction]) SK 3717 AS 6-1-171
After these [stems], a case-ending that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* is udātta:

The mention of "ūṭh" and "upadhā" must be made [in the rule]; otherwise, it would apply here [incorrectly] in the case of *akṣadyuvā*.

It should not be argued that because the phrase "not after a word with an udātta on the final syllable" (na antodāttāt) is understood [from the previous rule] in the case of subsequent reference (anvādeśa),
there is no such final udātta in that instance either.
Because the rule *idamo 'nvādeśe 'ś anudāttaḥ tṛtīyādau* (Pāṇini 2.4.32) prescribes the enclitic *aś* as unaccented (*anudātta*) when used in subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*),

"paddannomāshṛn... (Pāṇini 6.1.63); thus, there are six [substitutions] beginning with *pad*:

A case ending beginning with *śas* is acute-accented when following [the words] *aṣṭābhiḥ* and *daśabhiḥ*.

After a word ending in the suffix *anum* (i.e., the present participle suffix *śatṛ*) which has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*), the feminine suffix *nadī* and case endings beginning with *śas* that start with a vowel (*ajādi*) shall be accented.
The first one, knowing [the path], makes it resound toward the call; why [is this] from the antodātta?
In the rule "dadhatī abhyastānām ādiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.189), the initial syllable is udātta;

In this case, one syllable is acute (udātta); because it follows [a stem] taught with a short *a* (*adupadeśāt*), the suffix *śatṛ* receives the low tone (*nighāta*) by Pāṇini 6.1.186 (*lasārvadhātuka*).
In place of an acute-accented vowel, when a *yaṇ* substitute occurs with a consonant preceding it, the following feminine suffix *nadī* and case-endings beginning with *śas* shall be acute-accented.
She is the instigator of true blessings;
she is the leader for the god Savitṛ who brings forth the cosmic order.
When *yaṇ* follows these two [vowels], the *śas*-class suffixes (*śas* and so on) shall not be acute-accented.

The suffix *matup* is udātta when it follows a word ending in a short vowel that has its final syllable udātta, as well as after [the suffix] *nuṭ*. Example:

After a word ending in the suffix *matup* which contains a short vowel and is oxytone, the following case-ending (*nāman*) may optionally be acute.

Because of the statement, "The syllable following *ṅ* is optionally unaccented (*anudātta*) in the case of *devasenānām abhibhañjatīnām*," it is not so here.

in *lulavitha*,

In a word ending with a *ṛt* suffix, the penultimate syllable shall be acute (*udātta*).
When [the offering] is in the Āhavanīya fire.

A preceding word that is connected with an acute (udātta) or circumflex (svarita) accent shall remain in its original form (prakṛti-svara),

Regarding the rule beginning with *udātta* and so forth: why [is it stated] so that, when the first member of the compound is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*), there should be only the final acute accent of the compound, as in *samapādaḥ*?
These seven, when they function as the first members in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, remain in their original form (*prakṛti*).
In the rule "tulyaśvetaḥ kṛtyatulyākhyā ajātyā" (Pāṇini 2.1.68), this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; for example,

"patayanmandayatsakham" (flying, gladdening the friend):
"mandayati mādake indre sakheti" means "the friend who gladdens the exhilarating Indra"; this is a locative tatpuruṣa compound.
"Black as a sword" (*śastrīśyāmā*) [is formed] by the indeclinable particle *nañ* according to the rule "of *nañ*, *ku*, and particles" (*avyaye nañkunipātānām*);
or else, this is not a sacrifice (*ayajña*).
What is the point of counting? For one who has bathed, even a momentary pleasure is untimely.
The suffix *iṣṇu* is applied after verbal roots meaning "to eat" [to form words denoting the agent].

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the final member is a word denoting color— provided it is not *eta*— the preceding member, which also denotes a color, remains in its original form (*prakṛti*): for example, *kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ* (a black-spotted deer) and *lohitakalpamāṣaḥ* (a slightly red bean).
The word *kṛṣṇa* ends with the suffix *nak*, and the word *lohita* ends with the suffix *itac*; [is] color [the same]? Is there "supreme black" (*paramakṛṣṇa*)?
Among colors, what is a black sesame seed? Is it "not other than black" (an-eta), or is it "black and other" (kṛṣṇa-eta)?
When these two words are the final members of a *tatpuruṣa* compound denoting a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the preceding member shall remain in its original form (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is that the water is as deep as the oar; this refers to *golavaṇa*.
The meaning is "as much as is given to a cow";
the word *aritram* ends in the suffix *-itran* and is oxytone (having the acute accent on the middle syllable);
it denotes measure (*pramāṇa*) as mere quantity or delimitation, and not specifically length alone.

AS 6.2.5: In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the first member] retains its original accent when it means "an heir to wealth" (*dhanadāyāda*).

In a tatpuruṣa compound, when these two [words] follow, the first member, which expresses an obstruction, remains in its original form (prakṛti-svara).
The delay in going and the difficulty in speaking arise as obstacles; because of a deficiency in the necessary causes, the act of going occurs after a long time and is accompanied by hardship.
What is the obstruction?
It is dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).

When the word *pada* signifies a pretext (*vyāja*) as the final member of a compound, the preceding member retains its original stem form (*prakṛtisvara*) in that *tatpuruṣa* compound; for example, *mūtraprasthitaḥ*.
The word *mūtra* ending in the suffix *ghañ* is [formed as] *uccāra*;
the word *uccāra* ending in the suffix *ghañ* has its final syllable accented by virtue of the rule *thāthaghana-kap-dhrasva-śuṅga-thālañām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144).
In the case of an indication (apadeśa), what is the station of Viṣṇu?
In a Tatpuruṣa compound where the word *nivāta* follows, provided it denotes a shelter from wind, the first member retains its original form; for example, *kuṭīnivāta*.
The word *kuṭī* (meaning "a small hut" or "sheltered wall") ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*,
while the word *kuḍya* (meaning "a wall") ends in the suffix *ḍya*.
Others say that *yaganta* means protection; [if so], why does he live in a windless place (*rājanivāte*)?
This word *nivāta* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "side" (*pārśva*).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the word *śārada*, which denotes something other than "produced in the rainy season" (*ārtava*), follows, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). For example:
*raju-śāradam udakam* ("water from the autumnal harvest").
The word *śārada* means "fresh" (*nūtana*); its analysis within its own constituent parts (*asvapadavigraha*) is "just recently drawn up from the rope."

The word *rajjū* is derived from the root *sṛj* with the suffix *asun*, and its first syllable is udātta according to Pāṇini 6.1.157; how much more so, then, is *uttamaśārada* [which is not subject to that rule] when it does not denote a season (*anārtave*)?
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound following these two [words] when it denotes a genus (*jāti*), the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
The Kaṭha is the Adhvaryu;
the word *kaṭha* ends in the suffix *ac* according to the rule *pacādyac*, denoting the decoction of the gatekeeper.
Therefore, from the rule *vaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.104), the suffix *ṇini* is applied; and by the rule *kaṭhacarakālluk* (Pāṇini 4.3.107), there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix.

In the word *dauvārika*, derived from "one appointed at the gate" (*dvāri niyuktaḥ*) with the suffix *ṭhak*, the accent falls on the final syllable. [The question is: why is it specified as being "in the sense of a genus" (*jātau*)?
The supreme Adhvaryu priest.
Of these two, the former is by nature like his father; what similarity [could there be] in this?
In this context, the meaning of the compound is "being highly honored" (paramasadṛśa), not "resemblance" (sādṛśya).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound that is a *dvigu* where the final member denotes a measure of length, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), except in the case of the seven eastern [countries].
"Seven years is its measure; [the suffix] *mātrac* is always elided after *lodhiga* when expressing measure.
Thus, there is elision (*luk*) of the *mātrac* suffix.
The word *prācya* is udātta on its first syllable;
that which is both *prācya* and *saptasama* is *prācyasaptasama*. [The question is: why is the term *dvigu* mentioned?
Is a *vrīhiprastha* the standard measure, or is it equal to seven times the maximum?

In a Tatpuruṣa compound followed by the word *vāṇija*, the first member, when it denotes either that which is to be traversed (*gantavya*) or merchandise (*paṇya*), retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
"Madra-merchant" and "cow-merchant" are examples of the seventh-case (locative) tatpuruṣa compound.
The word *madra* ends in the suffix *rak*;
why is it that "it should be gone to" (*gantavyā*) is not [the case] for a supreme merchant?
In a tatpuruṣa compound where the final member is a word denoting a neuter gender, such as *mātra* and others, the same [shortening] occurs when these follow.

The word *bhikṣāmātra* means "of an equal measure to alms"; the term *bhikṣā* ends in the suffix *ap*, according to Pāṇini’s rule *guror hal aḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.103). This is the innovation of Pāṇini.
According to Pāṇini, the word *śabda* has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*);
the word *nanda*, ending in the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* group), begins with the root *nand*.

The shadow of a wall.
In these two subsequent examples, where the *tatpuruṣa* compound expresses "beneficial for," it is likewise [the case]:

a holiday from study is dear to students;
milk-rice is the pleasure of Brahmins.
The *anadhyāya* (period when study is forbidden) called *chātrapriya*;
the words *brāhmaṇa* and *chātra* have their final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the accent of the suffix;
[the question is] "what is the purpose of [stating] *prītau*?"
The happiness of a king.
When the word *svāmin* follows, the preceding member likewise denotes "one's own"; as in *gosvāmī*,
does it mean "one's own"?
The supreme master.
The tamer, the master of the house, in the home.
When the word *pati* follows, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound denoting lordship (*aiśvarya*), these [words] do not retain their original form; for example:
*bhūpatiḥ* (lord of the earth) from *bhuvaḥ patiḥ*, and *vākyapatiḥ* (lord of speech).
The lord of the mind,
the lord of the one who desires to marry again.
In the aforementioned context, the word *bhuvana* ends in the suffix *kyuṅ*, according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.2.20: *bhūsūdhūbhrasjibhyaḥ*. Thus, it denotes the Lord of the World (*bhuvanapati*).
Possibility is the determination of existence.
There is the apprehension of going,
the obstacle to going, and that which is closest to going.
Whether his departure is feared, or he is afflicted, or it is conjectured that he is very near— what could be more proximate than such a conjecture?
One who was formerly wealthy is called "āḍhyapūrvaḥ. (SK 3756; AS 6-2-22)
The word *pūrva* (prior) is used in its technical application (*vṛtti*) to denote that which has existed previously; for example,
in the case of "that which has existed previously," as opposed to *paramapūrva* (absolutely unprecedented).
In these cases, the preceding [member] remains in its original form (prakṛti).
Extending as far as Madrasa,
with Gāndhāra as its center,
and bounded by Kaśmīra.
Is "madrasaveśam" a synonym for "madrasadeśam" in the sense of proximity?
A field together with its boundaries is "with boundaries" (*samarthāda*), such as "the field with the boundaries of Caitra" (*caitrasamaryādam*).
In *vispaṣṭakaṭukam*,
the word *vispaṣṭa*— being an immediately preceding prefix— is accented on its first syllable according to Pāṇini 6.2.49.
What is more distinct than salt? What is more excellent than virtue?
One who is clearly a Brahmin;
one who is clear, variegated, and manifest.
Endowed with wisdom and skillfulness.
Fickle and skillful.

When the word *avama*—which has the substitutes *śra*, *jya*, or *kan*—or a word meaning "evil" (*pāpa*) occurs as the second member of a compound, the first member, provided it denotes an abstract state (*bhāva*), remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). For example:
*gamanaśreṣṭham*.
Superior in going,
inferior in going, and lowest in going.
If going is most wicked, as stated in the verse beginning with "śretyādi," how can going be beautiful?
In the sense of an abstract state (bhāva), what is it that is gone by means of this? It is "going" (gamana); "going that is excellent" is *gamanashreyaḥ*.
"Ke" means "let it not be so" in the case of a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa).
AS 6-2-26: In a *karmadhāraya* compound, [the feminine suffix] is applied after *kumāra* and *śramaṇā*.
The word *kumāra* has its acute accent on the final syllable [when used as a noun]. (Pāṇini 6.2.27)

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, when *pratyenas* follows, the first syllable of *kumāra* is udātta; thus, in *kumārapratyenāḥ*, [it means] one whose sin (*enas*) has departed, i.e., one who is free from sin.
Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.114:
*pūgā gaṇāsteṣūktaṃ vā*. This sūtra states that for the names of *pūgas* (assemblies) and *gaṇas* (groups), the suffixes prescribed for them may optionally be applied when they are mentioned as such.
In the case of *kumāracātakāḥ* and *kumārajīmūtāḥ*,
because the initial syllable lacks the udātta accent, the form remains simply *kumāraśca* according to Pāṇini 2.1.60.
Before these [suffixes], the preceding [element] remains in its original form (*prakṛti*).
That which has five *aratnis* as its measure is "five-aratni"; that which has existed for ten months is "ten-month-old" (*daśamāsya*);
that which has existed for five months is "five-month-old" (*pañcamāsya*).
Under the governing rule "tam adhīṣṭo vā" (Pāṇini 5.1.80), the suffix *yaP* optionally follows a *dvigu* compound; for example,
*pañcakapālaḥ*.
The *pañcakapāla* consists of five potsherds, five portions, and five bowls.
By the rule *phiṣ* and *naḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ*, the word *pañcan* has its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*).
[Question: What about *pañcāśvaḥ* in the list beginning with *iganta*?
In a Dvigu compound, what [is the rule]? For example:
*paramāratniḥ*. (SK 3764)
The word *bahu* is likewise [used] in the sense of "many," as in the expression *bahvaratni*.
*bahumāsaḥ* and *bahukapālaḥ*:
the word *bahu* has its final syllable accented.
When *yaṇ* is substituted for it, [the rule] *udāttasvaritayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.4) applies, as stated in SK 3765 and AS 6.2.31.
In a *dvigu* compound, the first member of these two [words] may optionally remain in its original form (*prakṛti*): for example,
*pañcadiṣṭiḥ* or *pañcavitastiḥ*.
A word denoting time other than [specific] times, ending in the locative case, remains in its original form when followed by words such as *siddha* and so forth.
*Sāṅkāśyasiddha* means "perfected at Sāṅkāśya"; *sāṅkāśya* ends in the suffix *ṇya*, and *ātapaśuṣka* means "dried in the sun."
*bhrāṣṭrapakvaḥ*:
*bhrāṣṭra* ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*; *cakrabandhaḥ*: the word *cakra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

Is it because the accent on the locative case-ending (*saptamī-svara*), which was established by the rule for the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) but sublated by the rule for the whole (*kṛt-svara*), is here being restored?
These [words] remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*) when the following member (*uttarapada*) expresses that which is to be avoided or denotes a part of a day or night.
The god rained all around Trigarta during the forenoon and the afternoon.
In the *upapūrvarātra* group,
the words beginning with *apatrigarta* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on their first syllable.

Since Bahuvrīhi and Tatpuruṣa compounds have already been established, this [rule] is for the sake of the Avyayībhāva; namely, that after *apa* and *pari*, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) alone denotes the thing excluded,
because it is only those two [prepositions] that possess the sense of exclusion.
Even the constituent parts of day and night are indeed excluded from those two;
why [is it said] "excluded" with respect to fire?
The word *prati* is compounded with a word denoting fire (*agni*) [to form an avyayībhāva compound].

In a *dvandva* compound denoting members of the royal class (*rājanya*) ending in the plural number, when it refers to the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, the first member retains its original form (*prakṛtisvara*); for example:
*śvāphalkacaitrakāḥ* and *śinivāsudevāḥ*.
The word *śini* is acutely accented on its first syllable; by metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇayā*), it refers to his descendant.
Why [is the term] *rājanya* used?
[To exclude cases such as] *dvaipyabhaimāyanāḥ*.
Those born on an island are *dvaipyas*;
the youthful descendant of Bhīma is *Bhaimāyana*;
and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis—these are not *rājanyas*.
The mention of "rājanya" here is for the purpose of including those Kṣatriyas who belong to lineages consecrated [as kings];
why then is the plural number used, since these [lineages] are not so many?
Are Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva a dual compound? Are they the "Vṛṣṇi youths," meaning the young princes of the Vṛṣṇis?
Are the Kurus and Pañcālas among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis?
In a dvandva compound, a preceding member that expresses a number retains its original form; for example,
*dvādaśa*.
The form *trayodaśa* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation) with the substitution of *trestraya-* and an udātta accent on the first syllable.
In a dvandva compound consisting of pupils who have as their subordinate [member] their teacher, the first member retains its original form; for example, *pāṇinīya-rauḍhīyāḥ*.
By this accentuation, both of these [words] are udātta in the middle;
the inclusion of the term "having the teacher as a subordinate member" (*ācāryopasarjana*) is a qualification of the *dvandva* compound,
so that the entire *dvandva* may be understood as having the teacher as its subordinate member.
Therefore, why is it not said here that "Pāṇini" and "Devadatta" are [the names of] teachers?
Regarding the term "antevāsī" (resident pupil), what do the grammarians of the Vedic tradition say concerning the treatises of Āpiśali and Pāṇini?
In a *dvandva* compound of these [words], the first member retains its original form (*prakṛti*).
Kārtaka and Kaujapa—
these two, Sāvarṇi and Maṇḍūkeya, are formed with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "this belongs to Kṛta" and "this belongs to Kujapa."
The word *mahat* [is used] by its own original form (*prakṛtyā*) in the ten [items] beginning with *vrīhi*.
Mahāvrīhi,
Mahāparāhṇa, Mahāgṛṣṭi.
*Maheṣvāsaḥ*,
*mahāhailihilaḥ*,
and *mahacchabdaḥ* have the acute accent on the final syllable.
This accent applies only to this specific compound as prescribed by the rule *sanmahat-parama-*, etc.; it does not apply here in the case of *mahato vrīhiḥ* (*mahadvrīhiḥ*).
And [the word] "great" [is optionally neuter], according to Pāṇini 6.2.39.
The *kṣullakavaiśvadeva* and the *mahāvaiśvadeva*:
[the former is so called] because it takes away hunger (*kṣudham lāti*), thus it is *kṣulla*.
Therefore, in the case of *ajñātā* and so forth, which [word] has the acute accent on the final syllable? (Pāṇini 6.2.40).
The words *uṣṭrasādin* (camel-rider) and *uṣṭravāmī* (female camel-rider) are derived from the root *uṣ* with the suffix *ṣṭran*; thus, the word *uṣṭra* has its initial syllable accented.
*gosādaḥ* (the word *gosādaḥ* [is formed]).
One who possesses cows and so forth is a cowherd (gosārathi).

AS 6.2.42: In these seven types of compounds, as well as in those beginning with *dāsībhāra*, the preceding member retains its original form (*prakṛti-svara*); for example, *kurūṇāṃ gārhapatam* becomes *kurugārhapatam*.
It should be stated that the suffix *kur* occurs after the root *vṛj* when followed by the affix *up*.
*vṛji-gārhapatam*:
*vṛji* has its first syllable accented; *rikta-guruḥ*: *rikta* is heavy.
According to the rule *rikte vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.2.15), the word *rikta* has its first syllable udātta. [The compounds are:
*asūtā jaratī* = *asūtajaratī*;
*aślīlā dṛḍharūpā* = *aślīladṛḍharūpā*.

The word *aślīla* has its first syllable accented because it is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). That which possesses *śrī* (prosperity/beauty) is *ślīla*; the suffix *-lac* is applied here according to the rule for the *sidhma* group.
The substitution of *l* for *r* occurs because [the word] belongs to the *kapilakādi* group;

"pārevaḍavā" is a compound meaning "like a mare on the far shore," formed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) with the sense of "as it were" (*iva*), involving both the compounding and the non-elision of the case-ending.
The word *pāra* is oxytone because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group;
*taitilakadrūḥ* is [a compound] where *kadrūḥ* belongs to the *taitila*s. [The term *taitila*] ends in the suffix *aṇ*, meaning "the descendant of Titilin" or "a student of Titilin."

The word *paṇya* is acute on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *yat*; however, it should be stated as an exception (*vārttika*) that this applies when it forms a name, as in *paṇyakambalaḥ*.

In other cases, where it refers to a blanket that is to be sold, there is simply the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound, for this specific accent is prescribed by the rule *kṛtyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.154) regarding compounds formed with gerundives.
The compound *dāsībhāraḥ* means "the burden of a female slave.

In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *devahūtiḥ*, it is desired that the initial member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), even though no specific rule has been prescribed; all such cases are to be understood as included under the category of *dāsībhāra* and similar formations.

"He [is] for wealth, he for *puraṃdhī*. In the word *puraṃdhī*, the suffix *ki* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* (3.3.93), meaning "that in which the body (*pura*) is placed" (*dhīyate*).
The absence of elision (*aluk*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The word *pura* is acutely accented on its first syllable by virtue of the rule *phiṣ* (Pāṇini 1.1.45), as it does not fall under the scope of the *nabviṣaya* rule (Pāṇini 6.2.43).

When the subsequent member of a compound expresses the meaning of that which ends in the fourth case, the word ending in the fourth case remains in its original form (prakṛti-svara); for example, *yūpāya dāru* becomes *yūpadāru*. (SK 3778)
When the word *artha* follows, a word ending in the dative case remains in its original form (*prakṛti*); for example, *devārtham*.
When followed by a word ending in a *kta* suffix, a word in the dative case retains its original form [and does not undergo sandhi] in the expression *go-hitam*.
When followed by a word ending in a *kta* suffix, a preceding word not ending in *iṣṭhan* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*).
Those formed into rows have the word "śreṇi" as their first member with the acute accent (udātta); those formed into groups [have the same].
The word *pūga* is oxytone in a *karmadhāraya* compound; for example,
what was done by a guild (*śreṇi*) is called *śreṇikṛtam*.
What is there to be done or left undone when there is no finality?
In a compound, when followed by a word ending in the suffix *kta*, a word ending in the accusative case retains its original form; for example, *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*.
The word *grāma* in the compound *grāmagataḥ*, meaning "gone to the village," is udātta on its final syllable due to the *niṭ*-accent.
In the case of *ahīna*, why is it stated that [the prefix] has passed beyond the wilderness (*kāntāra*) and is free from affliction (*anupasarga*)?
This is an exception (apavāda) to the rule stated in *Thātha-SK-sandarbhah* 3878: "There is no attainment of happiness here.
[See] SK 3782.
AS 6.2.48: When a word ending in *kta* that expresses the object (*karman*) follows, a word ending in the third case retains its original form (*prakṛti*), provided it is *tvotāsaḥ*.
Struck by Rudra, struck by the Great King;
Rudra is the one who roams.
What is the use of a chariot for the action? One who has gone by chariot is called "rathayātaḥ.

When a word ending in the suffix *kta* follows in the sense of the object (*karman*), a preceding *gati* that is not separated by another word retains its original form; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [AS 6.2.140] *thā-tha-siṭ-kasvatu-tum-khalarthānām*.
Has the immediate successor raised up the family priest?
But when the first member is a *kāraka*, only the accent of the suffixes such as *-tha* (in *sthā*), which is later applied (*satiśiṣṭa*), remains— as in *dūrād āgataḥ*.
When a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *t*, other than the word *tu*, follows, the preceding *gati* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*).
[In the phrase] "the two powers of Agni, the most manly" (*agnerāyo nṛtamasya prabhūtau*), [the *gati* remains unchanged].
In *saṅgatiṃ goḥ*, [the substitution of] *kṛt* is an exception to [the substitution of] *svar*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "before a suffix beginning with *t*"?
What will one who is merely talkative do?
In the case of a form ending in *tṛc*, why is it that [the suffix] *atau* is adventitious (*āgantu*)?

AS 6.2.51: In a word ending with the suffix *tavya*, the final syllable is acute-accented (*udātta*), and the preceding prefix (*gati*) is also [acute-accented] immediately; furthermore, both of these [the suffix and the prefix] occur simultaneously as their original forms (*prakṛti*). Example:
*anvetavā u* (*anvetavā u*).
An exception to the rule regarding the *kṛt* suffix *svar*.
(Pāṇini 6.2.52)

Regarding the rule that when the suffix *va* follows a verbal root ending in *an*, and the prefix *añc-* follows, those [prefixes] which are *parāñc-* remain in their original form (*prakṛti*): why is it specified "not ending in *i*" (*aniganta*)? [Counter-example: *parīṇatya*. Why is it specified "ending in *va*" (*vapratiyayānte*)? [Counter-example: *pratyakṣam*. Why is it specified "when *añc-* follows" (*añcau pare*)? [Counter-example: *pratyagbhyām*. Why is it specified "those which are *parāñc-*" (*ye parāñcastān*)? [Counter-example: *udaktam*. Why is it specified "in their original form" (*prakṛtyā*)? [Counter-example: *udaktam*. Why is it
Let them go back; let them go back from the sound of the thunderbolt. Slay him right here! Strike down his manly powers and drive them away!
What is the example for the suffix *vapr*?
It is *udañcana*. (SK 3787)

In the case of a word ending in the suffix *v* (the *ap* suffix), even when it contains the root *añc*, the forms *nyak* and *udak* remain in their original base form (*prakṛti*) before the word *uttāna*; thus,
[the compound] is *nyaṅṅuttānaḥ*.
According to the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇ*, the vowel *a* of the root *añc* is svarita; thus, *adhyaṅ*. (SK 3788)
AS 6-2-54: In *īṣatkaḍāraḥ*,
this word *īṣat* is accented on the final syllable.
In the case of *īṣadbheda* and similar compounds, the accent is governed solely by the rule for *kṛt*-suffixes (Pāṇini 6.2.139).

When the first member of the compound denotes a measure of gold, it may optionally remain in its original form when the word *dhana* follows; for example, *dvisuvarṇa-dhana*, meaning "wealth whose measure is two suvarṇas. Even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, this option prevails because it is taught later [in the rules].
What is the gold? What is the measure of the wealth consisting of a prastha?
Among wealth, what is gold-worth?
A necklace of coins.
Or rather, the word *prathama* retains its original form when expressing novelty.
The meaning is that he is now engaged in studying grammar for the first time;
the word *prathama* is derived from the root *prath* with the suffix *am*.
"Is it not soon?
"Indeed, he is the first grammarian.
AS 6.2.57: Optionally, [the first member] retains its original form in the case of *katarakaṭhaḥ*.
The mention of *karmadhāraya* is for the sake of subsequent rules;
however, in this case, it is already established simply because it is mentioned by its specific technical name (*pratipadokta*).
AS 6-2-58: *āryakumāraḥ*,
*āryabrāhmaṇaḥ*.
The word *ārya* has a svarita accent on its final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ṇyat*;
[the question is] "is *ārya* [used here]?"—
as in *paramabrāhmaṇaḥ*.
Regarding the phrase "brāhmaṇa, etc.," does it mean that "noble kṣatriya" (āryakṣatriya) is a *karmadhāraya* compound? Indeed, it is so.
In a *karmadhāraya* compound, the words *brāhmaṇa* and *kumāra*, when standing before [another word], may optionally remain in their original form (*prakṛti*).
*rājabrāhmaṇaḥ* and *rājakumāraḥ*:
the separation of the rule is for the sake of subsequent purposes.

With his feet washed, what is the finality [of his state] when the mouth of the bag is open?
Why [is it] preceded by a prefix? [As in the example:
*śuṣkamukhaḥ*. (SK 3845)

The section concerning the *uttarapada* (the second member of a compound) extends up to the end of the *āpāda* (Pāda 4); however, the first section [of this chapter] has as its limit the rule *prakṛtyā bhagālam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.179).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *karṇa* following a term denoting a color or a term denoting a characteristic is udātta on its first syllable. (Pāṇini 6.2.112)
Is Karṇa white-eared, spike-eared, or [simply] eared?
Is he "White-footed" because of his color-characteristic, or is he "Beautiful-eared"?
The word *karṇa* is udātta on its first syllable.
Maṇikarṇa is used in comparison; gokarṇa [is used] in comparison.
In a bahuvrīhi compound, when the two members are names of the eyes, the suffix *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.113) is applied.
Śitikaṇṭha,
Kāṇḍapṛṣṭha,
Sugrīva.
Nāḍījaṅgha was in comparison like one with a donkey's throat.
He has the back of a cow, the neck of a horse, and the shanks of a cow.
Pāṇini 6.2.115: In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *śṛṅga* is acutely accented on its first syllable when it denotes a state, a name, or a comparison.

In this context, "state" (*avasthā*) refers to the specific stage of age of a cow or similar animal, characterized by the emergence of its horns, such as when the horns have emerged or when they measure two finger-breadths in length.
Rishyashringa is [the authority] regarding perception;
Upama regarding comparison.
Is "meṣaśṛṅgaḥ" (ram's horn) a *avasthā* (state/condition), or is it "sthūlaśṛṅgaḥ" (thick-horned)?
In a bahuvrīhi compound, these words following the negative particle *nañ* are udātta on their first syllable.
O crusher of enemies, my old age has become ageless and immortal.
"Immortality among the gods"—
what is the function of the negative particle (*nañ*) in *abrāhmaṇamitraḥ*?
What is it that conquers?
One who has no enemy.

Following the word *su*, with the exception of *loman* and *uṣas*, a word ending in the suffix *man* as well as one ending in the suffix *a* shall have its first syllable acute-accented, provided it does not follow the negative particle *nañ* or the word *su*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.
Performing good deeds, well-yoked, may he,
the immeasurable one accompanied by excellent prayers, carry us; auspicious to our cattle,
well-disposed, and full of splendor.
He fashions beautiful forms; what is the purpose of fashioning? Having performed his work, he dwells within the mind.

In the case of *surājā* (from *su-rājā*) and *alomoṣasī*, why is it that *sulomā* and *sūṣāḥ* do not become *kapi* (the suffix *kaP*), since the rule "after *kapi*, the preceding [element] remains as it was" (*kapi pūrvaḥ*) applies? This is the objection. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.135).
The suffix *ka* is applied after [the word] *susravas* to form *sukarmakaḥ*.
When followed by *soḥ*, these [words] are udātta on the first syllable:
*sāmrājyāya sukratuḥ* (*sāmrājyāya sukratuḥ*), *supratīkaḥ* (*supratīkaḥ*).
One to whom offerings are easily made,
possessing well-extended power and affection.
A two-syllable word ending in *yat*, *āt*, *u*, or *ū* that follows *su* is udātta in a bahuvrīhi compound, except for the words *adhāḥ* and *aśvāḥ*; e.g., *adhāsvaśvāḥ*.
In *suraṃthā ātithigve*, both *suraṃthā* and *ātithigve* have their first syllables udātta due to the rule *nitsvareṇāśvarathau*.
Why [is the word] *ādyudāttaṃ* mentioned?
He who has beautiful arms;
he who is golden among those who are not well-praised.
The word *hiraṇya* [is used] when three [years] are expressed; Pāṇini 5.1.29.
In a Bahuvrīhi compound, the word *su-* following *pari-* is udātta in Vedic;
as in *suvīre rayiṇā* (*suvīre svarayiṇā*),
and *suvīryasya gomataḥ* (*suvīryasya gomataḥ*).

The word *vīrya* ends in the suffix *yat*; in that case, the rule "that which ends in *an*, *ava*, etc., is not [udātta]" (Pāṇini 6.1.213) would prevent the initial udātta accent. Thus, the explicit mention of *vīrya* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [to the effect that such a prohibition does not apply here]; for if that were the case, the desired result would already be established by the preceding rule alone.
*upakūlam* (near the bank)
Near the shore, near the tuft, near the root.
Near the boundary,
near the axle, well-proportioned.
In the group of words beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*, why is there the inclusion of terms such as *kūla* (bank) and so forth?
In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, why is "upakumbham" used, rather than "paramakūlam"?
*dvikaṃsaḥ* (two *kaṃsas*)
Two churning-sticks,
two winnowing-baskets,
and two vessels for the parched grain.
In a *dvigu* compound, why is it that *paramakaṃsaḥ* is not [a valid example]? It is because it consists of two parts (*dvikāṇḍam*).
In a Tatpuruṣa compound ending in the word *śālā*, when it is neuter in gender, the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*) is acute-accented.
In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *brāhmaṇaśālam*,
why is it not [called] *dṛḍhaśālaṃ brāhmaṇakulam*?
In the case of *śālā*, what is *brāhmaṇasenam*? In the neuter, what is *brāhmaṇaśālā*?
Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.124 (SK 3858): In a Tatpuruṣa compound that is neuter in gender, the word *kanthā* as the final member is acute-accented on its first syllable.
What is the purpose of the neuter forms *sauśamikantha* and *āhvarakantha*?
The daughter of Dakṣa (Dākṣī).
In a Tatpuruṣa compound ending in *kantha* when used in the neuter gender, the first syllable of words such as *cihaṇa* is udātta; for example:
*cihaṇakaṇṭham*, *mandurakaṇṭham*.
While the term "initial" (ādi) is understood [from the previous rule], its mention again is for the purpose of making the first syllable of the preceding word udātta.
The words beginning with *cela* as final members [of a compound] have their first syllable acute; for example:
*putracelam*, *nāgarakheṭam*.
The *dadhikaṭuka* section on progeny consists of a censure of sons and others through comparison with rags and so forth; the compound is formed according to the rule beginning with *vyāghra*.
In the sense of reproach, what is *paramacela*? (Pāṇini 6.2.127)
Is "vastracīra" cloth like bark-fiber, or is it woolen cloth like bark-fiber? What is the intended comparison?
paramacīram SK 3862 AS 6-2-128 means "the very old."
Ghee-and-meat dish, ghee-soup,
and ghee-vegetable dish.
The compound [is formed] by the rule *bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.1.35). What is the purpose of the word *miśra*? [Consider the counter-example:
*paramapalalam*.
In a tatpuruṣa compound, [the first member] is udātta on its initial syllable.
Dākṣikūla, Śāṇḍisūda, and Dāṇḍāyanasthala.
*Dākṣikarṣaḥ* is a name for a village;
[is this] with regard to a name?
The highest bank (of the river).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, excluding a *karmadhāraya*, the final member *rājya-* is acute-accented on its first syllable; for example, *brāhmaṇarājyam*. Why [is this rule stated]? [To exclude cases such as] *akārājyam*.

In the case of *paramarājyam* and *celarājya*, the indeclinable vowel [of *para-* and *cela-*, respectively] takes precedence by virtue of the prior rule of prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), resulting in *kucelam* or *kurājyam*.
One who belongs to the class of Arjuna; one who sides with Vāsudeva.
The rule "provided it is not a *karmadhāraya*" applies here; thus,
*paramavargyaḥ* [is formed],
where *vargādi-* refers to the group of words beginning with *varga* that is included within the group beginning with *diś*.
[The suffix ṅīp is applied] after words denoting males.
In a tatpuruṣa compound, the word *putra* as the final member is udātta on its first syllable,
as in *dāśakīputraḥ* and *māhitāputraḥ*.
Is the son [the same as] the maternal uncle of Kaunaṭi? Is the male [the same as] the female?
The son of Dakṣī (dākṣīputraḥ) [is formed according to] Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.133.

A son derived from these [words] is not acute-accented on the first syllable; because of the inclusion of the term "ākhyā" (name), there is the inclusion of synonyms and their specific derivatives, such as *ācāryaputraḥ*.
The son of the preceptor,
the son of Śākaṭāyana, the prince.
The son of Īśvara,
the son of Nanda,
the son of the officiating priest.
The son of the officiating priest, the son of the *hotṛ*, those who are joined together, and the kinsmen.
The son of a maternal uncle,
kinsmen related through the mother and father, and relatives, as well as the son of a kinsman.
The term *bhrātuṣputraḥ* [is formed with a long vowel] by Pāṇini 6.2.134.
These [words], when following a word ending in the sixth case that is not *prāṇin*, are acute-accented on the first syllable in a *tatpuruṣa* compound;
for example, *mudgacūrṇam*.
Why is *apra-* mentioned? [To exclude cases such as *mudgaprati*].
Fish powder (matsyacūrṇa) [is used as a substitute for salt], according to Pāṇini 6.2.135.
With the exception of those ending in the sixth case, the words *darbhakāṇḍa* and *darbhacīra* have the acute accent on the first syllable.
sesame paste, mung bean soup, and radish greens.
Are the six [senses] the bank of the river, or is the cook the king?
What follows next?
The section on the adopted son (dattaka).
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound denoting a forest, the word *kuṇḍa* has its first syllable acute [when it follows a word meaning "grass"]; for example, *darbhakuṇḍam*.
In this context, the word "kuṇḍa" is used in the sense of similarity; is the forest a clay vessel?
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the final member is the word *bhagāla*, it retains its original accent.
Kumbhībhagāla, Kumbhīnadāla, and Kumbhīpāla.
These [words] have the middle syllable accented by virtue of the governing rule "by their own nature" (prakṛtyā), up until the point where it says "at the end" (antaḥ).
A word consisting of more than one syllable that follows *śiti* remains in its original form (as a *prakṛti-bhūta*);
for example, *śitipādaḥ*.
The word *pāda* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group;
the word *aṃsa* is [ādyudātta] because its suffix is marked with *ṇi*.
What is the point of Śibi?
Is he not one whose feet are worthy of being seen? Has he not honored [the guest]?
The term *śitibhasat* is *śiti*, with the initial vowel being udātta;
this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the original accent of the first member of a compound (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).
Pāṇini 6.2.139: In a tatpuruṣa compound, a word ending in a kṛt suffix following these [words] shall have its original accent (prakṛtisvara).
The weapon is of such a kind;
the two red, bold steeds that carry the hero.
The wood-cutter [is mentioned] with the adverbial suffix -kāra in the sense of "loudly."
Is it easy for you to go? Who is the agent of the Lord's action?
The genitive case here has the sense of "remainder" (śeṣa-lakṣaṇā);
the mention of the *kṛt*-suffix is for the sake of clarity.
In the example *prapacatitarām*, once the compound is formed with the element ending in *tarap* (*tarab*), the suffix *ām* is applied.
Regarding this, some say that the *aṅ* accent occurs because it is prescribed as remaining;
others say, however, that the mention of the *kṛt* suffix is for the sake of including forms such as *prapacati*.
AS 6.2.140: In these cases, both the preceding and following members of the compound remain in their original form simultaneously; for example, *vanaspatim* and *vanā*.
He who [glorifies] Bṛhaspati— the word *bṛhat* here is prescribed as having its first syllable accented—
[should] gladden the Lord of Śacī.
The word *śacī* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *śārṅgarava*-class,
as seen in the expression *śacībhir na*; thus,
*tanūnapāt* is so called.
Narāśaṃsa the vigorous one; [the lengthening of the vowel] is due to the rule of nipātana;
Śunaḥśepa.
After the suffix *uṅ*, both [the preceding word and the suffix] remain in their original form simultaneously.
O Indra and Varuṇa,
O Indra and Bṛhaspati, we— what [is] the deity?
In the case of the copulative compound *plakṣanyagrodhau*, why is it not like *agniṣṭomaḥ*?
Pāṇini 6.2.142: When the subsequent member is not *pṛthivī* and so forth, and is unaccented, the aforementioned [rule] does not apply.
For Indra and Agni, O bulls, what [is there]? From the non-earth and so forth, what did they produce, heaven and earth?
They produced heaven and earth.
The word *dyāvā* is prescribed as having the acute accent on the first syllable, while *pṛthivī* has the acute accent on the final syllable; [likewise] *somārudrau*.
By the rule *roderṇiluk ca*, the word *rudra* ends in *ra*;
*indrāpūṣaṇau* [is formed with] *pūṣan*,
which is an exception (*nipātita*) having the acute accent on the final syllable according to the rule *śvan-ukṣan-pūṣan*.
*Sukāmanthinau*: because *manthin* ends in *-in*, it is udātta on the final syllable.

The mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is intended as a qualifier for the subsequent member in the rule "when beginning with an anudātta," so that it does not become a qualifier for the *dvandva* compound itself.
The phrase "anudāttādau" (beginning with an unraised tone) is for the purpose of distinguishing the respective domains of the injunction and the prohibition.
This is a governing rule (adhikāra). (Pāṇini 6.2.144)
Now, for words ending in *tha*, *atha*, *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *itra*, and *ka*, when they follow a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*, the final syllable is acute;
as in *prabhṛthasyāyoḥ* (*pra̭bhṛ̱thasyā̱yoḥ*) and *āvasathaḥ*.
The suffix ghañ is applied [to form a noun], while kta is applied [to form a past passive participle].
The holder of the thunderbolt, praised by many (*dhartā vajrī paruṣṭutaḥ*). The analysis of the compound is: "praised in many places" (*puruṣu bahupradeśeṣu stutaḥ*). Thus it is explained.
Destruction is the cutting away of water.
Thus,
what is the means of purification?

In the word *govṛṣaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule beginning with "mūlavibhujādi"; this occurs precisely because the preceding element is a verb root (*gati*), an agentive factor (*kāraka*), or a subordinate word (*upapada*).
It has been well praised by you.
And following the analogy of *soru*, a word ending in the suffix *-kta* is oxytone when it occurs in the phrase *ṛtasya yonau sukṛtasya*. (In the womb of Truth, of the well-performed deed.
*Śaśaplutaḥ*.

Pāṇini 6.2.146: A word ending in the suffix *kta* is oxytone when preceded by a verbal root (*gati*), a kāraka, or an upapada, with the exception of words such as *ācita*. Example: *upahūtaḥ śākalyaḥ*.
Kauṇḍinya has been thoroughly consumed;
what has been accumulated does not come back.
established SK 3881 AS 6-2-147
In these cases, the final member ending in a *kta*-suffix is udātta-accented on its final syllable, as in *prabṛddhaḥ* and *prayutaḥ*.
This undertaking has the sense of "not being designated";
it is an open-ended class (ākṛtigaṇa).
In a proper name, the final syllable is acute-accented; e.g., Devadattaḥ.
From what source was Viṣṇuśruta born, and from whom did Rāmāyaṇa arise?

Regarding *dattaśruta* and *devapālita*, why is it that [the former] does not take the third case by the rule "from this restriction, in the sense of a name" (Pāṇini 1.4.92), whereas for the latter, the third case occurs by the rule "in the sense of the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2)?
Why is there this restriction regarding the *kāraka* (grammatical participant), so that it may apply as a restriction on the *datta* and *śruta* [terms],
and not such that the acute accent (*udātta*) occurs even after a non-*kāraka* within the *datta* and *śruta*?
It is well-known;
what [is the meaning] of "devakhātā" (divine-dug) as a benediction? It means "dug by the gods."
In this context, a restriction is intended as if [the rule] were *āśiṣy-eva* (only in the sense of benediction).
Therefore, in the example *anāhato nadati devadattaḥ*, this is not the name of a particular conch;
rather, by the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 6.2.48), there is simply the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound.
Pāṇini 6.2.149:

In a compound used in the sense of "one who has acted in such a manner" (*itthambhūte kṛtam*), the final member ending in the suffix *kta* shall have its final syllable accented with the acute (*udātta*).
The speech of one who is asleep and the song of one who is intoxicated are "done" (*kṛta*);
thus, the root *kṛ* refers to action in general and does not denote only the manifestation of what was previously non-existent.
By that [rule], even the act of prattling and so forth is rendered as the object;
this is an exception (apavāda) to the rule "the third case is used for the object" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.2).
A word ending in the suffix -ana, which denotes either an action (bhāva) or an object (karman), is udātta on its final syllable when it follows a kāraka [other than the agent]. For example:
*payaḥpānam sukham* ("the drinking of milk is pleasant").
Are the rice grains for the king's meal those that are taken by hand?
What is *dantadhāvana*? It is derived from the root *dhāv* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
What is an example [of a compound] formed from a *kāraka*?

AS 6.2.151: In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, these words which follow a *kāraka* [as the first member] have an acute accent on their final syllable; this is an exception to the accentuation rule for *kṛt*-affixes.
The path of the chariot, the manual of Pāṇini, and the exposition of Vedic meters.
The royal bedchamber,
the royal throne,
and the stable for horses.
Is *brāhmaṇayājakaḥ* and *gokrītaḥ* derived from a *kāraka*? Yes.
Regarding the combination of *prabhūta* with *tādau*, the accent is governed by *niti* (Pāṇini 6.2.51), as stated in the *Niti-SK-sandarbhah* (SK 3784) and *SK* 3886.
A word denoting excellence in Vedic study has its penultimate syllable accented acute (udātta).
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, by the rule "when the meaning is equal," the seventh case ending would have been expected; [here] what is the merit through the Veda? It is "Vedic merit" (*vedapuṇya*).
SK 3887 AS 6-2-153 māṣonam: "Less than a māṣa."

The term *māṣavikala* refers to a verbal quarrel; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the third member of a compound where it is the prior member.
In this regard, some maintain that the word *artha* here signifies the inclusion of the literal form itself—

as in the expression *dhānyārthaḥ*— whereas by the word *ūna*, which serves to indicate the meaning, there is the inclusion of things having that meaning. Since [the desired result] would be established simply by the fact of being explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*), the mention of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is for the sake of clarity.
A peace treaty is an agreement for a single purpose through a binding wager.
Mixed with sesame seeds and mixed with clarified butter—
what is this mixture?
Why [is it said] "sugar-coated grains" (*guḍadhānāḥ*) without a prefix, when they are mixed with sesame?

The inclusion of the term "with a prefix" (*sopasarga*) within the rule for "mixed" (*miśra*) is precisely the indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this principle]; otherwise, in the absence of sandhi, one would have to say *brāhmaṇamiśro rājā*.
United with the Brahmins, he attained a common purpose.

Words ending in taddhita suffixes having the sense of "produced from" (*saṃpādya*) and so forth, when following the negative particle *nañ* used in the sense of negating a quality, have the acute accent (*udātta*) on their final syllable. For example: *kārṇaveṣṭakikam* (produced from ear-rings), *akārṇaveṣṭakikam* (not produced from ear-rings).
One who deserves cutting is *chaidika*; one who does not deserve cutting is *acchaidika*.
That which is not beneficial for calves is *avatsīya*.
That which is non-afflictive does not lead to affliction;
what is the function of the negative particle *nañ*?
One who deserves a donkey-chariot is called *gārdabharathika*; one who deserves two donkey-chariots is called *dvigārdabharathika*.
What is the purpose of this restriction regarding qualities (*guṇapratiṣedha*)?
"Other than one who possesses a donkey-cart" means *agārdabharathika*.
For it is said that a secondary quality (*guṇa*) becomes the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning;
this rule applies where its negation is expressed.
The face does not meet [the ears] because of the ear-ornaments; thus it meets.
Does he study the Pāṇinian grammar? A Pāṇinian.
One who is not a follower of Pāṇini— what derivative suffixes (*taddhita*) can a non-Pāṇinian carrier possibly bear?
"Voḍhṛ" (the bearer) does not become "avoḍhṛ" (one who has not borne).

In the word *yayāti*, when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) ending in *-ya* follows as the final member of a compound, the final syllable of that member following the negative particle *nañ* becomes acute-accented (*udātta*), provided it refers to the negation of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedha*). For example:
a collection of ropes is *pāśyā*; "not a collection of ropes" is *apāśyā*.
What is to be brought about that is not for that purpose?
What is to be accomplished that is not directed toward that end?
What is the purpose of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) here?
Why is there a prohibition of the quality (*guṇa*) [in the case of *adeya*]?
That which is other than *dantyā* (the dental) is *adantyā* (non-dental);
therefore, when there is the mention of that which has such an *anubandha*, it does not include that which lacks such an *anubandha*.
Thus, it is not the case here.
The Vāmadevya [Sāman] is not [to be used].
A word ending in *a* or *ā* that follows the negative particle *nañ* is udātta on its final syllable when incapacity is understood; for example,
*apacaḥ*,
meaning "one who is not able to cook."
In the absence of [the ability to] draw, what is the initiated one who has not cooked?
It is simply the negation of a quality.
This is another [instance of] "pacādyac" [affixation].
When the negative particle *nañ* is followed by a word ending in *vat* or *vant* that has its final syllable accented (*udātta*), it is used in the sense of reproach; for example,
"a lazy fellow (*jālma*) who does not cook" is reproached as being unable to cook.
Non-distraction (avikṣipaḥ) [is the cause of the suffix -aṇ, according to Pāṇini 4.3.120].
A word following *nañ* (the negative particle) is udātta on its final syllable when it forms a name or denotes an insult, as in *adevadattaḥ*. (Pāṇini 6.2.166)
Words following the negative particle *nañ* shall have their final syllable accented acute (udātta),
as in *akartavyaḥ*.
The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied after the root *uk* (to go) when preceded by the prefix *an-*, forming the word *anāgāmuka*.
In the case of *alaṅkariṣṇuḥ*,

by the mention of the suffix *iṣṇuc*, there is also the inclusion of *khiṣṇuc* despite its having two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*), because of the force of the rule prescribing [the suffix] beginning with the vowel *i*; thus,
*anāḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*.
"Unpleasant and so forth" means that which is not pleasant,
that which is improper.
(ga) In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the forms *arāja* and *anāha* [are used] for *rājan* and *ahan*.
In common speech, the accent of the negative particle *nañ* remains as it was [before the compound].

An *āmantrita* (vocative) following *āmaḥ*, separated by one word, is not unaccented (*anudātta*).
"Are you cooking, Devadatta? "Yes. "At intervals, Devadatta? Are you cooking? "Yes."
What is the vocative? "Does Devadatta cook? What is [the vocative] when not in proximity?
"Are you cooking, Devadatta? (Pāṇini 8.1.56)
The verb ending in a personal suffix is not unaccented when it follows "ud-asrjaḥ" (O Aṅgiras, when you released) or "uśanti" (for they desire). (O Aṅgiras, when you released; for they desire.)

"But I shall explain to you [the usage] by means of particles (*nipāta*): *iti ha*, *iti tu*, *iti paśya*. Since this is already established, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), meaning that [the particle *iti*] occurs only in connection with these specific [particles] when they follow, and not with others."

In the phrase *jāye svārohāva ihi ehi*, the final *loṭ* (imperative) ending of the verb *ihi*, which is joined with another *loṭ* ending (*svārohāva*) expressing motion, receives the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
When these six [particles] follow, a finite verb (tiṅanta) is not unaccented; for example:
*devaḥ pacati cana*.
The god cooks; indeed, the god cooks as it were;
the god cooks the herd.
"The god cooks somewhat," "the god cooks repeatedly"—
what is the purpose of [the suffix] *agati*?
The god indeed causes to ripen.
In the case of *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, and *iva*, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is not unaccented; for example:
*devaḥ pacati ca khādati ca*.
This is so provided it does not follow a word denoting motion (*agateḥ*).
In the case of *devaḥ prapacati ca prakhādati ca*,
the prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule *ca-vā-yoge prathamasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.58) is set aside, while the second verb (*prakhādati*) is indeed accented with *nighāta*.
When used in conjunction with *ca* or *vā*, the first finite verbal form (tiṅ-vibhakti) is not unaccented.
"He tends the cows" or "he plays the lute," or "hither we pray for gain"—
this [first sentence] is dependent on a finite verb to be supplied from the subsequent sentences.

In the case of *yoga*, why is there the mention of the "first" [word] (*prathamā-grahaṇa*) even when two words have already occurred in conjunction, for the sake of the *nighāta* (elision of accent), so that it does not apply to a second word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)?
When there is a transgression of duty, the first case-ending (prathamā) used in connection with a finite verb (tiṅvibhakti) is not unaccented (anudātta).
"He goes himself by carriage" (svayaṃ harathena yāti) and "he causes the preceptor to go on foot" (upādhyāyaṃ padātiṃ gamayati)—
in these cases, there is a protracted vowel (*pluta*) according to *kṣiyāśīḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.104).
A first case ending not joined with *aha*, and a verbal suffix (*tiṅvibhakti*), are not unaccented when used in conjunction with *nānā*, *niyoga*, or *īkṣiyā*; for example:
*tvam aha grāmaṃ gaccha*.
In the case of a reproach,
he goes himself on horseback but leads his teacher on foot.

AS 8.1.62: Furthermore, it is stated that when these two [particles *eva* and *ca*] are elided, the first case-ending of a verbal suffix (*tiṅvibhakti*) is not unaccented; for example: *deva eva grāmaṃ gacchatu* ("Let the god indeed go to the village") and *deva evāraṇyaṃ gacchatu* ("Let the god indeed go to the forest").
The meaning is that he should go both to the village and to the forest;
thus, let the god go to the village,
and let Rāma go to the forest.
The meaning is that he should go either exclusively to the village or exclusively to the forest; here there is an elision of the particle *aha*, and that [particle] has the sense of "exclusively."
What is the restriction?
O King, "where indeed will you eat?
means "nowhere at all."
Only when there is no possibility [of the application of another rule].
When *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *eva*, or *ā* are elided, the first person verbal suffix (*tiṅvibhakti*) is not unaccented; for example, in *calope*:
*indravājeṣu no 'va*.
The rice grains are white; they milk white cows for the clarified butter on the day of the Vālakhilyas.
One should sacrifice with rice;
one should sacrifice with barley.
The day indeed belonged to the gods,
while this hand alone belonged to men.
When joined with these two [words], the first case-ending (prathamā) and the verbal inflection (tiṅvibhakti) are not unaccented (anudātta) in the Vedic language (chandas).
One animates the one unborn;
another guards the other unborn; of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the fig tree.
Why [is it said] "one" when two are capable?
The word "one" refers to the number and has no other purpose.
In a word where the word *yat* occurs, the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following it is not unaccented.
He who eats, that which is eaten today, or the wind that blows— in these cases, the effect is held to occur with an interval.
Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.67: After words such as *kāṣṭha* when they denote an act of honoring, the word expressing the person honored is unaccented; for example, *kāṣṭhādhyāpakaḥ*.
And the elision of the suffix *mal* should be stated (optionally):
*dāruṇādhyāpakaḥ*, *ajñātādhyāpakaḥ*.
This is intended as an exception to the rule regarding the udātta accent on the final syllable of a compound;
it applies to this specific compound and not here.
The reading "dāruṇamadhyāpaka" is the opinion of Vṛttikāra.

Since the inclusion of the word "pūjita" (honored) would already suffice for the purpose of including that which is honored through the act of worship, the explicit mention of "pūjita" is for the sake of obtaining the immediately preceding honored one.
This itself is the indicator that in this section, even when there is a mention in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not necessarily relied upon.
Pāṇini 8.1.68: After words such as *kāṣṭha* meaning "to honor," a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) expressing that which is honored is unaccented (*anudātta*).

Since the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) would otherwise result in the elision of accent (*nighāta*), and since this elision is prohibited by the rule *nipātairyadyadi...* (Pāṇini 8.1.30), this present rule [8.1.34] is an injunction. Furthermore,
because of the inclusion of the term *sagati* ("along with its preceding particle"), the preceding particle (*gati*) is also subject to elision.
It is desired that the inclusion of the prefix [gati] applies only when there is the inclusion of a verbal root; it does not apply here in the case of *yatkāṣṭhāṃ śuklīkaroti*.

When a word ending in a *su*-affix follows, a finite verb (*tiṅ*)— whether accompanied by a prefix (*sagati*) or without a prefix (*agati*)— is unaccented (*anudātta*) when it expresses contempt (*kutsane*).
He cooks it rotten;
he cooks it thoroughly rotten; he cooks it wrongly.
In the case of censure,
[the example is] *prapacati śobhanam* ("he cooks well");
in the case of *sup*, [the example is] *pacati kliśnāti* ("he cooks [so as to] distress").
It should be stated that "pacati" (cooks) [is used] in the sense of "belonging to a lineage" (*gotra*) at the beginning,
or as a reproach for the action.
Let there be no censure of the agent: "Devadatta cooks badly."
It should be stated that *pūti* has the suffix *an* as its indicatory letter (*anubandha*).
Therefore, because it has the suffix *an* with the indicatory letter *c*, it is udātta on the final syllable; or else, it should be stated that when it has many meanings, it is anudātta.
They cook it while it is putrid.
Is it the case that when one raises [the voice] with an *anudātta* accent,
it becomes a *gati*?
Datta cooks;
what is the use of slow-moving [horses] for going? O Indra, come with your tawny steeds that have the plumage of peacocks! (O Indra, come with your tawny steeds that have the plumage of peacocks!)
A word denoting motion is unaccented [when it follows another verb].
The inclusion of the term *tiṅ* in the rule "yatprapacati" is for the purpose of specifying that which possesses an acute accent (*udāttavat*);

otherwise, since prefixes such as *pra-* are dependent on the action (*kriyā*) they are connected with, the designation of *gati* would apply only to that [action] when it is a verbal root (*dhātu*) possessing an acute accent, and would not apply to the suffix (*pratyaya*).
What is the purpose of [specifying] "possessing an acute accent" (udāttavat)?
[It is to exclude cases such as] *prapacati*, which are the accents of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*).
Now, the manner of the movement of accents (*svarasañcāra*) in Vedic sentences is described: "I praise Agni" (*agnim īḷe*) is the first *ṛc*.
Regarding that, Mādhava maintains that the word *agni* is unaccented on the first syllable according to the rule "phiṣaḥ... (*Phiṭ-sūtra* 1) under the view that it is not etymologically derived;
however, in reality, it is [unaccented] because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group.
In the case of its derivation (*vyutpatti*), however, by the accent of the suffix *ni* (Pāṇini 3.3.92), the [final vowel] is unaccented because it belongs to a verbal root (*aṅgasuptvāt*).

Then, by the rule *ami pūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107), there is a single substitution (*ekādeśa*); and by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), that single substitute is accented acute (*udātta*).
By the rule *īḍe tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), there is a *nighāta* (anudātta accent) on *īḍe*; however,
in the *saṃhitā*, by the rule *udāttādanudāttasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.66), the vowel *i* becomes *svarita*.

According to the rule *svaritātsaṃhitāyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.39), the syllable *ḷ* undergoes *ekaśruti*—also known as *pracaya*. The word *puraḥ* is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix *asi* prescribed by the rule *pūrvādharāvarāṇām-* (Pāṇini 5.3.39). The word *hita* is also oxytone due to the accent of the suffix, because after the root *dhā*, the substitution of *hi* for *dadhāti* occurs according to the rule *dadhāterhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.42).

In the case of *puro’vyayam* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), there is the designation *gati*; then, in the compound formed by *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), since it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the final member accented (*samāsāntodātta*), the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) would apply, resulting in the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable as the prior member; furthermore, by the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the original accent of the *kṛt*-derived final member would apply, and by the rule *thāthādisvare* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), the accent of the *thā-thādi* suffixes would apply—thus, through successive supersession of each preceding rule, one might expect the accent of the prior member to be applied by *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49). However, [the correct form is established].

In the *saṃhitā* of the word *puraḥ*, when the accentual intensification (*pracaya*) would otherwise apply, [the vowel] following an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) becomes more depressed (*sannatara*), according to the rule *udāttasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ*; thus, it is the super-acute (*anudāttatara*).
For the word *yajñasya*, the accent belongs to the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Since the case ending is *suptva*, it is *anudātta*; consequently, [the preceding syllable] becomes *svarita*.
The word *devam* is formed with the suffix *pacādyac*.
The word *ṛtvij* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the *phiṭ-svara*, the accent of suffixes, or the *cit-svara*;

the word *hotṛ*, ending in the suffix *tṛn*, has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) by the *nit-svara*. The word *hotṛ* has its final syllable accented by the rule of the original accent of the second member of a compound (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*).
The word *ratna* is udātta on its first syllable according to the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 26).
In the compound *ratnadhāḥ* ("the holder of jewels"),

the accent is udātta on the final syllable, either by the general rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*) or by the rule that the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative is retained (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).

Having elided the *tamap* suffix, the *anudātta* (low-pitched) quality arises; from this, the *svarita* (circumflex) and *pracaya* (continuous) accents follow, and so forth—all of which should be inferred according to the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*).
Thus ends the section on accents (*svaraprakaraṇa*).
In this manner, a mere indication regarding Vedic words has been shown here. May this be for the pleasure of the illustrious Bhavānī and Viśvanātha.
